events.title: Tech world's calls for Jensen Huang to return to Nvidia are growing
events.summary: An online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement has drawn more than 160,000 signatures, with Elon Musk among prominent tech executives backing the campaign, according to the petition's website. Huang has discussed a potential return as Nvidia CEO with close confidants, the Financial Times reported. Major shareholders Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management have urged Nvidia's board to consider all leadership options, including Huang's potential return. An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia has drawn more than 160,000 signatures, as prominent tech executives, employees and shareholders rally behind the chipmaker's co-founder following his resignation last week. The "Stand with Jensen " campaign has attracted support from Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, according to the petition's website, which notes that affiliations are self-reported and not verified. Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993 and helped turn it into a dominant supplier of artificial intelligence chips, resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and board member last week following reports of extramarital affairs — including one involving a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor. The growing campaign to reinstate Huang adds a layer of complexity to the decision for Nvidia's board as it looks to put the controversy behind it, and coincides with reports that he is considering a comeback. Any potential return, however, faces significant hurdles. Nvidia's board is continuing an independent investigation into the conduct that led to Huang's departure. What's more, U.S. lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged America's artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet. Musk was among the most prominent tech executives to publicly back Huang's reinstatement, saying on X that he would sign a petition calling for the former Nvidia chief's return. "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," Musk wrote on X. He had previously also said it would be "an honor" to hire Huang. The campaign has drawn support from people identifying themselves as current and former Nvidia employees, shareholders and business partners, according to the petition's website. It calls on Nvidia's board to ensure a fair investigation into Huang's conduct and provide greater transparency around the circumstances of his departure. Some Nvidia employees have also publicly expressed support for Huang, with one engineer saying he had decided to leave the company following the CEO's departure. Darrell Dai, who identified himself as a robotics engineer at Nvidia, said Huang's vision and the engineering culture he fostered were key reasons he had stayed at the company. Another Nvidia employee, Vartika Singh, who said she had worked at the chipmaker for nearly eight years, praised Huang's leadership and personal support during a family medical crisis. "I have never worked for anyone quite like Jensen Huang, and I doubt I ever will," Singh wrote on X, describing his commitment to employees, researchers and startups. The push has also gained traction among major shareholders, with Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker urging Nvidia's board to consider all options, including Huang's potential return, in an open letter Friday. The investors called for a measured approach to choosing Nvidia's next leader, arguing that Huang deserved a fair process before the board made any permanent decision. Huang has discussed the possibility of returning as Nvidia's chief executive with close confidants, the Financial Times reported , citing multiple people familiar with the matter. One of his allies told the FT that supporters were assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his reinstatement and would seek backing from the White House. The efforts had Huang's support, the person added, according to the report. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company linked to the controversy, said recent media reports contained assertions about its business and supply chain that were not supported by verifiable evidence. The company said it had retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation and that Alice Huang, a woman reportedly romantically linked to Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and no longer holds any role there. Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei , CNBC reported earlier.

events.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
events.summary: The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". But while Alice Huang is said to have stepped down from her role as Megaspeed director near the end of 2023, there were suspicions that she was still heavily involved in the firm's operations, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS C4ADS said that Huang was still "practically in control" of Megaspeed even after she had handed over the reins of the firm. Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies. Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify. Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised. "That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls," the congressman told the Face The Nation programme. Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. A representative for Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times Sunday suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded. The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated to lead Nvidia is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing. The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next CEO from outside the company. On Friday, Bessent had blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process". The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate". China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

Nvidia shares rose after the Financial Times said Jensen Huang is discussing a comeback. Investors hope his return would calm worries and restore clarity on supply deals. Huang’s exit followed an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and his return is still uncertain. Nvidia is down 32% from its October peak and faces wider AI boom worries. Earnings on Nov 17 should show demand trends and may shape the stock’s next move. Nvidia shares may be poised for some relief after the Financial Times reported Jensen Huang is discussing a possible comeback to the chipmaker. A perpetual futures contract on the Hyperliquid blockchain referencing Nvidia’s share price rose more than 3% on the evening of Nov 15. Nasdaq 100 futures advanced nearly 0.9% before paring gains. Nvidia’s stock is coming off its worst week since April 2025, after Huang’s admission of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and quick ouster from the company. Huang has already been discussing the idea of returning , with backing from several Silicon Valley allies, according to the Financial Times report. Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management are among those that have urged Nvidia’s board to reconsider. “Markets are reacting positively because Jensen Huang remains synonymous with Nvidia,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. “His track record is exceptional, and the prospect of his return would restore a degree of clarity around future supply commitments – many of which were based on his personal handshake agreements that could otherwise have been at risk.” Prospects for an actual return by Huang remain uncertain. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is urging the company to make a “dramatic” leadership shake - up, and come clean about its compliance with export controls on its prized AI chips. Nvidia shares are down 32% from their October all-time high, with the Huang controversy adding to broader concerns over the sustainability of the AI boom. The company is due to report quarterly earnings on Nov 17, which should give investors insight into the outlook for demand. “Markets are desperate after non-stop bad news, and are looking for remedies,” said Anna Wu, an investment strategist and founder of Floodlines Research. “Even unconfirmed ones.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: Japan’s economy unexpectedly shrinks as inflation squeezes households
events.summary: The first contraction in four quarters underscores the uneven nature of Japan’s economic recovery. Japan’s economy shrank 0.1% in July-September, as households cut spending because of higher living costs, poor weather and weaker demand for cars and air conditioners. Capital spending rose 1.6% on labour-saving technology and AI projects, but net external demand cut 0.6 percentage point from growth as imports jumped. Economists said the dip is unlikely to stop the Bank of Japan’s rate rises, as inflation stays high and growth is expected to remain modest but resilient. TOKYO – Japan’s economy unexpectedly contracted an annualised 0.1% in the July-September quarter, government data showed on Nov 16 , reflecting weak consumer spending as households grappled with higher living costs. The first contraction in four quarters underscores the uneven nature of Japan’s economic recovery, with households remaining vulnerable to persistent inflation despite rising wages. Still, policymakers are unlikely to view the weakness as a brake on Japan’s moderate recovery, with resilient corporate activity, rising real wages and robust demand for artificial intelligence-related investment underpinning growth. “While growth was indeed negative this time, there is no need to be overly pessimistic about the result,” said Kento Minami, senior economist at Daiwa Securities. “My impression is that moderate growth is probably continuing.” Minami also said the results are unlikely to derail the Bank of Japan’s (BOJ’s) tightening path, as the central bank remains focused on inflation risks, adding that firm domestic price pressures and a global backdrop of higher interest rates leave little room for a dovish policy shift. The gross domestic product data compared with a median market forecast of 0.3% annualised growth in a Reuters poll, and followed a revised 1.7% expansion in the previous quarter. The reading translated into a quarterly fall of 0.02%, compared with the median estimate of a 0.1% increase. Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of economic output, fell 0.3%, compared with a market estimate of a 0.2% decline. Household spending was hurt by persistent price pressures and poor weather, including heavy rain and typhoons during the quarter. Demand for automobiles and air conditioners retreated following the temporary boost in the previous quarter from tax and regulatory changes. “Strong wage growth should support consumption, but higher prices linked to Middle East tensions will continue to squeeze household purchasing power,” said Masato Koike, senior ⁠economist at Sompo Institute Plus. Capital spending, a key driver of private demand, rose 1.6%, versus a market forecast for a 1.5% increase, backed by investment in labour-saving technologies and AI-related projects. Net external demand, or exports minus imports, knocked 0.6 percentage point off growth, compared with a market forecast for a 0.4 percentage point drag on GDP growth. Imports rose sharply as oil and other energy purchases recovered after Japan diversified procurement following disruptions linked to the war in the Middle East. The BOJ will closely scrutinise the latest data as it assesses whether the economy can withstand further interest-rate increases. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ has stepped up its policy tightening this year, delivering interest rate hikes in June and September. Many analysts expect the next BOJ rate hike as soon as December. A monthly survey of 37 economists by the Japan Center for Economic Research showed the economy is expected to grow 0.89% in fiscal 2026 and 1.02% in fiscal 2027, suggesting economists see growth remaining modest but resilient. Japan’s longer-term growth challenges remain in focus, with the International Monetary Fund projecting the country will slip to the world’s sixth-largest economy in nominal dollar terms in 2027 in dollar terms, overtaken by India and Britain. Japan is currently the world’s fourth-largest after Germany. REUTERS

events.title: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
events.summary: Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people. The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months. The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys. Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues. Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.” The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week . events.title: Apple launches research study to explore the use of AI for health
events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Text of this article November 15, 2026 UPDATE Apple launches research study to explore the use of AI for health The Apple Health AI Usage Study, conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, will evaluate trust, comprehension, and real-world health AI engagement Apple today announced the launch of the Apple Health AI Usage Study in the United States, a virtual research study and associated app designed to advance the understanding of how people interact with conversational health AI tools. 1 By examining what drives user trust, the quality of responses, comprehension, and everyday health actions, the study aims to inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for Apple and the industry. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” said Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness. “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.” The study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a leading clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals that generates answers using medical information from established sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine , Journal of the American Medical Association , and Nature . The study brings together medically grounded AI technology developed by OpenEvidence with an Apple-designed research experience. Participants will be able to ask the study app everyday health questions; explore complex medical information communicated with approachable language; and see linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations that ground each response. Participants can also choose to share HealthKit data types — such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results — to explore how personal data integration impacts relevance and understanding. Consumer health technologies powered by LLMs may at times offer responses that are incomplete or unclear, which is why research is critical to presenting health information to users with greater clarity. The study will also explore how health AI can potentially help participants better prepare for clinical visits with their own doctors. “Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine. “When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly. Connecting these tools, and rigorously studying what works, is how we’ll get there.” The study is designed from the ground up with privacy protections, transparency, and clinical guardrails, and study data will not be used to train AI models. Participants retain control over whether to share any HealthKit metrics or survey responses, and Apple has implemented security measures to protect the study data it maintains, as well as the confidentiality of participants’ information. The study app features safety guardrails that are intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed. Study Details and Availability The Apple Health AI Usage Study is open to up to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older across the United States. To join, participants must have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later. Download the study app to learn more about the study and choose to enroll. The study app is not meant to diagnose or treat any condition, or replace the advice of medical professionals. Participants should consult a doctor or clinician to address health concerns or verify medical information. events.title: Japan's economy unexpectedly contracts in third-quarter as elevated energy costs bite
events.summary: A Reuters poll of economists had estimated the economy to grow at 0.3%. While Japan's exports beat expectations for two of the three months in the quarter, net exports weighed on the economy as energy prices imports. The data comes amid expectations that the Bank of Japan could raise rates once more at its December meeting. Japan's economy unexpectedly contracted in the third quarter, shrinking at an annualized 0.1% compared to the previous quarter, as elevated energy prices impacted consumption and net exports. A Reuters poll of economists had estimated the economy to grow at 0.3% in the three months to September, while GDP had expanded at 1.4% in the previous quarter. Japan's exports beat expectations for two of the three months in the quarter, but net exports weighed on the economy due to higher costs of energy imports, cutting 0.6 percentage point from the country's growth. The GDP data could complicate Japan's policy normalization path, though there's still a 75.6% chance of the Bank of Japan raising rates by 25 basis points in December, according to LSEG. Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia Pacific at Capital Economics, also expects the BOJ to go ahead with the rate hike. "It looks increasingly likely that the Bank will have to tighten policy more aggressively than we've been anticipating as inflation is about to surge." The BOJ had declared that its 2% underlying inflation target had been met for the first time in 13 years at its meeting last month. Core inflation in September also hit its highest level this year at 2.1%, overshooting analysts' expectations. On an year-on-year basis Japan's economy grew 1.1%, its strongest growth since the second quarter of 2025. Theliant noted that this was owed to a lower base in the third quarter of 2025. Following the data release, the Nikkei 225 fell 0.62%, while the yield on the benchmark 10-year Japanese Government Bonds was at 2.885%. The yen weakened marginally against the dollar, trading at 159.76.

events.title: Founder of Guadalajara cartel dies in hospital after decades in prison
events.summary: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo was convicted of the 1985 murder of a US drug enforcement agent and a Mexican pilot. Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels, has died in hospital at age 80. Local security authorities said Felix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the western city of Guadalajara two days ago but suffered multiple organ failure and died at about 2pm (20:00 GMT) on Sunday. list 1 of 3 Guatemalan lawmaker and three police officers killed in armed attack list 2 of 3 Mexican mayor found alive after hours-long abduction list 3 of 3 Mexico arrests alleged major leader of Jalisco cartel Felix Gallardo, a founder of the Guadalajara cartel, was convicted for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent, a crime that made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers. Imprisoned since 1989, Felix Gallardo was held in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state, though his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health. Rising to prominence in the 1970s, the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in the ensuing decades. Born in 1946 in Culiacan, Sinaloa, a northwestern state that would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking, he worked as a police officer and a bodyguard for a local governor. Later, he gained a reputation as a powerful criminal capo known as the “boss of bosses”. Felix Gallardo and others set up their cartel in Guadalajara, the Jalisco state capital and a fast-growing economic powerhouse, becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale and to forge an alliance with Colombian drug barons, including Pablo Escobar’s Medellin cartel. His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and 1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials. His cartel also made innovations, such as using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent, supported by fellow kingpins like Rafael Caro Quintero. His legal battles stretched across decades. Arrested in 1989, Felix Gallardo was sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug trafficking and weapons charges tied to the Guadalajara cartel. While already jailed, he faced a separate prosecution over the 1985 kidnapping and murder of US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar. Camarena’s killing caused a diplomatic dispute with Washington, which pressured Mexico to arrest those involved. In 2017, a federal court found Felix Gallardo guilty in the case and imposed a further 37-year sentence. He denied responsibility for the killings. His rise and fall were portrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 hit Netflix series Narcos: Mexico. Felix Gallardo suffered poor health in his final years and was blind in one eye, practically deaf, and unable to walk on his own by the time Spanish-language US network Telemundo interviewed him in prison in 2021. He maintained his innocence. “Thirty-two years have passed,” he said. “That’s an eternity for a man who did not commit any crime.”

events.title: Black Friday and tax return scams - don't fall for these
events.summary: This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you. That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year. Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information. Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out. Is it really HMRC? Here's how to tell If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January. Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC. Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email , external , text message , external or phone call , external claiming to be from HMRC is genuine. "Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer. New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October. There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information. To avoid being caught out, HMRC says: it never contacts people by email, text or phone to tell them they are due a refund or ask them to claim one it never asks for personal or financial information by email or text message it never leaves threatening voicemails about legal action or arrest Is it a real deal? Here's how to check In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered. Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy. "When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check. "No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy." The bank also advises doing these four things: Pause and check , rather than being blinded by a countdown timer Pay safely using a credit or debit card via a trusted payment service, not a bank transfer to a stranger Open an official website or app yourself rather than clicking on links in emails, ads or social posts Talk to a friend, family or your bank if you think something does not feel right, and calling your bank straight away if you think you've been scammed Doing these things now will help you save money at Christmas Published 7 days ago Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams Published 19 October Watch our pick of standout clips from across the BBC 0:57 Aftermath of deadly Leeds car crash. 00:00:57, play video Aftermath of deadly Leeds car crash 1:10 SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth. 00:01:10, play video SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth 1:12 Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia. 00:01:12, play video Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia 1:00 Can AI save lives in landslides? events.title: After a nationwide ground stop, US faces aviation infrastructure questions
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? Trump has requested $50bn for upgrades, but Democratic lawmakers are asking for transparency before spending more. Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all flights in the United States for nearly four hours due to a reported equipment failure. It was only the second time since the attacks on September 11, 2001, that such an order was given. list 1 of 3 US air travel in chaos after rare nationwide ground stop halts flights list 2 of 3 US blames system upgrade for longest nationwide FAA ground stop since 9/11 list 3 of 3 What forced the US to ground all planes? A router switch, we now know More than 9,000 flights were cancelled, and an estimated 1.5 million passengers were left stranded. Officials blamed the disruptions on an upgrade gone awry. The routers used to communicate with aeroplanes in mid-flight had suddenly stopped working , and pilots were no longer able to speak on their usual frequencies. As of Sunday, officials were still working to return the system to normal. “As we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News, while acknowledging continued delays. But the situation has led to scrutiny over whether the nationwide ground-stop could have been prevented. While President Donald Trump has blamed a lack of funding from Congress, critics say billions of dollars have already been allocated for badly needed upgrades. The work, they say, is what has lagged behind. Democratic lawmakers have also questioned the Trump administration’s choice of contractors to install the upgrades. “Secretary Duffy and the Federal Aviation Administration have received historical and monumental investments over the last two years,” Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro said in a statement on Sunday. “Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner.” Duffy has indicated that investigations are ongoing into what caused the malfunction on Friday. But he has described the problem as starting at “a remote FAA location” where workers from the defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wire with fibre optic lines. A router used for communication reportedly began to malfunction, sending out 1,000 attempts to log onto the FAA’s system every four or five seconds, overloading the entire network. In an interview on Sunday with NBC’s Meet the Press, Duffy stopped short of blaming L3Harris. “Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris that was doing the work for us? Was it a fault of the router itself? We have to do that investigation and make sure we take precautions,” he said. Though Duffy did suggest he preferred to part ways with the company, which owns a significant chunk of the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure. “I want to get away from L3Harris and get to a new one, but they own the network,” Duffy told Meet the Press. “I can’t cancel the network that they own, and I operate on.” L3Harris has existed since 2019, following a merger between the Harris Corporation and L3 Technologies. It is one of the largest defence contractors in the country, and its involvement with the FAA’s telecommunications network stretches back to 2002, when the Harris Corporation was awarded a billion-dollar contract to modernise the network’s systems. But Friday’s mass grounding was not the first time L3Harris’s systems were involved in flight delays and problems with communications during an upgrade operation. In November 2009, for example, the FAA’s network experienced a smaller outage as upgrades were being made to a router in Los Angeles, according to an agency investigation . “The most notable impact to the flying public was the inability of the FAA to process electronic flight plan data,” a report explained. “As a result, these flight plans had to be entered into the FAA air traffic control systems manually, causing the delay of over 800 flights that morning.” In a statement after Friday’s grounding, L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA’s current probe and had already replaced 70 percent of the system’s copper wire with fibre optics. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” it said. Critics point out that many of the problems associated with the FAA’s telecommunications systems predate L3Harris’s involvement and stem from ageing infrastructure. The FAA has aimed for years to replace some 5,170 lengths of copper wiring dating to the 1960s, which is used by routers and other communication gear. Ageing copper, however, is just one of the tech problems the FAA faces.

events.title: SK Hynix to spend $1.35 billion over five years to support chip suppliers
events.summary: South Korea’s SK Hynix aims to strengthen its supply chain as competition intensifies in the AI chip market. SK Hynix will spend 1.4 trillion won over five years to support domestic chip suppliers and strengthen its supply chain as AI chip competition grows. It will help suppliers through research, testing, mass production and sales, including advance funding and support even if projects fail. A jointly funded 874.6 billion won testing facility, Trinity Fab, will open in May 2027 to cut costs, speed up testing and protect sensitive information. SEOUL – South Korea’s SK Hynix said on Nov 16 that it plans to spend 1.4 trillion won (S$1.35 billion) over the next five years to support domestic suppliers of semiconductor materials, parts and equipment, aiming to strengthen its supply chain as competition intensifies in the artificial intelligence chip market. The chipmaker also outlined plans for a jointly funded 874.6 billion won testing facility at its semiconductor complex in Yongin, south of Seoul, where smaller suppliers will be able to test products under conditions similar to those on commercial chip production lines. SK Hynix said its supplier support programme covers four stages – research and development, testing, mass production and sales. It aims to help smaller companies overcome financing and technology hurdles. The testing facility, named Trinity Fab, is a partnership between SK Hynix, the central government and local governments in South Korea. It is scheduled to open in May 2027. SK Hynix will contribute 443.2 billion won, the central government 373.6 billion won and local governments 57.7 billion won, according to the company. The facility will be housed within the first chip plant at SK Hynix’s Yongin semiconductor cluster, 40km south of Seoul, where the company plans to invest 600 trillion won to build four chip fabrication plants. It will include a 3,305 sq m cleanroom and equipment for processes including lithography, etching, deposition and inspection. Suppliers will be able to evaluate materials and equipment using 30cm wafers before deploying them on production lines. SK Hynix said the shared facility would help small suppliers reduce testing costs and shorten the time needed to bring products to market. It will be run by an independent non-profit foundation to protect intellectual property and commercially sensitive information. Under its research support programme, SK Hynix will provide up to 50% of initial development costs in advance and compensate suppliers for work undertaken even if a project fails to meet its targets. SK Hynix and financial institutions will also provide two trillion won in financing backed by the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation, while other programmes offer low interest loans and technical consulting to suppliers, including smaller sub-contractors. events.title: What a Tiny Chorus of the ‘Bring Back Jensen’ Tech Bros Gets Wrong
events.summary: A small band of rogue tech bros has ridden to Jensen Huang’s defense amidst a report from the Financial Times that Huang is huddling with allies, plotting a comeback as Nvidia CEO days after resigning, with a petition demanding “due process, not mob justice,” signed by a minority of tech voices who have gotten outsized attention, such as Elon Musk and Atreides Management managing partner Gavin Baker. One tech bro even said , “Nvidia would be wrong to fire Jensen. His marital indiscretions are between him, his wife, and a reprimand from the board,” as if that was all there is to the story. But this small circle of rogue tech bros is wrong. This is not a story about a woke inquisition or prudes regulating marital indiscretions and sex – and a Sam Altman-style comeback does not make sense. We were supportive of Altman’s comeback and knew Steve Jobs personally – and supported his firing and subsequent comeback . But these circumstances are materially different. There is no comeback here. Start with the conduct the defenders wave away, of Huang’s workplace affairs with direct subordinates. Huang admitted infidelity on Nov. 8. Days later, the New York Times reported a relationship with one of his direct reports. Nvidia’s code of conduct , which opens with a letter from Huang himself, names “personal relationships” as a conflict of interest. We had firsthand knowledge of Mark Hurd’s removal at HP over expense reports that concealed a personal relationship with a contractor, which was the right removal. Boards at McDonald’s, Intel and Nestlé similarly removed CEOs over relationships with employees. Workplace romances with bosses having affairs with married direct reports put those subordinates in an inherently compromised position; they are deleterious to the morale of those around them, raising questions of merit and favoritism. But when it comes to Huang and Nvidia’s woes, workplace romance is the least of it. The relationship that should alarm Americans the most was Nvidia’s “culture of noncompliance” on chip export restrictions to China, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it on Sunday with Larry Kudlow, irrespective of whether or not Alice Huang, who helped set up Megaspeed, was an actual Chinese spy. As Bessent said, was Nvidia “pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” Evidence points to a fifth or more of Nvidia ‘s compute revenue being tied to China The paper trail when it comes to banned Nvidia chips illegally making their way into China at scale, evading U.S. restrictions, is particularly damning for the company. Shipment records reviewed by the Wall Street Journal tie Megaspeed to nearly $12 billion in orders of Nvidia’s most advanced chips for Chinese buyers between early 2024 and mid-2025, despite a balance sheet that showed a measly $33 million in 2023., according to Culper Research. Documents reviewed by Bloomberg show that a company Alice Huang founded told China’s own central-bank credit registry that it held servers carrying banned H100, H200 and H800 chips in a Shanghai data center. Some were first sold to an official Nvidia cloud partner in Singapore and then subsequently laundered into China. In March, the Justice Department indicted Super Micro’s co-founder, who has pleaded not guilty, for allegedly smuggling $2.5 billion of Nvidia-powered servers through a Southeast Asian front, with dummy servers staged for inspectors. And where do such chips end up once they make their way into China? The Chinese Communist Party and the Chinese military, where they are used directly against the US. Reuters found that Northwestern Polytechnical University, blacklisted by Washington since 2001 and one of China’s “Seven Sons of National Defense,” bought two Nvidia H200s just last month. It researches missiles and military aircraft. A WireScreen study of more than 3,800 Chinese military and government procurement records found export-controlled accelerators, including Nvidia’s A100s and H100s, going to buyers across the People’s Liberation Army, including its Rocket Force, its Cyberspace Force and the equipment arm of the Central Military Commission. Worse yet, China is training its own supposedly superior AI models on banned Nvidia chips, and likely distilling U.S. frontier models in order to create supposedly lower-cost “open source” models. A former researcher from OpenAI, in an original forensic analysis and GPU “fingerprinting ,” found patterns strongly suggesting that six AI models from four of China’s leading labs were initialized on Nvidia Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China – a highly disturbing finding which raises questions about whether Chinese AI “innovation” is actually just stolen U.S. intellectual property masquerading as Chinese ingenuity. By the researcher’s own account, the findings do not show where the chips were located or how access was obtained. So many of these tech bros have it exactly backwards. Beijing did not want Jensen out. Beijing wanted Jensen’s chips, and got them. All the while, Huang assured the world there was nothing to see. “There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion,” he disingenuously told Bloomberg in May 2025. That October he declared Nvidia’s AI-chip business “100% out of China.” Nvidia now says it put Megaspeed on an internal block list in June 2025. Yet for months afterward its spokespeople kept vouching for the customer, insisting spot checks found every chip where it belonged. Culper Research revealed just how disingenuous Nvidia’s claims were. Its review of Singapore and Malaysian filings found Megaspeed’s Malaysian arm had been financed through a Singapore entity, Apex Enterprise Solutions, that Culper ties to Alibaba , and had imported $4 billion of servers from Aivres, the U.S. arm of Inspur, whose Chinese parent Washington blacklisted over its work for China’s military. Nvidia’s assurance that Megaspeed had no Chinese shareholders said nothing about who was paying for the chips. That does not even begin to factor in the possible charges of accounting fraud that plaintiffs’ attorneys will surely bring against Nvidia as the truth emerges, given how Nvidia was accounting for all these Asian transactions and the possible impact to its revenues, earnings and stock price. Nvidia reports China at about 7% of revenue, or $12.4 billion in the first half of this fiscal year. events.title: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis
events.summary: Prime minister promises ‘root-and-branch rethink’ of support for young people as Milburn report advises sweeping changes to some benefits Andy Burnham: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”. Burnham said the government would intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fell behind, and “long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state”, including providing more opportunities for vocational training in schools. Writing in the Guardian, the prime minister said ministers’ response to Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into the crisis of youth unemployment in the UK would not be “a traditional … reform” but “societal and generational”. He promised to reduce the number of Neets – 18 to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training – which topped a million this year for the first time in more than a decade. Hoping to head off opposition from leftwing MPs in his own party, who rebelled to block Starmer’s welfare changes last summer , Burnham said the government would “invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on”, but said the support “will have to come with responsibilities”. “If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can. Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point,” said Burnham. Milburn’s long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s . Some young people will lose their personal independence payments and the right to claim the health element of universal credit, and instead will get a new youth allowance paid at the standard rate of universal credit. The government has also announced it will expand a taxpayer-funded scheme aimed at helping young people into work to under-25s who have been claiming benefits for a year. Eligible 18- to 24-year-olds will be “guaranteed” a fully funded, six-month job matched to their skills after 12 months on universal credit. The Liberal Democrats said the six-month offering was worth “very little” without a job at the end of it. Before the publication of the report, Milburn said the government would have to be “candid with people”, that it would take 10 years for the benefits bill to come down, and investment would have to be made upfront. Addressing critics calling for the benefits bill to be immediately slashed, the former health secretary told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “There’s no such thing as a free lunch. If you are going to will the ends, you’ve got to will the means. I don’t think there’s a single person in this country who believes that it’s tolerable to have one million young people, aged 16 to 24, who are not in education, employment, or training.” Pat McFadden acknowledged that Milburn’s review would have an “element of compulsion” for Neets and there would be people who would receive less in benefits than currently. The work and pensions secretary said the UK had to become more like countries that had dealt with youth unemployment more successfully, such as the Netherlands, where the youth desk would “literally knock on your door” and offer options of training or work. But he denied that Milburn was proposing a ban on young people claiming health-related benefits. “That’s not what he’s saying. He’s saying if you have a long-term disability, that means you can never work,” he said. “You will actually get more than you will now. He’s saying that if you have extra costs, there will be a benefit you can apply to for extra costs. He’s also saying there should be a local fund for short-term needs, and for other people, he’s saying there should be more support to get into work. Change was necessary, he added, because the number of young people claiming personal independence payments (Pip) had doubled since the start of the decade, while the number of young people on the health element of universal credit had increased by 80%. Burnham hit out at the Conservatives and Reform, who have called for deep and immediate cuts to welfare, with Kemi Badenoch vowing to slash the bill by £36.1bn by 2030 if the party wins the next general election. Under the plans 70% of child benefit disability-related claims linked to ADHD and “milder” behavioural disorders and learning disabilities would be cut, with Labour calling the proposals “ a charter for human misery ”. The shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, acknowledged the plans could mean around half a million children losing disability-related payments.

events.title: Zambia’s copper boom attracts billions in investment, but who benefits?
events.summary: Workers’ rights, environmental concerns and local businesses remain at the centre of the debate. Lusaka, Zambia – Zambia is attracting billions of dollars in mining investment as it seeks to become a significant supplier of minerals critical to the global energy transition. But as foreign companies expand operations and new projects come on stream, questions are mounting over whether common Zambians are benefitting from the country’s growing mineral wealth. President Hakainde Hichilema said more than $12bn had been invested in Zambia’s mining sector since 2022, as the government pushes to increase copper production and attract new investors. Leading investors include Canadian companies First Quantum Minerals and Barrick Mining Corporation, India’s Vedanta Resources and China Nonferrous Metal Mining Group (CNMC). Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH) has also emerged as a leading investor after committing $1.1bn to recapitalise Mopani Copper Mines, previously owned by Glencore. The investment gave IRH a 51 percent stake in the mine, with state-owned ZCCM Investments Holdings retaining 49 percent. Alongside large-scale mining projects, the Copperbelt province has also seen the expansion of smaller Chinese-owned mineral-processing plants, some sourcing ore from artisanal and small-scale miners. Their growth has raised concerns about safety standards, regulatory oversight and environmental protection. The government has sought to restore investor confidence through tax incentives and a more predictable fiscal framework, following years of frequent changes to mining tax policies under the former Patriotic Front government, which ruled Zambia between 2011 and 2021. Unlocking mineral wealth and adding value To accelerate mineral exploration, Zambia is undertaking a nationwide high-resolution aerial geophysical survey aimed at improving geological information and identifying previously unexplored mineral deposits. The survey is now about 98 percent complete, according to the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development. The government has set an ambitious target of increasing annual copper production to 3 million tonnes by 2031, from less than 1 million tonnes in recent years. “We can do with our copper, cobalt, nickel, lithium, manganese and rare earth metals, which we now know we have in this country for our people, what the UAE has done with oil and gas for its people and their economy,” Hichilema told delegates at the Zambia Mining and Investment Forum in Lusaka on October 19. Beyond increasing production, Zambia is also seeking to expand value addition to copper, a key material in electric vehicles and renewable energy infrastructure. Historically, the country has exported copper cathodes to China and other industrialised countries. But the government wants Zambia to play a more active role in the global transition to a low-carbon economy by developing domestic mineral processing and manufacturing capacity. Africa’s two leading copper producers, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Zambia, are also exploring a partnership with South Africa to develop an electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry. “DRC and ourselves are doing something on EV materials so we can build a joint venture with South Africa, which is ahead of us in the motor industry, so that the motor vehicles produced out of South African production lines have Congolese and Zambian inputs of the EV battery,” Hichilema said. The proposed partnership reflects growing efforts by African mineral producers to move beyond exporting raw materials and capture a greater share of the value generated by the global energy transition. However, turning these ambitions into reality will require more than increased mineral production. It will also depend on the development of local industries, skilled labour and infrastructure capable of supporting large-scale manufacturing. Workers question their share amid mining boom While foreign capital is driving an expansion of Zambia’s mining sector, trade unions say local workers are yet to see meaningful improvements in their working conditions. “Inasmuch as the copper prices are going up and we have seen an increase in the amount of investments, we are experiencing same employment conditions – things are not any better for a mineworker,” Stephen Mwaanga, secretary of the National Union of Miners and Allied Workers, told Al Jazeera. Despite higher copper prices, Mwaanga said, mining companies were also grappling with elevated production costs, including higher fuel prices, which he linked to the US-Israel war on Iran, affecting traffic via the Strait of Hormuz. The wider Southern African region has also faced drought conditions associated with El Nino, putting additional pressure on electricity supplies.

events.title: Intel sued by shareholders following 29% stock plunge
events.summary: In the lawsuit, shareholders said Intel was too slow to disclose information about how slowing PC sales and an inventory glut would weigh on revenue. Intel shareholders sued the chipmaker, saying it hid the impact of weak PC sales and high inventory before a 29% share price plunge. The suit, led by the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, says Intel delayed warnings while raising US$23 billion in stock in mid-August. Intel blamed supply shortages and an "unprecedented memory crunch" for weaker PCs; the case seeks damages and names Lip-Bu Tan and David Zinsner. Intel has been sued by shareholders who accused the US chipmaker of defrauding them by concealing the impact of a prolonged slowdown in personal computer sales that caused its stock price to plunge nearly 29% in a single day. In a proposed class action filed on Nov 13 in the San Jose, California, federal court, shareholders led by a Michigan pension fund said Intel was too slow to disclose information about how slowing PC sales and an inventory glut would weigh on revenue. The shareholders said Intel’s problems with PC sales and excess inventory outweighed data centre construction and other benefits related to the artificial intelligence boom. They also said Intel had the motive and opportunity to defraud by raising capital in mid-August, halfway through its “disastrous” third quarter, when it sold US$23 billion (S$29.6 billion) of stock at US$95 per share. The sale came as Intel looked to build out its chip contract manufacturing business, a key part of chief executive Tan Lip-Bu’s business strategy. Shares of Intel closed on Nov 13 at US$59.66. Intel did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Nov 15 . Tan told analysts that he was disappointed by manufacturing supply shortages, an “unprecedented memory crunch”, and resulting softness in PCs. “We need to address these challenges with urgency,” Tan added. Like many other large technology companies, Intel has poured money into manufacturing, but supply disruptions have made it harder to benefit from growing demand for data centre chips. Meanwhile, rising memory prices have made PCs more expensive, weighing on demand. The Nov 13 lawsuit, led by the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, seeks unspecified damages for Intel shareholders between July 23 and Oct 29. Tan and chief financial officer David Zinsner are also defendants. Intel shares are up 62% in 2026 through Nov 13, though they have slid from their recent peak of US$142.35 on June 30. REUTERS

events.title: Eisenkot says Netanyahu can’t remain Israel PM amid alleged vote meddling
events.summary: Members of an Arab-led party were reportedly arrested before Israeli elections based on unfounded evidence from the prime minister’s office. Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cannot “remain at the helm of government for even one more minute” amid reports alleging Netanyahu’s office engaged in electoral interference. Eisenkot, tasked with forming Israel’s new government , launched a scathing attack on his rival on Sunday, just a few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government . list 1 of 4 Iranophobia: Netanyahu’s bid to transform fear into political survival list 2 of 4 Can Netanyahu launch a strike on Iran before he leaves? list 3 of 4 Will Democrats try to strip US-Israel initiative from Pentagon funding? list 4 of 4 Israel coalition talks put Arab party leader under pressure over Hamas “The conduct of outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his inner circle poses a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” Eisenkot wrote on X. Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 published a report earlier on Sunday alleging Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, lodged a complaint with the police commissioner’s office against members of the United Arab List (Ra’am) party on the eve of Israel’s October 27 election . Norden reportedly directed police officers to an alleged intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu’s office. Based on information from the source, about 14 police officers raided the homes of three Ra’am members without a warrant and arrested them on suspicion of bribery to incentivise voting, according to Channel 12. Netanyahu subsequently launched a campaign against Arab-led parties throughout election day. After they won a record 19 seats, he made unproven accusations of electoral fraud. The three men were released after police determined the information from the purported intelligence source was unfounded. The Channel 12 report also alleged that David Zini, the head of Israel’s internal intelligence agency Shin Bet, requested the attorney general’s office to wiretap five Palestinian-Israeli Knesset members on election day over suspected election interference, but the request was later rejected. “I call for an immediate investigation into the affair and for the police and the Shin Bet to immediately clarify the details that have been published,” said Eisenkot, a former army chief. Netanyahu’s Likud party called Eisenkot’s statement “outrageous incitement” against the prime minister. On Friday, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of fuelling a “racist and violent” campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel during the elections to cling to power. Netanyahu renewed his appeal to Eisenkot to form a unity government on Saturday, but the opposition leader called the plea a “bluff”. However, Eisenkot had confirmed talks between his Yashar party and the Likud party over the proposal for a shared government. Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot’s bloc has yet secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.

events.title: I went back to India when my H-1B was rejected. Now I have 2 public companies and am a judge on Shark Tank India.
events.summary: Kunal Bahl's H-1B rejection kickstarted his entrepreneurial journey in India. Kunal Bahl Kunal Bahl's entrepreneurial ambitions in the US were crushed when his H-1B visa was rejected in 2007. He chose to return to India, where he cofounded a company with his high school friend. He's since taken two companies public, invested in over 300 startups, and is a judge on Shark Tank India. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kunal Bahl, the 43-year-old cofounder of the Indian digital commerce holding company AceVector Limited and investment firm Titan Capital. It has been edited for length and clarity. Entrepreneurship was always on the cards for me. An H-1B rejection just fast-tracked it. I grew up in New Delhi, and then I went to the University of Pennsylvania in the US for a program that blended an engineering and business degree. While I was in college, a bunch of big things happened in the tech sphere: Google went public, and Facebook became viral. By 2006, which is when I graduated, it was all the rage. The internet economy was taking off. I had a lot of business ideas, but it became clear that I could not start a company because of my visa status. I was on an F-1 visa , and I first needed to find an employer who could sponsor my H-1B, then lay out a pathway into Silicon Valley. From there, I'd try to start my own company. I interned at Microsoft during my junior year and returned in October 2006 in a full-time role after graduating. Then my H-1B visa petition was rejected While waiting for my H-1B visa selection, I was counting down the days until my Optional Practical Training , a temporary yearlong work authorization after graduation, would expire. I remember vividly that, in June or July of 2007, I got an email that said my H-1B petition had been rejected. For a moment, I didn't understand. It was unfathomable to me that, if I worked at a company like Microsoft, my H-1B visa would not be approved. I checked with the Microsoft team. Looking at their faces, I gathered that there was a finality to the rejection . The company was very nice about the situation, suggesting that I work in the Microsoft India office and try again for the H-1B after a year. At no point had I considered moving back to India . But I gathered myself up and decided that if I go back to my country, I'd work for myself, not for Microsoft. No time wasted starting my company I no longer had the baggage of having to figure out this H-1B situation. I felt liberated because I didn't have to worry about visas or green cards. So I called up my best friend from high school, Rohit Bansal, who was working in a financial institution at the time. We used to sit next to each other in class and talk about starting a business together. I asked if he wanted to do something together. He said, "Great, let's do it." Our company was incorporated on September 12, 2007, a few days before I touched down in India. Building a startup in India in 2007 was a challenge India has a hot startup ecosystem now. That cannot be said of the India of 2007. The country had very few internet users and smartphones, and digital payments were few and far between. Things were pretty dull, to be honest. I was not returning to the promised land or a burgeoning startup ecosystem. Even launching a startup was frowned upon. People would ask, "You guys have a good education, so why didn't you get a job? Does nobody want to hire you?" We started as a physical coupon book business, because Indians love a good value. But getting funding was a challenge. Angel investors weren't common then. We had both saved up a bit from our year working corporate jobs and pooled our savings — about $60,000 in total. That became our seed capital. We stayed with our families for food and accommodation, and worked out of a small office in the basement of a residential building in Delhi's furniture market. We had neighbors complain about people going in and out of the building late, because Rohit and I would work 20 hours a day to get our business off the ground. Our company pivoted from being an online couponing platform like Groupon to one of India's first e-commerce platforms, called Snapdeal. Now we have two publicly listed companies that we spun off from the original coupon book business. We wanted to give back to the startup ecosystem in India, as well. In 2011, once we had built up some capital, we started investing in early-stage startups and formed Titan Capital . Over the last 15 years, we've invested in more than 320 startups, many of which have gone public. I'm now also a judge on Shark Tank India. The India of today is full of opportunity In hindsight, my not getting the H-1B visa was serendipitous, though it hurt at the time. It was part of a larger plan: I had to return to India and help the next generation of founders. It was easy for me to pack up my bags and come back because I wasn't married and didn't have children. And I know it's far more difficult for those who have dependents living with them in the US, like children or parents. So I do empathize with workers facing immigration struggles in the US. That said, India has changed drastically since the time we started our company. India now has a billion internet users. There's ubiquitous smartphone penetration. There are so many coworking spaces for startup founders. There is a high talent density. There is a robust funding ecosystem. The startup tech scene is front of mind for the government. There is no better time to come back to India. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported
events.summary: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport MIAMI -- Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries. The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said. Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle. On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft. The NTSB said Sunday that preliminary information showed the UPS plane was instructed to give way to the Copa Airlines flight but did not stop. The UPS aircraft had substantial damage, while an assessment of the Copa plane had not been completed, it said. The NTSB said it opened an investigation and expected a preliminary report to be released within 30 days. The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said. UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened. “We cannot speculate on the details of the incident,” UPS said in a statement. “The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information.” The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people. 2 Americans die in suspected drowning incident in the Bahamas 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China
events.summary: Microsoft has announced massive price rises for commercial cloud services in India and New Zealand, but a substantial reduction in China. The software giant sells its cloudy services in many local currencies, at an equivalent rate to the prices it charges in the USA. As exchange rates shift, so do the prices Microsoft charges around the world. Microsoft last week announced the new charges that will come into effect from January 1, 2027, and the news isn’t pleasant for customers in India, who face an increase of 15.7 percent for cloud services and up to 20 percent for some on-prem offerings. New Zealand customers face a ten percent price hike. Customers in China, where Microsoft relies on a local partner called 21Vianet to deliver its cloud, will see costs fall by up to 8.5 percent. Australian buyers will see costs fall by 4.5 percent. The only nation not in Asia on Microsoft’s list is Norway, where prices will ease 5.9 percent. Sega Japan hits double trouble Sega has just had a rotten week that saw it battle a data leak and an outage. The outage impacted the company’s ALL.Net and Aime services, which connect arcade games across different locations. The services include administrative features for arcade operators, plus services for gamers including pre-payment to play, high score and profile recording, and networked gaming. Sega suspended some ALL.Net and Aime services on November 1 after discovering unauthorized access to servers. At least thirteen games and services were then unavailable until around November 15. The company hasn’t explained what went wrong, but assured customers the incident was not a data breach and that payment information was safe. But data did leak for those who subscribe to some Sega newsletters. Sega uses a third-party outfit called Arara Co. to send some emails, and it leaked email addresses. No other personal data leaked from Arara. Sega has nonetheless warned newsletter recipients to watch out for suspicious messages. Alibaba floats chip unit Chinese tech giant Alibaba last week announced its intention to float its T-Head chip design biz on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The filing announcing the spinoff describes T-Head as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China,” suggesting Alibaba doesn’t think buyers in the rest of the world are keen to acquire its chips. T-Head going public “allows a more efficient deployment of Alibaba Group’s financial resources,” the filing states, and should also mean the chip design outfit can more easily find third-party customers. India bans export of dead batteries The government of India last week banned the export of “Lithium-Ion battery Black Mass” – a powdery substance created during the process of recycling batteries. “It contains recoverable quantities of critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese,” according to the government’s announcement of the ban, which argues the measure “will increase domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, thereby reducing import dependence and the associated foreign exchange outgo. It will also strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage and clean-energy technologies.” “Further, the measure will advance the circular economy and ‘urban mining’, reducing reliance on primary mining, while supporting environmentally sound recycling of this hazardous material within the country in accordance with applicable environmental regulations.” Japanese giants to investigate orbiting datacenters Five giant Japanese companies – NTT, Mitsubishi Electric, MUFG Bank, the Development Bank of Japan, and telco NTT DOCOMO – last week signed a memorandum of understanding that will see them jointly explore development and operation of a mega-constellation of satellites. The five “will examine the technical and business feasibility of commercializing a diverse range of services enabled by mega-constellations, including communications, Earth observation, satellite-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), and space data centers.” Mitsubishi already works with the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to jointly develop and manufacture rockets. The two banks regularly back big infrastructure projects, while the two NTT entities have advanced comms expertise. The five companies didn’t set a deadline for delivery of a plan. If they do decide there’s a business opportunity, they’ll likely need to look beyond Japan for launch capacity as JAXA does not currently possess a re-usable launch vehicle and operates at a modest launch cadence compared to private launch operators. ®

events.title: Musk, Uber co-founder join call for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia
events.summary: Elon Musk and several tech heavyweights are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief. Elon Musk, Travis Kalanick and over 158,000 others want Jensen Huang back as Nvidia chief after his Nov 12 resignation over two extramarital affairs. Supporters say Huang made Nvidia central to AI and ask the board to “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Some investors back all options, but US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants an outside chief and a “dramatic shake-up” over chip smuggling concerns. SAN FRANCISCO – Tech tycoon Elon Musk and an Uber co-founder are, as at Nov 15, among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief. The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Huang resigned on Nov 12, ending a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded after revelations he had two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate. Alongside the SpaceX chief, the tech heavyweight signatories include Tim Sweeney, founder and chief executive of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator. Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”. More than 7,500 signatories identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce. The support illustrates the unique standing of the leather-jacketed executive, who is seen as a godfather of artificial intelligence within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing data centres and start-ups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”. But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang championed open AI models, including Chinese ones, and fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei. According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return with people close to him, and one of his allies says he is assembling a crisis team of executives to seek White House support. On Nov 13, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open. In Washington, however, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued on Nov 15 that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News, demanding that the company explain whether it had knowingly turned a blind eye to the smuggling of its chips to China.
