events.title: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
events.summary: Bharat Semi , an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere. The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027. India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets. The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview. “Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch. Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision. Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system. The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027. The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market. Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe. “It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said. In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility. The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility. events.title: Americans fear the worst after Pentagon doomsday prepping, ‘Black October’ cyberattacks, stock crash, spy scandal, Microsoft outage, and airport chaos
events.summary: The past month has seemed like one battle after another, and it’s taking a toll on Americans who are starting to feel like everything is breaking at once. October began ominously after the Pentagon launched an initiative on Sept. 30 called FORTRESS , which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains. The plan envisions portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage, and microgrids that can disconnect bases from civilian power networks. It also calls for strategic reserves of munitions, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts, and medical supplies. Then came a month of cyberattacks that hit hundreds of companies and institutions around the world. Targets included the Federal Election Commission, Sony, John Deere, Oracle Health, Burger King Japan, and the State Bank of India. The hacking spree was so widespread that it was dubbed “Black October.” Cyberattacks even reached freezers across Europe and at U.S. military bases, with temperatures hiked high enough to spoil frozen food. France blamed the freezer hacks on Iran, which had previously vowed to retaliate against the U.S. and its allies for the war against the regime. Adding to the unease was the U.K. government’s campaign urging Britons to keep canned food, bottled water, and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption. Cybersecurity experts also rushed to fix vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language that’s used in nearly 70% of all websites. The National Security Agency warned the vulnerability could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers. Black October reached a crescendo with the largest crypto heist in history: North Korean hackers swiped $6.3 billion from Binance . Days later, U.S. voters delivered a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans, as Democrats swept races across GOP strongholds in midterm elections. Several candidates who campaigned on pushing back against data centers rode to victory in the so-called blue tsunami, threatening the AI boom that has powered the U.S. economy and stock market in recent years. While stocks jumped in the immediate aftermath of Election Day, they suddenly tumbled with top indexes suffering the worst losses since Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariff shock in April 2025. Tech companies saw especially steep declines, and on Nov. 5 the Nasdaq 100 marked its worst single-day performance since March 2020—during the early panic over COVID-19. Markets regained some ground as dip-buyers rushed in to snap up bargains. But then another bombshell came last weekend, when Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. After a separate affair with an Nvidia employee emerged days later, Huang stepped down as CEO from the AI chip giant he cofounded. Nvidia stock plunged as markets anticipated tougher restrictions on its chip exports, while the sudden loss of Huang, who hadn’t designated a successor, put at risk all the “circular” financing deals he made with companies throughout the AI ecosystem. In addition to the stock carnage, the spy scandal also highlighted China’s extensive industrial espionage efforts , which could tip the scales in the AI race that may determine economic and military supremacy. Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Wednesday. Then on Thursday, Microsoft’s suite of software tools went offline, shutting down email and calendars as well as collaboration and AI functions. The company attributed the outage to a technical issue—and not to cyberattacks or AI. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” it said . Workers around the world felt paralyzed by the Microsoft outage, so many suspected it had a role in the FAA’s order to ground planes at all U.S. airports on Friday, forcing airlines to cancel or delay thousands of flights. Microsoft said it had no indication that the ground stop was related to its global outage. The FAA later blamed its drastic move on an upgrade from copper wire to fiber-optic cables at a communications node in Arkansas. The changeover caused routers across the air traffic control system to be flooded with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Because it disrupted some radar feeds, the FAA ordered the ground stop to ensure safety. It was lifted about four hours later. Still, when the problem first emerged on Friday, it was so alarming the White House situation room and national security apparatus went into action . The FBI, the director of national intelligence, the Defense Department, the NSA, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency all got on a call to compare notes. They didn’t see any chatter or “footprints” that are normally associated with a cyberattack, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. But on Sunday, he didn’t completely rule one out . “We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor,” Duffy told Fox News Sunday . “But we’re open. If we see something else, we’re going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement.” The cumulative effect of all the disruptions has put Americans on edge. A cruise ship that overturned in New Orleans after getting hit by a tanker on Friday didn’t help either. Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, who was stuck at Newark Liberty International Airport, told the Associated Press “There’s a lot of weird stuff going on” and wondered if it was all part of some form of attack. “We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore,” he added. “They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.” Maxine Gustafson, a 34-year-old physician assistant from Minneapolis, was at Chicago’s O’Hare airport when she admitted to the AP that the week’s mishaps made her feel afraid and helpless. “It makes you think, like, is this a cyberattack?” she said. “We don’t have control over a lot of this stuff.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Woolworths apologises after customers report drained gift card balances
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Woolworths customers report hundreds of dollars stolen from digital gift cards The gift cards were purchased following a 4 per cent discount promotion through Everyday Gifting. ( Supplied ) Dozens of Woolworths customers say their digital WISH gift cards have been drained. Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of e-gift cards and is investigating. Customers who contacted the ABC say they purchased their cards after a 4 per cent promotional offer on Everyday Gifting. Dozens of Woolworths customers say they have lost hundreds of dollars after discovering their digital gift cards were drained by transactions they did not authorise. The ABC has been contacted by customers across Australia who say their Everyday WISH gift cards, purchased through the Everyday Rewards website or app, were spent by someone else. Some customers have reported losing up to $500, with transactions appearing at stores in different states from where the cards were purchased. Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting "a number of" customer e-gift cards, apologising to those affected and saying it is investigating the reports as a priority. Complaints first appeared on Australian bargain-sharing website OzBargain last week, with similar reports subsequently emerging across Facebook and Reddit. All of the customers who contacted the ABC appear to have purchased their gift cards during a promotional offer through Everyday Gifting that advertised a 4 per cent discount. Everyday WISH gift cards can be redeemed in store and online at participating Woolworths Group retailers and partners, including Big W, BWS, Dan Murphy's and Cellarmasters. The complaints reported to the ABC so far involve Everyday WISH cards purchased digitally through the Everyday Rewards website or app. ( Supplied ) Deborah Kellie, from Brisbane, said she lost $500 after purchasing an Everyday WISH card last Monday. "I have been an Everyday Rewards customer for ages, and I usually buy my rewards cards through the RACQ," she said. But Ms Kellie said a promotional email from Everyday Gifting advertised a "great deal", offering an extra 1 per cent discount on WISH gift cards compared with RACQ. "So I thought I've got to go shopping next week, I'll get one from them [Everyday Gifting] instead." Two days later, she discovered the entire balance had been spent at a Big W store in Doncaster, Victoria, despite never having used the card or shared its details. In Sydney, Michael Bennett said he had also switched from buying the WISH gift card through the NRMA app after seeing the 4 per cent discount offer in the Everyday Rewards app. He said he purchased a $400 WISH gift card through the app on November 9. But when he attempted to use it at a Woolworths store in Hornsby on November 14, the card had disappeared from his digital wallet. Deborah Kellie says her gift card was drained in another state two days after she purchased it. ( Supplied ) After checking the balance through a link in his email, he discovered the money had been spent. The transaction history showed $400 had been spent at a Big W store in Pagewood, in Sydney's east, on November 12. Mr Bennett said he had not shared the gift card details, his mobile phone had remained in his possession, and his Everyday Rewards account was protected by a complex password and two-factor authentication. He also said the gift card had never been physically printed. "Woolworths warn customers to treat gift cards like cash," Mr Bennett said. Suspecting a cybersecurity breach, Ms Kellie said she cancelled her Visa card as a precaution. She said she made three attempts to contact Woolworths customer service, but was unable to speak to anyone despite waiting for more than an hour on the phone the first two times. On her third attempt, Ms Kellie said an automated message advised the company was receiving an increasing number of calls before disconnecting her. She subsequently emailed Woolworths screenshots and details of the transactions and lodged a report with cybersecurity authorities. The report has since been referred to Queensland Police for assessment in correspondence seen by the ABC. Following ABC enquiries, a Woolworths spokesperson advised customers who notice an unrecognised transaction to contact its Gift Card Support team at giftcard@customerservice.woolworths.com.au . Customers can also log into the Everyday Gifting website and register their details on the homepage. "Our team will work directly with customers to determine the appropriate next steps, including issuing replacement e-gift cards for customers impacted," the spokesperson said.

events.title: What to know about summer jobs, from where to find them to thinking 'strategically'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts What to consider before hunting for a summer job There's an influx of hospitality, retail and tourism jobs over summer, economist Blair Chapman says. ( ABC News: Sam Ikin ) If you're looking for a few extra hours of work or desperately trying to save before university begins, a summer job could be the right fit for you. These seasonal roles can simply be about earning extra cash, but it could help you discover what you love (or hate) doing for work. It could even help with starting a new career. Ben Walker was 16 when he got a casual job at his local supermarket in Sale, in regional Victoria. Ben Walker's first casual job led to ongoing part-time work. ( Supplied: Ben Walker ) The 21-year-old says that led to the part-time job that now supports him while studying game design at university. In the beginning, Ben says he learnt a lot from interactions with people outside of school and cricket. "The people skills, I think, are massive," he says. Why summer is a good time to get a job There is an influx of roles in hospitality, retail and tourism ahead of Christmas and summer, says Blair Chapman, the chief economist at employment service Seek. "In Australia we get the double dose of Christmas and summer," he says. Retail picks up from early November (because of Black Friday sales), and online shopping has led to an increase in warehouse or "pick-packer roles" too, Dr Chapman says. And given cost-of-living pressures and airfare prices, more Australians are likely to holiday closer to home this summer, he says. "That sort of domestic-driven tourism might pick up because people can't afford to go overseas." Dr Chapman says there is also "a bit of an evolution" in who is looking for summer jobs. "There's a cost-of-living crunch and people are looking for that second job to help supplement their income," he says. What are the benefits (other than pay)? Grozdana Manalo says her first job as a barista began a "love affair" with coffee and helped her build confidence and communication skills. Why a job 'that's just a job' works for these people The dos and don'ts of job hunting while still employed The steps first home buyers can take while saving for their deposit "It also showed me just how hard and long some people work and made me really appreciate being a uni student," she says. She's now a career services manager at the University of Sydney's Business School. "Summer jobs can also help students discover what they enjoy, and just as importantly, what they don't," Ms Manalo says. Seasonal and casual roles can also help young people develop professional skills, she says. "Teamwork, communication, problem solving and time management — all important skills no matter what job or career you pick in the future." Thinking strategically when applying for jobs Irma Mooi-Reci is a professor of sociology at the University of Melbourne and the CEO of a company specialising in workforce data and skill gaps. She would like young people to think "more strategically" about summer employment. "Is it because you want to pay your bills? Is it because you want to have that experience or get a reference? Or is it because you want to get that first permanent job?" she asks. Economic report dubs 2026 'year of AI' A new economic report by consultancy firm Deloitte says the AI "winners" will be organisations that combine human and machine strengths, with recruiters saying human judgement will still be key. It's worth looking for a job that complements your career goals and whether an employer will see the experience as relevant, Professor Mooi-Reci says. "Find something that you like doing, that you feel passionate about and learn as much as possible." Professor Mooi-Reci says young people can become overwhelmed by information and fearmongering about the job market, the value of their degree and artificial intelligence. "Don't be afraid, but think strategically," she adds. How to find a summer job (and avoid exploitation) If you're after seasonal work, Ms Manalo recommends looking for roles advertised on social media and job boards, or simply walking into local businesses and asking if there are positions available. She says there are also "hidden job markets", which is why so many positions are filled before they're advertised. "This is all about leveraging your personal networks and making it known that you're looking for work," she says. If you're young or have never been employed before, understanding workplace rights and responsibilities is very important, Ms Manalo says.

events.title: South Korea’s instant ramen giants take their spicy rivalry global
events.summary: For nearly four decades, NongShim has dominated South Korea’s instant noodle market with its signature Shin Ramyun. NongShim is fighting Samyang overseas with a 200 billion won Busan export plant for Shin Ramyun, which will lift export capacity by 70% and support global growth. Samyang’s Buldak has become a viral hit, lifting overseas sales above 80% of revenue and helping it overtake NongShim in some markets, including China and Europe. Both firms are expanding fast as the global instant-noodle market grows, and NongShim wants to double global noodle sales by 2030 and enter the stir-fried noodle market next year. SEOUL – For nearly four decades, NongShim has dominated South Korea’s instant noodle market with its signature Shin Ramyun. But when South Korean ramen became a global phenomenon, it was a rival that captured the world’s appetite – and investors’ imagination. Samyang Foods did it with its Buldak, which became a viral sensation with global fans filming themselves eating the intensely spicy noodles on social media. The craze pushed Samyang’s overseas sales above 80% of revenue – compared with NongShim’s 37% – and lifted its market value to nearly four times that of its rival. Now NongShim is spending heavily to rebuild investor confidence. At the heart of the push is a 200 billion won (S$190 million) factory for NongShim’s iconic Shin Ramyun in the port city of Busan, the company’s first dedicated export plant and home to what the company calls the world’s fastest instant-noodle production lines. The facility will boost NongShim’s domestic export capacity by 70% as it seeks to regain ground lost to Samyang overseas. “We may have been somewhat slow in responding to global demand early on because our products were so deeply loved at home for so long,” said Ji Songha, NongShim’s head of global marketing. A decades-old domestic rivalry between two of South Korea’s biggest food makers is intensifying overseas. NongShim and Samyang, both based in Seoul, are racing to capitalise on a K-food boom that has pushed Korean noodles into mainstream supermarkets from the US to Europe, just as the global instant noodle market is projected to grow about 23% to US$63.3 billion (S$81.5 billion) by 2030. NongShim’s new six-storey complex, which opened in October, is designed to produce 600 packets a minute on each line – twice the speed of conventional setups. Inside, raw dough takes barely seven minutes to become a shelf-ready packet of Shin Ramyun. Guided by artificial intelligence sensors and automated mixers, the noodles are rolled, flash-fried and boxed at blinding speed. The factory will nearly double NongShim’s annual domestic export capacity to 1.2 billion packets, and raise its total global capacity to 6.2 billion across Korea and four factories in the US and China. Production from Busan will initially be directed to Japan, Europe, Australia, India and South-east Asia. NongShim aims to double global noodle sales to 5.4 trillion won by 2030, which would lift overseas sale to more than 60% of revenue. Such growth would also elevate it to the global top five instant noodle makers alongside Nissin Foods Holdings and Maggi-maker Nestle. NongShim’s push puts it head-to-head with Samyang. The Buldak maker is rapidly gaining ground in overseas markets where NongShim dominated, having already overtaken it in key markets like China and Europe. It is on track to become the third-largest instant noodle seller in the US in 2026 – right behind NongShim, according to Euromonitor International. Samyang is also accelerating its global expansion, and announced last week it would invest more than 131 billion won in a new Vietnamese production line. Its first overseas plant in China is set to open in January. For NongShim, the test will be whether the new capacity translates into faster sales growth and improved profitability. The company’s valuation could get a lift from a rebound in US sales and increased output from the Busan facility, according to Hanwha Investment & Securities analyst Han Yujung. NongShim’s push for overseas growth has a promising early start – sales of Shin Ramyun abroad jumped 36% in the first half of 2026. Still, Samyang commands a valuation premium over NongShim, its stock is trading at 13.4-times forward-earnings versus the latter’s 11.4 – meaning investors are paying more per won of projected profit in anticipation of faster growth. NongShim is also borrowing from its rival’s playbook. To court Gen Z shoppers abroad, it has leaned into pop culture – launching limited-edition Shin Ramyun tied to Netflix’s K-Pop Demon Hunters and setting up booths at fan conventions globally. It also plans to roll out a new stir-fried Shin Ramyun in 2027, entering the soupless-noodle category that propelled Buldak’s global success. “We cannot yet claim that we are outperforming Samyang in many international markets,” Ji, NongShim’s marketing head, said. “But we are studying and benchmarking what Samyang has done well.

events.title: Dems' Denver victory party previews 2028 battles
events.summary: DENVER — Thousands of Democrats gathered here this weekend for a giddy postelection summit, reveling in their party's historic midterm victories and touting the center-left strategy they say powered them. But some progressives saw the event as a lavish, out-of-touch affair bankrolled by billionaires — exactly what Democrats just campaigned against. "I'm all for celebration, but perhaps a fancy retreat does not exactly meet the tenor of the moment," said Josh Orton, president of the liberal group Demand Justice and a veteran of Bernie Sanders' 2020 campaign. Why it matters: The competing views of What's Next, the buzzy confab held by the influential centrist organization Majority Democrats, offer an early glimpse of the ideological battles over health care, money in politics and other issues that will define the party's 2028 presidential primary. Zoom in: Democrats in the Mile High City were practically vibrating with happiness, still not quite able to believe they'd won back both chambers of Congress and flipped deep-red states such as Mississippi and South Carolina. "The vibes are excellent," Delaware Rep. Sarah McBride, a member of the Majority Democrats, said in an interview. "The last high-water mark, we were all in our houses on Zooms," she added, referring to the 2020 presidential election. "This is the first time there's been an undeniable capacity to celebrate widespread wins in the last decade." Free drinks flowed. Political operatives sported bomber jackets embroidered with the phrase "Majority Democrats." Speakers were immortalized in rock concert–style posters on the walls. For a brief moment in Denver's Mission Ballroom, the often-in-disarray Democratic Party looked united. Several presidential hopefuls downplayed the party's divides in speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said onstage that ordinary people don't give "a damn" about "where we fall on some imaginary political spectrum." Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin quipped in her address that elected officials who were fighting over progressives vs. moderates had "missed the plot." The other side: But others in the party weren't interested in all the kumbaya. Young protesters sneaked into the event and heckled House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), shouting "You're a f**king traitor!" while calling for Medicare for All and impeachment. Some audience members were palpably annoyed, yelling "Shut up!" Another flashpoint emerged over high-dollar donors and super PACs. Majority Democrats — which is largely funded by a billionaire couple and describes itself as an alternative to both the "activist left" and a "gerontocratic establishment" — is already in the crosshairs of the Lever, a progressive publication. Majority Democrats' funding has been the focus of reporting by the Lever. The group tussled with the news site over the Denver event, initially denying it press passes and later blocking one of its journalists from interviewing an elected official. David Sirota, founder of the Lever, said the group's actions were "Trump-like attempts at retribution." But there was a silver lining for the outlet: The back-and-forth generated the single biggest influx of new subscribers in its history, he said. What they're saying: "What's Next was an overwhelming success: It brought together 3,500 Democrats from across the political spectrum to talk about what worked this cycle and where we go next," said Majority Democrats spokesperson Vidhya Jeyadev. "This cycle, we won seats that had been written off for a generation and proved there is no one way to be a Democrat." The intrigue: Some potential 2028 candidates in Denver tried to portray themselves as unifiers who can bridge the party's divides. New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim, who declined to rule out a 2028 bid, said, "I understand" where the protesters were coming from. "People are furious," he added.

events.title: Trump blames Biden for airline ground stop
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Trump breaks silence after airline ground stop to blame Biden administration Donald Trump says the Biden administration was "a disaster" for the Federal Aviation Administration. ( Reuters: Aaron Schwartz ) Donald Trump has made his first public comments on the weekend's air travel issues, blaming the Biden administration for leaving "a broken system". He has also called on Congress for more funding to upgrade America's outdated air traffic control systems. Thousands more US flights have been cancelled, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warning travel disruptions would continue for another day. The Trump administration says the air travel havoc triggered by a no-take-off order on Friday could drag on for another day, pushing back its timetable for a return to normal. Nearly 2,000 more flights were cancelled on Sunday and questions remained over how such chaos could unfold in the world's largest economy, a country that prides itself on its technological prowess. Stranded passengers wandered through chaotic US airports for a third day. Officials have blamed Friday's flight chaos on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables. US says wires to blame for grounded flights The US government has blamed a nationwide aviation shutdown which has disrupted more than 20,000 flights on a program to replace copper wires with new fibre ones. On Sunday, President Donald Trump ended uncharacteristic days of silence on the ground stop, but only to blame his predecessor, Joe Biden, for the debacle. Mr Trump insisted he inherited a mess from the Biden administration and said Congress, which his party controlled for two years, must approve funds to upgrade America's outdated air traffic control system. "The Biden administration was an FAA disaster," Mr Trump said, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration. "Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began." FAA chief Bryan Bedford said on Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans stranded at airports would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday. Sean Duffy has also blamed prior administrations for dated systems. ( Reuters: Eric Lee ) But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Sunday morning that it would take longer to get planes, crews and travellers to where they needed to be. "So, in the airspace, we're going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow," Mr Duffy told America's ABC News. "We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that." Mr Duffy also flatly rejected calls for his resignation over the travel chaos, insisting he inherited woefully outdated air traffic control infrastructure such as, he said, radar equipment dating back to the 1960s. "So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I'm the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me," Mr Duffy said in an interview on CNN. As of Sunday afternoon, more than 1,880 flights within, into or out of the United States had been cancelled, according to the travel monitor site FlightAware. What we know about why US flights were grounded Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for a communications outage. The Trump administration has blamed Friday's nationwide ground stoppage — meaning no planes could take off — on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines. Friday's disruption was only the second time such a ground stop had been issued in US airspace, among the busiest in the world, since the 9/11 attacks. Mr Duffy has appealed for $US50 billion ($74 billion) in funds to upgrade and modernise the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to "meet this moment". But Democrats quickly pounced to say Congress under Trump's Republicans could already have done this.

events.title: Some Dems' 2028 strategy: Make America Nice Again
events.summary: Some Democrats weighing 2028 campaigns for president believe the midterms proved that Americans have soured on Trump-style, scorched-earth political warfare and want a brand of politics that's nicer and more optimistic. Others aren't so sure. Why it matters: Democrats' midterm blowout has prompted a debate over the lessons of 2026 — whether voters in the 2028 primary will want their own ruthless fighter after two more years of President Trump, or will be itching for a more unifying figure. Zoom in: That divide was reflected in several potential 2028 contenders' comments around the midterms. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg told his supporters that the end of the Trump era "means a politics where we can check the news and actually feel our blood pressure come down a little." In his reelection victory speech, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told supporters that "you declared that you could not be more ready for an end of this ruthless chaos and cruelty." In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom — who led the successful ballot measure to create more Democratic House seats in response to Trump's redistricting push in red states — boasted that California "fought fire with fire." Newsom mocked Democrats who he said would have responded by merely writing op-eds in the New York Times. "Donald Trump is not screwing around, nor are we," Newsom said at a preelection rally, adding that he was proud of leading the "most un-Trump state in America." The big picture: The midterm results provided an argument for each side. Several key victories for Democrats in red states came from candidates preaching decency, or voters recoiling from vicious Republican attacks. In Kansas, Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said one of his campaign's big ideas was "decency" — and that he wanted to become the "best friend" of Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.). In Ohio, Gov.-elect Amy Acton told her supporters that "basic decency is on the ballot" after her opponent and Vice President Vance defended an attack ad featuring Acton's mother, from whom Acton had been estranged since childhood after accusing her stepfather of sexual abuse. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, a seminarian and the first Democrat to be elected statewide in three decades, said that "love my neighbor" informed his approach to politics. In Denver last week at a gathering of Democratic leaders, Talarico pressed the point: "It's been 10 years of this kind of politics — politics as blood sport, politics as trolling and owning and name-calling, politics as professional wrestling. It tears families apart. It ends friendships, and it leaves us all feeling terrible all of the time." The other side: Other Democrats who won key races embraced something like Newsom's edgier approach by pledging to fight fire with fire, and to not unilaterally disarm against Republicans. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said on the campaign trail that when his opponents go low, he doesn't take the higher ground. He prefers to take them "to the mud and choke them out." He added that too many Democrats "tell you they're fighting, only to show up with a strongly worded letter." Reality check: Hamilton, Acton and Talarico had unifying messages, but they and their allies also ran tens of millions of dollars in negative ads against their Republican opponents. In 2008, Barack Obama also had a larger theme of change and unity but ran a campaign that unapologetically attacked his opponents.

events.title: England stun Spain to end La Roja’s 43-game unbeaten run
events.summary: Spain suffer first defeat since March 2024 after losing 3-2 to England in Madrid despite grandstand finish. England held on with 10 men to record a stunning win over Spain in Madrid in one of the great UEFA Nations League games. The visitors had seen their hosts parade their World Cup trophy on the pitch before the game, but raced into a 3-0 lead inside an hour, before being reduced to 10 men on 65 minutes and having to cling on in a dramatic finale to pip Spain to top spot in Group A3 on goal difference. It was a record 10th straight away win for the Three Lions, and it inflicted the first defeat on La Roja since they went down 1-0 in a friendly against Colombia in London in March 2024. The 43-game run saw them crowned European and World Champions along the way. England produced a stunning start and might have been ahead inside the opening minutes, but Unai Simon made a brilliant reaction save to claw away Jude Bellingham’s close-range effort. The visitors were irresistible in the first half, pressing high and denying the hosts time and space to find their rhythm, and Spain were unable to register a shot on target in the opening 45 minutes. England led 1-0 at the break after Harry Kane latched onto Elliot Anderson’s pass in behind and drew a foul from Pau Cubarsi in the box. Following a brief VAR review into Anderson’s challenge on Marc Cucurella in the build-up, Kane stepped up to convert the penalty. He fired to the right of Unai Simon to register his 93rd Three Lions goal on his 127th appearance in the final seconds of the half. The visitors doubled their lead eight minutes after the turnaround as Declan Rice’s curling corner was met by a powerful downward header from the unmarked Ezri Konsa, his Arsenal teammate. The hosts were in disarray four minutes later, when some slick counterattacking saw Bellingham slot through into space on the right of the box for the on-rushing Ben White to drill a low shot past Simon at his near post. The game changed 25 minutes from time when Jarell Quansah was dispossessed in his own half, and Anderson was shown a straight red card for denying a goalscoring opportunity by putting his arm on Lamine Yamal as he raced into the box. After VAR confirmed the decision, Mikel Oyarzabal sent James Trafford – recalled in place of Jordan Pickford in goal – the wrong way to give the hosts hope. They piled on the pressure and reduced the arrears further on the break on 75 minutes, when Yamal’s first-time cross from the right was swept in off the post by substitute Nico Williams. La Roja laid siege to the England goal in the closing stages as they sought a goal to extend their unbeaten run and claim top spot in Group A3. But Trafford produced a stunning double save in stoppage time, diving to his right to parry a shot from Fermin Lopez, then somehow bouncing up to turn the follow-up from Aymeric Laporte around the upright. England held on to secure first place in the group on goal difference after both sides finished on 15 points. Both sides will find out their Nations League quarterfinal opponents next March when the draw takes place on Friday. England is set to face one of the three A-Group runners-up, other than Spain, while La Roja will face one of the other three group winners.

events.title: 'We slept here': Flight delays linger but schedule is back on track for Monday
events.summary: U.S. flights are expected to return to near-normal levels on Monday as airlines scramble to get back on track. Flight disruptions lingered two days after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours, with more than 3,400 flights canceled or delayed on Sunday. Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the issue on a router that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. U.S. flights are set to run close to normal on Monday as airlines scramble to get back on track after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday. Disruptions lingered on Sunday with thousands more flights canceled and delayed. Close to 2,000 U.S. flights were canceled as of 4:45 p.m. ET and more than 7,500 were delayed, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware, down from the 6,697 cancellations and 9,000 delays on Saturday, and Friday's 9,201 cancellations and more than 7,400 delays. American Airlines had the most cancellations on Sunday at 805 flights, about 13% of its schedule, followed by Delta Air Lines with 360 cancellations, or 7% of its schedule, according to aviation data firm Cirium. The airlines' home hubs of Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport and Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, respectively, saw some of the most severe delays in the U.S. Meanwhile, JetBlue Airways canceled close to a third of its flights. "We slept here," said Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from New York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter's birthday trip. They were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta Air Lines , they decided to make good use of the extra time: after strolling through Central Park, they went window shopping on Fifth Avenue. But when the flight was canceled, the standby list for a backup flight looked grim, and their original Midtown hotel was charging about $700 for an additional night, the two slept at LaGuardia on Saturday. She said they found wheelchairs to sleep in outside security. Duffy blames L3Harris network for longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11 Hundreds of flights into Newark, New York, Philadelphia disrupted after Verizon fiber line cut The government shutdown is over. The air traffic controller shortage is not Aviation industry pushes Congress for air traffic improvements, more hiring Why the U.S. doesn't have enough air traffic controllers FAA system outage disrupts thousands of flights across U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday tied the issue to a router and work to update from copper wires, a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies , to a fiber-optic system. FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over to fiber optic. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday afternoon. Customers told CNBC they were booked on several flights before getting on board. Justine Fritz, who works in sales for a consumer goods company, was in New York for a business event on Friday. She tried five different flights before getting on a flight to Houston, then flew four hours out of her way to get back to Minneapolis after her Saturday flight was canceled. Fritz said she had so many boarding passes that TSA wouldn't let her through security at first. "It's been bananas," she told CNBC at the gate. Fritz said she made the best of it by shopping and getting a haircut, but she's still disappointed. "I'm missing the first hour of the Vikings game," she said. Martin said her trip home with her daughter will take even longer. Delta booked them to Memphis, and her husband will drive the four hours from Birmingham to pick them up. Shortly after the groundstop, the longest since 9/11, Duffy pushed Congress for as much as $50 billion for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system. A day later, Democratic lawmakers pushed back, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress's approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years. "Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again," said Reps. Rick Larsen (D.-Wash.), ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Rep. Andre Carson (D.-Ind.), ranking member of the aviation subcommittee, said in a joint statement. events.title: An Nvidia engineer says he's quitting because Jensen Huang was ousted: 'So disappointing'
events.summary: Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia this week after admitting to an affair. Erik Flyg/Bloomberg via Getty Images An Nvidia engineer said he left the company after former CEO Jensen Huang resigned. Huang resigned last week after admitting to an affair. The board is investigating whether Huang was the " target of a foreign intelligence effort." An Nvidia engineer said he's left the company because of former CEO Jensen Huang's departure . Darrell Dai, a senior research engineer in the company's robotics sector in Shanghai who has worked at Nvidia for a little over a year, according to his LinkedIn profile, announced the decision in an X post on Saturday. At the time of writing, the post had amassed over 104,000 likes. "Jensen's vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close," Dai wrote. In the post, Dai wrote that he admires Huang's "willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious," citing the tech founder's commitment to CUDA and positioning the company for the AI boom. What matters most, Dai wrote, however, is the culture Huang established at Nvidia. "Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees' Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard," Dai said. He added, "That is why this has been so disappointing." Nvidia's board of directors is now searching for a new CEO after Huang resigned on Thursday. Earlier in the week, Huang admitted to having an affair, and Nvidia launched an investigation into whether he was "the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The New York Times and Reuters later in the week reported that Huang had also developed relationships with two Nvidia employees. Nvidia's board of directors says it is considering both internal and external candidates, and there's already a number of names in the ether, including former Apple CEO Tim Cook. Meanwhile, a growing movement that includes some Silicon Valley heavyweights is urging the board to reinstate Huang . Elon Musk and Replit CEO Amjad Masad have promoted a petition demanding the board bring Huang back. "Organizers and signers are concerned that Jensen may have been forced out without due process and without even a few days to make his case. It's exactly why we are asking the NVIDIA Board to explain," the organizers said on the "Stand with Jensen" campaign's website. Others, however, say Huang's behavior was too reckless to bring him back. Yorkville's senior managing director, Dan Ives, said he doesn't see Huang making a comeback at Nvidia. In an X post, Ives said "no one individual" can replace Huang, but his era is coming to an end. "We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO. It's about moving forward for Nvidia and it starts Tuesday with earnings as Colette leads NVDA ahead (for now)," Ives said on Sunday. Ives called the idea "ridiculous" given the "legal/Board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles." Last week, Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, chair of the Senate Banking Committee, wrote on X that Huang's resignation doesn't absolve him, executives, or the company of "responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws." In his X post, Dai said the most difficult aspect of the situation is coming to terms with Huang's resignation before receiving a proper explanation. "I have felt that engineers' perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard," he said. "That gap has been more painful than I expected." Dai said he understood that some aspects of the situation can't be shared immediately, but that doesn't change the feeling of being left out of a decision that impacts the entire company. "A company's greatness comes from its leadership, its governance, and the people who turn its ambitions into reality. Employees' trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too," Dai wrote. Business Insider has reached out to Nvidia and Dai for comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Vance may wait until late spring to reveal 2028 plans
events.summary: Vice President Vance won't make a final decision on whether to run for president in 2028 until after the new year — and may wait until late spring to announce his intentions publicly, two sources with knowledge of his plans tell Axios. Why it matters: Vance remains the early favorite to succeed President Trump as the GOP's presidential nominee, but the party's midterm losses have complicated his political future and could reshape the 2028 field. People familiar with Vance's thinking say he's genuinely undecided about running, and that his decision-making timeline was in place before the midterms. Advisers caution that the timing could change, however. Vance is still discussing a potential bid with his family, including his wife, Usha, following the birth of their fourth child, the sources said. The big picture: Vance allies say the midterm losses haven't changed his standing as the early 2028 GOP front-runner, citing his donor network, political infrastructure and name recognition. Vance co-founded the secretive Rockbridge Network , which could anchor his presidential fundraising operation. The group met in Houston after the midterms. As Republican National Committee finance chair, Vance has cultivated relationships with major contributors. He also has ties to technology donors Peter Thiel, David Sacks and Elon Musk — the world's richest person and the GOP's biggest financier. Vance campaigned nationwide for the midterms, building relationships with GOP activists and officials who could prove valuable in 2028. Behind the scenes: Vance's closest political advisers believe he should run in 2028 and that he's likely to do so, according to a person close to the vice president. But the GOP's midterm losses have given Republicans who want to move on from the Trump administration an opening to argue for a different direction in 2028. Vance likely will have to answer for the Trump administration's record in 2028, potentially complicating his presidential ambitions. Vance privately opposed the Iran war, and some Republicans interpreted his post-midterm criticism of the conflict as an effort to distance himself from Trump's decision to attack Iran. The intrigue: Republicans close to Vance see Trump's continued presence as another reason to delay announcing his 2028 plans. Vance is wary that launching a campaign too early could shift attention away from Trump and risk alienating him. Trump said that "a lot of people didn't like [Vance's] comments" about the Iran war, but added that he wasn't among them and insisted their relationship wasn't affected. Zoom in: While Vance weighs a presidential campaign, a few other Republicans are doing so as well — namely Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who's been among the most active Republicans preparing for a potential 2028 run. Cruz's team has held meetings about a possible run, according to people familiar with his operation. But many Republicans, including some Cruz allies, doubt he could seriously challenge Vance, particularly if Trump endorses the vice president. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is viewed by some Republicans as a potentially more formidable rival to Vance. Rubio has attracted support from influential GOP figures, including megadonor Ken Griffin . But Rubio repeatedly has said he would support Vance if the VP were to run, and Rubio's workload as secretary of state and national security adviser has left him without Vance's ready-made political operation. Other potential Republican contenders include former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. DeSantis has been particularly outspoken , calling the GOP's midterm losses a near "extinction-level event" and pointing to Florida's Republican victories as a model for rebuilding the party. events.title: Cut national insurance for under-25s to create jobs, Milburn report to say
events.summary: Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill National Insurance (NI) paid by businesses on workers aged under 25 should be gradually lowered to encourage companies to create jobs for young people, a major review of youth unemployment will say. A report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will suggest the government should reduce NI costs over five years for people aged between 21 and 24 years old, starting in retail and hospitality. Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms. Milburn will say the number of young people not in employment, education or training - known as Neets - was not started by the NI rise. But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing". The independent report, which has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday, will also make recommendations on reducing the UK's benefits bill. Milburn has said the government spends £22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive. There are nearly one million so-called Neets aged between 16 and 24 in the UK, according to data from the Office for National Statistics. He will recommend that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales. Milburn wants the government to provide a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support . Those who refuse to take up help could lose their benefits. Milburn is also expected to say that helping young people develop skills is pointless if there are no jobs available for them. The former health secretary will recommend doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000. But he will say this should only be done "when fiscal conditions allow". Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank. Milburn is set to say that given the UK's fiscal position, an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money. 'Government's foot firmly on my neck' But Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns three salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and the minimum wage. She said she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any. Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads". Salon-owner Collette Osborne says she is "inundated" with CVs from young people She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages. "I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said. Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters. "I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs." Milburn told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme he agreed with a recent move by Chancellor John Healey to slow down the equalisation of the national minimum wage across age groups. Labour had pledged in its manifesto to remove "discriminatory age bands" and close the gap between adult minimum wages and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds. But in his Budget, Healey said pay for that age group would rise from £10.85 to £11.27 an hour in April next year while people aged 21 and over will see their wages increase from £12.71 to £13.21. "I understand why because nobody wants to see young workers on poverty pay," Milburn said, but he said it "imposed a lot of costs on [the] government". "I think we have got to look very carefully at the convergence issue," he said. Milburn said he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers. "Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said. "The state has a responsibility to help them with that." On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit. People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales. McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029".

events.title: Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK urge Israel to allow aid into Gaza
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? The countries accuse Israel of preventing tents and other vital supplies from entering Gaza, despite the humanitarian crisis. Gaza floods leave 350,000 affected as UN humanitarian chief demands aid access Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom have ⁠⁠⁠⁠urged Israel to allow immediate and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza, highlighting that recent floods have “brought further suffering” for Palestinians living there. The countries’ foreign ministers co-signed Sunday’s joint statement , the latest international warning about the dire humanitarian situation in the besieged territory. list 1 of 3 70 bodies recovered from Gaza rubble, thousands still missing list 2 of 3 Who can force Israel to implement Gaza ceasefire deal? list 3 of 3 Palestinians reclaim Gaza’s shores with a swim for hope “People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance,” the statement said. “Yet 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza.” For years, Israel has restricted entry and exports into Gaza, home to more than 2 million people. But since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, Israel has placed the Palestinian territory under a full-scale blockade, limiting access to even essential supplies like food and water. Under the Geneva Convention, denying civilians access to humanitarian aid can constitute a war crime. “We today urge the Government of Israel to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza,” Sunday’s statement said. Heavy rain this month swept away tens of thousands of tents in the territory, leaving many without shelter. “This situation is entirely reversible”, Sunday’s statement said, “and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in”. More than 1.9 million people have been displaced in Gaza, according to the United Nations, many of them suffering displacement multiple times. As of November 1, the Global Shelter Cluster, a humanitarian organisation that coordinates with the Red Cross and the UN, estimated that Gaza residents need at least 1.7 million mattresses and 121,000 tents to face this season’s cold, rainy weather. During Israel’s genocidal war, entire neighbourhoods and cities were levelled. Some of the structures that remain are unstable. In September, at least 20 people were killed when a building they were sheltering in collapsed. Shelter is only one factor in the ongoing humanitarian crisis, though. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been plunged into poverty since Israel began its genocidal war. The price of basic goods has soared as incomes have shrunk due to the war and Israel’s tightened siege. Sunday’s statement follows a similar appeal from the UN’s Humanitarian Country Team of the Occupied Palestinian Territory on Friday. “The devastating impact of the latest rainstorm in Gaza was preventable,” the team wrote. “Children and adults were killed, critical services suspended, and thousands of family shelters flooded, swept away, or torn apart – not by the storm alone, but by policy decisions.” The European Union also released a statement on Saturday, expressing “grave concern” over the humanitarian crisis. It urged Israel to “allow immediate, unimpeded access” to humanitarian aid and “reopen all Gaza border crossings”. Sunday’s joint appeal also called on all parties to “implement the Comprehensive Plan for Gaza”, a plan unveiled in 2025 that called for an immediate ceasefire between Israel and Hamas. But attacks have continued, including on Thursday, when an Israeli air strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital killed six Palestinians. Israel is the subject of an ongoing genocide case before the International Court of Justice, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, have been issued arrest warrants by the International Criminal Court. They have been accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

events.title: UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset
events.summary: The UK will have a "voice in the room" but no vote on European Union food policies as part of a so-called "Brexit reset" to reduce red tape, EU relations minister Hamish Falconer has told the BBC. Prime Minister Andy Burnham hopes to agree a deal at a summit on Friday but critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker" but not a rule maker. Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules and said the deal could help bring down prices for shoppers. The reset would not involve any upfront payments, Falconer added, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment. Falconer said it was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. "The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said. The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit. The reset means they will be dismantled. In September, the Conservative Party said it was "raising the alarm" over the government's planned reset, saying it would leave British consumers and businesses "dangerously exposed, with no input on how regulations are made or power to reject them". Both the Conservatives and Reform have said they would undo the planned reset if they were in power. Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU. Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said the deal would help bring down costs for firms importing food. "This will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves," he said. He said currently "pages and pages" of form-filling meant some suppliers had given up exporting to the EU and some products, such as Lincolnshire sausages, meant they were almost impossible to export at all. Some M&S trucks require over 300 pages of documents for food exports, from export health certificates, phytosanitary certificates, visits from vets and border check paperwork. Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats. "The amount of paperwork you would need to do, the amount of uncertainty - you have to have it in the right pen colour, if it's not black, it might be refused," Falconer said. "If you're selling Cox apples from Kent, they have to wait a day before they go into the European Union." The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling. Falconer said the impact of the reset deal for food would be an additional £5bn. The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP. This wider agreement includes aligning emissions trading rules, and agreeing to a youth mobility scheme, as well as the reset on food trading. Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included. Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said. But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules. He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found. UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D. Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations. Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area. He said there were bound to be compromises and trade-offs in any deal but that where the UK had advantages the government wanted to make sure "those aren't lost under the deal". Crisp flavourings a contentious area Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK. "I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said. Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said. Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations. "The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

events.title: More MNCs choose Singapore for HQ, but outsized workforce no longer a given
events.summary: The number of foreign HQs in the Republic has increased from about 770 in 2019 to 1,030 in 2024, reflecting an almost 34% jump, according official statistics. More MNCs are choosing Singapore as a global or regional HQ, with foreign HQs rising from about 770 in 2019 to 1,030 in 2024. HQs no longer mean more staff in Singapore, with some firms keeping lean teams and moving routine work to lower-cost markets, experts said. Companies still value Singapore for its neutrality, tax incentives, talent and strong business climate. SINGAPORE – More multinational corporations (MNCs) are anchoring their global or regional headquarters in the Republic, but the move no longer entails having a larger workforce here as compared with other markets. The number of foreign HQs has increased from about 770 in 2019 to 1,030 in 2024, reflecting an almost 34% jump, according to official statistics. Over the same period, the number of resident professionals, managers and executives employed by foreign HQs rose by less than 8%, from 12,700 to 13,700. This is the latest available data, with preliminary figures for 2025 due to be released in early 2027. Experts told The Straits Times that foreign firms have steadily continued to set up HQs in Singapore, without committing to an outsized headcount. Patrick Na from professional services firm TMF Group said: “Foreign HQs have been growing since 2019, and Singapore keeps pulling in new ones, especially the higher-value strategic ones. The numbers are still going up.” He added: “A regional HQ does not automatically mean ‘the place with the most people in the region’ any more. These days, it is often a leaner set-up focused on senior decision-making, strategy and key functions, while a lot of the middle-layer operational and coordination jobs get moved to lower-cost locations.” Ray Tay, co-founder and managing director at business advisory and immigration firm VIVOS, observed that many foreign companies with Singapore HQs had fewer employees here than in neighbouring lower-cost markets such as Malaysia or the Philippines. He said the trend, which started around a decade ago, progressively grew as manpower costs in the Republic rose. “Covid totally supercharged it because every staff from top to junior learnt to use teleconferencing tools, and other remote working or collaboration tools became more prevalent,” he added. Despite this, Tay said foreign firms still saw value in designating Singapore as HQ, for reasons including its “efficient, no-nonsense image”, neutrality and tax incentives. He pointed to the Economic Development Board’s International Headquarters Award, which encourages companies to set up or expand their global or regional HQ activities in Singapore. The incentive offers a concessionary tax rate of 15%, 10% or 5% on a firm’s qualifying income, provided it meets conditions including hiring additional skilled employees. Local and foreign companies in Singapore are by default taxed at a flat rate of 17% on their chargeable income. Among businesses with HQs in Singapore is French cosmetics and skincare brand Clarins. Its subsidiary here, which was incorporated in 1992, serves as its regional HQ with nearly 200 employees. This is fewer than some other regional markets which the firm operates in, such as China, where it has more than 1,000 employees, and Japan, with almost 350 employees. Clarins president and chief executive Jonathan Zrihen told ST: “Singapore’s importance goes well beyond headcount. It is a place where we develop talent, shape strategy and make decisions that guide our business across the Asia-Pacific and, in travel retail, worldwide”. He added that Singapore has over the decades remained “the ideal hub” to support the firm’s development in the region. “It offers a neutral, central and highly efficient base, ideally located within the region, with a strong pool of international talent who can work across cultures. “It also provides a very stable and trusted business environment. That rationale has held over time,” Zrihen said. French cosmetics and skincare brand Clarins has nearly 200 employees at its regional headquarters in Singapore. The pharmaceutical subsidiary of Japanese giant Meiji Holdings has also put prominence on Singapore by selecting the country as its ASEAN strategic hub. Kensuke Hata, managing director of Meiji Pharma Asia, which started operating in Singapore in April, said the Republic supports the company’s marketing and business strategies, as well as initiatives in ASEAN. He added: “As our activities grow, we will continue to build the capabilities we need in Singapore in a thoughtful and sustainable way. “We see its value not only in scale and number of employees, but also in the quality of its regional responsibilities and contribution to patient access across ASEAN.

events.title: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
events.summary: We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.” “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.” Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return .) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here . Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days. Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned. But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia. And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all. Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about. But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive. So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key. Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out. Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago. And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly. But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more. Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind. I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America. I mean, there’s two sides of this coin.
