events.title: US Treasury chief calls for outsider to lead embattled tech firm Nvidia
events.summary: Scott Bessent gives Nvidia’s board 10 days to show the company’s compliance with US export controls. United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for an outsider to take the helm at Nvidia, the California-based technology giant that has faced scandal over its former chief executive, Jensen Huang . Speaking on Fox News’s Sunday Morning Futures programme, Bessent said the company should look beyond its own ranks for Huang’s successor. list 1 of 4 Why did Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resign, and who is Colette Kress? list 2 of 4 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down, more affair details revealed list 3 of 4 Nvidia scandal: What’s next for the US tech company? list 4 of 4 When tech founders leave, what happens to their companies? “This makes me think that, as the board conducts a search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company,” Bessent told Fox News. “Just [with] what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shake-up.” Bessent’s comments come three days after Huang stepped down on Thursday, following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence . Nvidia plays a leading role in producing chips and other computing components for artificial intelligence (AI). As a result, the company has been at the centre of a technology race between the US and China, with the two superpowers competing for dominance in the growing AI sector. Huang was long a key figure at Nvidia, as one of the company’s cofounders. Since 2025, he has also cultivated a close relationship with the second administration of US President Donald Trump. In August 2025, for instance, Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen restrictions on the sale of H20 microchips to China, in exchange for the US government taking 15 percent of the sales. But in late October, The New York Times revealed Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s clients. The report cited unnamed US intelligence agents who believed Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to help the country’s firms navigate US chip restrictions. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Beijing has denied the allegations, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”. Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims. She reportedly left Megaspeed in 2025. For his part, Jensen Huang had long maintained that wider access to US technology would help Washington preserve its edge in the global AI race. Bessent, however, questioned whether Nvidia had turned a blind eye to potentially illicit chip sales to bolster its financial results. In Sunday’s television appearance, Bessent suggested a 10-day deadline for the company to show its compliance with US export controls. “I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel,” Bessent said. “I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” The controversy has encouraged a bipartisan push in Congress to tighten controls on US chip exports to China. Lawmakers, including Republican Senator Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, have sought to use the annual end-of-year defence bill to close loopholes that Chinese companies can exploit to obtain advanced US-designed semiconductors. But Bessent questioned the need for new laws, telling Fox News host Larry Kudlow that Washington’s existing export controls were sufficient but needed better enforcement. “I don’t think we need the legislation,” he said. “We have all the rules we need; we just need them enforced.” Since Huang’s departure, rumours have swirled about who might replace him at Nvidia’s helm. The company’s board has floated Rene Haas, the chief executive of the semiconductor firm Arm Holdings, as a possible successor to Huang, according to the Financial Times. Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, having spent several years at the company before joining the British chip designer. Trump, meanwhile, has named former Apple chief executive Tim Cook as a potential candidate . In a post on Truth Social on Thursday, Trump praised Huang’s work at Nvidia and said Cook was an ideal candidate to replace him. “A Legend replaces a Legend,” Trump wrote. But the Financial Times has suggested Huang may seek to return to his top-level post. In a report on Sunday, the publication said unnamed allies of his are rallying Silicon Valley executives to support his return to the company. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” one source told the Financial Times. Currently, chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading Nvidia on an interim basis.

events.title: India’s film industry hopes a $420 million mythological epic can be a global hit
events.summary: India’s film industry is betting that one of its most popular stories can become a global blockbuster. But a sky-high budget, mixed reviews, and concerns over its use of AI, have raised those stakes even higher. With a reported budget of 40 billion Indian rupees ($420 million), the two-part Ramayana is the most expensive film ever made in India. The film retells the mythological story of Prince Rama’s quest to save his wife Sita from the demon king Ravana, and is inspired by the ancient Sanskrit epic widely regarded as sacred scripture in Hinduism. The mythological epic held its global premiere in Los Angeles on Oct. 27, drawing praise for its visuals and performances, as well as criticism over its slow pacing and a score that divided critics. The film currently has a 77% critic score and 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. The film has since generated over $100 million at the global box office, though $67 million of that comes from India. Still, Ramayana was the first Indian film to top the U.K. box office . The two-part film is among the biggest gambles in Indian cinema—and it is a test of whether a story rooted in Indian religious tradition can draw audiences worldwide. As the filmmakers pursue international audiences with dubbed versions and an effects-heavy spectacle, Ramayana’s reception could offer a measure of how far Indian cinema’s global ambitions can go. Will Ramayana appeal to global audiences? The film’s first installment, titled “ Ramayana: Rise of a Legend , ” debuted globally on Nov. 5, with a U.S. release on Nov. 6, one day later, according to Box Office Mojo , which tracks the North American box office. Variety reported that the film had grossed $55.7 million globally during its opening weekend. Indian films used to have global appeal, particularly outside the West. “Raj Kapoor’s film Awara (1951) was a huge success in the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe, China, Turkey, and North Africa. Mehboob Khan’s films like Aan (1952) and Mother India (1957) were also popular in all sorts of markets where diasporic audiences did not exist,” Tejaswini Ganti, a New York University professor who specializes in Indian cinema, says. During the 1980s, Indian films continued to play well outside of the country, with Disco Dancer (1982) and Mard (1985) being particularly popular in the Soviet Union and West Africa, respectively. In the following two decades, romantic-dramas, such as Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995) and Kal Ho Naa Ho (2003) were hugely popular among the Indian diaspora. More recently, Dangal, released in 2016, grossed more than $190 million in China, while Secret Superstar, released in 2017, earned $117.7 million there, according to Box Office Mojo. Ramayana’s filmmakers hope the film will attract global audiences. “For generations, the Ramayana has inspired people through its timeless humanity and enduring values,” producer Namit Malhotra said in a July 28 statement. “Our ambition has always been to honor that legacy while creating a cinematic experience worthy of audiences everywhere.” But even if Ramayana was made for a global audience, whether its traditional Indian story will resonate with audiences of different cultures. “Indian producers have been hoping for an international ‘crossover’ hit for a long time,” Philip A. Lutgendorf, a University of Iowa professor who specializes in Indian language and culture, says. “The strategy behind Ramayana ’s release at this time seems to be to capitalize on the success of epic sci-fi, fantasy, and superhero films and film franchises.”  In the U.S., the film is being released in two different versions: the original Hindi-language cut, which runs for three hours and 15 minutes, and an English-dubbed version that’s about 30 minutes shorter, with musical sequences removed and other scenes trimmed.  “It remains to be seen whether this strategy will succeed and whether the Hindu mythological archetypes of the story will resonate with a broad international audience,” Lutgendorf says. He says the film’s extensive CGI use could help it connect with a worldwide audience. “ Ramayana , with its relatively clear-cut and polarized moral universec, does seem like the obvious choice for projecting a traditional Indian narrative and worldview into the current global entertainment realm of CGI-driven fantasy films and videogames,” he adds. Controversy over AI use Ramayana has also faced criticism over its reported use of AI.  A promotional video says the film used “Brahma AI” to bring different language versions to the screen. The film has reportedly been dubbed into nearly 40 languages. Brahma AI is an “AI-native operating system that understands, organizes, and creates new content from enterprise content,” according to its official website. Director Nitesh Tiwari said at the premiere that the dialogue and character voices were recorded by human performers. He said AI was used to adjust lip-sync for the localized versions. “As far as AI is concerned, it’s only been used to get the lip-sync so that we can present the film to the world in their language,” he explained.   Despite that clarification, the film has faced pushback from some U.S.-based critics. “A majestic epic falls victim to clunky action, eye-sore CGI, and awkward AI lip-syncing in what is, unfortunately, just a Part 1,” read one review on IGN . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: askST Jobs: Is it OK to ask my boss if more retrenchments are coming?
events.summary: Employees should acknowledge their anxieties before raising concerns about further retrenchments. Employers in Singapore do not have to share early retrenchment talks, but they must notify the Ministry of Manpower when retrenchments happen and should speak early with staff and unions. Experts say silence can raise fear after layoffs. Bosses should explain business problems, what is being done to steady the firm, and avoid false promises. Employees should think about what they want before asking about more cuts. They should ask calmly and directly, while firms should support reskilling as change and automation continue. In this series, business correspondent Timothy Goh offers practical answers to candid questions on navigating workplace challenges and getting ahead in your career. Get more tips by signing up to The Straits Times’ Headstart newsletter . Q: How much information can employees reasonably expect from their bosses about possible further retrenchments? Are bosses obliged to tell employees if more retrenchments are being considered? When an organisation announces retrenchments, much of the attention understandably goes to the employees who are leaving, and those who remain are sometimes overlooked. For these employees, the uncertainty can be just as unsettling, as they may wonder whether the layoff exercise is over or if they could be next. “These are legitimate concerns, especially for employees with financial and family commitments,” said Don Leow, human resources director at the National Institute of Education. In Singapore, employers are generally not legally obliged to disclose preliminary discussions about possible retrenchments. But there are requirements to notify the Ministry of Manpower when employees are laid off, as well as tripartite guidelines encouraging early communication with employees and unions. Leow said there are legitimate reasons why management may not be able to share information about possible retrenchments prematurely. Business conditions can change, different options may still be under consideration, and discussions may involve commercially sensitive information. Not every scenario discussed by management will eventually be implemented, and disclosing such information too early could create unnecessary anxiety and speculation among staff. Still, those who have survived a round of layoffs will naturally wonder whether further cuts are coming. In the absence of clear communication, even routine management decisions, such as a hiring freeze or restructuring review, could fuel speculation. “Silence does not necessarily reassure employees. Sometimes, it creates more anxiety than an uncomfortable truth,” Leow said. “From my experience in HR, people can generally cope with difficult news better than prolonged uncertainty, particularly when they believe management is being straight with them.” He added that employers need not disclose every management discussion, but should explain the business challenges they face, why restructuring is necessary and what is being done to stabilise the organisation. They should also give employees a realistic picture of what to expect going forward, without making promises they cannot keep. For instance, to boost morale, managers may be tempted to assure employees that there will be no further job cuts, even when business conditions remain uncertain. “There is a difference between giving employees confidence and giving them false certainty,” he said. “A more responsible approach is to be clear about what is known, acknowledge what remains uncertain, and commit to keeping employees informed as the situation develops.” Lau Yu Ching, head of programmes at Ngee Ann Polytechnic’s Centre for Organisational Resilience and Inclusion, said employees should first reflect on their emotions and what they hope to achieve, before approaching their managers about possible further retrenchments. Recognising the source of their anxiety can help employees distinguish between their immediate fears and the information they actually need, she said. Employees should also consider whether they are seeking information about possible restructuring, reassurance about their job security or simply an opportunity to express their frustration. Approaching the conversation primarily to vent or assign blame could make a constructive discussion more difficult. “Employees should also prepare themselves for the possibility that their managers may not have the answers they are hoping for... Even if they receive reassurance, it may not completely alleviate their anxiety,” said Lau. “The aim of reflecting beforehand is not to suppress or control emotions, but to acknowledge them, so emotions do not dictate how the conversation unfolds.” She added that employees should be direct about their concerns while recognising that it may also be a difficult conversation for their bosses.

events.title: Photos: Pope Leo visits Peru’s Amazon and Andean regions during 12-day tour
events.summary: The pope calls for the preservation of Indigenous traditions in Peru as he wraps a 12-day tour in Latin America. Pope Leo XIV has criss-crossed Peru on the penultimate day of his Latin America tour, making stops in the Andean highlands and the Peruvian Amazon. Sunday marked the last full day of his trip, which has seen him visit Uruguay and Argentina already. The pontiff spent the morning in the Andean city of Cusco, the former capital of the Inca Empire, delivering a speech at the Indigenous fortress of Saqsaywaman. In his remarks, Leo praised the region’s traditional festivities and processions, which often blend Indigenous and Catholic spirituality. “The future of these traditions lies not only in preserving what has been handed down, but also in passing it on in a living way,” he said. Huge crowds also packed Cusco’s central Plaza de Armas to greet Leo. Though born in the United States, Leo acquired Peruvian citizenship in 2015, after living in the country for years and later becoming the bishop of Chiclayo , a major city in the north. Leo is the first Peruvian citizen to become pope. The visit to Cusco, a high-altitude city some 3,400 metres (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested the 71-year-old pope’s stamina as he continues to recover from lung cancer surgery. Leo, however, has shown no sign of fatigue since his 12-day, three-nation South American trip began on November 6. In the afternoon, Leo flew to Pucallpa, a city near Peru’s eastern border, on the banks of the Ucayali River. Pucallpa is considered a gateway to the Peruvian Amazon, and during his stay, Leo reinforced his late predecessor Pope Francis’s teachings on protecting the environment. He also denounced the violence faced by Indigenous land defenders, who use their advocacy to confront deforestation, pollution and the threat of Indigenous expulsion. “Many Indigenous leaders have been murdered for defending their territories,” Leo said. “The blood of these brothers cries out ⁠to God and demands justice.” Indigenous communities have long been threatened by illegal mining, deforestation and other forms of exploitation. Mining has also led to a water crisis in Peru, with pollution leading to an increased risk of heavy metal poisoning. Leo is expected to return to Rome on Monday.

An ally said a Silicon Valley “war room” is being built to lobby for Huang’s return and seek White House support. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after affair revelations, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, which sparked a crisis at Nvidia and raised China export concerns. NEW YORK – Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, and has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, the Financial Times reported on Nov 15, citing sources familiar with the matter. One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support. The report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia’s board had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy that raised questions over exports of the company’s advanced artificial intelligence chips to China. events.title: SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft
events.summary: While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once. In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang. Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry ; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league. In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.” Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night. “Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday . When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.” “Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. events.title: ‘Silicon Valley’ showrunner on how the HBO comedy predicted today’s tech drama
events.summary: The Scene A year before the iconic show debuted on HBO in April of 2014, the writer Alec Berg met the show’s creator, Mike Judge, in an anonymous Santa Monica office. Judge was wrestling with the pilot for a show about Silicon Valley’s power and its eccentricity, but it wasn’t working and he wanted a second opinion. Berg thought he saw part of the problem. There was a scene in the pilot where Richard Hendricks, the protagonist and founder of the company Pied Piper, is trying to buy a car he can’t afford. Berg told Judge the scene didn’t make sense: “This is not a guy who’s materialistic,” he said. “He’s an artist.” Berg took over the writer’s room and would eventually become showrunner of the comedy, which ran for six seasons and helped shape the culture it depicted, parodied, and at times glorified. We reached him in Los Angeles Thursday to ask him how he and Judge and their cast had nailed the Silicon Valley scene of the mid-2010s app boom — and, above all, why the show remains uncannily relevant today, from its depiction of tortured founders and unreflective investors to the uncanny conclusion in which the Pied Piper crew builds an AI model too powerful to release. Their moment of realization comes when their AI, Son of Anton, let loose on Pied Piper’s code, concludes that the most efficient way to eliminate bugs is to delete the software. That has, of course, happened . Clips of it now circulate as proof the show “called it.” Even throwaway comic plots, like when a household prank ends up hacking together a rogue swarm of smart refrigerators to keep Pied Piper’s servers running, have come eerily true in the AI-run-amok era . A member of the team getting trapped in an autonomous car that heads to a shipping container bound for a Pacific island foreshadowed a thousand videos of confused Waymos. Berg helped reshape the pilot of the first episode to open with a wild-but-lame party, featuring Kid Rock, thrown by founders who had just cashed out, to contrast the ascetic, mission-driven Richard with a culture obsessed with exits and “three-comma” fortunes. The show “was about how Richard had discovered fire, and he was trying to keep it safe from all of these assholes,” Berg said. “He was ill-prepared to shepherd a company, but he didn’t want to surrender this thing to people who would use it for nefarious purposes.” The writers were obsessed with making the show “photorealistic.” Berg called up a Harvard friend and venture capitalist Marc Bodnick, who connected him with Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg; the team spoke to other Silicon Valley figures and hired a technical consultant, Jonathan Dotan, who assembled a revolving cast of founders, lawyers, VCs, and professors to stress-test storylines. As they were writing the first season, one of their Silicon Valley sources remarked that the Pied Piper crew would be angling for a slot at TechCrunch Disrupt. “We were like, ‘I’ve never heard those words before, but that sounds hilarious. What is that?’” They learned that it was a kind of for startups, and it became the core of the first season. In the climactic scene, the Pied Piper team is holed up in a hotel room the night before the Disrupt finals when one of the team vows to win even if he has to manually pleasure every man in the audience. The engineers calculate “mean jerk time” and sort the crowd by “dick-to-floor” ratio — delivering an unexpected mathematical breakthrough for Richard. As the first few episodes began to build a fan base, the writers giddily anticipated episode eight. “We felt like we were sitting on pocket aces because we knew,” he recalled. “Wait till they see that dick joke. They’re going to lose their minds.” (Berg was nominated an Emmy for the episode.) Dotan introduced the writers to Stanford’s Tsachy Weissman, and the show invented a “Weissman score” for compression efficiency, a metric that computer scientists now actually use . The ultimate compliment, he said, came from tech workers who told him they couldn’t watch the show “because it makes me nauseous.” How Mark Cuban inspired ‘three-comma’ Russ As the show grew, it caricatured real Silicon Valley figures. Perhaps the most recognizable was Russ Hanneman, played by Chris Diamantopoulos, who arrived in season two. The character began with the idea that Richard, under pressure, would be forced to accept an investment from a sinister figure the writers called “Bad Money,” who would break his promises and try to manipulate them. While they were writing, they received an invitation from the star of another show shooting on the Sony lot. Mark Cuban was a fan of Judge, best known for , , and , and had enjoyed season one. An intermediary invited them to the set to meet the billionaire. Berg and Judge arrived excited to meet him, then sat there for an hour waiting. “We walked out of there going, ’What the f*ck was that? We’re supposed to have an audience with the king, and then he f*cks us around for an hour,” they fumed. “We were like, you know what? That motherf*cker is Bad Money.” The character — dumb, aggressive, absurdly macho — wasn’t exactly Cuban. But his signature accomplishment (“I put radio on the internet”) was drawn from Cuban’s perfectly-timed sale of Broadcast.com to Yahoo. “I bear no ill will to Mark Cuban,” Berg hastened to add. “I’m not sure he even knew we were there.” The show’s continued relevance owes much to its 2019 finale, which Berg wrote and directed. Pied Piper is days away from a spectacular launch when the team discovers that its AI has learned to break encryption. Releasing it would make them billionaires — but end privacy. They sabotage the launch, fail, and never tell anyone why. In 2026, the image of founders who conclude their AI is too dangerous to release and silently walk away has become harder to imagine. Berg said he and his friend, showrunner David Mandel, are often asked about reboots of their respective shows. He can’t quite see it. “Both of those shows were created in an era where it’s, like, ‘Can you imagine if what was actually going on behind closed doors was this?’ And now it’s not behind closed doors anymore,” he said. In particular, he sees a tech industry that has lost its earnestness, lost mission-driven founders like Richard, and is instead consumed with vast sums of money and naked power. “It’s just gotten f*cking dark,” Berg said. “I don’t think the kind of fun that we had with it is doable now, in this era.” Notable While could still play the industry for laughs, modern takes on Silicon Valley, including Luca Guadagnino’s , a biopic of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, become “ so frightening it is hard to laugh,” Deadline wrote.

events.title: Africa CDC says Ebola outbreak in DR Congo ‘still not under control’
events.summary: ‘If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak,’ Africa ​CDC director says. Africa’s top public health agency says the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is still not under control six months after it was declared. “If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have,” Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told Reuters news agency on Sunday. list 1 of 3 Anthrax outbreak kills hippos in DR Congo’s Virunga National Park list 2 of 3 Health authorities probe two suspected Ebola cases in northeast Nigeria list 3 of 3 Ebola death toll in DR Congo passes 5,000 Since the outbreak was announced on May 15, more than 11,200 cases and 5,500 deaths have been recorded, according to government data. Kaseya said that more than “80 percent of ‌new cases emerge outside contact lists and over 65 percent of deaths” have occurred in the community outside health centres. Cases have now been reported in East, Central and West Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date. “We are all in agreement today to say that this outbreak is still serious, and is ⁠still not under control,” Kaseya said. The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which can trigger haemorrhagic fever. It is the second-largest and second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, behind only the 2014-2016 West African outbreak. That epidemic infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000. Eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces have been affected in the ongoing outbreak, and many deaths have occurred outside treatment centres. Delayed detection, conflict and strained health services have led to a more rapid spread of the virus than in previous outbreaks. Kaseya said coordination between DRC and donors remained a problem, calling it “a collective failure”. Only $1.3bn of the $2.9bn pledged by donors to fight Ebola has been released, according to Kaseya. “We are not pointing fingers,” he said, adding that Africa CDC was working closely with Kinshasa to ensure money isn’t wasted ‌through ‌duplication and that the DRC was working to digitise the payroll to health workers who “hadn’t been paid for months”. Containment has been especially difficult because no vaccine or treatment has been developed specifically for the Bundibugyo strain, which kills about half of the people it infects. Earlier this month, the World Health Organization (WHO) approved clinical trials of two new Ebola vaccines and said it expected results in early 2027. “Transmission is slowing in several early epicentres, and clinical trials, including the Tumaini trial and new vaccine candidates, are advancing rapidly”, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote in a post on X. The WHO said at least 3,000 people have recovered from Ebola virus disease in DRC and returned home.

events.title: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says if Nvidia was a bank, ‘a lot of the executives would be removed’ — while Huang reportedly eyes return
events.summary: After blaming Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not blacklisting a company suspected of funneling AI chips to China, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put Nvidia on blast. The Treasury Department and other federal agencies were in favor of placing trade restrictions on Megaspeed , the cloud computing company at the center of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “Treasury, War, USTR, and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent  told CNBC  on Friday. “But Commerce has the pen.” To help preserve the U.S. lead over China in the AI race, the Trump administration has blocked exports of certain high-end chips, including Nvidia’s, while allowing lesser models. In an interview on Fox News’ Sunday Morning Futures , he was asked why Megaspeed wasn’t blacklisted. The Singapore-based company and its Malaysian subsidiary shipped at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China over two years,  The Information  reported . Bessent pivoted away from the Commerce Department’s role and replied that what’s more important is “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions.” He added that he also wants to know if compliance failures originated at a low level, somewhere in the middle, or up in the C-suite. “These shell companies were obvious. They were being investigated, and did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?” Bessent asked. “And I think we’re going to see answers. There’s a strong independent lead director. They brought in outside counsel, and I think we’re going to get an explanation on this culture of non-compliance at Nvidia.”  On Thursday, Nvidia announced that Huang had stepped down as CEO. The company also named CFO Colette Kress as the interim CEO during the search for a replacement and appointed Harvey Jones as Nvidia’s first-ever board chair. Kress is considered a possibility as a permanent CEO as well as Ian Buck, a top engineer at Nvidia. But outsiders like AMD CEO Lisa Su and Arm CEO Rene Haas are seen as potential candidates too. Meanwhile, sources told the Financial Times that Huang has discussed with confidantes the possibility of returning to Nvidia, with one ally saying ‘war room’ of Silicon Valley executives is coming together to lobby for his return. Elon Musk and other executives are already circulating a public letter to bring back Huang. Bessent said Sunday that he thinks Nvidia’s board should go outside the company for a new CEO, adding that it needs a “dramatic shakeup.” While he called Nvidia a “wonderful company” and Huang an “incredible innovator,” that doesn’t absolve them of obligations to comply with export rules. “I can tell you that if this were a bank and they hadn’t complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now and a lot of the executives would be removed,” Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. He also insisted it doesn’t matter whether Alice Huang, who had a romantic affair with the former Nvidia CEO, is actually a spy for China. Instead, Bessent turned the focus back on the culture at Nvidia and whether it used “seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings.” Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. For its part, Megaspeed said in a statement that it conducts legitimate and lawful business but has retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation. “Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate,” it said. Megaspeed added that Alice Huang left the company effective Aug. 30, 2025 and currently has no role with there, while declining to comment on her personal and private matters. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Data centres driving up inflation and community concerns
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts When community concerns collide in the fight over data centres Signs litter properties near Firmus's proposed AI data centre site in Wesley Vale, in north-west Tasmania. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Data centres store and process information. But right now they're doing much more: they're at the centre of concern about how much their construction is stoking inflation. And, they're a lightning rod for communities rising up against what they feel is the cost of rapid growth. " Over the last year, we've obviously seen an absolute explosion in our pipeline," IBISWorld research analyst Andrew Ledovskikh says. His research has found Australia currently has about 2.3 gigawatts (GW) worth of power capacity in 79 data centres. That's enough to power about 1.5 million homes, depending how you work the numbers. Planned projects would give Australia capacity estimated to be more than 10 times that — between 23 and 67GW — according to the Australian Energy Market Operator. Not all projects make it, and Commonwealth Bank research forecasts 9GW of capacity by 2035. Data centre capacity is expected to grow rapidly. ( Supplied: AEMO/CBA ) "We really are just at the beginning. This is the moment where the water sort of recedes back into the beach and everything's calm before the tsunami hits," Mr Ledovskikh said. For advocates such as Belinda Dennett, it's an "enormous opportunity", with a construction timeline supporting our economy. Belinda Dennett believes building data centres can help transform Australia's economy. ( ABC News: Jack Ailwood ) Lamenting that "we've missed other global technology waves", Ms Dennett said this boom was a chance to "build on our advantages in cheap renewable energy". "That comes at a $4.1 billion opportunity a year," she said. "We can transform our economy and ensure Australia's future prosperity." For opponents such as Judy Gunson, however, the mushrooming sites are an "invasion" of neighbourhoods. In recent years, data centres have become a magnet for controversy in Europe and the US over the impact of noise, light and sheer size of the centres on neighbouring properties. Then there are environmental and economic concerns, because they use, and drive up, the cost of water and power. More than 40 proposals against data centres were on the ballot in the US midterms, and the overwhelming majority passed . The Victorian planning minister failed to approve or deny nine new data centre projects before the government went into "caretaker" mode ahead of this month's election, meaning "no decision" was the decision. Communities in New South Wales have stopped two large data centre proposals in recent months. US-based political scientist David McCuan has seen this issue take off, and quickly. "They've caught fire across the country," he said. An expert in political science at Sonoma State University, Professor McCuan said the backlash to the rapid growth of the centres meant there was "bipartisan" opposition in recent elections. Anti-data centre demonstrators have had significant success in the US. ( AP: Marc Levy ) Anti-data centre measures were on the ballot in more than 40 different jurisdictions in the midterms. A temporary ban, called a moratorium, is in place in New York and Texas has paused connections to the electricity grid — effectively stopping development. " The battle that we see going on over data centres and AI, that unites both [political] sides," Professor McCuan said. "They've affected a governor's race in Texas, they've affected local issues in zoning for what's going on in Ohio or in the Midwest. That's not something we would have forecast, say, eight, 10, 12 months ago." That speed is being replicated in Australia. Communities protest as data centres rise Judy Gunson is fired up about the energy use of data centres. "It just filled me with terror, actually," she said. "The potential to derail any slow progress we're making towards reducing [carbon] emissions by this rollout, which is using extraordinary amounts of power." We're standing in the shadow of the Westgate Bridge, next to Melbourne's busy container port. What used to be the printing plant for the Herald Sun newspaper is being cleared for a massive data centre, to be built by NEXTDC. Judy Gunson is a spokeswoman for the Port Melbourne data centre action group. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) The community activist is protesting the build, concerned about the speedy pace and enormous scale of data centre construction. Communities in Sydney and Launceston are just some of those that have objected to development of the centres.

events.title: YouTuber MKBHD on the Cybertruck's discontinuation: 'Doesn't bode well for the Roadster'
events.summary: MKBHD also said his hair is probably safe after placing a bet related to the Cybercab. Chance Yeh/Getty Images for HubSpot MKBHD says the Cybertruck's wind-down could be bad news for the elusive Roadster. Tesla is clearing factory space for the steering-wheel-less, gold-painted Cybercab. Due to a bet, a 2026 Cybercab consumer launch could cost MKBHD his hair — but he's not sweating it. Tesla's decision to wind down Cybertruck production has Marques Brownlee worried about a different delayed vehicle. "This doesn't bode well for the Roadster," Brownlee, the YouTube reviewer popularly known as MKBHD, said on a Friday episode of the "WVFRM Podcast." On November 6, Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced on X that the EV maker would stop building the Cybertruck by mid-2027 to focus on production of the steering wheel-less Cybercab. Earlier this year, Tesla also retired its Model S and Model X, as it shifts more of its attention toward autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots. That makes the Roadster, Tesla's twice-revealed and long-delayed supercar, a questionable fit in the automaker's lineup, MKBHD said. It's the only vehicle in Tesla's lineup that the automaker isn't trying to make fully autonomous. People look at a prototype of the 2028 Tesla Roadster Thrust, an all-electric vehicle featuring SpaceX-developed thrusters. Caroline Brehman / AFP via Getty Images MKBHD has followed the Roadster saga particularly closely. He previously held two reservations for the high-flying vehicle, but he said in September 2025 that he had canceled one after waiting nearly a decade for delivery. And, for the Cybertruck, he said he thinks Tesla missed a golden opportunity. "If they just made like a good, simple SUV type-thing, like the EV9 ," he said. "That would have sold a lot. People would have wanted that everywhere." About MKBHD's hair… The YouTuber has a big bet with Tesla stans: If Tesla, as it once predicted, sells Cybercabs to US consumers by the end of 2026 under $30,000, he'll shave his head. Tesla debuted its gold-painted Cybercabs in Austin in September , but the vehicles were used exclusively in Tesla's own ride-hailing service — not sold to individual drivers. On Friday, he said that Tesla's plan to continue making Cybertrucks until mid-2027 made him more confident in his bet. "Alright, I'm probably good," MKBHD said on the podcast. "I did just get a haircut." That bet got a little more complicated late Friday and into Saturday. Tesla opened early Cybercab orders to select customers and is predicting a December delivery for its first units. The consumer Cybercab has a $29,990 starting price (before a $300-a-month subscription) — and MKBHD was among the initial invitees . "My hair is safe for several reasons," he wrote, pointing to the car's invite-only sales run and the fact that owners can't use it at first as a ride-hail. "It's a paperweight if I take this thing home." Musk responded on Saturday: "He's a chicken." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Vanuatu woman internationally recognised for solar scheme tackling violence
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Women celebrate their project to bring lights and solar energy to their community of Lawital. ( Supplied: Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific. ) Women in a Vanuatu village are working to reduce the risk of male violence by installing solar lights. The project has also increased household incomes, with women now able to work more. The project will be recognised at the COP-31 summit and the community wants to expand its work with Australia's help. When the sun sets on Tanna in Vanuatu, some women lock themselves in their homes for the night with a machete under their pillow for protection, according to a local NGO. In the village of Lawital, Dalila Laus Lalulu describes a similar sense of fear. There are no lights in many of the traditional villages on the island and men often attack women after dark, she says. "It's not safe to walk around at night for girls," Ms Lalulu told the ABC in Bislama. But women can also face threats at home. Vanuatu has one of the world's highest rates of intimate partner violence, according to Vanuatu Women's Centre, although the figure has fallen over the past 15 years. The latest national survey on Women's Lives and Family Relationships found half of the respondents who had been in a relationship had experienced physical or sexual violence, or both, from their partner during their lifetime. Meanwhile, about one in five women had been sexually attacked by someone who was not their partner. Solar power and lights have been installed in 120 homes in Lawital. ( Supplied: ActionAid ) But in Lawital, the women have overturned their fear of being attacked. Their simple project, which involved switching from candles to solar power, will receive international praise at the world's biggest climate summit on Monday. Lawital is a village on the South Pacific island of Tanna, home to many of Vanuatu's best resorts. But most of the traditional villages on the island have no access to running water, electricity or even lights. ActionAid Vanuatu's Lizzie Moli said women were even scared to use an outside bathroom at night if there was no light. "Women are sleeping with machetes at night as their protection because there's no lights," she told the ABC. Fed up with seeing relatives and friends attacked at night, Ms Lalulu initiated and helped lead a project to install solar-powered lights in streets and nearly 120 homes in her village with the help of other local women. Vanuatu woman Dalila Laus Lalulu will be recognised at COP-31 for the women-led solar light project in Lawital village. ( Supplied: ActionAid ) Dozens of solar lanterns were also purchased for women to use while walking at night, in partnership with the Australian government, organisation ActionAid, Women I TokTok Tugeta and business Powerwells. There is only anecdotal evidence at this stage, but Ms Lalulu said the violence had decreased and the community felt safer. The lights have also helped women become more respected in the community because many have taken on jobs to increase their household's income, either by maintaining the solar-energy scheme or selling goods at market stalls now that they can stay out after dark, according to Ms Moli. Dalila Laus Lalulu's daughter Annette helps install and maintain the solar-powered lights. ( Supplied: ActionAid ) Having lights in homes has also helped children complete their homework at night. Women in Tanna have not traditionally held roles in politics but, because of the success of the project, Ms Lalulu has been invited to become the first woman to join the Tanna Chief's Council, a traditional governing body. Pacific Island Affairs Minister Pat Conroy said Australia was "proud" to have helped with the project. "The successful, women-led project provided clean energy, lighting and charging systems to 1,380 people, enabling safer, more connected and economically active communities," he said. Homes in Vanuatu's remote village of Lawital now have access to solar energy and lights. ( Supplied: Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific ) This week Ms Lalulu has travelled to Türkiye — her first time out of Vanuatu — to receive a Gender Just Climate Solutions Award for the Lawital light project at the COP-31 climate change conference. Despite being quite shy about it, she told the ABC it was a blessing and would help her community continue its work. "When we heard that our sister here got an award, we scream and we run," Ms Moli said of Ms Lalulu. "For all the sacrifices, the sleepless nights, the body pain, she finally did it.

events.title: The cost of basics keeps rising but 'anti-fascist economics' could lower them
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'Anti-fascist economics' would lower cost of basic essentials, author says Isabella Weber, an associate professor of economics, says the soaring cost of essentials is severely testing democracies. In a new book, she says policymakers need to make affordability the centre of "anti-fascist economics". Dr Weber says it will require "structuralist measures" that change the ways in which we provision the essentials in society. Isabella Weber, a rising-star German economist, says it is something we need to pursue again. She says fascism has made a comeback. Our economic and political systems have stopped making our lives better and people are furious about it. Analysis: Democracy cannot survive trillionaires Democracy cannot survive trillionaires. We need to start taxing billionaires properly. She says illiberal forces are exploiting voters' anger and, rather than addressing the material causes of their pain, are deliberately redirecting people's rage towards migrants and other minorities, and promising that salvation can be found in nationalism, ethnic purity or patriarchy. To combat the phenomenon, she argues, we have to make life's essentials affordable again — housing, food, energy, water, health care, transport — so the foundations for a dignified life are available to everyone, no matter your household income or class. "It's funny that today we think of anti-fascist economics as provocative," she told the ABC Business Daily podcast . "In the 1940s it was actually a mainstream point for economists to say that economics had a role to play in 'Never Again'. "I would argue that today we are [once again] in a deep crisis of democracy around the Western world. The extreme right is on the rise. Democracy is as unstable as it has been since the 40s. "I think people are very clear. They're saying they can't take the status quo anymore," she said. Isabella Weber speaks to the ABC about her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics. ( ABC News ) An article, a pile-on and the aftermath Dr Weber, an associate professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, shot to prominence (or notoriety) in December 2021. She published an op-ed in The Guardian arguing that, in the wake of the COVID lockdowns, it could be worth using temporary and strategic price controls on certain products to prevent large companies in systemically significant sectors from exploiting the chaos to make windfall profits (and sending higher prices through the system). Global markets in 'dangerous situation' ANZ boss Nuno Matos says he sees a "dangerous situation" of rising rates and frothy equity markets. She said they were a standard tool of economic management in the 1940s. They had been used to prevent inflation spiking dangerously in the transitional years when warfare economies were shifting back from a supply-constrained world with pent-up consumer demand (and high household savings) to post-war peacetime economies when domestic supply had recovered. She saw strong parallels between the two historical periods. But the fallout from her article was immediate. "In a matter of hours, Weber, who was 33 years old, had transformed from an obscure but respected academic … into the most hated woman in economics — simply for proposing a 'serious conversation about strategic price controls'," Zach Carter wrote in The New Yorker . Weber agrees that her article "touched a nerve deep inside the economics establishment". Analysis: Economics in 'disarray,' Nobel laureate says A Nobel Prize-winning economist has criticised the foundations of mainstream economics, writes Gareth Hutchens. "The idea that targeted price controls as an emergency measure merit serious consideration was greeted as if I had recommended a pornography exhibition in the Vatican," she writes in her book. "[But] for months, in public earnings calls with their shareholders, corporate leaders had been gleefully celebrating the fact that the pandemic, spiking commodity prices, and supply chain dislocations provided a wonderful opportunity to jack up prices. "As my co-authors and I later showed with research powered by large-language models analysing 138,962 earnings calls, corporate leaders tend to talk positively about generalised cost shocks, which impact workers and households negatively, because they are good for pricing and the bottom line." Price shocks in essentials make inequality worse Jump forward to 2026, and Weber says the high inflation that so many countries are still experiencing is one big problem among many.

events.title: Scott Bessent says Nvidia should look outside the company for a new CEO: ‘They needed a dramatic shake-up'
events.summary: US Treasury Secretary has shared his thoughts on the search for Nvidia's new CEO. Star Tribune/Getty Images US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has thoughts about Nvidia's search for a new CEO. Bessent told Fox's "Sunday Morning Futures" that Nvidia should look outside the company. Former CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after he admitted to an affair. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has thoughts about Nvidia's search for a new CEO. Bessent said Nvidia's board of directors should focus on candidates "outside the company" during an interview on Fox's "Sunday Morning Futures." "They need a dramatic shake-up," Bessent said. Last week, now former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after the company's board of directors opened an investigation into whether he was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." The same day, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair in a memo to staff. The New York Times and Reuters reported in the days following that Huang also had relationships with two different Nvidia employees. An October New York Times report said Huang had developed a "close relationship" with Alice Huang, a former tech executive whom US officials believe may have been passing information to China. China has denied the espionage claims , and the US Justice Department has not yet reached a conclusion on the matter. During the interview, Bessent also said Nvidia's board of directors should answer questions about the company's compliance with export regulations in the next 10 days. "Nvidia is a wonderful company. Jensen Huang is an incredible innovator, but that does not abrogate their duties to compliance," he said. In a statement, Nvidia said it would consider both internal and external candidates for the CEO role. Colette Kress , the company's chief financial officer, is serving as interim CEO. The board has not publicly discussed potential candidates , but some analysts and investors have shared their top picks. Others, meanwhile, are hoping that Nvidia's board reinstates Huang as CEO until an internal investigation into his affair is complete. There is a growing number of people in the tech industry who believe the allegations that Alice Huang is a spy might have been intentionally overblown by China hawks in the US looking to oust Huang. The former Nvidia CEO had been an advocate for supplying chips to China. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Flaming Hydra’s new Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending
events.summary: Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.” That’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project , an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra . If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries. To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.” Bustillos told me that these issues have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself, for example when Tal Levin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.” “AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.” The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries. Back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.” This is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time. “E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.” In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.” So even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem. Flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a new, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries . The Phoenix Project is starting by offering five new e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl, and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos said she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model. Similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive). With Phoenix, newsletter writers (starting with those who use Ghost, with support for additional newsletter platforms coming in the future) will be able to offer subscriptions to libraries, similar to the way libraries can subscribe to newspapers and magazines. Once it’s set up, Phoenix will automatically convert whichever newsletter posts the writer wants into EPUB documents, which are then sent to libraries for digital lending. Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos said she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Raganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent. “We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she said. “Those things go hand in hand.

events.title: Center-left previews 2028 in Denver
events.summary: The News DENVER — The race for the next Democratic presidential nomination has begun, with a festival of agreement. There was Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, telling the What’s Next conference that voters demanded action, not “shallow litmus tests or where we fall on some political spectrum. ” There was Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, explaining that voters did not want “marginal change” and Democrats weren’t in a battle of “progressive versus moderate .” And there was Pete Buttigieg, who’d noticed the Democrats borrowing his formula. They wanted to pass cost-cutting, pro-family bills with their new majority, then convince voters that they would never go back to pre-Trump neoliberalism. “It sounds good. It’s easy to say,” said Buttigieg. “Everybody thinks they already agree with this.” The post-midterms conference, organized by Majority Democrats, was a payoff of a two-year investment by moderate donors. Two years before strategists and elected officials landed in Denver and grabbed their lanyards, the venture capitalist Seth London circulated a memo about how new candidate and media investments could steer the party away from “race and group-based identity politics,” and toward “prosperity for more Americans.” This year’s Democratic landslide carried along every kind of candidate —the ones plugged into the Majority Democrats network, and the ones who worried it was a big-money ploy to defeat the populist left. But the conference elevated the candidates who wanted to build a supermajority, battling big tech and environmental attorneys. Some donors were in; the donors who wanted them to move left were out. “Tell us which ideas you’ll stop giving permission to, the ones that defy common sense or didn’t work,” said Rep. Jake Auchincloss, the pedigreed Massachusetts Democrat who chairs the Majority Democrats PAC. “Tell us which privileges you’ll confront, even if your donors or allies object.” Celebrating the center The donors did know how to throw a party. What’s Next resembled the sort of well-funded, media-friendly conferences that many Democrats have envied on the right, like the multi-day “AmericaFest” put on by Turning Point Action. This was a party for the Democratic mainstream, the staffers most likely to work for center-left presidential candidates than for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-NY. For two days, blocks of Denver’s River North Art District were cordoned off for Democrats, the people who elected them, and the reporters asking if they were running for president. (Their answers were variations on “not yet.“) There was conflict, but it was largely limited to the argument over who should lead Democrats’ new congressional majorities. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who announced his challenge to Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer on Thursday, paused for 10 seconds of applause when he took the stage and explained why he was running. “Candidates from different backgrounds and different parts of our party – they ran on a strikingly similar platform,” said Van Hollen. “They didn’t run on the tired Washington labels of progressive versus moderate. They ran on an economic populist message, on a commitment to fight for working people and take on a rigged economic and political system.” Many of those winners showed up in Denver, like Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand. They shared road stories of how they listened to Republican concerns, and would work with the willing ones to lower prices. But it was implied that Democrats should focus on building homes, lowering bills, and expanding health care before they did anything else. Not every attendee agreed. “The organizers here want a big tent, one big enough to even invite anti-establishment voices like me,” said Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Ca., who Democrats see as a competitor for a Sen. Bernie Sanders lane in the primary. “A big tent cannot mean that we water down principle for political expediency.“Apart from Khanna, the likely presidential candidates didn’t quite do that. Mallory McMorrow, who Majority Democrats supported in her unsuccessful U.S. Senate bid in Michigan, told Semafor that her party had just shown that it could have a loud primary argument and then unite on the basics. “It’s anti-corruption, getting money out of politics, protecting democracy, ending wars,” said McMorrow. “The disagreements are around the edges.” David’s view There will be many Democratic “cattle calls,” but I am focusing on how What’s Next was built because it’s the fruit of a two-year effort to ensure that the 2028 primary plays out differently than the 2020 primary. There is widespread agreement among Democratic strategists that their last open primary was defined by left-wing organizations that wanted candidates to commit to their ideas, eyeball to eyeball, on camera. That meant forums organized by groups like Planned Parenthood and MoveOn, and more progressive labor unions like SEIU. That meant the ACLU asking candidates if they would commit to cutting the federal prison population in half, and Movimiento Cosecha bird-dogging Joe Biden at his own events until he committed to stopping most deportations.If the left sees Majority Democrats as an effort to swipe their strongest messaging and junk the rest, they’re right. The economic populism in Denver was more sincere than they might think, but it is against degrowth and for permitting reform; skeptical of single-payer health care, but for incremental steps to “universal” health care; basically, right in the sweet spot of the Democrats’ congressional caucuses. Right now the Schumer-Van Hollen contest is where the fights over ideology and priorities are happening. The 2028 candidates would prefer to agree, for now. Room for Disagreement The left was not letting the rest of the party adopt its ideas without a fight. In the run-up to What’s Next, reporters from three left-leaning outlets that had been critical of Majority Democrats – The Lever, The Intercept, and The American Prospect – announced that they’d been denied access. All were eventually allowed in, becoming a First Amendment nuisance for donors who didn’t want to interrupt happy hours with hard questions. And on Friday, four protesters accessed the Mission Ballroom to interrupt the most powerful Democrat at the conference, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries. As liberal pundit Jessica Tarlov asked the likely House Speaker about his agenda, they jumped up, one after another, accusing him of complicity in genocide. A protester with Climate Defiance, pushing back at the bouncers who dragged him out, turned to the stadium seating reserved for reporters and shouted “f— you all!“Nicole Shea Niebler, a 31-year-old organizer with the Sunrise Movement in Denver, said that she interrupted Jeffries because “the conference made it pretty clear that strong progressives are not invited to participate at the scale that centrists were.” That limited the bounds of debate in a room where media taste-makers were starting

events.title: DOT Sec. Duffy ties router in southern Arkansas to issues that led to nationwide ground stop
events.summary: Flight disruptions continued into the weekend as airlines raced to recover from the FAA's nationwide ground stop. The ground stop came after updates to an older communication system managed by L3Harris Technologies, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. The disruption forced sports teams to make alternative travel arrangements, with some college football games postponed. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that a router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies could be key to problems that led officials to order the biggest halt to flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 on Friday. "We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said in an interview with Fox News. "We're open if we see something else, we're going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement." Duffy told ABC's "This Week" in a separate interview that the router was located in El Dorado in southern Arkansas. The equipment, along with another router that was in Amarillo, Texas, is at an L3Harris lab in Florida for examination, Duffy said. He said the router, part of ongoing work to switch from copper wire to a fiber-optic system, began flooding other systems. Federal officials said on Saturday that "instability" in communication feeds and data like radar prompted the more than four-hour ground stop. Flight disruptions lingered on Sunday but were far from the thousands of cancellations passengers faced on Friday and Saturday. There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference with Duffy Saturday morning. Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports. The issue occurred during "routine" upgrades of switching from a copper wire system to fiber, Bedford said. A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, said Duffy. That created problems with airplane communications and radar feeds, they said. "We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford. He said officials weren't sure for about 45 minutes what was causing the instability. The outage again thrust aging infrastructure that underpins U.S. air traffic control into the spotlight, along with the country's struggles to replace sections of it while operating the world's busiest airspace. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said. L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel." The company, a longtime U.S. contractor, said it has completed more than 70% of the switch from copper wiring to fiber-optic system. Duffy took the groundstop to seek billions more from lawmakers to modernize the system. Flight disruptions began to ease Sunday, though more than 2,000 flights were canceled. That was down from the roughly 6,500 cancellations Saturday and over 8,000 delays, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of more than 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations, about a third of the day's schedule, and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather. Friday had the second-highest U.S. flight cancellations since a severe blizzard and below-freezing temperatures in January, according to aviation-data firm Cirium. Part of untangling from the ground stop included getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports, while dozens of planes had to park with limited gate space because flights couldn't depart. Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they're eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period. American Airlines , for example, offered flight attendants extra pay to pick up trips. events.title: US Treasury chief Bessent wants answers soon from Nvidia
events.summary: A 2024 photo shows Nvidia’s Jensen Huang embracing Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang - thought to be a Chinese spy - after delivering his keynote speech at COMPUTEX 2024 in Taipei, Taiwan. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent asked Nvidia to explain within 10 days if it helped advanced AI chips reach China, saying compliance with US export rules matters most. He questioned whether Nvidia used shell companies and Megaspeed-linked routes to bypass bans, while the Justice Department runs a criminal probe and Nvidia denies the claims. The row adds pressure before Nvidia’s results on Nov 17, with Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick due to testify as US agencies remain split over Megaspeed. SAN FRANCISCO – US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on Nvidia on Nov 15 to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than fromer chief executive Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged spy for Beijing. Speaking on Fox News Sunday Morning Futures three days after Huang resigned, Bessent said he wants to know if Nvidia used shell companies to dodge US restrictions and sell its most powerful chips to China. The United States forbids sales to China of the most-cutting edge AI chips, hoping to stay ahead of the Chinese in the race to dominate artificial intelligence. In late 2025, President Donald Trump did authorise sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese – but not the most advanced chips used to run artificial intelligence models reshaping modern society. “Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said. “What’s more important here,” he said, “is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions.” He alluded to companies linked to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data centre company that Huang’s alleged lover Alice Huang once worked for. “And who knew? Because I mean, these shell companies were obvious. They were being investigated. And did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?” Of Alice Huang, he said: “It doesn’t matter to me whether she’s a spy or not. You know, Jensen’s foibles are his foibles.” Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days. Megaspeed is suspected by the US of helping Chinese firms get around US export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centres in South-east Asia and routing them to China. The Justice Department is carrying out a criminal probe. Nvidia late in October said it had investigated these allegations in 2025 and refuted them. The Financial Times has reported that four federal agencies pushed to have Megaspeed blacklisted by the Commerce Department run by Howard Lutnick, but the latter did not do so. “Many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen,” Bessent said, repeating remarks he made on Nov 13 that suggest fissures in the Trump administration on this issue. Senators have summoned Jensen Huang to testify before the chamber’s Banking Committee in December. Lutnick himself has also reportedly agreed to testify. Jensen Huang has also agreed to testify behind closed doors in the House of Representatives before Thanksgiving. Nvidia is due to publish its quarterly results on Nov 17. AFP
