events.title: Bessent calls for ‘dramatic shakeup’ at Nvidia, urges outside CEO
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a “dramatic shakeup” at Nvidia and urged its board to hire an outside CEO following Jensen Huang’s resignation. Bessent questioned whether Nvidia pursued potentially illicit chip sales to boost earnings and suggested other executives should face scrutiny. The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, both of whom are expected to accompany President Donald Trump to China this week. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings. Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls. "I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said in an interview on Fox News. The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump's handling of the matter. Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter. Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO. Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia's problems extended well beyond Huang. "If this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed," Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Bessent also questioned Nvidia's financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell. Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a new methodology based on customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling Bessent's remarks came two days after he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government's export blacklist for months. "But Commerce has the pen," Bessent said. The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce's failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place. Lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family's financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners. Cantor said Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said. There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information. Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia's H200 to China . Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut. Bessent's latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang's departure.

events.title: Under pressure, Lutnick joins Trump in China
events.summary: Howard Lutnick is expected to travel on Air Force One with the president to China this week as the commerce secretary fights to regain his footing after clashing with Trump officials over Nvidia and China chip controls, according to people familiar with the matter. President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Lutnick has become the target of Washington finger-pointing for slow-walking Commerce Department restrictions on certain AI chip exports to China, as well as his close relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week after admitting to an extramarital affair with an Nvidia customer suspected of being a Chinese spy, and media reports of two affairs with subordinates. The woman, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, which the US is investigating for improper chip smuggling into China. Republicans are accusing Lutnick of defying Trump — and warning his job could be on the line — after reports emerged that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials had pushed the commerce secretary to place the Nvidia customer, Megaspeed, on a blacklist of companies that pose national security concerns. Treasury “has been pushing for this for months” but Commerce “has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC last week. Bessent, who has directly criticized Lutnick’s handling of the matter, is also expected on the trip. A senior US official told reporters ahead of the China trip that the Nvidia scandal “should not really have any bearing on the trip.” “These are national security matters that we develop in the administration interagency process, and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there,” the official said. ‘Nine lives’ They have accused Lutnick of allowing the chipmaker to indirectly sell more advanced chips to China than previously known or allowed under US export control laws, through loopholes he has so far declined to close. He’s also been criticized for giving Nvidia unfettered access to rule-making that would impact the entire industry. The White House has said it “maintains complete confidence in the secretary.” Lutnick had been expected to attend Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World convening this week alongside OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Amazon’s Andy Jassy, and hundreds of other CEOs, but will instead be with the president. And while plans could still change, Lutnick’s inclusion in the trip signals that Trump wants to keep Lutnick around long enough to at least accompany the president to China for his visit with Xi. “This guy has nine lives,” a person close to the White House previously told Semafor. “How many does he have left?”

events.title: Transportation secretary still doesn’t totally rule out that a cyberattack may have hit the FAA, and the FBI is assisting the probe
events.summary: Air traffic is returning to normal after a nationwide ground stop on Friday, but the investigation into the root cause is just starting, and the federal government hasn’t dismissed the possibility of a cyberattack. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters Friday night it “doesn’t appear” that a cyberattack was involved though he admitted that “there’s nothing certain right now.”  Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expressed confidence Saturday that foul play wasn’t involved, and reiterated that message on the Sunday talk shows—but still qualified his statements. In an interview with ABC’s This Week , he said the director of national intelligence, the National Security Agency, the FBI, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency were all on a call together with “our intelligence partners” after the FAA’s communication problems emerged. They didn’t see any chatter or “footprints” that are normally associated with a cyberattack, he added. Instead, the FAA has zeroed in on a copper wire line that was being updated to a fiber-optic cable by contractor L3Harris. “We felt pretty comfortable that this was an internal network issue that’s owned and operated for us by L3 Harris, not an outside a factor,” Duffy said. “We feel pretty good still today that it is not a hacking event. But if the FBI comes in and says ‘no, we found something,’ obviously we’ll share that with the American people. But we have no indication that this was a hack.” In a briefing on Saturday, Duffy explained that the changeover to the fiber-optic cable caused routers across the air traffic control system to be flooded with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Because it disrupted some radar feeds, the FAA ordered the ground stop to ensure safety. It was lifted about four hours later. The installation took place in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a router from that location is now at an L3Harris lab in Florida with FAA staff, he told Fox News Sunday , adding that the FBI is offering assistance and suggesting a cyberattack still hasn’t been totally ruled out. “We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor,” Duffy reiterated. “But we’re open. If we see something else, we’re going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement. But at this point, we don’t think [a cyberattack] was the cause.” While the router in Arkansas is under scrutiny, a separate one in Amarillo, Texas, also acted up, raising another question about the disruption. Duffy said the upgrade in Texas had been done weeks earlier, but started to broadcast data into the FAA network at the same time as the Arkansas router. He told CBS’s Face the Nation that the FAA is investigating why that happened, noting both routers are at the L3Harris lab in Florida where the FBI is offering support. ABC asked if sabotage has been ruled out, and Duffy replied “we’re looking at a full suite of issues with the router and with the installation.” The FAA knows who performed the installation, and Duffy called the technician a “good American patriot” who is believed to be a veteran as well. “So we don’t think that someone tried to sabotage the network on the install at all,” he added. “But we don’t actually have the root cause, which is why we do the investigation with our L3Harris partner on the network and the FBI and the FAA.” For its part, an L3Harris spokesperson said Saturday that the company has been modernizing the communications infrastructure for the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA.  Along with its telecom partners and the FAA, L3Harris added that it has completed more than 70% of the conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. “We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks T he Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34. While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “ it’s make or bake time ”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead. Warnings of mounting risks, unprecedented heat and disasters such as August’s glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border can engender a sense of paralysis or unreality. The leaders of both host countries prompted anger last week: the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, publicly extolled his country’s oil reserves , while Australia’s Anthony Albanese failed to mention fossil fuels in his speech. But for all its flaws, the UN climate process remains crucial. There is no other mechanism to broker a global green transition. Mr Burnham’s appointment of a climate security adviser , Madeleine Alessandri, should focus minds in the UK. Kemi Badenoch’s rejection of net zero has undermined an important cross‑party consensus. Ministers, who must soon make a decision on Rosebank oil and gas field , must realise that economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would dwarf any benefits. Governments of countries that are far poorer than the UK cannot be expected to turn away from coal and oil if rich countries keep investing. A resolution to derive 35% of energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 will be agreed this week if objections from fossil fuel producers can be overcome. Attempts to undermine the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change must also be resisted. It provides the science on which the process depends. Increased accountability on climate finance is urgently needed too. Poor countries cannot be expected to put up with endless delays . A large majority of the global public recognises the threat from global heating and wants action by governments. Of course, this takes courage and leadership: people may back a green transition in the abstract, but be more resistant to changes that affect their lives. But those pushing for a faster shift away from fossil fuels, at Cop31 and at a national level, should be emboldened by the way that public awareness and support have grown: they are on the side of the future, while their opponents are stuck in the past.

events.title: TechCrunch Mobility: The Nvidia backup plan for China’s self-driving industry
events.summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility ! I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition. Web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he said the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else. These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy. The former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem. Nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve. I spoke to Leo Wang , the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle company Pony.ai , this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China. Demand is already far greater than supply, Wang said, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said. Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap. “If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he said, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.” When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang said Chinese companies have already been preparing. “If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he said. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. Although cost-effectiveness-wise, probably it’s not the best choice yet. But still, it’s an alternative way that already exists and which is more mature than a few years ago.” May Mobility plans to use the Volkswagen all-electric ID. Buzz for its global ride-hailing platform. The company said it is targeting the deployment of more than 10,000 autonomous vehicles through 2031. This does not mean that VW’s MOIA group is ditching Mobileye, I have been told. Instead, VW told me, the company is offering an automated driving-ready base vehicle to other companies that develop their own self-driving systems. (This was just presented last month during Nvidia GTC in Berlin.) Newmo , a Japanese robotaxi startup, raised a ¥20.8 billion (roughly $135 million) round led by KDDI. ParkBee , a Dutch parking technology company, acquired Mobian’s city and parking operations. Port , an urban logistics company, raised €14.5 million in a round led by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Balnord. Lucid reported Q3 revenue of $350 million, below Wall Street expectations, and it is still losing money. Although its Q3 net loss did narrow to $830.9 million. Notably, the EV maker increased its delayed draw term loan from its largest shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, to $1.75 billion. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating a Waymo software recall from a year ago that was issued after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses. The agency said that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software update intended to fix the problem. Sources familiar with Waymo tell me that there have not been school bus-related incidents since March. I have not been able to independently verify that with the Austin Independent School District. The Tesla Cybertruck will live on through next summer, but production will ultimately end , according to Elon Musk, who defended the polarizing steel-clad truck.

events.title: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response | Andy Burnham
events.summary: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response Alan Milburn’s review will mark a watershed moment for our approach to welfare and childhood. This is how I’m determined to create change Report: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis A generation of young people did not wake up one morning and decide they did not want to work. The fact that a million 16- to 24-year-olds are now not in education, employment or training (Neet) is not their fault. It is ours, as politicians. We have failed to give them the support they need as they have grown up in a tougher world. This has become an economic catastrophe for the country – and a moral one too. Sixteen years ago, the Conservative government took a deliberate decision to make young people bear the brunt of the cuts they chose to make. Those becoming adults today are the children of austerity. At four years old, with Sure Start centres closed, too many were already beginning school behind, without the support they needed to catch up. By 12, too many had seen youth clubs shut down and had fewer places to go in their communities with the closure of libraries and leisure centres. Teenagers in need of mental health support were told to wait months or even years . And, by 18, millions had passed through an education system that told them their technical talents were not worth as much as the abilities of their academic peers. A country focused on the future would make young people its priority for investment – not the target for cuts. It would give all young people a path in life, giving them confidence and hope for the future. Britain has done neither. It is time to acknowledge that this failure has left too many young people ill-prepared for the challenging world they now face. And, of course, that has costs. Under the Conservatives, the welfare bill shot up by £114bn . What is the Tory solution now? To punish those young people once again. The crude cuts they are proposing to the welfare bill would simply compound the mistakes they made in government. They would drive children into poverty and increase levels of family homelessness even further, piling further pressure on councils, the NHS and other public services. This is not “reform”. It is a path to higher public spending and broken services. The way I see it is that we have two choices: we can either invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on; or we can continue to pay the price for failure. I choose the first. The time has come for a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world. To bring down the welfare bill for good, we have to act at the different stages where young people can fall behind. We must intervene long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state. Next week, Alan Milburn’s review into young people and work will be published. I want it to be a watershed moment. We have an opportunity to change the way we think about welfare and the way we think about childhood. Because the two cannot be separated. For too long, we have waited until young people reach adulthood and then tried to deal with the problems that have built up over the years. Under this government, we will start much earlier, making sure children have the support they need at the moments that matter most. It is what I call a whole-childhood approach. It means, in the early years, giving every child a proper start. Those who start school behind too often never catch up. To stop these children from falling through the cracks, we must build an education system which offers support with wider needs, such as mental health, and values all talents. This brings me to a change I am determined to make as prime minister. I will build an education system in England based on the principle of parity between academic and technical routes, that gives all young people a path in life, a confidence in their abilities and tells them they are equally valued. For too long, Britain has praised the graduation cap and looked down on the hard hat. New technical pathways in school will start to put that right. We will open up opportunities for young people to learn new skills and get good jobs where they live. When they approach adulthood, we will make sure they do not face a cliff edge. We will guarantee good work experience and employment opportunities. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more The government will consider Milburn’s recommendations carefully and respond in full in the coming weeks. But I can say now that our response will not be in the manner of traditional Department for Work and Pensions reform. It will be societal and generational. We will rethink supporting childhood – shifting government spending from paying for failure to investing in success. Of course, that support will have to come with responsibilities.

events.title: Trump breaks silence about FAA nationwide ground stop, blames Biden administration
events.summary: Trump’s first public comments on the FAA nationwide ground stop came Sunday morning, as he blamed the Biden administration and called for Congress to provide more money. The more-than-four-hour stop triggered widespread cancellations and delays, and investigators were still determining the root cause. President Donald Trump on Sunday made his first public comments about Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration, blaming the Biden administration for making an "old and broken" air traffic control system worse . Trump also urged Congress to approve more funding to modernize the system. The ground stop lasted more than four hours Friday, disrupted flights nationwide, contributed to thousands of cancellations and delays, and affected hundreds of thousands of passengers. "The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster," Trump wrote on his social media platform. "Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began." The president added that his administration has "the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems," but said that "we need Congress to give the money, FAST!" Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA last year as part of a major tax and spending package. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has said that the aging air traffic control system will need more funding for a broader overhaul. The FAA said its equipment became unstable after a high volume of data flooded its network. The agency said contractor work at one site may be related and that the underlying cause remains under investigation . Nationwide FAA ground stops are rare. Before the Nov. 2026 shutdown, the last two were after the Sept. 11 attacks and a brief FAA computer outage in January 2023.

events.title: I was a single mom of 4 boys. The hardest part wasn't always the money or exhaustion but the judgment.
events.summary: The author raised four boys on her own. Courtesy of the author I raised four sons alone while working multiple jobs and struggling to make ends meet. Strangers constantly pitied us and made my boys feel like they were a burden. I learned to ignore their judgment and protect the happiness we had built together. A woman was following us at the grocery store. It took me a few aisles for my hackles to rise, to get that weird Spidey-sense tingle that something wasn't quite right. I was focused on my sons , aged 2, 3, 7, and 9, trying to smooth over little skirmishes about whose turn it was to pick out the cereal, push the cart, or hold my hand. The easy, regular bickering that was the backdrop of our lives. After about three aisles, I noticed this woman. Older, alone, watching us. Staring at us. I was so conceited about my sons that I assumed she was charmed by us until she walked over and said, "Are all of these children yours?" I was 30 years old. Young for this many children or really any children at all. I told her yes, these were my sons, and she dropped the same three words I have since come to loathe with every fiber of my being. "You poor thing." Said always with a cluck of the tongue or a sad shake of the head. My children, always within earshot, told in so many words and so many ways that they were less valuable because they were many and I was one. An unwanted death knell to the happy, regular life we were enjoying mere moments ago. I heard this so often A version of this conversation happened with absurd frequency when my sons were growing up. Strangers would notice that I was on my own with four sons and that I needed to get the details. "Are all these yours?" was often the opening salvo. A question that was no one's business, a question that turned my sons, my lovely, funny, beautiful boys, into things. I always answered, I'm not sure why. Maybe I hoped for a different response , a positive affirmation of what I saw. "Wow, they're all so good!" or "They all look so much like you," or some other compliment to warm me and bolster me or keep me going. Because it was not easy raising the boys on my own . We never had any money, no matter how many jobs I worked. We rented houses we could barely afford and sometimes couldn't afford at all. We moved a lot. We lost so many little heirlooms in those moves, which breaks my heart to this day. We rarely had a car. We walked everywhere. It was lonely to be a single mom It was lonely too, raising the boys on my own. Always a little unsure if I was getting it right. I was desperate for confirmation that we were OK. I would have given anything for a kind comment from a stranger, just to hear that we seemed OK. That we seemed like a nice family even if we were broke. Instead, I always heard "you poor thing ." Or "those poor kids." Or maybe worst of all, "how awful for you." A condemnation of us and our life together. Decision made. We were awful. We were to be pitied. I can't tell you how much harder strangers made things for me as a single mom. Their comments made me feel ashamed of myself. Nervous, anxious to make sure those "poor kids" behaved to avoid further judgment. These strangers and their comments made my sons feel as though they were a disappointment to me. And in some ways, I think I let them. Too many times after a stranger called us "poor things" or clucked sadly or shook their heads, I snapped at my kids. Told them to stop arguing, stop goofing around, stop being regular little boys. It was like I stepped outside myself and saw us as poor things too. That day in the grocery store was my final straw. Something clicked in me. I didn't cause a scene, fight with her, or call her out for her dumb comment. I just didn't let it in. I smiled at the boys. I let them get Count Chocula and strawberry Pop-Tarts as a weekend treat. I started building a little mental bubble around us against strangers, one that would protect us for years to come. Keep us sane and grounded through decades of struggle, both financial and emotional, when the kindness of strangers might actually have made life a little easier. I just wish I didn't have to. events.title: ‘SNL’ parodies Jensen Huang and other tech billionaires: ‘May I pleasure you in an industry secret?’
events.summary: The 'Saturday Night Live' cast as tech billionaires Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Peter Thiel. Saturday Night Live/NBC John Mulaney and the "Saturday Night Live" cast poked fun at the Nvidia scandal this week. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO last week after admitting to an affair. Former 'SNL' cast member Bowen Yang returned to play Huang: "It's me. Jensen 'hide your wife' Huang." This week's "Saturday Night Live" cold open was a who's-who of the AI revolution. Comedian John Mulaney kicked off the episode by playing a CIA officer conducting national security training for tech billionaires. Specifically, how to identify a spy. Mulaney's character is joined by Palantir cofounder Peter Thiel (James Austin Johnson), OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (Ben Marshall), Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline), Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg (Andrew Dismukes), and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane). "America needs you to learn the difference between a woman who actually wants to have sex with you, and a woman who is clearly a spy," Mulaney said. "You all saw how former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned this week after he was caught having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy." Last Sunday, Nvidia's board of directors said it would investigate whether Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort" on the same day he admitted to an extramarital affair in a memo to staff. Huang resigned from his position days later. On "Saturday Night Live," Mulaney's character empathized with the tech billionaires. "Look, I can't imagine how disorienting this has been for you. To go from these bug-eyed little weirdos to being gods," Mulaney said. "Never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you, A: survived, and B: been given all the world's wealth and power." Mulaney asked the tech executives why someone "very beautiful" would be interested in them. "Because I have a good personality and normal, human mannerisms?" Marshall's Altman said. Zuckerberg, played by Dismukes, guessed it's because "she's comforted by my Meta glasses recording her at all times." Wickline's Amodei theorized it's because "she's using me... for my body." Mulaney then asked the group to pretend an attractive woman approached them at the bar and asked, "What are you working on?" Amodei and Zuckerberg weighed in. "I would say, Madam, what a pleasure to see you this evening. May I interest you in an industry secret?" Amodei said. Zuckerberg said he would "assume that she wanted to sleep with the man who created the Metaverse, as all women do." Near the end, former 'SNL' cast member Bowen Yang returned as Huang. "It's me. Jensen 'hide your wife' Huang," Yang says as he joins the other tech billionaires. "Ladies, when you invite Jensen over, you know what's about to go down. The S&P 500." He added, "That's right. I'm into BDSM: Breakin' da stock market." Nvidia lost more than $500 billion in market value over the last week. Yang's Huang cautioned his fellow tech executives against being like him. "Remember, women don't like guys like us. That's how we became guys like us," he said. In real life, some Nvidia loyalists are hoping the board will reinstate Huang . Nvidia's board of directors said it's considering internal and external candidates for the permanent CEO position . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: After-game snacks have become a whole new way for parents to show off. I joined in, but stuck to a budget.
events.summary: The author said that after-game snacks prepped by parents, like the one her sons received after a baseball game, have gone beyond just food and sports drinks. Courtesy of Rachel Morgan Cautero.. I was taken aback when my son got his first after-game snack of the season. More than just snacks, these bags now have toys and other goodies for kids to enjoy. I leaned into the trend when it was my turn, but I stuck to a budget. My boys are playing baseball this season, and besides marking practices and games on my calendar, I also signed up to bring the snacks after a few games. After seeing my kid's first after-game snack, I am so glad I didn't go first. That's because these after-game snacks were a whole thing. Our first was a cute reusable gift bag filled with a baseball card, a woven baseball necklace — and the snacks. I was floored. I'm also a bit embarrassed to admit that I immediately logged into my Amazon account to start planning my own over-the-top snack. I usually don't mind being the "extra" mom, but this one got me thinking: are kids' sports snacks the new birthday parties ? In other words, is this yet another chance for parents to go above and beyond, all in the name of a good theme? And to what end? I surveyed my players Before I went all in with the after-game gift bag snacks, I asked my boys what they wanted. My older one was ambivalent about the extra treats, but had a few requests for the snacks, like Joyride candy and chips. So I focused more on that, though I did buy the popular "baseball drip" themed gift bags for the treats. The author said she surveyed her sons to see what she should put in the after-game bags when it was their family's turn to provide them. Courtesy of Rachel Morgan Cautero. My youngest is into arm sleeves, specifically compression arm sleeves that baseball players wear to keep their muscles warm and protect their skin from the sun and turf. Of course, at 6 years old, they're purely decorative, but I honored his request and included a cheap version of the arm sleeves in the gift bags for his team. And when I say cheap, I mean about $1 per pair, which I felt OK about. I kept a budget in mind I know it can be easy to blow your budget in the name of a good theme. I've hosted enough kids' birthday parties to learn this one firsthand. That's why, when I decided to up my game (pun intended) for after-game snacks, I set a budget. I knew I wanted to spend no more than $5 per kid. With 12 kids on the team, $60 was my limit. The author said that after-game treats, like this one provided by another parent, have gotten more elaborate. Courtesy of Rachel Morgan Cautero. Buying in bulk, planning ahead when ordering from Amazon, or splitting up non-treat items like baseball cards, candy, and temporary tattoos are other budget-friendly ways to join in on the trend. My boys have gotten all in their after-game treat bags this year and have been happy. Along with the cute bag and arm sleeve, I included a carb-heavy snack and a Gatorade, since experts suggest including healthy carbs and hydration in after-game snacks. I leaned into the trend I was honestly a little surprised the first time I saw one of these treats after a game. Do parents really need another task on their to-do list? What's wrong with orange slices and Gatorade? Absolutely nothing, but I enjoy a challenge and leaned in. I'm probably an "extra" mom myself. My kids' birthday parties are always big and a bit over-the-top. One year, we rented a petting zoo for my 5-year-old's farm-themed party. Another year, it was a video game truck for my 7-year-old. But I don't do it all. For example, we've never done advent calendars or treats for their classes on their birthday. We also don't do cute matching outfits for school picture day, family Halloween costumes, or boo baskets. What I've realized is this. You can go big for your kids, but you can't do it for everything. You have to pick and choose your things, or you will drive yourself crazy. Did I choose to lean into the after-sport snack as one of my extra things? I sure did. But it made my kids — and their teammates — smile, so I guess I'm OK with it. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The tech products we enthusiastically recommend this holiday season
events.summary: We’ve been reviewing a bunch of new gadgets and hardware at TechCrunch this year: dumb phones , bird feeders , health trackers , slushy machines , AI mattress pads , you name it. Sometimes we think they’re unnecessary and expensive , but other times, we try out devices that we love so much that we go out and buy them ourselves. If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season. We’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year. What can we say? We’re nerds. We work for a tech website. But after trying devices from the usual suspects as well as some wildcards, we have recommendations. Evidently, 2026 was the year we fell in love with the pocket-sized e-reader. Xteink X3 ($55) – a budget pick for someone techy It’s an e-reader so small that it can fit in your wallet, or even magnetize to the back of your phone. Do you dream of a world where instead of scrolling Instagram when you’re waiting in line for coffee, you actually opt to read books? There’s really something special about the X3, and it’s only $55 during Xteink’s Black Friday sale. Fair warning, it takes some fiddling with to set up, and it has no integration with Kindle, Libby, or any other apps, so only buy this for someone willing to do a bit of Reddit browsing and tinkering to get it up and running. XTeink X4 Pro ($99) – it has a backlight! If you aren’t planning to magnetize the XTeink to your phone, you’ve got to go with the X4 Pro . It’s slightly bigger, but it has a backlight, which makes it way more versatile. After using both the X3 and the X4 Pro, I find that the backlight really is a game changer, since I do a lot of reading in bed — plus, I like my Pop Socket wallet a bit too much to displace for the X3, and I’d rather just carry an extra credit card-sized device than risk forgetting my actual credit and ID cards, which I have grown too used to having on my phone. Boox Palma Pro 2 ($400) – a phone-sized e-reader without the drawbacks If I’m being honest, reading my colleague Aisha Malik’s review of the Boox Palma Pro 2 is making me want to buy one. I love using the Xteink e-readers, but they don’t connect to any outside apps. As a hardcore Libby power user (a phrase I am saying in earnest sincerity), it’s a bit frustrating that I can’t get my library books on Xteink e-readers. The same goes for apps like Kobo and Kindle, where any e-book you already own cannot be transferred out of the Amazon ecosystem unless the publisher agrees, which most do not. If you’re looking for an e-reader with a screen that’s actually book-sized, my favorite that I’ve used is the Kobo Libra Colour , which is $259. The Amazon Paperwhite line is great, but c’mon, Amazon. Branch out! Hey, we’ve all got to eat. And if you want, you can make that eating process overly techy. Why not? Ember Mug 3 ($99) – for the tea lover who’s really particular The Ember Mug 3 is the latest iteration in Ember’s line of coffee/tea cups that actually stay warm. Our reviewer Lauren Forristal especially appreciated that you no longer need to use your phone app to change the mug’s temperature, which seems like it would be really annoying! This mug is perfect for gifting to someone, or to put on your own wishlist — you might not want to spend $99 on a mug for yourself, but these sorts of luxury, nice-to-haves are what holidays are made for! Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer ($449.99) – two appliances in one! Ah, Ninja, the premiere company in the business of turning every appliance into a two-in-one air fryer. I jest, but at least Ninja knows it’s onto something. Despite the high price point, Lauren says that this new product made “a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one.” You can’t buy more counter space (without moving), but you can buy more versatile appliances. GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro ($499.99) – if your fridge has a built-in ice maker, you just won’t understand Sure, there are cheaper ice makers on the market. But Aisha clarifies that this is the ice maker for “those who crave what’s called ‘the good ice.’” If you feel so passionately about the ice in your beverages that you know what she means, then maybe this is for you. What they really want is a Mac mini or Claude subscription, but if that’s out of budget, we have some other ideas that might impress your AI-pilled, vibe-coder loved ones… Open AI Codex Micro ($230) – for the Codex evangelist When I asked my colleague Lucas Ropek what about his favorite product he reviewed this year, he mentioned the Codex Micro . Some hard-core coders — who the product is aimed toward — have found this thing less than pleasing, but Lucas seems to have had fun figuring out this first attempt by OpenAI at hardware. Best case, it’s a productivity game-changer for your friend who has a hardworking team of AI agents within the OpenAI ecosystem.

events.title: Trump's border crackdown faces a new blue wall of governors and House members
events.summary: Voters have handed Democrats every House district touching Mexico and all four border-state governorships. Why it matters: Starting next year, the sweep gives Democrats new leverage over state resources, border spending and legal challenges during President Trump's final two years. By the numbers: Democrats last held all four governorships — California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas — in January 1979, according to National Governors Association records . 10 for 10: Democrats swept all 10 House districts touching Mexico for the first time since 2008, according to an Associated Press analysis . Three flips: JoAnna Mendoza ousted Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani in Arizona. Bobby Pulido and Katy Padilla Stout flipped Republican-held seats in Texas. Four attorneys general: Democrats also won the top legal offices in all four border states, including Texas , where the party hadn't won an attorney general race since 1994. State of play: Trump built his immigration crackdown around the southern border. He declared a national emergency on his first day back, expanded the military's role and border barriers, and launched a sweeping deportation campaign. Southwest border apprehensions dropped roughly 91% in the 12 months through August compared with Biden's final 12 months, according to FactCheck.org's October analysis . The crackdown has also reached further into American communities, with ICE arrests surging during the summer of 2026. Zoom in: Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa's defeat of Gov. Greg Abbott could bring the most immediate border changes. Abbott spent about $11 billion on Operation Lone Star, deploying state police and National Guard troops and building Rio Grande barriers, according to the Texas Tribune . Hinojosa, Texas' first Latina governor-elect, has questioned that spending. She can rethink state deployments and enforcement priorities, though existing laws and federal authority limit her options. Democrats also flipped the Texas House and elected a Democratic attorney general, giving Hinojosa allies in funding and legal battles. Republicans retained the state Senate. The intrigue: Outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed more than 20 lawsuits against Democratic immigration policies and defended Gov. Greg Abbott's border crackdown. His Democratic successor, Nathan Johnson, has vowed to challenge unconstitutional federal border tactics — potentially turning the office from a powerful Trump ally into an adversary. What we're watching: Several Democrats newly elected to represent border districts in Washington campaigned on both strong border security and pathways to citizenship for longtime undocumented immigrants. Bobby Pulido, who flipped a Texas GOP-held seat, said in his launch video : "Yes, we have to get the criminals out and secure the border. But we can do that without destroying families and our South Texas economy." He also told the Texas Tribune that one of his congressional priorities will be codifying a pathway to citizenship. JoAnna Mendoza, who flipped an Arizona seat, also backs a strong border and legal pathways to citizenship. That aligns with many border voters' views: An October N+ Univision/YouGov survey found 56% of Texas Hispanic voters thought immigration enforcement had gone too far. Yet 62% wanted border security and a pathway to citizenship for longtime undocumented immigrants pursued together — suggesting Democrats can make gains without abandoning enforcement. Zoom out: Trump's tariffs and immigration crackdown have rattled businesses that depend on trade and shoppers from Mexico, giving Democratic governors another reason to challenge Washington. Laredo businesses report fewer customers, while merchants near San Diego's border crossings say tougher immigration enforcement has hurt foot traffic and hiring. Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs pressed Washington over tariffs and trade uncertainty. Manufacturers near Santa Teresa, New Mexico, have put projects on hold amid tariff threats and uncertainty over trade rules.

events.title: Two planes collide on taxiway at Miami airport one day after national grounding
events.summary: Two people injured after wingtip of Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck nose of United Parcel Service Boeing 767 Two planes collided with one another on a taxiway at Miami’s international airport on Saturday night – a day after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an hours-long nationwide ground stop due to communication issues affecting multiple air traffic control centers. In a statement, the Trump administration-led FAA said the wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck the nose of a United Parcel Service Boeing 767 “while the airplanes were taxiing at Miami International Airport”. Two people reportedly had minor injuries in the collision and subsequently received medical treatment. The FAA said it was investigating the matter, which was reported at about 9pm local time. According to the FAA, air traffic controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight before the collision. “The Copa flight was taxiing to the gate and the UPS flight was taxiing for departure to Bogotá, Colombia,” the FAA said. A passenger on the Copa flight, Cesar Ferreira, spoke to CNN about how screams from those around him clued him in to the emergency. “We were taxiing after landing at a normal speed when, all of a sudden, I heard the chatter around me getting louder – followed by a collective scream and then the impact of another aircraft hitting ours,” Ferreira said. “Inside the cabin, we felt the plane jerk abruptly sideways. At first, some passengers started freaking out, but the Copa crew reacted quickly, getting everyone to remain seated.” Copa Airlines said in a statement that it “regrets the disruption this incident may cause our passengers”. “The safety of our passengers and crew is our top priority, and we will cooperate with authorities as they investigate,” the airline said. The airport said flights were directed to other taxiways, so airport operations were not affected. “We are aware of an incident involving one of our aircraft on the ground in Miami ,” UPS said in a statement. “Our crew is safe, and we are committed to working with authorities to determine what happened. The safety of our employees and the public is our highest priority.” The weekend was marked by thousands of flight delays and cancelations in the wake of a four-hour FAA ground stop on Friday which the Trump administration said stemmed from routine but botched maintenance aiming to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber optic cables. Trump administration transportation secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday and Sunday blamed the need for the maintenance on a lack of congressional funding – though critics have said the White House has not spent the money it has been apportioned to upgrade the infrastructure supporting the US’s air travel system.

events.title: Trump heads to Asia with hopes of shifting the momentum after midterm setbacks hurt him at home
events.summary: President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week and he's aiming to shift the momentum after Republican losses in the midterm elections WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week, hoping to make some big attention-grabbing moves on the world stage after his party suffered deep losses in the midterm elections , diminishing his standing at home. The Republican president is using the international trip to try to shift momentum, and he is poised to make a splash with a historic three-way meeting with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia to talk about their nuclear stockpiles. Trump has long boasted about leveraging his relationships with the leaders of two of America’s biggest global adversaries, though he has failed so far to achieve major breakthroughs with them. He first heads to the Philippines to meet on Tuesday with Southeast Asian leaders who look to the United States for help countering Beijing's aggression in the region. Trump will then go to China on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. There, he will have his third face-to-face meeting this year with Xi and see Putin, too. A year ago, Trump used a similar Asia trip to agree on a trade truce with China and secure investment pledges from Japan and South Korea. This time, Trump is going with his party no longer in control of Congress as of January and with attention beginning to turn to a crop of presidential hopefuls who aim to replace him in 2028. “I think he, like other presidents, has figured out that in a moment where things are really hard domestically: Get on an airplane and go international,” said Kurt Campbell , a former deputy secretary of state in Democratic President Joe Biden's administration and chairman of The Asia Group, a consultancy. It's a pattern followed by some of Trump's predecessors. Democratic President Barack Obama flew to Beijing days after his party lost the Senate in 2014 to negotiate carbon emission targets with Xi. Republican President George W. Bush went to APEC in Vietnam after the GOP lost control of Congress in 2006, though the Iraq War hung over his travels. The White House said Trump will sign a trade deal with Thailand in Manila as well as a host of commercial deals and will be the “guest of honor” at a leaders' dinner. In Shenzhen, he will focus on trade issues before the meeting with Xi and Putin. Trump is leaving as airlines struggled to get passengers onto flights after a nationwide ground stop on Friday led to thousands of flight cancellations. Trump and his officials have blamed their predecessors, a contractor and Congress for the problems. Trump is about to be bogged down at home in ways that may curb what he can do overseas. His tariffs and war with Iran proved to be poisonous with voters. Going forward, Trump's ability to threaten import taxes or military assaults — two of his major foreign policy tools — will be limited by Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill in the new year. Just last week, in a newfound vulnerability, his push to boost artificial intelligence was complicated when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved. Huang had traveled with Trump on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. Trump has argued that America needs to preserve its leadership on AI and warned of dire consequences if China wins that competition. But Trump does not plan to confront Xi on the issue, said administration officials who insisted on anonymity as a condition for previewing the president’s plans on a call with reporters. The officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip. Even though the administration is discussing ways to close loopholes and further prevent Chinese businesses from using advanced chips made by Nvidia and other U.S. companies, the officials said they do not expect the restrictions to cause retaliation by Beijing. Trump will be accompanied by Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla, who is the world's wealthiest man and a frequent adviser to the president. Musk spent at least $445 million to try to help Republicans keep control of Congress, and Democrats are keen to investigate his ties to the administration. Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Trump may find it easier to be in the company of foreign leaders than his own crumbling coalition at home. But his words and actions at the summits are now more likely to draw scrutiny in committee hearings when he returns to Washington. “We’re going to have a very close eye on it," said Rep.

events.title: When the boss has an affair, the whole family business can pay the price
events.summary: Fallout from ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair is the latest reminder of the shared toll paid when patriarchs cheat F rom Profumo to Petraeus to Gary Hart , Bill Gates and Bill Clinton , history is littered with older men in positions of great responsibility having affairs with mostly younger women that put their jobs, businesses and reputations at great risk. Now we have the former Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang. These men – smart, respected, powerful – make decisions that simply baffle the rest of us. If they’re so intelligent, how could they not see how things were going to end up? The answer is they’re men. And when there’s a younger woman who shows interest, well … We all love a bit of schadenfreude now and again. But it’s not so fun for the employees, shareholders, partners and others who work alongside these men. And it’s deeply unpleasant for their families, particularly when they work in the same business. Jensen Huang’s family is feeling that right now. His son, daughter and son-in-law all have prominent positions at his company. His daughter is married to another Nvidia executive. And they’re not alone. And when it happens at a smaller business, the impact is even worse. Huang’s company is so well known that the world knows of his indiscretions. But people live in their own worlds, and in my client’s world, pretty much everyone in the company knows what’s going on with the cheating spouse. Some surveys claim that as many as 20% of people have admitted to cheating on their partners. There are 34m small businesses in the US with almost a third being family owned. So the odds are that there are other moms and dads (probably dads, given that 61% of businesses are still owned by men) making the same mistakes. I have clients in this position. And their children working in their businesses are going through the same horrible experience. Hopefully, the children working in family businesses have positions where they are not directly reporting to mom and dad. Hopefully there’s an organizational structure and policies in place that separates them from ownership and treats them as any other employee. Whether the owner of the company – even if it’s the mom or dad (again probably the dad) – is having dalliances on the side should be of no matter. They’re doing a job in the company. They’re not a part of this. But unfortunately they are. It’s still their parents. There’s still an unsaid thing amongst the rest of the employees that not only are they the kids but they’re also likely to be the future owners of the company. Their behavior inside the company walls is being watched as closely as their parents. Suddenly, their parents’ behavior is now reflected on them. Can they also be trusted? And yet I don’t feel entirely sorry for the Jensen kids or any kids working for their parents where a similar situation occurs. They’ve enjoyed the perks of being the owners’ offspring. They’ve likely been given opportunities they wouldn’t necessarily get if they worked for someone else. They know what they signed up for. The hope is that Huang’s children, and the children of any business owner going through the same situation, learn and turn it to their favor. When a responsible CEO cheats on their spouse, it calls into question their overall ethics. When the affairs become a circus like Jensen’s – or even in the smaller world of my clients – the ridicule it creates undermines their authority. People look at my cheating clients like they’re a joke. They wonder how they could do something so blatantly stupid like having an affair with an employee in an environment where their children work? They question the judgment of the very leader who runs the company that provides their livelihood. The kids should stand by both their parents, accept that mistakes were made, but show to the world that it’s still their family and that they love them. But they should also take the opportunity to show their fellow employees, and the world, that they wouldn’t behave the same way.

events.title: FBI raids and a recycling firm: how a promising US mayor wound up at the center of a bribery scandal
events.summary: As Oakland residents watch ex-mayor Sheng Thao stand trial, the scandal has come to symbolise wider frustrations T wo years ago, residents of Oakland, California , woke up to a shocking scene: their mayor’s home was being raided by the FBI. Agents were seen carrying dozens of boxes from the hilltop home of Sheng Thao, the city’s 38-year-old leader, as part of an investigation constituents would later learn alleged her participation in a pay-to-play scheme with the city’s recycling contractor. It was a stunning moment for Thao, who was elected to lead the Bay Area city in 2022 and was once seen as a promising young mayor in a city that has long grappled with economic inequality and a reputation for violent crime. Her story of growing up in a refugee family and overcoming domestic violence and homelessness to become the first person of Hmong descent to run a major US city resonated with readers confronting questions about equity and representation that came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, and made her the subject of glowing media profiles . As mayor, Thao revived the city’s Ceasefire violence-reduction strategy and brought in a much-needed infusion of revenue through the sale of the Oakland Coliseum sports complex. But her tenure was far from smooth. At the time of the raid she was already facing a heated recall campaign grounded in her perceived failure to address the city’s mounting public safety and homelessness crises – one that would see her ousted from office in November 2024. Two months later, Thao was indicted on federal corruption charges, and eventually replaced by longtime progressive congresswoman Barbara Lee in a special election. Now, Oakland is anxiously watching the final chapter in this political drama unfold as Thao and three co-defendents stand trial over the alleged bribery scheme. Having just concluded its fifth week of hearings, the case is rich with soap-opera-esque plot points, from an alleged beating at a recycling company’s headquarters to text threads in which co-defendants celebrated the plot that would make them “$100 million dollars richer” and touted that “money buys everything”. Proceedings are expected to conclude later this month, with Thao facing six federal counts in total. If found guilty, she could face up to 20 years in prison. To the frustration of other witnesses , Thao, who has a constitutional right not to testify, has yet to take the stand. The saga has left residents disappointed and reopened longstanding frustrations about a city that has everything it needs to thrive – a prime location on the bay, a diverse population, a burgeoning arts and culture scene, and a growing economy – but a government that struggles to deliver basic services or answer for its shortcomings. “When the news [of the FBI raids] broke, there was a wide range of feelings from the community,” said Stephanie Tran, president of the Oakland Chinatown chamber of commerce, of the fall from grace of a mayor who offered representation to Oakland’s sizeable Asian-American community. “Many were, quite honestly, just disappointed, even sad,” she said, that an Asian woman in such a high position of power was now associated with this controversy. The bribery, conspiracy and fraud charges against Thao rest on claims that during her 2022 campaign, David and Andy Duong – a father and son whose family runs California Waste Solutions, the company that provides Oakland’s recycling services – paid for negative mailers attacking her rivals and promised her romantic partner, Andre Jones, a $300,000 no-show job. In exchange, prosecutors allege, Thao promised to extend the company’s multi-million-dollar city contract, appoint the Duongs’ preferred people to important municipal positions, and buy shipping containers converted into homes for unhoused people from a company the Duongs ran with a business partner. All four defendants have pleaded not guilty, with their lawyers denying the existence of any bribery scheme. Thao’s legal team did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. Darwin BondGraham, news editor at local non-profit media outlet The Oaklandside, said the courthouse has been frequented by members of Oakland’s political class. But when it comes to everyday Oaklanders, many just want the mess behind them. “The trial is accounting for things that happened when Oakland bottomed out during the first few years of the pandemic,” BondGraham said. “I think people moved on.” What many want is simple: a City Hall that fixes the potholes, answers 911 calls and acts with accountability. But in Oakland – which has faced recurring budget deficits for decades, leading to substantial staffing shortages and hundreds of millions in deferred maintenance – these basic services are not a given. Those are the sorts of core concerns that pushed Emily Wasserman, a mother of two living in the city’s Laurel neighborhood, toward local advocacy. In 2024, Wasserman was ready for change.

events.title: The typical homebuyer in 2026 is older, richer, and loves the suburbs
events.summary: NAR's Profile of Homebuyers and Sellers highlights the characteristics of housing market participants. Organic Media/Getty Images The National Association of Realtors released its profile of homebuyers in 2026. The typical homebuyer is nearly twice as old as they were in 1981, when NAR started its report. Buyers also have a degree, make more than average money, and choose the suburbs over the city. The housing market hasn't been inspiring for prospective homebuyers lately. With many potential buyers waiting on the sidelines as interest rates rise, home sales are taking a hit. In 2024 and 2025, existing home sales were identical, at 4.06 million. However, that number fell to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October 2026, according to the National Association of Realtors. It's the lowest number in over a decade. "Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023," NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said. "As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010." So who's still buying homes? NAR released its annual Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. This year's report covers home sales between July 2025 and June 2026, offering a snapshot of the economic climate and housing market over the past year. Since the previous report, the median homebuyer age has dropped slightly, while their income has grown considerably. Buyers also resoundingly favor the suburbs. Here's what the typical homebuyer looked like in the past year, according to NAR. The median age of a homebuyer dropped to 58, down from its peak of 59 last year. Marnie Griffiths/Getty Images The steady increase in the median age of homebuyers has been a talking point for years. When NAR published its first report in 1981, the median age of all homebuyers was 31 — now it's up to 58. For first-time homebuyers, that number stayed put at 40, while the age of repeat homebuyers also stayed flat at 62. While the age of first-time buyers is usually the report's main talking point, the median age of repeat buyers has increased at a faster rate since 1981. Even though the median homebuyer age was 58, the most common homebuyer was in the range of 65 to 74 years old — that age group made up 26% of all homebuyers. More married couples bought homes than single buyers. Morsa Images/Getty Images Homebuyers figured it was easier to go in on a house with another person than alone. Married couples accounted for the largest share of homebuyers by a wide margin. Sixty-three percent of all homebuyers were married. The amount of single women homebuyers slightly decreased to 20% — after doubling since 1985 — but they are still more common than than single men, who accounted for 8% of all homebuyers. The gap between single women and single men homebuyers was only a 2% difference in 1985 — 11% and 9%, respectively. The typical homebuyer's household income is well above the nationwide median. Luis Alvarez/Getty Images According to the US Census, the median household income reached its peak in 2025 at $87,460. Homebuyers this year make well above that, with a median household income of $120,000. For first-time buyers specifically, that number is $100,000. Most homebuyers are empty nesters. Alina Rudya/Bell Collective/Getty Images The typical buyer bought a house with three bedrooms, two bathrooms, and 1,900 square feet of space; enough room for children or extra guests. Most buyers, however, were without kids. Homebuyers with no children under 18 living in the home accounted for 74% of buyers. Buyers with one or two children made up 10% of buyers, and those with three or more children made up 6%. Most buyers have at least one college degree. TK Nataba/Getty Images Today's homebuyers are highly educated. NAR's survey found that 30% of buyers have a bachelor's degree, followed by 27% with a master's degree, MBA, or law degree. Just 16% are high-school graduates. College graduates tend to have higher incomes than people without degrees, which may help explain their higher homeownership rates . The suburbs are the place to be. There are a handful of metropolitan areas where there's more than a 70% chance of home prices falling in the next 12 months, according to CoreLogic. Michael Godek/Getty Images The suburbs are the "It" place for the typical buyer. This year, 48% of all buyers purchased homes in suburban neighborhoods, compared with 21% in small towns and 14% in rural areas. It's a reversal from recent years. In 2022, the share of buyers purchasing homes in the suburbs fell below 40%. Small towns and rural areas attracted an influx of buyers that year, narrowing the gap between suburban and small-town buyers. As more Americans gravitate toward suburban areas, the shift suggests the pandemic-era rush for more land and space in smaller towns and rural communities is easing. The typical buyer doesn't want to share walls. The typical homebuyer prefers a detached home. Gregory Bracco/Getty Images The typical homebuyer would rather not share walls with neighbors. This year, 80% of homebuyers chose detached homes. By comparison, townhouses accounted for 7% of purchases, while duplexes and condos made up 4%. With buyers continuing to favor the suburbs , it's not surprising that condos, often concentrated in urban areas, are getting less love. Repeat buyers are dominating homebuying. Home in Seaside, Florida. adamkaz/Getty Images The real estate market is increasingly a tale of the haves and have-nots. NAR's survey shows that first-time homebuyers are struggling to keep up. In 2026, the typical buyer had already purchased one or more properties. Repeat buyers, whether purchasing a new primary residence or a vacation home , accounted for 78% of all home purchases. Repeat buyers are also much older than they were in the past. In 2026, their median age is 62, compared with 36 in 1981. "Repeat buyers are driving the housing market," said Jessica Lautz, NAR's deputy chief economist and vice president of research. "Unlike first-time home buyers, repeat buyers have seen their housing equity grow rapidly over the past decade, enabling them to trade up for larger homes or move into more desirable locations. These are often moves by choice rather than necessity." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Social Security and the blue wave: What could happen to payroll taxes and senior tax breaks
events.summary: As Social Security's trust funds face looming depletion dates, lawmakers elected during the midterms may make changes that affect the taxes Americans pay. Raising or eliminating the payroll tax cap to help fund Social Security has been a popular policy choice among Democrats, and even some Republicans are getting on board with the idea. Another change, a recently enacted senior tax deduction of up to $6,000 per individual, is set to expire in two years. New leaders may decide whether to extend that tax break. Congress has six years to enact changes to Social Security to prevent cuts to retirement benefits. Senators elected in the Nov. 3 midterms will be in office when the deadline arrives, and their decisions may be critical in making tax changes that can affect Social Security. During the midterm campaign season, tax policy surfaced in the debate over Social Security in two different ways. Many Democrats, and some Republicans, called for high earners to pay more in Social Security payroll taxes, while many Republicans touted a recently enacted tax deduction for adults 65 and older. The diverging tactics come at a crucial moment for reform: The first could increase revenue flowing into the program. The second reduces eligible older adults' income taxes and can lower the taxes some beneficiaries pay on Social Security benefits, reducing program revenue. Social Security trustees' latest projections show the trust fund used to pay retirement benefits may start to become depleted in 2032, when 78% of benefits would be payable. Lawmakers do have some leeway — if the program's retirement and disability trust funds are combined, depletion would be pushed out to 2034, when 83% of scheduled benefits would be payable. But that's still a haircut for retirees — and it's coming soon. "We've waited too long already, and the consequences are that the gap has grown larger," Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said of Social Security's shortfall. On the campaign trail, midterm candidates largely avoided specifics on how they would reform Social Security. However, raising the payroll tax cap, also known as the taxable maximum, was a popular choice among Democratic candidates. That would require people who earn more than the cap, currently $184,500, to begin contributing payroll taxes for their earnings above that amount. Meanwhile, some Republican candidates said they would extend the temporary senior tax deduction of up to $6,000 per eligible individual that is set to expire in 2028. Midterm elections 2026 live updates: Economy, inflation and voter concerns Midterm elections guide: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisions These Senate races may help determine the fate of Social Security Social Security: How much money beneficiaries may lose if Congress does nothing The deduction, part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed in July of last year and billed as a senior bonus, was among the factors that moved Social Security trustees' retirement trust fund depletion projections three months sooner, according to an annual report released in June. Here's what experts say could be in store now that Democrats have won control of the House and Senate. Social Security is a pay-as-you-go system that relies on payroll taxes from workers to help make monthly benefit payments to millions of Americans. In 2026, earnings up to $184,500 are subject to that tax. Workers and employers each contribute 6.2% of pay up to that threshold, while self-employed individuals pay 12.4%. The wage cap will rise in 2027 to $192,300. It adjusts higher annually to reflect incremental changes in the average wage index. On the campaign trail, some House and Senate candidates said the cap should be raised or eliminated entirely so high earners contribute more. Following the election, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who is expected to become the next chair of the Social Security subcommittee, said on X on Nov. 7 that his proposal to increase benefits by at least $2,400 per year and "scrap the cap" on earnings subject to Social Security taxes would be a "top priority." Outgoing Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., responded on X that the plan would "put a 12.4% tax" on people who are not millionaires or billionaires. The idea of higher payroll taxes has broader support. A national survey fielded in February found most respondents — 79% — support raising taxes for wages over $400,000, according to the University of Maryland School of Public Policy. The change was the most popular option tested among the 2,509 adults surveyed. Rising income inequality has meant the payroll tax cap no longer covers 90% of earnings, though that percentage was expected to remain constant when lawmakers enacted the last major reforms to the program in 1983, according to research from the Roosevelt Institute, a New York-based liberal think tank.
