events.title: The ultimate adulting task: signing up for health insurance
events.summary: Not many 22-year-olds share DJ Mikunda’s enthusiasm for health insurance coverage. “You know what sounds like a good Friday night? It’s looking at health insurance,” he joked. But Mikunda has a reason to be eager. He has gone without coverage since he left home and started working in 2023. He’s now a manager at a gas station in St. Louis. In years past, he has looked at plans on the health insurance marketplace at healthcare.gov — but the options proved overwhelming and a bit too expensive. “I feel like I’m a well-informed individual,” Mikunda said. “I try to stay updated on what a deductible is and what the premiums are and copays. And I’m still finding myself a little bit lost.” To sort through the basics, HealthQ introduced Mikunda to independent assister Jackie Shrago , who has been helping people navigate the insurance marketplace since the early days of the Affordable Care Act. The QTip: Search for a free “independent assister” on healthcare.gov to better understand your insurance options. Income Drives the Conversation Shrago started by asking Mikunda about his income. How much money you expect to make in the coming year determines whether you’re eligible for reduced monthly payments. The system uses a sliding scale for households making less than 400% of the federal poverty rate — which means, for 2027 enrollees, an individual with no children can make up to $63,480 and still qualify for a discount. A person in their mid-20s making $50,000, for instance, would get an average 23% discount, according to KFF’s subsidy calculator . For someone making $30,000, the tax credit would cover nearly three-quarters of the cost. It’s important to estimate next year’s income as accurately as possible. If you end up making more than anticipated, you may owe money back to the government. “The last thing you want is a surprise when you file your income taxes,” Shrago told Mikunda. Short-Term Affordability vs. Long-Term Needs Then, Shrago pivoted to the other considerations: How much can you afford to pay every month? And what kind of coverage do you really need? It’s a personal decision about financial planning and risk tolerance, balancing up-front payments with out-of-pocket costs. Mikunda knows he’ll need regular doctor visits and prescription medication, because he has a chronic joint condition that has gone virtually untreated since he started working and lost Medicaid coverage. So he might consider stretching his monthly budget for a plan that covers more of the medical cost. Those financial trade-offs drive much of the decision, forcing you to find a “comfortable medium” between the level of coverage you want and the amount you’re willing to pay, Mikunda said. Gather Your Decision Team There’s much to consider, especially for a first-timer. But one-on-one help is available at healthcare.gov . If you click on the link to “ Find local help ,” you can filter specifically to search for “independent assisters” like Shrago in your ZIP code. Unlike insurance agents and brokers, assisters are forbidden from charging for their services or receiving compensation from insurance companies. (The brokers listed at healthcare.gov far outnumber the independent assisters, but the assisters are findable.) Shrago also recommends starting the selection process early enough to step away and think. “If you’re dealing with something that is uncertain enough and you feel really awkward about it, you don’t need to make a decision today,” she said. “Take your time and think about it.” Assisters tend to have the least availability right before the federal marketplace’s Jan. 15 deadline, so reach out early. People and Policy The Trump administration cut funding for independent assisters and navigator nonprofits by roughly 90% in 2025. When making that announcement, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said the program was inefficient , costing more than $1,000 per person enrolled. The reduction in funding means fewer people helping. In Ohio, for example, the number of paid navigators serving state residents dropped from 50 to five at the start of open enrollment in 2025. Katherine Ruppelt and Emily Siner at Nashville Public Radio contributed to this report. HealthQ is a health series from reporters Cara Anthony and Blake Farmer, approachable guides to an unapproachable healthcare system. It’s a collaboration between Nashville Public Radio and KFF Health News . KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF . This article first appeared on KFF Health News and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License . events.title: Gen Z believes using AI is making their colleagues dumb and lazy—but may paradoxically see it as key to their own promotion, Wharton says
events.summary: Last year, researchers from Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University revealed startling evidence about the impact of using AI on how—and how hard—people think, finding that among more than 300 knowledge workers, leaning too much on AI tools like ChatGPT was associated with diminished critical thinking skills . The study, mirrored by results from MIT-led research , suggested that even using AI for low-stakes tasks such as proofreading “can lead to significant negative outcomes in high-stakes contexts,” like writing legal documents, the study authors wrote. For the young generation of digital natives navigating AI anxiety around keeping up with peers using the technology and AI displacing them from jobs, the fear of the technology making people dumber is dominant. But that hasn’t stopped them from using AI—even when they’re explicitly told not to. A Wharton-led survey published earlier this year, conducted in partnership with Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation, found young people are ramping up their AI use, even as their concerns about it causing lazy thinking persist. A survey of nearly 2,500 U.S. adults between the ages of 18 and 28 completed in October 2025 found 79% of respondents believed AI makes people lazier, and 62% said they had concerns it makes people less smart. “What we find is deep ambivalence on how Gen Z is thinking [about] using AI,” Benjamin Lira Luttges, a postdoctoral scholar at Wharton who led research for the report, told Fortune . Despite these fears, Gen Zers have increased their AI usage. Pew Research Center data published in June found 66% of people ages 18 to 29 have ever used an AI chatbot, such as ChatGPT, up from 55% in 2024. However, 37% of those young adults said they believed the impact of AI on them over the next 20 years would be negative, the most pessimistic attitude of any age group surveyed. The paradox of Gen Z’s willingness to use AI at the office, even amid persistent worries about the technology’s impact on critical thinking, lays bare the young generation’s complicated feelings toward AI, according to the report’s authors. After all, Gen Z’s fraught relationship with AI runs deep. Nearly one-fifth of the generation is worried about AI displacing them at work, yet they lead the workplace in AI adoption .  Though they require some decoding, Gen Z’s tangled attitudes toward AI can be critical in designing a path forward for the technology, more broadly, to be best integrated into the workplace, Lira Luttges suggested. “Young people lead the adoption of new technologies, and a lot of things that are often seen as fringe, as not mainstream, are adopted by young people and eventually become part of the mainstream,” he said. “So in a sense … looking at Gen Z is a way of looking towards the future of work.” What are Gen Z’s fraught feelings toward AI? Lira Luttges speculates the biggest mental factor informing Gen Z’s attitudes toward AI is simply a bias toward immediate gratification , a disposition more prominent in younger, developing minds. “There’s a legitimate tradeoff between benefits and costs that you get from using AI,” he said. “Our brains are wired to prefer smaller, immediate rewards versus long-term, delayed rewards.” As Gen Z grapples with finding or keeping jobs, as well as scaling their career ladders, job performance bolstered by an AI boost may hold more appeal than the less tangible threat of critical thinking skills loss. Similarly, even if an employer does not want an employee using AI for certain tasks, those workers, particularly if young, might consider getting their tasks done efficiently as more important, particularly if the risk of getting caught is slow, Lira Luttges noted. Anyone—not just Gen Z—could also fall victim to the better-than-average effect , a statistically impossible phenomenon of most people generally believing they are above average at a certain task. Gen Z survey respondents, for example, may see themselves as AI power-users, Lira Luttges said. Sure, AI could atrophy critical thought capabilities and make other people lazy, but not those filling out the survey. How will Gen Z shape the future of work? To maximize how AI is used in the workplace, employers should not ban AI, but rather embrace ambivalence toward it, the report authors argued. According to the survey, respondents who reported using AI more frequently worried less about its impact on intelligence and motivation, indicating AI anxiety may resolve over time. But resolving AI anxiety doesn’t address the question of AI use impacting critical thought. Some future-of-work experts, including Mark Beasley, professor and director at North Carolina State University’s Poole College of Management, believe a critical thinking gap, not an AI skills gap, will pose a serious threat to organizational pipelines and business operations. Beasley told Fortune the threat AI poses to entry-level jobs could mean insufficient training and experience for middle- and eventually upper-tier positions in the near future. “The biggest risk organizations face is just being stagnant,” he said. But as long as workplaces are intentional about how they implement AI, Lira Luttges said the technology won’t have a significant impact on critical thinking. “For every task, there are two kinds of efforts,” Lira Luttges said. “There is effort that is germane to the task, that is intrinsic to the thing that you’re doing, and that kind of effort is the effort that you put in, and gets translated into learning. But there’s a lot of effort that is just there, that’s just like friction, that doesn’t really teach you anything.” “You should outsource the crap, not the craft,” he added. A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Jan., 30 2026. events.title: I was juggling a $99K job, a baby, and caring for my mom with Alzheimer's. Getting laid off was a relief.
events.summary: Elizabeth Stephens is the primary carer for her mom, Gail, who has Alzheimer's disease and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). Courtesy of Elizabeth Stephens Elizabeth Stephens struggled to juggle her roles as carer to her mom and toddler with office work. Eventually laid off, she was relieved to no longer carry so many responsibilities. The single mother used her severance and dipped into her savings to stay afloat financially. This story is based on an interview with Elizabeth Stephens , 45, an HR worker-turned-carer from Lancaster, Texas. It has been edited for length and clarity. I asked to transfer from Houston to Dallas in my HR role at a leading insurance company because I was very worried about my mom, who lived there. It was June 2024, but she'd been having issues with high anxiety and forgetfulness for around two years. She'd always been very neat. Then she was the opposite. Mom started to become overwhelmed Stacks of papers started to pile up in her house, and she felt overwhelmed by letters from Medicare and about retirement stuff. She loved decorating for each new season, but her fall decor stayed up for a year. What is your situation regarding long-term care for yourself or your loved ones? To share your story with a Business Insider reporter, please fill out this quick form . She was referred to a neuropsychologist and failed all the tests . Then, after an MRI and a PET scan, she was diagnosed in October 2024 with Alzheimer's disease and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). Stephens noticed that her mom's previously neat house had become cluttered. Courtesy of Elizabeth Stephens I wasn't completely surprised. It was the confirmation that made me cry in the clinic. I was glad I'd made the move to Dallas, especially because I was pregnant. At first, Mom stayed in her own house, around 25 minutes away from mine. I had my son in January 2025, and later put him in $1,100-a-month day care while I worked at my office in downtown Dallas. I worked out a routine where my friend would go over and check in on her in the morning. I'd stop by in the evening after picking up the baby. I made sure she ate dinner. It was nice because she read books to her grandson, even though he was still very much an infant. Things got stressful Then, one night in October last year, as I was getting ready to leave, my mom followed me to the car, carrying a big bag. She announced she was either coming with us or wandering the streets all night. Of course, she moved into our house. Things got physically and mentally stressful as I tried to juggle my $99,000 job with my family life. I would go between my mom and my son, trying to get them dressed and breakfasted before work in the morning. She would resist getting out of bed for her day care center , which cost $90 a day, while he would run all over the place, refusing to put his clothes on. Stephens with her mom and baby son. Courtesy of Elizabeth Stephens After I'd dropped them off at their separate locations, I'd drive 45 minutes to work in heavy traffic and arrive at the office exhausted. It felt as if I'd run a marathon before I logged onto my computer. Then, I did the reverse in the afternoons before making dinner. I took shortcuts like buying all-in-one meal kits and ready meals, but they were expensive. I employed private carers for Mom to pick up the slack. A friend and a cousin did it for love and either refused payment or charged only $10 an hour. Agency rates went as high as $35 an hour. I felt relieved when I was laid off Somehow, we survived six months until March 2026. Mom had fallen at home and was in rehab when I got "the" call from work. As soon as I saw the HR VP join, I thought, "Oh, this is a layoff conversation." There had been a lot of voluntary early retirements and layoffs, and I knew I wouldn't necessarily be exempt. I was entitled to 24 weeks of severance and health insurance through subsidized COBRA. I honestly felt relief. Something had to give. And, in this case, it was my career. Fortunately, I had done a good job of saving and setting up a 401(k) plan with a decent percentage match. Stephens with her mom and son, celebrating the 2025 holiday season. Courtesy of Elizabeth Stephens Mom's Social Security , retirement funds, and Medicare just about covered her outgoings, such as the two- or three-times-a-week daycare, and I have used my severance so far. We're also considering selling or renting out Mom's house. I have made safety modifications in the bathroom, including grab rails, a shower bench, and a handheld shower. And I bought Mom a more suitable bed. Right now, my goal is to make sure she, my son, and I are all looked after. It's the reason I bring in help for babysitting and respite care. My philosophy has always been that "you can pay for peace, or live in chaos." I launched a podcast for carers The plan is for Mom, 73, to live at home with me as long as possible. When it's no longer feasible, in accordance with her wishes, I will look for a place where she can receive the care she needs. Meanwhile, I'm figuring out my next steps in my working life: something related to eldercare and dementia care . I run a monthly memory café for caregivers and their loved ones. I also launched an independent podcast to help us feel seen and heard. It's called "What Ordinary Looks Like." To me, the daily routine of caring looks a lot like love. events.title: I moved back in with my parents 3 years ago to pursue my dream career. I wish I'd considered the drawbacks first.
events.summary: Although I am grateful to live at home while I pursue a new career, I hope to move back out on my own soon. Mia Minkova At 26, I moved back to my childhood home in London to focus on pursuing my comedy career. It's been tough building relationships and reacting to rejection while under my parents' roof. I'm grateful to live rent-free and have access to London's comedy scene, but I'm ready to move out. When I walked into my first Sunday stand-up class , I had no idea it would change my life. A year and a half later, I was ready to leave my plans behind and commit to my dream of being a professional stand-up comedian — so much so that I moved from bustling Berlin to my suburban West London childhood home. I hoped being in the orbit of the clubs that launched my favorite entertainers would make it easier to land gigs with real progression and fill me with inspiration, all while being able to worry less about money and live at home in the mecca of English comedy. However, returning home at 26 after eight years of independence was a challenge. Three and a half years later, there are a few things I wish I had considered before the move. There's more opportunity in London, but also more limitations and competition I've been able to land several comedy gigs over the past few years. Mia Minkova A metropolis like London is full of potential opportunities, whereas a smaller scene can often have more accessible ones. What Berlin lacked in clear-cut paths to a professional comedy career, it made up for by offering me significantly easier chances to practice. This was largely due to the city's smaller size. I'd spend maybe half an hour each way traveling to shows, if not less, and didn't have to seek out "bringers" (audience members comedians bring in exchange for getting stage time — common in big cities like London and New York). It also felt easier to get booked for longer sets, leave as soon as I was done, or socialize after a show. Supporting new acts on the main stages, such as the legendary Cosmic Comedy, was also common. Home in London, I'm connected to the network of one of the world's great entertainment capitals and more opportunities. However, they're pretty spread out — and I now often spend way more time (sometimes up to five hours total) traveling to and from performances. I'm also dealing with more competition (not that it doesn't push me to improve), and the admin involved in booking spots in new places does take away from time I used to dedicate to writing. I've gotten used to putting on a brave face even after I've bombed on stage or received a rejection Trying not to worry my parents too much has made it tougher to wallow after a rejection or a bad set. Mia Minkova Failure is an intrinsic part of success, especially with stand-up comedy. You try a joke, and it bombs. You travel hours and hours to perform a show for free to barely a handful of people. Within the industry, these are known pain points, for better or worse. I've recognized that pursuing a career in comedy can involve a lot of rejection and many public mistakes or disappointments. However, my family hasn't, and they worry about me. It can be hard to live with parents who have only ever seen you excel academically, and therefore struggle to understand why you'd trade that certainty for an artistic path of highs and lows — especially when they immigrated for a better life, and yours can seemingly be full of obstacles. From the outside, I see how my path to this dream job can seem a little harrowing. When parents were a phone call away, it was much easier to uphold a fake-it-till-you-make-it attitude. Face-to-face, it's hard for me to hide my low moments after a not-so-great gig or rejection email. I miss being able to wallow a bit without the fear of worrying someone else. It's been hard to find privacy and deepen my personal relationships People often ask how living with my parents affects my private life. Well, I'll say this: I'm currently single. Out of choice (I didn't say whose choice). I'm lucky to say I've never felt awkward going out on dates. Of course, bringing anyone home is a different matter. C'est la vie. Ultimately, I've prioritized my dream career over dreams of living in a rom-com. I don't believe that all art must come from heartbreak, but the thrill of romance is undeniable, and it is a fire that's become a little harder to kindle. My friendships have also been affected, as most of my friends don't live nearby. Girls' nights have dwindled, though having stand-up obligations in the same evening window certainly hasn't helped. Unfortunately, it's taken me a long time to realize that having a rich private life is essential to making art. In some ways, writing was easier when I had a more booming social calendar. There are certaintly perks, but I ultimately underestimated some of the costs of living at home as an adult Although I'm grateful to have lived at home, I'm ready to branch out. Mia Minkova I'm grateful to have lived rent-free for several years. It's given me a creative runway to instead put my money into improv courses, writing classes, and even into my first full split bill at the Edinburgh Fringe — a massive comedy festival. I've also been able to start doing spots at London clubs championing new acts, and I don't take these opportunities lightly. However, I'm ready to stand on my own again. I'm looking for a stable day job so I can move out — ideally somewhere in London closer to the action — and keep doing comedy. My creativity needs room to make mistakes, and I want a space where I can make them. Some say comedy is tragedy plus time, but I tried to rush the clock by moving home. Next time, I'd be more patient. Berlin gave me plenty of stage time, and I'm not sure I appreciated it. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The race to build autonomous war robots faces a problem that self-driving cars don't. There are no rules of the road.
events.summary: War robots have to be able to function in environments without proper roads or rules, but with plenty of chaos. Andrew Kravchenko/Bloomberg via Getty Images Militaries are increasingly using ground robots, and manufacturers want to make them more autonomous. But battlefields present challenges that self-driving cars don't face. There are no reliable roads or traffic rules, and battlefield conditions constantly change. War robots are becoming a growing presence on modern battlefields, and defense manufacturers are pushing to make them more autonomous to further reduce the risks to soldiers . But making uncrewed ground vehicles that can drive themselves into battle presents a challenge that self-driving cars don't. The number of robots in military arsenals is soaring, particularly in Ukraine, where they fire weapons, attack positions, and carry wounded soldiers , all while their operators remain farther from danger. Greater autonomy would allow fewer soldiers to operate more vehicles, let troops stay farther from the front, and allow robots to keep going when communications are disrupted. A chaotic battlefield, however, is far different from safe, well-mapped roadways. Robots have to navigate muddy tracks, forests, and dangerous terrain while facing enemy attacks. Terrain, conditions, and targets change constantly. And there are no rules. No speed limits, no predictable traffic, and no guarantee of safety. Robots work under constant threat of attack. Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images German defense technology company ARX Robotics makes GEREON robots, autonomous systems that have been used by Ukraine and procured by the UK. David Roberts, CEO of the company's British arm, told Business Insider that, when it comes to making self-driving vehicles, companies working on civilian roads face a less challenging environment. "Roads are structured," he said. "They've got rules. Roads are wide enough for cars to drive down. They have markings to tell a vehicle what to do and when to do it." In war, "there are no real rules," Roberts continued. "You don't quite know if someone's going to step out in front of you or be in the long grass in front. It's a very challenging environment in the first place to build autonomy." Mike McGinty, the CEO of British firm Digital Concepts Engineering (DCE), whose X-series ground robots have been procured by the British Army, also spelled out the differences. A street is "flat, of a guaranteed surface. It's marked. It's a track. It has a left and a right. It's signed," he said. And it's unchanging. "The same street's there tomorrow." "True autonomy is an extremely hard problem on cross-country ground," he said. "If you see a line on the ground, is it a hole, a log, a burn mark, a shadow, a crocodile, a person?" Robots are becoming a growing presence in conflicts, especially in Ukraine. Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images That doesn't mean it's easy to develop a self-driving car or taxi. "The truth is it's still extremely difficult," McGinty said, but developing autonomous uncrewed ground vehicles for war is a much more daunting task. The push for battlefield autonomy Autonomy can mean anything from following preset routes to independently navigating to a destination. Capabilities in Ukraine have grown, with AI helping robots navigate when Russian electronic warfare cuts communications. Ukraine's robots have limited but growing autonomy. Yevhen Titov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Autonomy remains limited. Roberts said that most robots in Ukraine are simply remote-controlled, with autonomy in "very niche areas," such as following waypoints if they lose their operator connection. He said autonomy needs to evolve beyond what has been demonstrated in Ukraine. The GEREON robots that ARX Robotics makes run on Mithra, a software layer that connects their sensors, AI, and autonomy functions. The "supervised autonomy allows a single soldier to task and oversee multiple systems simultaneously, delivering more mission output with fewer personnel," the company says. Roberts said the "ability to tell a vehicle to go to a certain place on the battlefield is very much where we are working at the moment." ARX's robots can already follow waypoints, detect people, avoid collisions, and make safety stops, he said. The next step is at the mission level, and he predicted that, within the next year or two, battlefield management systems will be able to tell vehicles where to go. "I don't think that this is something that anyone has actually got deployed yet, but I think there are a number of companies who are working on that sort of problem set." McGinty said Ukraine's current level of autonomy typically allows operators to control robots remotely, calling this the level of autonomy that DCE had "mastered." "Full autonomy is still a very difficult technological step," he said. "So someone will take it, but it won't be us because we're not the software company doing that." ARX Robotics' GEREON robot is used by Ukraine's forces. Angelika Warmuth/REUTERS DCE's robots can be fitted with a Marionette kit, which enables remote control and supports autonomous features, including software developed by other companies. Oleksandr Yabchanka, head of robotic systems for Ukraine's Da Vinci Wolves Battalion, told Business Insider that ground robot autonomy in Ukraine "is still in the early stages of development," but units want more to protect their soldiers. "The future of both aerial drones and unmanned ground systems lies in the development of autonomy." Multiple projects are underway. Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform Brave1's grant program, for instance, calls for "autonomous logistics" robots that can independently return to base and move autonomously if communications are lost. Ukraine has integrated AI into aerial drones , which have been more prominent in this war, as well as fixed weapons, and it is increasingly being incorporated into ground robots as the country pushes for greater autonomy in its uncrewed warfighting systems. The aim is to enable a single soldier to  oversee multiple pieces of equipment  simultaneously. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Why would anyone want a smart fridge? | Dave Schilling
events.summary: Why would anyone want a smart fridge? After a hack in France, internet-enabled appliances are looking even less appealing – especially before the holidays We are deep into the holiday season now, past Halloween and a mere two weeks away from American Thanksgiving . I’ve already given up taking care of my body, surrendering fully to gluttony, vices, and going to bed at 7pm because it’s pitch black outside. I’ve begun to hibernate like a slothful bear, my blanket and pillow never too far from my grasp. The only thing closer to my hands than my bedsheets is a slice of cold pizza. I just want to eat in peace, thank you very much. Grocery retailers are keen to take advantage of holiday-related binge eating, developing and releasing ever-more-depraved festive novelty foods to subdue us into carb-induced slumber. In the UK, Marks & Spencer is expected to unleash hoards of weird, miniature packages of comical junk, affectionately known as “ picky bits ”, to prevent your digestive system from ever idling into park. “Ham and Barber’s Cheddar Crumpets”. “Twelve Mini Chicken Kyivs”. “British Melton Mowbray pork pie”. These dishes either sound like a thing a tertiary character orders in a Harry Potter novel or the last meal of a 60s British gangster. In America, we have Trader Joe’s . There’s no fun name like “picky bits” for the plastic tubs of slop they sell in the refrigerator section. Instead, we turn to our spouses and partners and mumble: “Pick me up some of that crap.” Toffee-flavored cheddar cheese. Pumpkin spice yogurt dip. An advent calendar … for dogs. I don’t begrudge anyone for cramming their shopping carts with intentionally whimsical perishable food products for depressed people. Overeating is a better use of your hibernation time than drunk-driving into an Arby’s at 2am. This is a holiday rite of passage: the junk food gauntlet. It’s as crucial to the festive season as a decorated tree and a surplus of good cheer. But what if I told you that with the press of a button, the entire picky bits industrial complex could collapse before we even have a chance to open our canine advent calendars? In France last month, supermarket refrigerators across the country were shut off remotely by Iranian terrorists . Other European countries have been hit with similar attacks, which occasionally lead to food having to be thrown out. My entire body goes numb thinking about what it would do to US and British citizens if their supermarkets were similarly affected during the holidays. Can I muddle through another family get-together without a large, rapidly-warming bowl of chicken uncured bacon ranch dip to soothe my anxiety? Doubtful. The chaos would be unprecedented. It’d be like Judge Dredd, Blade Runner and The Purge rolled into one, but with worse catering. You might be wondering how someone even hacks a fridge. Well, industrial fridges like the ones hacked in France are operated remotely via computer. It makes some sense that large-scale operations like grocery stores need to have the ability to make temperature changes quickly, without a bunch of fumbling around with knobs and buttons. But internet-connected fridges are available to consumers, too. Refrigerators from brands such as LG and Samsung allow regular people to change the temperature of their fridge from a smartphone app. My house is not nearly big enough to require me to adjust the settings on my appliances from another room. I only have six rooms (counting the bathrooms, with which I am very familiar during the holidays). Once again, technology aims to solve a problem that doesn’t exist. All we’re doing is trying to get closer to the God-level control of everything at the push of a button. The issue with that is: if we are God to our machines, then the devil also exists, and he knows how to code. Maybe there are a few useful applications of this technology for those of us who are supremely lazy. Some fridges have cameras and AI capabilities that tell you what food is inside, so that you might maintain a clean, tidy food storage system – one that tells you when your groceries are about to go bad. As though your actual human eyes and hands don’t work. That old broccoli is in there. Do I need a computer to tell me what my poisoned nose already can sense? Yup, that’s rotten food. Confirmed. Until there’s a robot that can take the food out for me, move it to the compost bin, and hose down the interior, I’ll pass on the smart fridge. I’ve already pointed out that computers have overwhelmed our cars , but this feels far more ominous. I need my holiday trash. I need my 2,000-calorie tandoori chicken bites. I can’t function without uncured ham and swiss cheese pockets. This is existential. It goes beyond mere sustenance. This is my emotional support during trying times. If black-hat hackers can shut off my fridge and spoil my food, I might start picking my hair out or nibbling on one of my less crucial digits.

events.title: I'm a psychologist who studies couples—5 signs you've fallen into a common rut: 'It builds through small habits that each look harmless'
events.summary: Psychology and Relationships I'm a psychologist who studies couples—to avoid feeling 'quietly resentful of each other,' make 1 simple change Health and Wellness 3 habits that can help you build lasting friendships Psychology and Relationships Emotionally intelligent couples ask 1 question every morning: Psychologist Raising Successful Kids Harvard- and Stanford-trained child psychiatrist: 5 habits of parents who raise highly resilient kids Raising Successful Kids I've studied over 200 kids—parents who raise resilient, successful children teach them these 6 lessons early on Couples today, especially ones who've been together for many years, are vulnerable to a silent, almost invisible and slow-growing "relationship disease." I call this condition coexistence without contact. Couples living with this "disease" share a home, a bed and a schedule while living in almost entirely separate daily realities . In her book "Reclaiming Conversation," for example, MIT sociologist Sherry Turkle describes the modern experience of "being together, but also being elsewhere," and argues that it undermines our capacity to have the conversations that count. Real conversations require both people to be present. As a psychologist who specializes in relationships, I see couples having fewer of those real conversations and being less present with each other. They build systems for running a shared life. They work out who handles the mornings, who books the appointments, which chores belong to whom and how the week gets planned. These systems are a genuine achievement, and they're indicative of good management. But a relationship isn't a company you're trying to run. A company improves when you divide responsibilities clearly and let each person own one area. A relationship is more complicated than that. In my experience, what holds two people together is overlap, along with conversation and genuine connection. It builds through small habits that each look harmless, but get out of hand because you repeat them for a decade. In my experience, three of them do most of the damage: Giving in to exhaustion. By the end of a hectic workday, neither partner has much energy or attention left. You might default to independent phone scrolls or, at most, a conversation about the logistics of tomorrow. Adopting an over-optimization mindset. We bring the tools of work home because they solve real problems. Shared calendars and clear divisions of labor do reduce friction and boost efficiency. In private relationships, though, this can result in a well-functioning household where neither partner is particularly involved in the other's life. Avoiding friction on purpose. Couples might learn, after a few painful arguments , to steer around certain topics and conversations. Both partners might mistake less conflict for progress, even though the trade-off can be contact and connection. 5 signs you're coexisting without connection In my experience, this issue shows up in five fairly predictable ways. 1. Your conversations have stopped drifting You confirm the plumber is coming Tuesday, agree on who's collecting your daughter from band practice and decide what to do about your mother's birthday. But while you settle things and close loops, you never get to the strange thing a colleague said in a meeting, the article you read on the train or the fact that you've been contemplating leaving your job. These tangents you're missing are how you keep learning about a person you already know well. Looking at your phone can feel easier than starting a conversation. So you head to bed at different times, scroll for 20 minutes and turn the lights off without saying anything. That window when you unwind together and talk before falling asleep matters because being tired can lower your filter. People say things at 11 p.m. that they might not have shared at 8 p.m. You both know about the dentist on Thursday and the school thing on Friday because the calendar told you. Mornings become a matter of getting everyone out of the house on time, and you leave knowing your partner's schedule without knowing what they're dreading in it. A calendar can tell you where your partner will be but not how they feel about being there. You catch up on errands, admin, repairs and the people you owe a visit. Against a backlog like that, splitting up is simply the better strategy, since two people working separately cover far more ground than two people doing the same job together. But you've already spent five days mostly apart, and the weekend is sometimes the only real opportunity to close that gap. An idle Saturday might look like waste, but an "unproductive" weekend is sometimes exactly what a relationship needs. 5. You stop arguing about what to do with free time It's easy enough to go your separate ways whenever you do have downtime. You have your shows, your partner has theirs and the one you watch together is a compromise neither of you is enthusiastic about.

events.title: Bad jobs or benefits? Milburn should force employers to help the young | Richard Partington
events.summary: Bad jobs or benefits? Milburn should force employers to help the young Long-awaited final report will call for benefit cuts but lack of entry-level jobs is also driving the crisis ‘I’m scared about my future’: young people on the stress and desperation of jobseeking A generation is being sold short. Almost a million young people are not in education, employment or training (Neet). Austerity and the Covid pandemic cast a lengthy shadow, AI is upending the jobs market, and the cost of living is soaring – all under the microscope of the social media age. On Tuesday, Alan Milburn’s final report on young people and work will bring Britain to a fork in the road: either continue on this path of state and market failure or sharply change direction. It will be a big test for Andy Burnham’s government. Milburn will call for controversial benefit cuts for under-25s in exchange for a legal guarantee of a job or training. Alongside changes to education and health, his plan will take a decade to implement. Behind his argument is a principle Labour has struggled with – that restricting benefits to encourage work is a good idea. The system clearly is not working. Milburn makes the case eloquently – pointing out that for every £1 spent on job support £25 goes on benefits. But there are also important caveats: change will count for nothing unless employers play their part; half of all Neets are not on benefits, and bad jobs and a lack of entry-level opportunities are far bigger drivers of Britain’s youth jobs crisis than the generosity of the benefits system. Last week, the Bank of England deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told me Britain’s young people were bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” , with employers freezing recruitment amid the war in the Middle East. Unemployment among the under-25s has risen at the fastest rate since the 2008 financial crisis to reach its highest level relative to the total for all ages since the early 1990s. Young people now make up about 40% of all unemployment. All of this compounds a drop in entry-level jobs over the past two decades. The Saturday job died long ago, while to make matters worse, those positions at the start of the career ladder are most at risk of automation or replacement by AI. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the places in Britain with the fewest job vacancies have the highest Neet rates. Highlighting stark regional divisions, young jobseekers in Rotherham face a sixfold gap in opportunity relative to their peers in the Cotswolds. The preferred fixes called for by employers are tax cuts, looser regulations, and holding back rises in the youth minimum wage. But while policy costs are unquestionably a factor to consider, and the state could do more to help young people get ready for work, the problems go much deeper. When Milburn’s report comes out, corporate Britain will be out in force to show willing. Amazon, Marks & Spencer, Shell and Pret a Manger are among those who have already spotted the PR opportunity to showcase their efforts. But most are doing nowhere near enough. Of course it costs time and money to run youth outreach programmes, work experience schemes and to help recruits who need support to get up to speed – especially in tough economic times. But the consequences from not doing so are becoming increasingly clear. Almost half of jobseekers under 25 surveyed by the organisation Youth Employment UK think employers were unsupportive. Stories of the applications black holes and the catch-22 of companies demanding experience – even for entry-level roles – are all too commonplace. In Britain’s youth jobs crisis, issues with the quality of work on offer and opportunities for progression also play a part. Low paid, insecure jobs are rife – most notably in places with the highest Neet rates. Over the past quarter of a century in-work poverty has increased. Among working households, the relative poverty rate is almost a fifth (18%) compared with 13% in the mid-1990s. Figures this month show people’s job satisfaction has dropped to the lowest level recorded by the British Social Attitudes survey. Among young people it is particularly gloomy: separate figures show most believe that not everyone can go as far as their talent and hard work will take them. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Young people are more likely to find insecure work , only to end up jobless again within weeks. More than one in 10 are on zero-hours contracts. For many that flexibility is welcome and can be launchpad to a career – a point seized on by employers’ groups. But despite the gig economy boom of the past 25 years, Britain’s Neet rate has only fallen below 10% once. Countless studies show badly paid and insecure work is linked to poor mental wellbeing . Across all types of jobs, almost 1 million people in Britain suffer from work-related stress, depression or anxiety .

events.title: Poundland pins rescue hopes on Yorkshire Tea, Pot Noodle and Gloria Gaynor
events.summary: Chain restocks stores in operation named after singer of I Will Survive, as US owners release some of withheld funds Poundland’s under-fire US owners have released funds to help the stricken discount chain restock shelves temporarily, keeping hopes of a rescue deal alive in the run-up to crunch talks with the government. In an emergency resupply effort codenamed “Operation Gloria” by senior Poundland staff, about 16m grocery items were dispatched to 600 shops in the UK and Ireland over the weekend. The name comes from the Gloria Gaynor song I Will Survive, which soundtracked a defiant video posted by Poundland on social media showing pallets of Yorkshire Tea and Pot Noodles making their way from depots to the shelves. The US investment firm Gordon Brothers earlier agreed to unlock £21m of £50m that it had been withholding, amid accusations it was endangering the business. The money will provide breathing space while rescue talks continue, ensuring that suppliers continue sending goods to branches during the crucial pre-Christmas trading period. Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the end of last month, throwing the fate of its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers into uncertainty. Last week the chain won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors , giving it until 26 November to find a buyer. The company and Gordon Brothers are now heading for a frantic period of talks with potential buyers and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds. Discussions could be soured by allegations – denied by Gordon Brothers – that the US investment group is more interested in protecting its own interests by breaking up the business despite signs of a dramatic improvement in its trading performance. Gordon Brothers bought Poundland from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1 and claims to have rescued the company from collapse when nobody else would. However, the US business has faced criticism from MPs, who have accused it of “predatory capitalism” and extracting millions of pounds as Poundland found itself on a knife-edge. Liam Byrne, the chair of the business select committee, has likened Gordon Brothers to “the wolf of Wall Street, on the British high street”. Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures, since acquiring Poundland. Gordon Brothers has denied freezing any funds that should have been available to Poundland, and pointed to loans that it has provided to prop up the company. Reynolds plans to meet Poundland and Gordon Brothers before the deadline to stave off administration runs out, according to a report by Sky News. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He and Andy Burnham have expressed concerns about Gordon Brothers’ conduct, with the prime minister asking why the US company has yet to accept an offer for a business that employs 11,000 people. Poundland has said it is in discussions with three potential buyers. Bids from the investment groups Xyra Group Holdings and Innovest are understood to have relatively little chance of success. Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish company, is Poundland’s preferred bidder but progress has stalled over the repayment terms of a loan from Gordon Brothers. A number of high-street retailers, including Tesco, are eyeing up some of Poundland’s shops. A Gordon Brothers spokesperson said: “Funds will be released to allow payroll to be made in full this month, while additional funds continue to be released to support Poundland’s ongoing trading. “While our preference remains a sale of the whole company, we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation.” The Guardian approached Poundland for comment. The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade declined to comment.

events.title: UAE engineering firm Kent heads for record order book despite Iran war
events.summary: Kent, the Dubai-based energy engineering company owned by Saudi Arabia's Nesma & Partners , expects to end the year with a record order backlog as Gulf producers press ahead with major projects despite months of disruption caused by the Iran war. The company is on track to meet its revenue target of about $1.5 billion this year and deliver on earnings, chief executive John Gilley told The National in an interview in Abu Dhabi. The war involving the US, Israel and Iran, which began in late February, has disrupted energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and damaged critical infrastructure across the Gulf. But it has also generated a wave of work for engineering contractors with a deep presence in the region, from repairing damaged plants to building export routes that avoid the strait. Rystad Energy estimates the cost of restoring energy infrastructure damaged in the conflict could reach $58 billion. Kent is helping energy producers in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE assess damage to plants after the attacks. While some repairs are relatively minor, others require extensive planning before operations can resume. "We're very proud of the fact that we'll probably hit budget this year at a time when supply chains have been massively disrupted," Mr Gilley said. Kent's order backlog was nearly $3 billion by the end of 2025, much of it concentrated in Gulf countries, and was expected to reach a record by December. Its contracts with Adnoc Gas are progressing, including a $1.1 billion deal to expand the Asab and Buhasa gas processing plants under Adnoc Gas's $5 billion Rich Gas Development project . Supply chain bottlenecks have slowed progress, but Kent still aims to deliver on schedule, Mr Gilley said. New urgency for bypass pipelines Gulf producers are accelerating projects that allow them to export crude without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Aramco has started work to expand its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, while Adnoc is fast-tracking a new West-East pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. Mr Gilley said he did not see a major change in strategy from oil companies, but the war has transformed how such projects are viewed. "In the past, when these types of projects, which really don't add any production, are talked about, they're always on a slow burn," he said. "Now the risk rating and the benefit for the project have increased exponentially, so they're much more likely to go ahead." Kent does not expect to significantly increase capital spending next year, relying instead on its 5,000 to 6,000 engineers worldwide, including teams across five offices in India. Iraq emerges as major market Iraq is becoming a "very, very large" market for Kent as international oil companies expand their involvement in the country's energy sector. The company has a major framework agreement with Basrah Gas Company, works with BP at the Rumaila oilfield and with China's Sinopec, and has secured a new contract with BP at Kirkuk. Mr Gilley expects ExxonMobil , and potentially Chevron, to return to Iraq, creating opportunities for contractors at major fields, including Majnoon. LNG a key growth area Mr Gilley expects liquefied natural gas to remain a major growth area over the next decade, and Kent is pursuing opportunities linked to Mozambique's LNG developments. However, volatile prices complicate the long-term supply agreements needed to finance projects costing billions of dollars, he said, and contractors rarely share in the upside when commodity prices rise. "When the prices of gas and oil reduce, our customers ask us to reduce our rates," he said. "But they never get us to increase our rates when they make such profits." Kent is also expanding into data centre engineering, advising operators on grid optimisation and renewable electricity supplies. Mr Gilley said the business was "absolutely flying". "The world is addicted to two things: energy and data," he added. "The problem with increased demand for data is the increased demand for power. As an offering, we can do both." Kent has reduced its carbon intensity by 43 per cent, exceeding a 30 per cent reduction target set for 2027, and aims to achieve net zero by 2040. That does not mean retreating from hydrocarbons, particularly in the Gulf, where production costs and emissions intensity are relatively low. "We'll continue to proudly produce fossil fuels," Mr Gilley said.

events.title: 10 challenges facing the real estate industry in 2026, according to young leaders
events.summary: Business Insider's 2026 Rising Stars of real estate share the biggest challenges facing real estate. Alyssa Powell Business Insider has announced its 2026 class of Rising Stars of Real Estate. We asked 10 about the biggest challenges facing residential and commercial real estate. From AI to high interest rates and economic uncertainty, here's what they had to say. The real estate market has felt anything but normal in 2026. High interest rates and home prices have turned off many would-be buyers , even in some of the country's previously hottest markets . New taxes affecting high-end properties , coupled with broader economic uncertainty , have also prompted wealthy buyers to question whether it still makes sense to buy or invest in real estate in their cities — or look elsewhere , even overseas . These challenges are likely to carry into next year. But Business Insider's 2026 Rising Stars of Real Estate say it's not all doom and gloom. Some rising stars see a bigger role for agents as buyers and sellers try to make sense of a complicated market. Others are experimenting with AI to manage and grow their businesses. And in some markets, like Miami and New York, they say demand is picking up again. Here are what 10 of this year's rising stars say are the biggest issues facing real estate and how they think the industry will adapt. Agents can't get by just knowing the basics. Photo Courtesy of Joey Ben-Zvi Joey Ben-Zvi, founder of the real-estate firm Ben-Zvi Group, says technology has made data and information more accessible, leading some buyers and sellers to believe they can navigate a transaction on their own, without an agent. "Consumers have more access to information than ever before, which is ultimately a good thing, but access to information isn't the same as being in the trenches on a daily basis and staying deeply connected to the product and consumers, along with having the experience, judgment, and relationships necessary to navigate a complicated transaction," Ben-Zvi told Business Insider. While Ben-Zvi believes agents remain fundamental to the homebuying and selling experience, he says knowing the basics is no longer enough. "I think the industry is going through a necessary evolution," Ben-Zvi said. "Agents can no longer rely solely on access to listings or information. They have to demonstrate real value through their expertise, creativity, negotiation skills, and ability to solve problems." Data will become even more critical. Photo Courtesy of Saharsh Chordia Saharsh Chordia, the 33-year-old vice president of strategy and analytics at Cortland, said that data will become much more important. The challenge, he said, is turning the vast amount of data generated by physical assets into actionable insight. "Real estate is fundamentally a business built around physical assets, yet much of the industry's data remains fragmented and underutilized," Chordia said. "AI will play an important role, but the organizations that create a meaningful advantage will be the ones that can effectively collect, structure, and learn from information generated across their portfolios." Data centers could hurt some types of properties. Photo Courtesy of Michael Dillon Michael Dillon, a 31-year-old vice president at Prime Finance, said data centers and power-adjacent properties could drive changes in what traditional property types benefit and suffer. He noted that it's unclear how an AI-driven economy could position certain asset types over the long term. "For a lender, that means underwriting not just the building today, but folding those questions into our view of durable demand for that specific property over a ten-year horizon," Dillon said. AI is "Our biggest challenge but also our newest advantage." Photo Courtesy of Alex Dobosh Alex Dobosh, an associate director at HKS Real Estate Advisors, sees artificial intelligence as real estate's biggest challenge, and potentially one of its greatest opportunities. It's not hard to see why. Americans are turning to platforms like ChatGPT for real-estate advice, home-construction guidance, and help with the buying and selling process. Business Insider has even written about homebuyers who have successfully used AI as their real-estate agent . Dobosh doesn't see AI as a reason for agents to panic. He says it can be a powerful tool for professionals willing to embrace it. His firm is already doing so. "Our biggest challenge is also our newest advantage, which is AI," Dobosh said. "It can be overwhelming to see how it's changing our world. We are leveraging it every single day to source business and help our clients, but also because we refuse to fall behind." The wealth gap will continue to grow. Photo Courtesy of Landy Liu Landy Liu, the 33-year-old founder of Foyer, a "401(k) for homeownership," expects 2027 to be another year of affordability concerns. "We are facing a structural squeeze on consumers that is leading to a dramatic evolution of the homebuying experience," Liu said. Liu, who founded Foyer to give first-time homebuyers more support throughout the process, said a lack of affordable homes has widened the wealth gap. "The industry needs to fundamentally change to better support younger Americans and other consumers at a lower cost," he said. There's a housing shortage and an affordability crisis. "Demand continues to rise across all five boroughs, but land, construction, labor, and financing costs make it extremely difficult to build projects with a meaningful share of affordable units," McGrath told Business Insider. events.title: Minister backs legal right to job support for young people
events.summary: Watch: Pat McFadden refuses to rule out that some young people might lose benefits The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment. Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague". McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed. But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers. It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work. His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales. Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans. Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade. However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year. Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job. He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness. How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted. Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service. Watch: Helen Whately says legal guarantee of work or training for under-25s 'doesn't make sense' Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this." He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to." He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today". Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added. Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending. But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs". She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing. Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said: a sustainable reduction in welfare spending cannot be achieved in two or three years, warning that "crude cuts" to the benefits system would create other additional costs for government GPs should not be responsible for signing sick notes declaring people unable to work ministers should "look very carefully" at Labour's manifesto commitment to phase out the reduced minimum wage for those aged 18-21, adding that moves towards this had "imposed a lot of cost" on firms It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage. From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently. It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year . How have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Tell us about your experience. events.title: ‘Nobody else is going to save us’: the direct action group taking on the UK’s banks, bailiffs and water firms
events.summary: Community union Acorn is helping people fight unfair bills, AI decision-making and housing injustices as cost of living crisis deepens Y asmin didn’t expect to find herself sitting across a negotiating table from executives at one of Britain’s biggest water companies. But her growing frustration with her water bills had led her to launch a national campaign. The 34-year-old single mother from Manchester had endured unexplained charges and a nine-month wait for a water meter. She went to the community union Acorn to propose a campaign that would in time force four large water companies into negotiations. United Utilities eventually apologised for its handling of her case and credited £250 to her account. It is the latest in a series of direct actions by Acorn targeting the cost of living crisis, from challenging councils over bailiffs to confronting banks over housing policies. Rather than wait for government intervention, members say they are taking matters into their own hands and forcing powerful institutions to negotiate directly with them. “Joining the union has given me so much confidence,” Yasmin said. “Because nobody else is going to save us. We can only save ourselves, right? And save each other.” Founded in Bristol in 2014, Acorn began by organising renters against rogue landlords and evictions, before expanding into wider campaigns on cost of living. Its members propose, debate and vote on campaigns at branch level, with issues of wider significance referred to regional or national committees made up of elected members. National campaigns can also be proposed at conferences and put to a membership vote. On 20 August, Acorn staged nine protests as part of its national Dignity Not Debt campaign, forcing Yorkshire Water, Severn Trent, United Utilities and Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water into negotiations and securing concessions. Acorn state that Yorkshire Water agreed to stop sending bailiffs after vulnerable customers, while Dŵr Cymru pledged not to use artificial intelligence to make debt-collection decisions or contact vulnerable people. Dŵr Cymru confirmed discussions with Acorn. United Utilities committed to avoiding AI in customer dealings and establishing a direct route for Acorn members to resolve complaints, according to the group. The company confirmed talks and said it would review individual cases. Severn Trent agreed to explore writing off debts accumulated since September 2021 and widening access to discounted bills for low-income households, with the company confirming it had incorporated Acorn’s suggestions into its existing plans. Andy Burnham’s government has offered a £100 payment to help 20 million households with soaring energy bills, but the prime minister has since said his first budget did not go far enough. Acorn members are testing whether collective action can achieve what politicians say they cannot. In Bristol, members have spent two years campaigning against the city council’s use of bailiffs to recover unpaid council tax and other debts. After negotiations produced what they considered an inadequate offer, they voted to escalate their campaign, disrupting a full council meeting and prompting its cancellation. The council’s leader, Tony Dyer, criticised the disruption, saying it had interrupted an update on a cyber-attack affecting schools and prevented debate on furniture poverty. Sam Kidel, Acorn’s south-west area organiser, said the council had previously promised to protect people who received council tax reductions from bailiff action, but campaigners wanted those protections extended to other low-income and vulnerable residents. “There’s people getting a £30 parking fine and then it’ll get sent to the wrong address, or the person doesn’t open the letters because they’ve got mental health issues,” he said. “And then they end up getting bailiffs sent and the bailiffs add hundreds of pounds of fees on top.” Kidel said the organisation’s experience showed why members were unwilling to rely solely on politicians to tackle rising living costs. “We don’t feel like our democracy is working. If it was working, we wouldn’t be constantly being pushed into debt by energy bills, by rising council tax, by rising rents,” he said. “So we’re not going to wait around for politicians to sort that out.” He pointed to a previous national campaign against TSB, in which Acorn targeted 32 bank branches over mortgage conditions restricting the length of tenancies landlords could offer. Within days, he said, the bank entered negotiations and agreed to change the policy, a change TSB confirmed it had made in 2024, attributing it to a product review. In Leeds, Usman Akhtar, 26, the chair of Acorn’s local branch, helped organise a blockade of a Yorkshire Water facility near Bradford. Growing up in a cold, mouldy flat with his brother and single mother had drawn him into housing activism. But conversations with residents revealed how often housing insecurity was compounded by utility debts.

events.title: ‘Shameless venality’: how a flurry of lawsuits has thwarted Trump’s self-enrichment schemes
events.summary: Courts have issued stinging rebukes to president’s ‘blatant’ financial ploys as pro-democracy groups defend ‘government of laws, not of men’ pillar Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes. Several lawsuits were filed in 2026 against Trump’s schemes to benefit his bottom line by reducing potential tax liabilities, boosting his Truth Social platform financially by offering big investors early access to his posts, and helping Republicans by using federal funds to pay for highly partisan ads touting Trump’s record in the run-up to the midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered a heavy defeat. The major lawsuits against Trump’s financial ploys have been the handiwork of several nonpartisan groups including Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center. In response, judges in Florida and New York used strong language to condemn and help nullify some of Trump’s financial stratagems. Florida judge Kathleen Williams castigated a Trump scheme backed by the justice department to settle a $10bn lawsuit he filed against the Internal Revenue Service over an old leak of his tax information to the New York Times. Williams ruled that the Trump backed deal to set up a $1.8bn slush fund to pay alleged victims of political persecutions under Joe Biden and giving him immunity from IRS audits before May 2026 was “premised on deception” and a “fraud against the court”. In a separate legal blow to Trump in the closing weeks of the campaign, the president was rebuked by a federal judge in New York, for channeling $20m of public funds to run ads touting his administration’s achievements. The ads were widely attacked as campaign ads and propaganda. Former judges and ex-DoJ lawyers say that he Trump moves to boost his bottom line and political drives with backing from DoJ lawyers exemplify various kinds of Trump “corruption”. Stacey Young, a former DoJ lawyer who set up Justice Connection last year as a network to defend the justice department workforce and the rule of law, told the Guardian: “The justice department’s leadership believes it has one chief client: President Trump. They have allowed him to use the department to protect his financial interests, punish his enemies, and reward his friends. “Thanks to the efforts of some of the country’s best litigators, the people of the United States are pushing back and standing up for the ideal that we remain a government of laws, not of men.” Further, retired federal appeals court judge J Michael Luttig said: “The courts have recently begun to strike down Trump’s countless schemes of blatant and shameless venality and corruption in the forms of self-enrichment, bribery, and extortion. That is the through-line of these three cases and the numerous other cases to come.” For Luttig, the court rebuffs are part of a broader trend of federal courts also rejecting as unconstitutional major presidential initiatives including tariffs and birthright citizenship. Luttig’s analysis was underscored by a July lawsuit filed by Democracy Defenders Fund and a coalition of 35 ex-judges, including Luttig, to kill a key piece of Trump’s proposed settlement of his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS by establishing a $1.8bn fund to pay alleged victims of political persecution that could have helped some January 6 Capitol rioters. The DoJ dropped the slush-fund idea after Williams ruling and some political blowback by Congress. But despite Williams’s legal objections and sharp criticism from Democratic senators, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, a provision is still in effect providing immunity to Trump, his family and the Trump Organization from investigations and prosecutions of past tax matters by the IRS as compensation over a leak of his tax returns. In her ruling, Williams charged that the plaintiffs initiated the lawsuit “for an improper purpose – to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy for a ‘settlement’ that had no viable basis in law or fact”. Williams’s scathing opinion in mid-July noted that Trump was on both sides of the issue and that the court itself was perhaps “the victim of fraud”. Williams concluded that the plaintiffs had acted in bad faith by “collusively filing a lawsuit with claims subject to multiple dispositive defenses solely to provide cover for a collusive settlement”. Citing language from an earlier ruling, Williams said “this case is part of Mr Trump’s pattern of misusing the courts to serve political purposes”. In summary, Williams wrote, acidly, that the plaintiffs “pursued this lawsuit in bad faith for the improper purpose of dishonestly advancing a political narrative”. Trump’s lawyers in late July said they would appeal the Williams order.

events.title: Who’s duping whom? Cut-price versions of luxury items are Christmas hit
events.summary: From Aldi candles to Quince’s cashmere jumpers, cheaper dupes of high-end goods have gone mainstream. But is it fair? For fans of the festive season nothing is more Christmassy than lighting a super-sized botanical candle with its trim of orange slices and berries. But as the notes of cinnamon and clove fill the room will you be burning money spent on the White Company’s £95 “winter indulgence” candle that customers describe as the “scent of Christmas”. Or have you followed TikTok’s advice and bought the Aldi “dupe” for £25. Dupes are products that claim to offer a similar experience to a high-end item though do not claim to be that product. They were originally a Gen Z obsession but have become a mainstream shopping trend at a time of strained household finances. “No matter what age you are, how much money you’ve got to spend, everyone wants to ‘luxe it up’ with a dupe,” says Catherine Shuttleworth, a retail consultant and chief executive of Savvy Marketing. “The message is ‘why not be smart like me saving cash but still looking good’,” she says. “In the case of homewares, a high street dupe of a luxury branded candle can look and smell just as good as the real thing, and will your visitors really notice that your table lamps are from B&M not the White Company?” Dupe culture is being supercharged by social media, particularly TikTok. More than 30 million people across the UK now use TikTok each month, according to the company, with Gen-Z’ers admitting that seeing products sell out or go viral makes them more likely to buy them. Data firm YPulse has been tracking consumer attitudes to dupes for several years and Tori D’Amico, managing content editor, says: “The idea that a dupe can be a true replacement for a luxury item is still prevalent. Dupes are not shameful or embarrassing to own. Young consumers brag online about finding a good deal and share it with the masses.” YPulse’s most recent research found that 44% of UK 13- to 39-year-olds have bought a dupe in the past year. When asked, just over half (53%) of this age group agreed that “the quality of dupe/fake luxury items makes me less likely to want to purchase a real luxury item”. Dupes are particularly prominent in the beauty world but are also found in other sectors including food, furniture, homeware and designer fashion. US “dupe” retailer Quince, which sells upmarket products ranging from candles to cashmere sweaters, has just launched in the UK. Alongside each product on its website it suggests the saving you are making against more expensive brands. A £50 woman’s red cashmere jumper, for example, is pictured alongside graphics comparing it with jumpers from Cos and Reiss costing three times as much. Fragrance, in particular, is a popular target. There are more than 50,000 videos on TikTok under the combined hashtag #perfumedupe and #perfumedupes, where influencers rate imitation fragrances against famous names and tell viewers where to find them. With fragrances a sought-after Christmas gift the platform is awash with content extolling these cheaper scents. Instead of spending nearly £130 on Mugler’s Alien try Zara’s Violet Blossom for £15.99, suggests one. Or, if you can’t afford Le Labo’s Another 13, try Marks & Spencer’s Aura Ambrette, a snip at £22.50. In TikTok Dupeland budget supermarket Aldi is lauded as a perfume house with its Lacura brand tipped to offer substitutes for high-end favourites ranging from Paradoxe to Flowerbomb and Baccarat Rouge – for £7 a bottle. “These cut-price products are in focus right now as consumers look for cheaper alternatives in response to rising prices,” says Eric Mills from market research firm NielsenIQ. In a recent survey, 38% of UK consumers said that in the past 12 months they had switched to lower-priced brands to manage their shopping bills. “The buyers of these brands are often thought of as only younger consumers, but while Gen Z are key spenders, it’s millennials who account for the greatest proportion of sales,” he adds. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In a microcosm of what is likely happening elsewhere in the market, the number of people buying dupe fragrances online is up 17% in the past year which is ahead of the overall market. With the continued adoption of AI tools, Mills says: “It’s easy to imagine dupes gaining further traction, as consumers can simply ask a chatbot for a cheaper alternative to their favourite luxury scent.” With dupes copying well-known brands without pretending to be the real thing they occupy a space somewhere between authentic and fake. While consumers might love dupes, the targets are less enthusiastic. Celebrity makeup artist Charlotte Tilbury , whose £350m fortune stems from the sale of her eponymous beauty empire to Spanish fragrance and fashion group Puig, recently told the BBC that “when you dupe, you dupe the consumer”.
