events.title: Rivian, Lucid, Scout CEOs aren’t counting on Democrats to restore EV federal support after midterm wins
events.summary: The CEOs of electric vehicle makers Rivian Automotive, Lucid Group and startup Scout Motors told CNBC they're not counting on Democrats in Congress to restore federal support for EVs. EV makers have had to contend with flip-flopping regulatory help from Washington over the years. EV sales spiked last year before the Trump administration ended federal incentives of up to $7,500 to buy an electric vehicle, but they have since come down from that high. Leaders of several U.S. electric vehicle manufacturers said they're not counting on increased federal support for their businesses once Democrats gain control of Congress in January, but they said they'll gladly take it if it does happen. That was the overall sentiment from CEOs of Rivian Automotive , Lucid Group and EV startup Scout Motors during interviews with CNBC after Democrats' historic midterm election wins. "We've honestly constructed Scout from day one to be in an environment where we're not going to count on, let's say, legislation or count on things that may or may not be there," Scout CEO Scott Keogh , an automotive veteran, told CNBC on Wednesday. EV makers have had to contend with flip-flopping support from Washington over the years. The Trump administration has ended or rolled back support for climate change initiatives and EVs that were supported by the Biden administration, including an up to $7,500 customer incentive for purchasing an EV. Legacy automakers such as General Motors and EV startups alike had counted on such credits to help them boost their sales and assist in electric vehicle profitability. But now they don't have that same level of federal assistance. Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe said it's his hope that the Democratic-controlled Congress and Republican President Donald Trump can find middle ground to make progress for the EV industry, but Rivian's not counting on that. "We try not to plan for those sort of things. The reality is it's probably going to have less of an impact than we think," Scaringe said Nov. 6 following the election results. "I think we're going to actually have a lot of challenges getting things done." Fellow EV manufacturer Lucid , which is backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, is taking a similar approach. "You know, they say, 'Plan for the worst and … hope for the best.' That's all we can say," Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli told CNBC on Monday. "Anything positive, we'll take it." The lack of expected support comes as Democrats seem to be more focused on hot topics such as healthcare and data centers rather than climate change and support for alternative energy technologies such as EVs. CNBC previously reported that House Democrats plan to bring to the floor bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law last year. They also plan to focus on oversight of the Trump administration and affordability. Rachel McCleery, executive director of the nonprofit policy advisory Coalition for Reimagined Mobility at SAFE, said she believes affordability concerns also could include the cost of vehicles, including EVs. "I fully expect there will be legislative debates over what to do moving forward, including on EV and EV supply chain incentives," McCleery, a former U.S. Department of Treasury senior advisor and Ford Motor policy director, said. "Bringing down the cost of vehicles for U.S. consumers is top of mind for Democratic policymakers, and electric vehicles are a critical aspect of this agenda because of the multiple challenges greater EV adoption solves for." Scout's Keogh said if legislators decide to offer any type of support, he would prefer it to be for EV production, which could then have a trickle-down effect on vehicle pricing and help companies amid inflated costs. "I always prefer it on the production side," Keogh said. "Anything that can drive down production cost is going to, of course, get passed along to the customer." Affordability has been a concern for EV adoption as the vehicles typically cost more than traditional models with internal combustion engines. Sales of EVs spiked last year ahead of the Trump administration ending the up to $7,500 incentive after September 2025, but have since come down from that high. Cox Automotive reports the average price for a new electric vehicle as of September was more than $54,800, according to the most recent available data. That compared to the average overall industry at just over $51,100 last month. "Ultimately, incentives can help accelerate adoption, but the industry can't build its long-term strategy around them," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, Cox director of industry insight, said Friday. "The goal has to be making EVs affordable and compelling enough that they make sense for more consumers with or without an incentive."

events.title: Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on these 3 stocks for the long term
events.summary: Major indexes were volatile this week due to earnings from artificial intelligence companies, key economic releases, and the scandal involving Nvidia former CEO Jensen Huang. While short-term fluctuations could weigh on investor sentiment, it is prudent to maintain a long-term investment horizon. Investors looking for attractive long-term picks can track the ratings of top Wall Street analysts and gain key insights from their in-depth research on the macro and micro factors impacting stocks. Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance. Cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks will announce its fiscal first-quarter earnings on Nov. 18. Migration to the cloud and the rapid adoption of AI have increased demand for cybersecurity solutions provided by Palo Alto and its peers. TipRanks' KPIs tool for PANW shows the rise in the company's subscription revenue over the years, driven by the adoption of its AI and security offerings and contributions from recent acquisitions. Ahead of the upcoming earnings, Oppenheimer analyst Ittai Kidron reiterated a buy rating on Palo Alto stock with a price target of $450 . The five-star analyst said that his checks indicate upside potential from CyberArk and Chronosphere acquisitions and strength in the company's core businesses. Specifically, Kidron expects Palo Alto's Q1 FY27 next-generation security annualized recurring revenue to be about two percentage points above the midpoint of the guidance range and consensus, or $9.55 billion. He also sees nearly 1 to 1.5 percentage points of revenue upside compared to the guidance and consensus of $3.305 billion. Kidron expects management to remain conservative with its FY27 guidance and raise it by no more than the size of the quarterly beat. Additionally, Kidron highlighted that partner checks indicated above-plan performance in the quarter, driven by firewall-attached subscriptions and strength in Prisma SASE and XSIAM offerings. The analyst also expects results to gain from CyberArk cross-selling and better-than-expected performance of Chronosphere as OpenAI completes its migration. "While Prisma AIRS crossed $100M in ARR last quarter, the fastest product ramp in company history, partners still view CY27 as the first real revenue year," said Kidron. Kidron ranks No. 638 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 55% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.5%. See Palo Alto Technical Analysis on TipRanks. Next on this week's list is database software company MongoDB . Recently, BTIG analyst Gray Powell initiated coverage of MDB stock with a buy rating and a price target of $417 . Powell estimates that currently the size of the company's core addressable market is nearly $15 billion, with several tailwinds to drive more than 20% revenue growth over the next few years. Beyond its core document and vector businesses, Powell highlighted that MongoDB has exposure to about $72 billion of adjacent markets, projected to grow to about $121 billion over four years. With even modest share gains in adjacent markets, the five-star analyst believes that MongoDB can grow revenue at about a 24% annual rate over the next three years, above management's growth target of more than 20%. Contrary to the bearish narrative, Powell views AI as an emerging tailwind for MongoDB, with application modernization creating new workloads while making migrations faster and cheaper. He added that interviews with eight contacts were generally constructive and indicated faster legacy migrations, growing non-relational adoption, and early traction in Voyage AI and Vector Search offerings. Additionally, Powell sees upside to Atlas growth, driven by new products. "We see a meaningful product cycle led by MongoDB 9.0 and AMP, with Agent Engine and Atlas Infinite adding upside over time," said the analyst. Powell ranks No. 480 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13%. See MongoDB Technical Analysis on TipRanks. Membership-only warehouse chain Costco Wholesale recently announced a special cash dividend of $30 per share, payable on Dec. 4. The company also announced that its board has reauthorized a stock repurchase program of up to $4 billion, which will expire in November 2030 and replaces the current $4 billion program that is set to end in January 2027. Following the announcement, Oppenheimer analyst Rupesh Parikh reiterated a buy rating on COST stock with a price target of $1,160 . The five-star analyst said that the special dividend news is one of the key catalysts that he has been waiting for since Costco was added to Oppenheimer's top pick list in November 2025. Parikh highlighted that the special dividend the company announced is significantly above his estimate of about $20 per share.

events.title: My husband was an NFL head coach, but we raised our 3 kids with strict rules about money. Christmas meant just 4 gifts.
events.summary: Kiya Tomlin built her career around her husband's NFL schedule. Courtesy of the Tomlin family Kiya Tomlin is married to Mike Tomlin, who coached the Pittsburgh Steelers for 19 seasons. It was important to her that she maintain some independence, including financially. Too many middle-aged women feel invisible until they embrace their strength and experience, she says. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kiya Tomlin , founder and designer of Kiya Tomlin apparel . It has been edited for length and clarity. As the wife of an NFL coach , I was highly visible, but didn't feel seen. I was always acknowledged as someone's wife, and most conversations revolved around my husband's career. Even our house guests and parties became obligations tied to football, not opportunities to genuinely enjoy connecting with people. I am super proud of my husband and our three kids. But I'm more than just a wife and mother. When Mike and I met in college , I was planning to be a doctor until I realized a medical career wasn't feasible, whereas Mike's career could take him anywhere. Kiya and Mike Tomlin met in college. Ethan Miller/Getty Images That's when I started my fashion career . I'd been making my own clothes since I was 10, and fashion is a passion of mine. It was a career that I could schedule around the kids and do anywhere Mike's job took us. One of my best accomplishments is supporting other mothers I was raised by a single mom, who was a community college professor. We didn't have much money, and we were one of the few Black families in the New Jersey town where I was raised. I was also extremely small: in kindergarten, the other kids used to carry me on their hip like a toddler. I never felt like I fit in, and part of that was because I couldn't fit into or afford the clothes my classmates wore. That was problematic for me, so when I was 10, I asked my mom for a sewing machine. I started making clothes that looked like what the other kids wore, and over time I began making outfits that could help me stand out in a different way. That became my claim to fame. Today, one of my proudest accomplishments is manufacturing my clothing at my factory in Pittsburgh . My six employees who work there are all moms. Creating a flexible work environment that lets them prioritize raising their kids while also supporting their family financially has been amazing. Our family had an adjustment period after each season As Mike's career took off , football dictated everything in our lives. We built our family around that reality. During the season, Mike sometimes worked 20-hour days and slept at the training complex. Once he became a head coach, the hours were somewhat less intense, especially as technology improved. He could typically get home for family time on a Friday evening. As Mike Tomlin's career took off, his wife Kiya was at home with their three kids. Justin Edmonds/Getty Images I handled everything related to the kids. It was important to me to maintain my independence financially , emotionally, and spiritually. It wasn't always easy. After each season, there was a period of reentry. I'd spent the football season being the sole boss at home, and sometimes the way I did things wasn't the way Mike would do them. During those adjustment periods, I knew I had to relax, relate, and release. We didn't spoil our kids just because we could When I was growing up, money choices were based on a distinction: is it a want, or a need? Because funds were limited, I usually got my needs met, but often went without things I wanted. Once I was raising my kids — who are now 20, 24, and 25 — I didn't have many external financial limitations. But I didn't wait to raise spoiled kids, even if I could afford many of their wants. Mike and I often reflected on our own childhoods and took a pretty bare-bones approach with our kids. On Christmas, for example, we followed the four gift rule: something you want, something you need, something to wear, and something to read. The first year of instituting that was tough, but the kids adjusted. I'm excited to see where my strengths lead in middle age Today, I'm 52. My kids are grown, and Mike is retired, which means I'm untethered from many of the obligations that I've had for the last 30 years. I have more freedom than I've ever had as an adult. I'm excited to have this room to grow. I want to see what I'm capable of, with everything I've learned along the way. In middle age, women are finally at a point where we have experience, knowledge, and money. Yet, we're culturally overlooked. That can make us feel invisible, even when we know better. We need to acknowledge that we have this amazing set of strengths. We don't need to chase our younger selves; we need to relish the fact that every experience, challenge, and skill we've gained has made us who we are today. That principle has guided me as a designer, and now it's guiding me into the next stage of my life. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How Nvidia's scandal knocked thousands off your 401(k)
events.summary: Nvidia's near-30% stock plunge in the last month is a drag on the retirement savings of millions of Americans, many who may not realize just how much their investments are tied to the scandal-engulfed chip giant. Why it matters: Nvidia's enormous weight in popular index funds means even those who have never purchased a single share of the company could feel the pain of its corporate upheaval in their 401(k)s. The resignation of CEO Jensen Huang after he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy may have cost an average Baby Boomer thousands of dollars, according to an Axios analysis of outside estimates. By the numbers: Index funds held nearly half of the assets in large private-sector 401(k) plans in 2023, according to the Investment Company Institute. Those funds include investments tracking the S&P 500, and Nvidia accounts for roughly 8% of that index, according to Tom Graff, chief investment officer at financial planning firm Facet. That exposure rises to around 14% in growth-style index funds and can reach 25% to 30% in some technology and semiconductor funds commonly found in retirement plans, Graff said. Zoom in : For an investor with $100,000 in an S&P 500 fund, a 30% drop in Nvidia shares would knock about $2,400 off the value of that investment given an 8% S&P holding, assuming other stocks in the fund stayed flat. For a growth-style tech fund with 25% exposure to Nvidia, that decline would amount to $7,500 in lost value. An average Baby Boomer holds about $260,000 in their 401(k), according to Fidelity . A tech-style exposure applied to that amount of holdings would equate to about a $20,000 reduction. Yes, but: Remember, a drop in your investment's value doesn't mean you've actually lost that cash — unless you sell your holdings. Zoom out: The potential fallout extends beyond Nvidia itself. About 40% of the S&P 500 is tied to the AI buildout, for which Nvidia is central, providing much of the financing and infrastructure needed to fuel the tech boom. If Nvidia's troubles slow the pace of AI data center investment, the damage could spread to other stocks held in Americans' retirement portfolios, analyst Bob Iaccino notes to Axios via message. "A lot of people are starting to realize just how much Nvidia exposure they have in funds they thought were diversified," Graff told Axios. "You don't want too much of your retirement riding on whether Nvidia has a successful transition to new leadership or not," he added. Reality check: While Nvidia has come to define the AI trade, its competitors have also emerged as potential beneficiaries of the stock's decline. "The mindset has flipped very quickly to 'who might benefit from this?'" Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers told Axios. Chip-company AMD's stock went on a run, rising by more than 30% in a five-day stretch last week, contributing to a broader run in the semiconductor sector. Nvidia makes up a sizable portion of many semiconductor indices and ETFs, showing how rotation can keep bull runs alive even as single stocks falter. Hyperscalers with their own chip ambitions , which at times have looked competitive with Nvidia, have also beaten the growth of the S&P 500 index over the last five days. Reality check: For those who are direct shareholders, the widely held financial advice would always tell you not to lock in losses as a stock drops. It's very unclear what the investigation will unveil. Nvidia is set to report earnings on Tuesday, giving shareholders more insight into its latest quarterly performance. The bottom line: Americans don't need to own Nvidia shares directly to have their retirement savings tied to the company's successes, or failures.

events.title: I loved living in NYC and thought I'd stay forever. As my life changed, however, so did where I wanted to be.
events.summary: The author, left, thought she'd always want to live in New York. Courtesy of Hannah Howard I'd always wanted to live in New York, and when I finally did, I felt like I'd won the lottery. I loved so much about the city and thought I'd call it home forever. However, as my life changed, so did where I wanted to live. When I was in my early 20s, working at a tiny cheese and wine bar in Hell's Kitchen, my boss told me something I've never forgotten: New Yorkers aren't necessarily born in New York . They're born all over the world, but New York is in their hearts. I knew exactly what he meant. New York had been in my heart for as long as I could remember. I first visited when I was 7, sleeping on the couch of my aunt and uncle's West Village apartment. I remember begging my mom for a fluffy pink scarf from a street vendor. She said yes, and I wore it proudly as we wandered the crowded sidewalks. I loved the noise, the energy, the sheer number of people going about their lives. I loved that you could be almost anyone, dress almost any way, and still have to work pretty hard to be considered even a little bit weird. I decided then that I would live there someday. Getting to New York felt like winning the lottery When it came time to apply to colleges , I looked first at schools in Manhattan. Getting into Columbia felt like winning the lottery. I was the luckiest girl in the world, headed for the city I'd dreamed about since I was little. After graduation, I spent a few years in Los Angeles and Philadelphia. Both had their charms, but when a job brought me back to New York , it felt like a homecoming. The author loved living and working in New York. Courtesy of Hannah Howard I've always found something oddly soothing about New York's frantic pace. My brain moves quickly, bouncing between ideas, worries, and possibilities. The city seemed to operate at the same frequency. Its chaos somehow quieted my own. I loved walking out my front door and immediately being in the middle of everything. I could spend an afternoon wandering without a destination and stumble upon a new favorite bakery, a strange little shop, or an unexpected conversation. Even after more than a decade, a million apartments, terrible bosses, tiny kitchens, and eye-watering rent , the magic never wore off. Sometimes I'd be walking down the sidewalk, carrying groceries or rushing to meet a friend, and I'd look around and think, I live here. That lottery-winning glee never entirely disappeared. The author moved from New York when her life changed. Courtesy of Hannah Howard Then my life began to change In early 2020, as the pandemic upended the world, my husband and I left New York for rural New Jersey. We had a baby daughter and soon welcomed a son. Our days filled with diapers, naps, playgrounds, and the logistics of caring for two little kids. Instead of crowded sidewalks, we had a backyard. Instead of the subway, a car. I loved the breathing room. But I missed New York fiercely: the spontaneity, the restaurants, the friends, the possibility waiting outside my door. I assumed we'd eventually find our way back. New York was still my favorite city. Surely that meant I was supposed to live there. Then, in 2025, my husband's job brought us to Chicago . I was excited, but figured New York would always be the place I secretly wished we could return to. Chicago gave me something I didn't know I was missing We settled in Bucktown, a neighborhood of old brick houses, leafy streets, coffee shops, and families pushing strollers. We walk our kids to school, see familiar faces at the playground, and walk the 606, an elevated trail through our neighborhood, stopping for tacos or ice cream. There's a farmers' market where I buy flowers and a bus to the Lincoln Park Zoo. Chicago has excellent restaurants , museums, and endless opportunities to explore. But there's also more room to move, less friction in everyday life. I hadn't realized how much I wanted that. Winter is long, and making a new home takes work. But I feel surprisingly rooted here. I have the energy I loved about New York, alongside a neighborhood life that feels manageable with two young kids. I can have an ambitious career, wonderful meals, interesting friends, and adventure without every ordinary errand requiring a complicated plan. I still love New York; I just don't need to live there anymore On my last trip to New York , I was in town for a conference, staying in Midtown. One afternoon, I put on my headphones and walked down Broadway through Union Square and into The Village, a route I'd traveled a thousand times before. I popped into Eataly for a gelato, weaving around tourists and people hurrying somewhere important. Music played in my ears, and my feet knew the way. I remembered the different versions of myself who had walked these blocks: the college student thrilled to be here, the aspiring writer figuring out what came next, the newlywed. I missed my kids, back home in Chicago. I felt nostalgic for the city and those earlier versions of my life. But alongside that nostalgia was something unexpected: complete contentment. I was so happy to be in New York. And just as happy that I didn't live there anymore. The city hadn't lost its magic. I'd changed. I wanted to walk my children to school, know my neighbors, and have space for the ordinary pleasures of family life. I wanted a city that felt exciting without making everything quite so hard. For years, being a New Yorker was an important part of how I understood myself. I liked what it said about me: that I was adventurous, ambitious, curious, and willing to embrace a little chaos. But those qualities didn't disappear when I moved away. I can still love New York, visit often, and feel a jolt of happiness every time I step onto its sidewalks. I can still be the little girl in the fluffy pink scarf, dazzled by all that possibility. And I can be just as happy to go home to Chicago. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: ‘We are losing ground’: Professors log 55-hour weeks as pay stagnates and states question their workloads
events.summary: Public universities helped make American higher education a draw for students and researchers worldwide. Now lawmakers and governing boards from Kansas to Utah want proof that the professors who teach there work hard enough. Faculty say the premise is backward. Professors who spoke with Fortune describe 55-hour weeks, departments that have shrunk by as much as half, and raises that haven’t kept pace with inflation. “We are losing ground,” said Renita Coleman , a journalism professor at the University of Texas at Austin. As scrutiny of higher education grows , state legislators, governing boards, and administrators have started questioning how professors spend their time and whether they deliver enough for their salaries and job protections. Some have pushed to limit tenure . Others are demanding a detailed accounting of faculty responsibilities. Critics see tenure as a shield for underperformers. Faculty say that misreads the job Public confidence in American higher education has fallen sharply over the past decade. According to Gallup , 38% of Americans expressed a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in higher education in 2026, down from 57% in 2015. The share expressing very little or no confidence rose from 10% to 25%. The weakening trust comes amid a convergence of concerns, from rising college costs and questions about the value of degrees to political battles on campuses . Those frustrations have fueled skepticism of tenure, which grants professors permanent faculty status after they meet a university’s standards for teaching, research, and service. Tenure was designed to safeguard academic freedom. But the American Council of Trustees and Alumni acknowledged in July that the public increasingly sees it as “a mere promise of job security, even for incompetent or unproductive professors.” Against that backdrop, lawmakers and university governing boards in states including Wisconsin , Utah , Ohio , and Kansas have moved to tighten faculty accountability. They have imposed minimum teaching loads, more rigorous post-tenure reviews, and other requirements to ensure professors do their share. For Coleman, the assumption that professors ease up once they earn tenure couldn’t be further from reality. “If they would only follow us around for a while, they would see this is ridiculous,” she said. “The pressure, the way they think, as soon as we get tenure, you’re going to stop working.” Earning tenure can take half a dozen years, and by then the pace of the job is habit. The idea of slowing down can feel almost foreign, Coleman said. “By the time we get tenure, we’re so ingrained in this, we can’t stop,” she said. George Dehner , a history professor and department chair at Wichita State University, said the scrutiny often starts from a basic disconnect about what professors do. “If you think the faculty are scamming you and don’t really work hard…this idea that faculty are working four or six hours a week teaching classes is a deep misunderstanding of what faculty do,” Dehner said. He and his peers “easily” work 55-hour weeks, he added, though their contracts stipulate 40-hour weeks during the nine-month academic year. Kansas now requires written work plans and five-year reviews for tenured faculty Many universities have long used a rough 40-40-20 model for faculty time: 40% teaching, 40% research, and 20% service to the institution and broader community. In January, the Kansas Board of Regents, which governs the state’s six public universities, put those expectations in writing. Under its new policy , faculty at the three research universities (the University of Kansas, Kansas State, and Wichita State) must devote 40% to 55% of their workload to teaching, 35% to 45% to research, and 5% to 20% to public service. At the three regional universities, teaching rises to 60% to 75%. Every faculty member now needs a written work plan, and annual reviews are mandatory. Those who fall short of workload expectations are placed on an improvement plan, and tenured faculty with two consecutive unsatisfactory annual reviews face dismissal, reassignment, or an additional one-year improvement plan. Tenured faculty will also undergo a comprehensive peer review every five years, down from every seven. Dehner described the policy as a concession to lawmakers who had pushed to give the regents greater authority to revoke tenure . Rather than protecting faculty, he argued, the new requirements reflect the same suspicion that professors aren’t doing enough. “It is absolutely not welcome,” Dehner said. “It comes from a space where there’s a deep suspicion that faculty don’t do anything… that’s a bad-faith place to start. This belief that faculty are lazy and are scamming them [is] compounded by the fact that they have no idea what higher education people do.” Gamal Weheba , an engineering professor at Wichita State, also sees the policy as an attempt to appease legislators rather than a meaningful measure of productivity. Academic work, he argued, can’t be measured by hours spent in a classroom or an office. “It’s not just an idea of having a time card that I clock in and clock out before I talk to students,” Weheba said. “That can never happen.” The Kansas Board of Regents did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment. At a January meeting, Regent Matt Crocker said the new policies strengthen accountability for state higher education spending, the University Daily Kansan reported . “The question I seem to get all the time, especially being here in Topeka, is making sure I’m being a good steward for the state’s funding for higher education, and I think the program and policies help answer that question,” Crocker said. More work to go around, and fewer tenured professors to do it For faculty, one of the biggest frustrations with the new mandates is that they’re being asked to do more without more colleagues to share the load. When Coleman started teaching at UT Austin in 2005, her department had roughly 25 full-time tenured faculty members. Today it has about 18, a decline of roughly 28%. The same pattern shows up in Kansas. Dehner said Wichita State’s history department has shrunk from about 17 faculty members when he joined in 2004 to roughly nine today. In Weheba’s engineering department, the count has fallen from about 14 to eight. Nationally, about 32% of faculty members held full-time tenured or tenure-track appointments in fall 2023, down from about 53% in 1987, according to data from the American Association of University Professors (AAUP). The shrinking ranks matter because tenured faculty carry duties well beyond the classroom. They serve on university committees, advise students, help colleagues pursue research funding, and sit on search committees for new university leaders, a particularly time-consuming job amid the revolving door of college pre

events.title: An elite matchmaker says executives' biggest strength at work can make dating harder for them
events.summary: Talia Goldstein, Founder of Three Day Rule Matchmaking, says that successful executives can struggle with dating. Cadie Thompson/ Business Insider Having a high-paying job with power doesn't necessarily translate to an easy love life. The founder of Three Day Rule Matchmaking said execs can struggle with dating because it requires relinquishing control. She coaches busy leaders to slow down, open up, and trust the dating process. When it comes to finding love , successful executives often struggle with one thing they can't control: chemistry. In business, executives are used to getting what they want, they know what their end goal is, and they know what work needs to be done to achieve it, Talia Goldstein, founder of Three Day Rule Matchmaking, told Business Insider. But this strength in their professional life doesn't always translate to dating. "Some of the executives struggle because you can't control whether the person's interested in you, you can't control whether or not there's chemistry, and that can be very frustrating for these top executive types," Goldstein said. Goldstein said that executives hire matchmakers to help them save time and energy, two things that their job often gets the best of. But she said that her firm, which charges clients anywhere from $6,300 to roughly $100,000 depending on the membership, also provides its clients coaching to help them level up their dating game. "A lot of what we teach them is to slow down and to get vulnerable and trust the process," she said. "And that can be challenging for people who are so used to controlling their destiny." As part of this coaching, her firm also collects feedback from both parties after the date and uses that information to better understand how the client is perceived by matches. Without feedback, people repeat the same patterns and are left wondering why they can't land that second or third date, said Goldstein, whose firm's clients are split roughly evenly between men and women. "With matchmaking, we know exactly why. So it ends up making the process more enjoyable. And also you learn so much about yourself in this," she said. "I think it's the most valuable part of the service." Goldstein shared an example of a successful entrepreneur her firm worked with where every date he came back from the women would express liking him, but would then say the interaction felt more like one with a friend. Goldstein said the team was stumped as to why none of the women they were setting him up with were working out. Thanks to the feedback sessions, they soon learned their client was ending each date with a handshake instead of a hug. "That just felt like a business transaction and nobody was interested," she said. "And that one small change made such a difference. But on your own, you would never have figured that out." events.title: Ukraine's war robots are starting to down Russia's drones. It could eventually change the fight in the kill zone.
events.summary: Ukraine's war robot makers are increasingly looking at how the unmanned vehicles can stop drones. STR/NurPhoto via Getty Images Ukraine's war robots are starting to down Russian drones to defend themselves. They could eventually provide mobile air defense for soldiers in the kill zone. But the technology is still emerging, and widespread deployment remains a challenge. Ukraine's robots are increasingly able to down aerial drones, a capability that could eventually help soldiers move and fight in some of the war's most dangerous areas. The skies in Ukraine are full of surveillance and strike drones that make movement risky, particularly in the kill zone surrounding the front lines. Ukrainian units are increasingly trying to use robots there instead of humans, and companies are giving robots new abilities to take down drones. Oleksandr Yabchanka, head of robotic systems for Ukraine's Da Vinci Wolves Battalion, a prominent Ukrainian military unit, told Business Insider that Russian drones are one of "the key challenges" on the battlefield, and "I believe that ground-based robotic systems can play a significant role in addressing this issue. " With effective protection against those drones, he said, "the nature of combat operations along the line of contact could change substantially." He called defending the "low sky" by countering enemy drones a promising role for ground robots . Ukraine's skies are so full of drones that gaining a new way to combat them is a big advantage. Florent VERGNES / AFP via Getty Images Beyond leading front-line operators, Yabchanka also co-founded Defence Robotics UA, a non-profit that helps Ukrainian units adopt robotic technologies. "I have particularly high hopes for the use of ground-based robotic systems in defending the low-altitude airspace," he said. The kill zone Inside the kill zone, drones complicate movement, so robots are taking on new roles in logistics, casualty evacuation, and more. Some of these systems are equipped with weaponry and jamming equipment to take down hostile drones. Robots equipped for counter-drone missions could reduce the demand for short-range air defense units, which provide cover for infantry moving in and out, in the kill zone. Right now, these units face great danger and risk getting pinned down inside. These robots could also defend themselves as Russia increasingly targets them. Ukraine's ground robots are taking on more battlefield roles, including in taking down enemy drones. Diego Herrera Carcedo/Anadolu via Getty Images Mykyta Rozhkov, chief business development officer at Ukrainian robotics and technology company Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that robots are "becoming a main target" for Russia and are defenseless without added protections. Giving robots the ability to defend themselves could make them more survivable, while turning them into mobile air defenses could help protect troops. Rozhkov said makers are now "trying to find a way how we can defend against FPVs." Yabchanka said that when it comes to changing the kill zone, "it would be incorrect to promise that this will happen specifically within the next 12 months." But he said robots have already successfully stopped some drones, and "I believe this field has a great future." Robots vs drones Most of the technology in this space is still being tested or used on a limited scale, primarily to protect the robots themselves rather than provide broader air defense. Rozhkov said that while it's key to have uncrewed ground vehicles be capable of defending themselves, he expects to eventually see UGVs functioning as a mobile, short-range air defense system to try to clear the skies. His company is working with a partner on a system that uses cameras and sensors to find hostile drones and then engages them with a separate capability. He didn't disclose how it would engage enemy drones. Ukrainian soldiers' movement is limited by Russian drones and artillery, and robots helping able to combat those drones could help in the war's most dangerous areas. ARIS MESSINIS/AFP via Getty Images Other Ukrainian robot makers are also adding anti-drone capabilities, some involving smoke, nets, and shrapnel solutions. Robots are increasingly being fitted with weaponry like machine guns, and some companies have said that these weapons can stop enemy drones. Ukrainian company UFORCE, for instance, says it has destroyed enemy drones in ambush scenarios. The company's AI-assisted Predator weapons station can be mounted on robots to track and fire at drones. The 42nd Separate Mechanized Brigade previously described a machine gun mounted on a Liut robot shooting down Russian drones. Rovertech, which advertises itself as making "robots for the kill zone," is developing a system that uses sensors, AI-assisted detection, and a net launcher to stop incoming drones, while Ratel Robotics has started serial production on a protective system that includes net launchers on its robots. Ukraine's 100th Separate Mechanized Brigade said last month that it had deployed an active protection system using net launchers and shared a video showing one of its robots firing a net at an approaching drone, which then crashed to the ground. Some Ukrainian units have also driven robots carrying electronic warfare equipment forward to jam Russia's drones, but it's an emerging capability that has yet to see widespread use. Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, says armed robots are starting to be used against aerial drones, but it wants more, describing anti-aircraft weaponry and protection as priorities. Rozhkov said that soon, Ukraine's robots will have "more and more sophisticated solutions" to stop drones. He said it's essential because the first side that figures out how to stop small FPVs "will gain a huge advantage on the battlefield and can create dramatic results." events.title: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? | John Harris
events.summary: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? Nearly 2 million children are housed in dire conditions, anxious families are living out of carrier bags. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised T wo days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.” In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar era”. But by that point, he had also served notice that his commitment to a thoroughgoing council house revival might not be quite as cast iron as it seemed. The previous month, having insisted that all of the £39bn Rachel Reeves had promised to spend on the Starmer government’s Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) until 2036 should go on homes for social rent, he made something of a brazen U-turn , announcing that the allocation of the first £10bn would reflect the existing social homes target of 60%. But this was leavened with another bit of old-time Labour religion : “Councils built this country out of a housing crisis once before. Backed properly, and trusted to get on with it, they will do it again.” The clock, however, is loudly ticking. John Healey’s underwhelming budget could only find an extra £1.5bn for social and “affordable” housing – which, apart from anything else, once again underlined the fact that the latter term is often all but meaningless. Thanks partly to a downturn in private housebuilding, Labour’s manifesto promise to oversee the building of 1.5m new homes of all kinds in this government’s first term is simply not going to happen . All this feels as if it symbolises how swaths of Burnham’s policy agenda still seem to be missing, fiscally strangled, or in a frustratingly early stage of development. But hope remains alive: the unveiling of his 10-year plan – which he insists will appear this year – could conceivably flesh out the kind of ambition we heard from him over the summer, as could next year’s spending review (note: I try hard to sound optimistic sometimes, and that is this week’s attempt). At root, this is a story about people’s lives. It centres on depressed and anxious families living out of carrier bags and constantly moving from one friend or relative’s home to another, and thousands of children trying to lead relatively orderly lives amid the chaos of temporary accommodation. About 1.7 million children live in damp, mouldy, cold, or otherwise non-decent accommodation. Given that Alan Milburn’s report about young people and employment will apparently be published on Tuesday, we should also remember that the sheer impossibility of owning or even renting a secure home is a huge part of the reason why 16- to 24-year-olds feel so estranged and alienated from the everyday world of work, earning and somehow making a life. As Aneurin Bevan famously said, the language of priorities is the religion of socialism, and this one is self-evident. So where are we? Since Labour took office it has made some good moves: introducing restrictions – with more to come – on the right to buy scheme whose various iterations have so depleted our housing stock, increasing rents to boost social housing revenues and, perhaps most significantly of all, returning at least part of the political conversation to such matters. The biggest step of all, though, is the SAHP , and the billions beginning to be spent on it. That may sound impressive, but the first results of that programme are unlikely to even start to be seen until 2029 or so. Besides, the consensus among housing insiders is that on the optimistic reading, even if everything works out – which is dependent, among other things, on Labour winning another election – the result will be about 19,000 new social homes a year, totalling just under 200,000 in all. I am sure that everyone who works at the housing charity Shelter is now sick to death of reciting this statistical counterpoint , but they believe, quite rightly, that in order to meet the UK’s dire level of housing need, at least 90,000 new social homes need to be built each year between now and 2036, which is some indication of the gap between official policy and cold reality. History, moreover, suggests that our ambitions should be even greater. I have spent the last week immersed in Michael Foot’s magisterial biography of Bevan, the postwar Labour government’s health and housing secretary.

events.title: Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot
events.summary: Anthropic's IPO comes at a tough moment for the tech industry, which has been hammered by bad news, from struggling neoclouds to the crisis at Nvidia. Leading chipmakers and internet giants need the IPO to go well, as Anthropic has $900 billion in spending commitments, including $110 billion over 10 years with Amazon. "The numbers are just staggering," said Joe Fath, an investor at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager. Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , the tech industry is under mounting strain. Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market. With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon , whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars. In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic's spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI, are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process. Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus . It's on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google , though delivery won't start until 2028. "The numbers are just staggering," Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. "It's hard to get your head wrapped around it." Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips. By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic's $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments. The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time. "Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract." Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future. "In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus. Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment. It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025. Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds , which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country. Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress , who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.

events.title: Space data centers could end stargazing as we know it
events.summary: Sprawling networks of space data centers could make it nearly impossible for humans to stargaze. That's just one of the many risks that come with placing tens of thousands of AI computers into orbit, according to a new report. Why it matters: Most Americans don't want data centers built near them, but putting them in space brings a new set of problems. Threat level: "Companies and policymakers should proceed with great caution," top academic researchers warn in a report for the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum, an annual event hosted by the Japanese government. If space data centers proliferate, the "most visible points of light in the sky during much of the night in much of the world could be satellites, not stars," the report said, mirroring astronomers ' worries. If the U.S. military adopts the technology, the data centers could become potential targets during future space conflicts . Thousands of orbital data centers whipping around the Earth at 17,000 miles per hour mean a growing "risk of collisions" and dangerous space debris . Space data centers are solar-powered, but the vast number of rocket launches needed to put them in orbit generate greenhouse gases and black carbon emissions . What they're saying: Columbia University's David Sandalow, the report's lead author, told Axios there are still "unknown unknowns" about space data center impacts. "If this is going to happen, it should happen slowly and with care," Sandalow said. "Not just launching lots and lots of these things and, kind of, seeing what happens. ... There's big risks." By the numbers: Despite those concerns, investors and tech innovators are all in on space data centers. In 2025, around $197 million in investments were tied to orbital data centers, per market research firm Quilty Space. That figure has swelled to $1.11 billion so far this year. SpaceX has applied for a constellation of 1 million data center satellites, according to the Secure World Foundation . Starcloud and Blue Origin's Project Sunrise have ambitions for 88,000 and 51,600 satellites, respectively. Yes, but: Caleb Henry, Quilty Space's director of research, said that companies may be filing for more satellites than they will likely field. "They don't want to have to bump the number higher up later on," he said in an interview. "We're at a point where people are tallying paper filings as if they are substantive and real," Henry said, "and we just don't know that yet." The bottom line: Researchers warned that governments and companies need to wait until space data center "risks and impacts are better understood and well managed" before putting them in orbit.

events.title: Is Nvidia cooked without Jensen Huang?
events.summary: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . A post-Huang era We're about to learn just how much one person truly matters to the AI economy. Jensen Huang was larger than life at Nvidia. He was the AI boom's most recognizable evangelist, the chip maker's chief visionary and dealmaker, and the force behind Nvidia's ascent to the most valuable company on the planet. As Zak Jason writes, the cult of the tech founder has very much become America's religion . And Huang was "its most convincing saint." A week ago, Huang admitted to an affair and apologized to his family. Nvidia disclosed it was investigating whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. And then The New York Times reported a second affair, this one with an Nvidia executive who was one of Huang's direct reports. He resigned on Thursday. Huang's abrupt downfall is a stress test of founder worship. The market put a price on it: Nvidia's market cap tumbled $573 billion last week, more than all but 18 companies in the entire S&P 500. "It's like the Bulls without Jordan," author Stephen Witt, who wrote a biography on Huang, said on CNBC. "I don't know how they are going to replace this guy." That is the essence of key-man risk , as my colleagues Sarah E. Needleman and Tim Paradis reported. When one leader is so closely identified with the strategy, the products, and the culture, their departure can create a vacuum that no org chart (let alone one with 60 direct reports to the CEO) can immediately fill. Much of Silicon Valley came to Huang's defense in recent days. Sarah Guo, a venture capitalist, called him "one of the most extraordinary entrepreneurs of all time." Sequoia's Shaun Maguire said Huang's "contributions to American innovation and AI leadership cannot be overstated." A petition to reinstate Huang as Nvidia CEO circulated over the weekend, collecting more than 100,000 signatures, including those of Elon Musk and other prominent figures. Our own Alistair Barr also points to new reports that are casting doubt on the intelligence behind Jensen Huang's downfall. For sure, there are several examples of seemingly irreplaceable CEOs — Steve Jobs at Apple and Travis Kalanick at Uber — whose companies still thrived under new leadership. And even some of Huang's biggest proponents aren't standing by him. "No one was a bigger defender of Jensen than I was but there are rules about sex with subordinates," CNBC's Jim Cramer said on X . "Just because someone is brilliant doesn't mean he can do what he wants." The question is whether Nvidia, which lacked a defined succession plan, can prove to be more durable than its founder's legend . If it can't? Dick Costolo, the former Twitter CEO, floated an idea . "Prediction: 3-4 years from now, [Nvidia] will miss a quarter or two, and they will bring Jensen back to run the company," he said. "Like fame, everybody is outraged for 15 minutes, and there is nothing Americans love more than the comeback story." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Gen Z shatters America's political orthodoxies
events.summary: Young Americans are challenging beliefs their parents and grandparents once considered sacred — from socialism and Israel to Christianity . Why it matters: Neither party can count on old political loyalties to win over a generation increasingly willing to break with the past. Socialism: 35 years after the Soviet Union collapsed, some 57% of Americans ages 18–34 view socialism positively, compared with 43% for capitalism, according to a September 2026 Gallup poll . Among Americans 55 and older, 65% view capitalism positively, compared with 34% for socialism. Israel: Decades after Israel fought wars against neighboring Arab states, some 53% of Americans ages 18–34 sympathize more with Palestinians, compared with 23% who sympathize more with Israelis, according to Gallup's February 2026 survey . Christianity: After centuries as the overwhelming religious identity of Americans, only 54% of Americans ages 18–29 now identify as Christian, compared with 76% of those 65 and older, according to nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute's 2025 Census of American Religion , released in April 2026. Between the lines : The return of forces that voters haven't felt in generations can scramble their priorities all over again. After decades of relatively low inflation, prices surged during the COVID era, with annual inflation hitting 9.1% in June 2022 — its highest rate since 1981. In 2024, young voters who ranked the economy and jobs as their top issue favored Trump by 24 points , according to CIRCLE's analysis of AP VoteCast. Two years later, 78% of financially struggling young students backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 16% for Republicans, according to a November 5 CIRCLE analysis . State of play: Young voters showed both parties how quickly their support can shift between elections in last week's midterms. Some 66% of voters ages 18–29 backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 31% for Republicans, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE , citing preliminary NORC data. That 35-point Democratic advantage compares with a 14-point margin in the 2024 House election, according to separate Edison Research exit polling. Trump's 2024 gains among young voters , especially men, now look less like a lasting GOP realignment and more like a warning about how quickly younger Americans can change course. Zoom in: Socialism's fading stigma reached the ballot box in America's two largest cities. Democratic socialists now stand poised to lead New York and Los Angeles after Nithya Raman defeated Karen Bass in Tuesday's mayoral election, joining New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both built campaigns around affordable housing and inequality, tapping into younger Americans' financial frustrations. The bottom line: Young Americans aren't necessarily embracing socialism because they've rejected their grandparents' Cold War beliefs, PRRI CEO Melissa Deckman told Axios. They're questioning capitalism because their own economic experiences have left them disillusioned. "What they're seeing isn't working, and the American dream is increasingly out of reach for them," said Deckman, author of " The Politics of Gen Z ."

events.title: Nvidia's next CEO will inherit more than Jensen Huang's job
events.summary: Huang's exit leaves his successor with the task of rebuilding the trust of Nvidia's tens of thousands of employees amid intense public scrutiny. Getty Images Huang's exit leaves Nvidia's next CEO with the challenge of rebuilding trust and refocusing workers. His successor will need to keep day-to-day operations humming amid intense public scrutiny. Companies can't let extraordinary results be a license to follow different rules, a former Netflix talent exec said. During an NBA tech summit last year, former CEO Jensen Huang described having a management style at Nvidia built on open communication. "I spend all of my time being transparent," said Huang, who has long been lauded for steering the chipmaker's extraordinary rise. Now, reports of Huang's extramarital affairs — with a direct report, another employee, and a client suspected by US intelligence officials of spying for China — have exposed a gap between his professed commitment to candor and how he may have acted behind closed doors. Huang's exit leaves Nvidia's next CEO with a difficult task: rebuilding the trust of tens of thousands of workers at a company at the center of the AI boom . "When the CEO is having a romantic relationship with someone at the company, that can erode trust and engender cynicism," said Kim Scott, a former Apple and Google executive and cofounder of executive education company Radical Candor. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Refocusing on the work Huang ran Nvidia with a flat structure at the top, a setup he credited with helping the company move quickly. He worked out of a conference room, not a private office, and had dozens of direct reports. Nvidia didn't have a publicly disclosed succession plan. C-suite observers have said that the halo surrounding a successful tech founder, combined with an org chart light on top layers , can leave a company with a thin succession bench. After Huang's departure Wednesday, Nvidia appointed Colette Kress, chief financial officer, as interim CEO . The company launched a search for a permanent replacement, including both internal and external candidates. Kress, as well as whoever ultimately takes the reins permanently, will likely face a number of challenges. "The first thing employees want to know is: Is the company in good hands and will it continue to do well?" said Scott. "A lot of people are holding unvested options worth millions of dollars." Nvidia's new boss will have to navigate the intense public scrutiny surrounding Huang's exit, while ensuring day-to-day operations remain humming. "The combination of keeping people focused on the work while not pretending that the circus outside doesn't exist is really, really hard to do," said Katie Burke, chief operating officer of legal AI company Harvey. 'A grief process' There are no quick fixes in this situation. "Trust can be violated very quickly, but it's rebuilt slowly and consistently," said Alison Fragale, an organizational psychologist and professor of organizational behavior at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. The chipmaker's new leader will also need to help employees cope in the aftermath of the scandal and get back to work. That may be especially difficult for those who admire Huang and wanted him to stay, added Fragale. "It's like a bit of a grief process," she said. Meanwhile, other employees may be feeling betrayed or unsettled by the intense public scrutiny. "You can't pretend that everyone's family is not asking them what's going on," said Fragale. Nvidia's next leader will have at least one advantage in healing the company's culture, said Jessica Neal, a former chief talent officer at Netflix. Huang's departure shows that despite all of his achievements, he is still facing consequences for violating company standards. "One of the biggest mistakes companies can make is confusing extraordinary results with the permission to behave differently," Neal said. "Every time you make an exception for a high performer, you're sending a message to everyone else about what really matters. And over time, those exceptions become the culture." events.title: Binance targets full reopening of withdrawals by next week
events.summary: Binance said on Nov 14 that it aims to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week. SINGAPORE – Binance said that it aims to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week, as operations normalise for the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange after a security breach linked to North Korea saw US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) stolen from the platform in October . The company said on Nov 14 in a post on X: “This week, we reopened withdrawals for 87 networks. We will aim to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week.” Binance resumed withdrawals in phases earlier in November , after covering 95% of the US$6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform in what experts described as the largest cryptocurrency theft. The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the Binance hack, but Pyongyang has denied that. Blockchain investigation firms have attributed it to a North Korean group known as “TraderTraitor”. In its initial report on how hackers pulled off the heist, Binance detailed a multi-stage hacking endeavour that began in June and set off a series of security breaches culminating in the theft on Oct 29. The theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay customers in full. The company’s finance chief Kaiser Ng left the company just over a week after the heist , to pursue a new venture after more than five years at Binance. He was replaced by long-time finance executive Justin Yek, who was most recently vice-president of finance at Airwallex. Cryptocurrencies tumbled over the weekend, with Bitcoin slumping to a four-month low. The largest digital asset sank 5.7% in the US on Nov 14 and continued to drop in Asia on Nov 15 to as low as US$62,112, down a further 3.6% and its weakest since July 14. Second-biggest token Ether, which slumped 8% in the US session, fell another 3.4% on Nov 15 to US$1,711, its lowest since July 8. Crypto has been pummelled in recent weeks by a confluence of factors, including the expectation of higher interest rates, large outflows from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, an AI-fuelled risk-off mood and continued fallout from the recent US$6 billion Binance hack. Bitcoin has slumped about 25% since Oct 21. Its low for 2026 is US$57,742, reached on July 1. Large liquidation events – in which more than US$500 million worth of Bitcoin positions are wiped over 24 hours – are becoming a recurring feature in the market, as sharp swings repeatedly flush leveraged traders out of their bets. On Nov 13 , Bitcoin’s slide triggered the liquidation of roughly US$1.3 billion in long crypto bets over 24 hours, with Bitcoin positions accounting for the majority of that sum, according to Coinglass data . In the 24 hours through 7am on Nov 15 in Singapore, exchanges tracked by Coinglass recorded about US$2 billion of crypto liquidations, including US$774 million in Bitcoin and US$488 million in Ether. Long positions accounted for the vast majority of the liquidations. From Oct 30 through Nov 13, US-listed spot Bitcoin ETFs saw almost US$3 billion in net outflows. Richard Galvin, executive chairman at crypto investment firm DACM, said the impending initial public offering of artificial intelligence company Anthropic PBC may be drawing capital away from crypto. “Price performance looks very similar to what happened through the SpaceX IPO pricing period earlier this year,” Galvin said. “It appears crypto remains a short-term funding source, particularly for retail investors. This is in addition to all the other macro headwinds.” REUTERS, BLOOMBERG

Liberty Steel Dalzell, a plate mill in Motherwell, has struggled to pay its bills and workers in recent weeks, according to several people with knowledge of operations. The government said it was “closely monitoring” the situation at the plant, amid growing concerns over its survival. The National Energy System Operator (Neso), the government body in charge of keeping the lights on, filed a winding up petition against the company last month, according to public court records. It is understood that its debt, thought to be for electricity transmission charges, has now been repaid and the petition will be withdrawn. The Dalzell plant has an order to make 34,000 tonnes of metal plate to build the navy’s fleet solid support (FSS) ships. They are due to be built in Belfast by the Spanish state-owned shipbuilder Navantia in a £1.6bn contract. The financial struggles of Liberty Steel Dalzell and its owner, the Gupta Family Group (GFG) Alliance controlled by the metals tycoon Sanjeev Gupta, have cast doubts on whether the plates will ever be made. The Dalzell mill is the only one in Britain capable of producing the plates needed, but its output has been limited for two years because of shortages in working capital. The first of the 216-metre FSS ships, designed to carry munitions, food and other supplies for the navy’s Royal Fleet Auxiliary, is planned to be delivered in 2031. The contract was awarded to Navantia in the hopes of revitalising Belfast’s historic Harland & Wolff shipyard that built the Titanic. Several people in the industry and unions believe Dalzell could be part of an integrated British supply chain if it had working capital. British Steel’s Scunthorpe blast furnaces, now under government control, could supply metal to Dalzell to make the plates that are then used in Belfast to build the ships. However, the longer Dalzell goes without producing the steel, the more likely Navantia is to source the metal elsewhere. Navantia has already said it would build the first ship largely in Spain because the Harland & Wolff shipyard was not yet ready, in comments to the Financial Times in September. Unions have called for the government to protect the Dalzell plant. Alasdair McDiarmid, the general secretary of the Community union, said: “We need to see a viable plan for Dalzell’s long-term future – the workforce deserve nothing less. If Liberty cannot produce this now, the case for government intervention will be unavoidable. We simply cannot afford to lose this crucial asset for Scotland , and for the entire UK steel sector.” A government spokesperson said: “This has been a difficult situation for the staff and local community supporting Liberty Dalzell. We want to see the company operational once more, and are closely monitoring the situation. “Navantia UK has a ‘local first’ policy when it comes to suppliers for the fleet solid support programme. Ministers have encouraged Navantia UK to use UK suppliers, including for steel, where possible.” The Dalzell plant has produced some plate in recent weeks, using steel that is said to have been sourced from Kazakhstan, but that is not suitable for the defence contract. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Workers’ pay packets have been late twice in recent months, including at the end of October. Staff are also concerned because the pension provider Aviva said it was “currently unable to accept further pension contributions into the workplace pension plans for members of this scheme”. A GFG spokesperson said the company was “engaging with Aviva and the Pensions Regulator to fix this as quickly as possible”. It is also understood that the company providing security to the Dalzell site walked away over the weekend after its bills were unpaid. Gupta’s businesses have been under financial pressure for several years because of the collapse of his main lender, Greensill Capital, in 2021. Companies within GFG remain under investigation by the UK’s Serious Fraud Office for suspected fraud, fraudulent trading and money laundering. A GFG spokesperson said: “Like the rest of the UK steel industry, Dalzell faces tough operating conditions with energy costs far higher than the prices its international competitors pay. Despite that the plant has restarted and GFG are pursuing new commercial deals to bring more volume through the mill. “The Navantia contract remains in place and Dalzell’s UK slab supplier has indicated capacity from early next year.” A Neso spokesperson said the body could not comment on specific debt recovery cases.

events.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
events.summary: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto , the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness. One month before release, it is quiet at Rockstar’s headquarters. A lot of people have finished their labour on the game and are taking time off in the run-up to launch – a well-deserved rest after more than 10 years of development. Those who remain here are caught in the strange no man’s land between finishing a piece of art and releasing it into the world. When it does come out, GTA VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of entertainment ever made, projected to shift tens of millions of copies and earn billions in its first year; its predecessor, 2013’s GTA V, sold 230m copies. In the midst of a horrible time for the games business, full of studio closures layoffs and soaring development costs, a whole industry is relying on GTA VI to give it a shot in the arm. On one near-deserted floor, a screen shows a countdown to the release date. For many players, meanwhile, the 13-year wait for a new Grand Theft Auto has become unbearable. When footage of GTA VI made its glitzy premiere on Netflix, it almost took the streaming giant’s servers down. Its first trailer has been viewed 300m times on YouTube alone. Across the world, people have booked days off work on 19 November to experience this event together – one of those increasingly rare shared global cultural moments in an age when we all live in our own algorithmic content bubbles. There is a slightly strained atmosphere at Rockstar North, and not just because of the pressure of GTA VI’s impending release. Over in Glasgow, Rockstar is also defending a high-profile employment tribunal case over the dismissal of 34 of its employees last year, who claim they were fired because they were involved in union organisation efforts . The case was due to wind up in October, but will now drag on right up to Grand Theft Auto VI’s release. A few days before my visit, head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe was testifying in court as former employees and their reps at the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) protested outside. Today, Kolbe is sitting in front of me with Rob Nelson, co-studio head of Rockstar North and one of the three creative leads on GTA VI, showing me what the studio has spent more than a decade and, by independent estimates that Rockstar will not confirm, more than $1bn making. On screen, Jason and Lucia – two young criminals on the run – are on their way from a bar to a nightclub, walking through downtown Vice City as the last vestiges of sunlight disappear and the streets become bathed in fluorescence. He is tall, square-shouldered, in a T-shirt and shorts; she has her hair up in a ponytail, wearing one of those merciless long-sleeved crop tops that almost nobody can pull off. After dancing with each other at the club, part of a crowded mass of virtual people gyrating in neon UV-reactive mesh tops, they will each don a cap, sunglasses and a bandana over the face, and hold up a jewellery store before escaping into the night in a beaten-up car, the boot stuffed with holdalls filled with cash and sizeable firearms, evading the cops by driving right through a cornfield in an apt echo of Bonnie and Clyde. Lucia is the first woman to have headline billing in a GTA game, part of a long lineage of criminal protagonists who range from the straightforwardly psychopathic (GTA V’s Trevor) to the unexpectedly sympathetic (GTA IV’s Niko Bellic, and San Andreas’s CJ). GTA VI is both her story and Jason’s.
