events.title: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
events.summary: Illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital. Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help. The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital.  When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container. “They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said. Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt their family. “Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going to give me locked up.” Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how, weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground. “I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement. “He stated many.” According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.” In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe. Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences. The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged with murder. But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell. His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.  In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to prison. A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024 — and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs while pregnant.  Courtney Haney at a family member’s home last month in Dothan, Alabama. Her daughter was born healthy, but Haney spent four months in jail for prenatal drug use. A. Wallace for ProPublica Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January 2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed the treatment offered by the court. “During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”  As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek justice in this case,” he said. Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied, “That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital. “If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email. Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her organization has identified 2,298 cases of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy. Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for pregnancy loss appear to be on the rise compared with the years before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion. “Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting worse.” Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and eye. In that time, something shifted.  “I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.  She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. She also wasn’t sure if she and her daughters could safely leave him. events.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left company in August 2025
events.summary: A woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang leaving a restaurant after attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in Taipei in May 2025. Megaspeed said on Nov 15 that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , whose ties to former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang raised US national security concerns, had officially left Megaspeed on Aug 30, 2025, and has no current role there. The Singapore-based cloud-computing company is an Nvidia business partner in the Asia-Pacific region and has been in the spotlight after reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom the US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang’s personal and private matters,” the company added in a statement. In October 2025, the New York Times reported that Megaspeed was under US investigation over whether it helped Chinese customers obtain Nvidia computer chips subject to Washington’s export controls. China has denied the allegation and Megaspeed has not been found to have violated ​the rules. “Megaspeed is aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence, ” it said in the Nov 15 statement. The company said it conducted “legitimate and lawful business” and had retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation. It added that its operations and supply chain controls were designed to comply with applicable laws and regulations, including US export-control requirements. Alice Huang became the controlling shareholder of Megaspeed in March 2023, according to Washington-based research group C4ADS, which reviewed corporate records. The US government and Nvidia did not respond immediately to Reuters requests for comment on Megaspeed’s statement. REUTERS

events.title: Tata heir questions big bets as US$185 billion group feud deepens
events.summary: Noel Tata, chairman of the trusts that control Tata Group, questioned whether some of the conglomerate’s biggest investments are being executed with enough discipline. Noel Tata questioned whether Tata Group has enough discipline in major projects, as the group pours billions into semiconductors, aviation, electronics and EV batteries. The feud has deepened over capital allocation, governance and a possible Tata Sons listing, with Tata Trusts resisting outside shareholders and saying a public listing could change “the Tata way”. A confidential analysis said semiconductors, electronics and aviation need more than two trillion rupees in extra capital, while Tata Trusts remain “100% behind” national projects but want tighter execution. MUMBAI – Noel Tata, chairman of the trusts that control Tata Group, questioned whether some of the conglomerate’s biggest investments are being executed with enough discipline, deepening a dispute over capital allocation, control and a potential listing of its holding company. The clash has widened as the group commits billions of dollars to semiconductors, aviation, electronics and electric-vehicle batteries, while the trusts that own 66% of Tata Sons resist a listing that would bring outside shareholders into the closely held parent. The dispute now reaches beyond succession and ownership to how a group generating about US$185 billion (S$238.3 billion) in annual revenue is funded, governed and run. “The question is, do we have the discipline when we execute projects, and not the direction?” Tata said on Nov 14 at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi. “How will projects with a long gestation period succeed if we don’t have discipline?” Much of the expansion has been pursued under Natarajan Chandrasekaran, the professional executive who has led Tata Sons since 2017. A confidential analysis prepared by Tata Trusts and reviewed by Bloomberg News estimated that semiconductors, electronics and aviation would require more than two trillion rupees (S$27.33 billion) in additional capital. The governance dispute widened after Tata Sons’ board backed Chandrasekaran for another five-year term on Sept 17, despite Noel Tata’s opposition. A spokesperson for Tata Sons did not immediately respond to a request for comment on his remarks about execution, capital allocation and a possible listing, sent over the weekend. Tata companies generated about US$185 billion in revenue in the year through March and own businesses ranging from Jaguar Land Rover to Tetley tea. Tata Trusts owns 66% of Tata Sons, and profits from group companies ultimately help fund philanthropy. That ownership structure has also allowed Tata Sons to support businesses through periods of weak returns or heavy investment. Noel Tata has argued that a public listing, and the arrival of thousands of outside shareholders, could make that model harder to sustain. “My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way,” he said. With 30,000 to 40,000 shareholders, “profit may take precedence over philanthropy”. Pressure to go public intensified after the Reserve Bank of India classified Tata Sons as an upper-layer non-banking financial company, a designation that carries listing requirements. The Trusts have opposed that outcome and explored a restructuring aimed at keeping the parent private. Noel Tata said the Trusts remain “100% behind” investments in projects of national importance, even as he called for greater discipline in how the group executes them and allocates capital. events.title: Pasta, pies and paperwork errors: the reality of Brexit food checks
events.summary: Delayed deliveries and inspection hold-ups among issues facing hauliers navigating post-Brexit border processes Three small boxes of spinach and ricotta cannelloni destined for a supermarket in Gibraltar languish on an EU inspector’s bench at the Eurotunnel terminal in Calais . They have been removed from a truck laden with perishables for British food lovers on the Rock – Morrisons steak and ale pie, family-size blocks of Morrisons cheddar cheese, ‘M’ Best coleslaw from Avondale foods in Craigavon in Northern Ireland and long-life milk. “We have been here nine hours now. It is very difficult,” said the lorry driver, Daniel Vasco, as he prepared to restart his 24-hour drive from London to Gibraltar. An official says the truck had originally planned to cross from England on a ferry from Dover but arrived via a freight train instead with the prerequisite dossiers of customs and food health certificates filed for arrival a few miles away. “We had to create 78 different files,” she explains, adding the pasta had to be removed because of a simple error. “The health official had put today’s date rather than the use-by date of 16 November on the paperwork,” said Olivier Colin, the director of customer service for Eurotunnel in France. This is the reality of Brexit and business is brisk. A few metres away in a refrigerated unit lie two pig carcasses wrapped in cellophane alongside several pallets of fresh food removed from different trucks that morning. The French official explains that when they opened the truck the found they had fallen from their hanging positions and with a risk of contamination had, under the rules, to be removed and destroyed. Paperwork that includes export health certificates, customs paperwork, veterinary certificates related to meat and transit documents did not exist when the UK was in the EU’s single market. Next Friday Andy Burnham and EU leaders are expected to sign a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal which will make exports of fresh food, drink and animal products such as leather easier. But without a full return to the single market, not all checks will disappear. Customs declarations will still be required along with other red tape. A report published last Friday by the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) showed that small to medium-sized businesses were worst hit by the Brexit checks. It is understood the earliest the new SPS deal will be implemented is January 2028. This is because of the need to pass legislation in the UK to realign continuously with EU regulations on food and animal products. For Getlink, the owner of Eurotunnel, it should restore some lost trade but it will also mean dismantling some of the €60m (£50m) Brexit infrastructure now made redundant. Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, said: “We would have preferred not to invest the money … but we decided not to complain, not to whine and say: ‘Ok, this has been decided by British citizens and, like it or not, it is our responsibility not to turn the new controls into a huge bureaucracy.’ “We carry 26% of the trade between Europe and the UK. That is why we invested,” he added noting however that trade had declined just over 20% in both directions since Brexit with exports of poultry and eggs in particular collapsing. Peter Roberts, the commercial strategy director for freight at Eurotunnel, said: “We have put everything we possibly can in place to make it as quick as possible but we can still end up with three packets of pasta on the table because someone made a paperwork mistake. When that paperwork is lifted it will be good for us, good for the driver, good for trade and the economy.” The efficiencies achieved over six years since Brexit are evident on one freight train over the Channel tunnel where the Guardian joined drivers. Just three of the 33 trucks and vans were redirected for checks on arrival – one for SPS checks and two for customs paperwork. Among those cleared to go is Gavin Woodward, bringing M&S labels to a food client in Belgium. He is returning with waffles but he recounts how in the past he has been stopped occasionally if he had “high-risk” cargo, which in his case, is chilled sliced ham. Carlos, a Spanish driver, is driving back to Spain after delivering fruit and veg from the Murcia area in Spain to Tesco in the UK. “I am stopped two to three times a month,” he says. “A deal will make a difference. Once I was stopped for two or three days. I was carrying meat.” Earlier this week, the Defra report showed that many small and medium-sized exporters had stopped exporting to the EU completely since Brexit. It cited a report by Aston University estimating that an SPS agreement “could boost UK agri-food exports to the EU by up to 22.5%”. A separate House of Lord report on Friday cited government estimates that the SPS deal “would increase GDP by up to £5.1bn by 2040 (up to 0.14%)“. “It could be a gamechanger,” said Leriche.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Cambridge museum celebrates the world's first business computer with films, family activities, and a little Python Vintage fun: Prodding AI agents using retro hardware just because you can 13 days ago Give him a hand: Dev publishes 25-year-old Palm OS tools to GitHub October 15, 2026 Spies, prime ministers, and balls: The BBC Domesday project @ 40 October 4, 2026 YouTube lunatic designed and 3D printed a working mechanical calculator September 30, 2026 A 1980s PDP-11 is still running Unix – and now you can watch September 23, 2026 Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all. The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children. The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories." Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids. Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it. LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013 . It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge . The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011 . The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory. The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948 . EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I . ® Amazon loses first batch of broadband satellites launched on custom rocket United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan LEO didn’t reach orbit Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China PLUS: SEGA Japan suffers outage and data leak; India bans dead battery exports; Alibaba chip unit to float; and more Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data PARTNER CONTENT: Real-time endpoint data keeps AI-driven IT operations accurate, fast and under control Most affairs don't matter except to the people involved.

events.title: ‘We will chase them down’: Debt collectors pursue claims exceeding $2m linked to Lao Huo Tang
events.summary: Debt recovery companies FDR Services and A.S.K Debt Recovery SG said they were separately pursuing claims amounting to more than $550,000 and close to $2 million respectively. Debt collectors say they are chasing more than $2 million in unpaid supplier claims linked to Lao Huo Tang Group, with visits to outlets and repeated failed contact attempts. FDR Services says it is handling $550,795.58 in claims from three suppliers, while A.S.K Debt Recovery SG says its cases approach $2 million across several businesses and creditors. The dispute adds pressure on the group, which has faced CPF arrears cases and a winding-up order for Singapura Heritage Food Hall, while management and Thomas Hong have not responded to latest queries. SINGAPORE – An unassuming mixed rice stall in Bedok Reservoir Road became the focus of debt collectors on a quiet afternoon on Nov 12, as they pursued unpaid claims from businesses linked to the Lao Huo Tang restaurant chain . The visit to Le Xin Mixed Veg Rice was among a series of attempts by debt recovery agencies to recover unpaid invoices involving companies linked to Thomas Hong, the founder and chief executive of Lao Huo Tang Group. Hong has held directorships in several food and beverage businesses. According to corporate records obtained by The Straits Times, he is listed as a director of companies such as Lao Huo Tang Investments, Lao Huo Tang Canton, Singapura Heritage Food Hall, Kenny Rogers Roasters and Le Xin Mixed Rice. He is also a shareholder of Lao Huo Tang Investments and has previously served as a director of other F&B companies. At the stall on Nov 12, debt collectors from FDR Services encountered an elderly man whom they believe to be Hong’s father. The commercial debt retrieval agency said the man declined to assist with their attempts to recover payment and indicated that he would contact the police. The visit to Le Xin Mixed Veg Rice stall in Bedok Reservoir Road was among many attempts by debt collectors to recover money owed to suppliers of businesses under or associated with Lao Huo Tang Group The collectors subsequently left a notice at the premises. Speaking to ST, FDR said it is pursuing claims totalling $550,795.58 on behalf of three suppliers, while another agency, A.S.K Debt Recovery, said it was handling claims approaching $2 million involving businesses associated with the restaurant group. It is unclear whether the amounts being pursued by the two agencies overlap. The claims involve various companies and outlets operating under several food brands. The amounts have been provided by the agencies and have not been independently established as debts owed by Hong personally, though he has become the central figure in the debt collection agencies’ pursuit of unpaid claims. More than $550,000 allegedly owed to 3 suppliers FDR said it was handling claims by suppliers that provided vegetables, meat, frozen food and other food products to restaurants and food stalls operating under various brands believed to be linked to Hong. According to documents provided by the agency, one vegetable supplier was pursuing $335,494.97 in allegedly unpaid invoices for deliveries to several outlets, including those at NEX, Jurong Point, Causeway Point, The Star Vista, Sun Plaza, Waterway Point and Seletar Mall. Of this amount, $63,740.21 was allegedly owed for deliveries at NEX, more than $59,000 at The Star Vista and $51,488.37 at Jurong Point. The invoices date back to 2025, with some outlets allegedly failing to settle payments for several consecutive months. FDR initially handled nine cases involving the vegetable supplier when they were referred to the agency in April. Its portfolio subsequently expanded to include claims from other suppliers, taking the reported total to $539,810.91. This was later revised to $550,795.58 after additional cases involving a meat supplier were included. The claims involve several companies, including Lao Huo Tang Investments, Singapura Heritage Food Hall and businesses operating other food brands. Another agency pursuing claims approaching $2m Separately, A.S.K said it was handling claims approaching $2 million involving several suppliers and creditors of businesses operating under or associated with Lao Huo Tang Group. In a statement to ST, the agency said one client had identified $356,138.36 in outstanding invoices across 10 accounts involving various outlets. These included $52,684.16 allegedly owed at The Star Vista, $50,360.43 at Waterway Point, $46,674.85 at Jurong Point and $36,277.32 at Bukit Panjang Plaza. The same client was also pursuing payments involving other businesses, including Singapura Heritage and Kenny Rogers, taking its total claims to approximately $570,000. Two other clients were pursuing more than $50,000 collectively, while another separate matter involved close to $1.2 million.

events.title: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader. He’s even eyeing the White House
events.summary: An Elon Musk acolyte, Tesla driver, and serial entrepreneur, Teague Egan was imagining ways of breaking into renewable energy in 2018 while he took a vacation to Bolivia. He learned about the country’s salt flats, their lithium reserves potential and, eventually, about the industry’s antiquated lithium mining techniques. “As an entrepreneur, I knew there had to be a better way. That was my ‘aha’ moment,” said Egan, now 38. He really began to think about how the lithium-ion batteries in Tesla’s electric vehicles are made and their massive global growth potential. He quickly founded EnergyX—short for Energy Exploration Technologies—and this year became the only company mining lithium commercially in the U.S. with modern direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology at its new Project Lonestar site in East Texas . This summer, EnergyX also opened a project in Chile extracting 170 metric tons of lithium a year. But these are still just demonstration plants. The real growth is about to begin, he touted. “EnergyX is just going to keep our head down and move towards commercialization,” Egan told Fortune . The plan is to commence construction next year. EnergyX aims to bring its Black Giant lithium project in Chile online by the end of 2028 with a first phase producing 7,500 tons per year and expanding to 52,500 tons annually by 2030. Project Lonestar in Texas would quickly follow with a 15,000-ton facility in 2029 and growing to 50,000 tons by 2031. These are admittedly aggressive timelines, but Egan is confident the progress will pick up quickly after achieving a watershed moment in October of inking its largest customer. But first, let’s take a quick step back. Two years ago, The Wall Street Journal ran this headline about Egan: “He Wants to Be the Lithium King. Run for President. And Live to 150.” The wording is brash but not inaccurate—yes, he says he still wants to occupy the White House and live well past 100—and he comes across as an over-the-top tech bro. Many didn’t take him seriously. Egan went to work proving the doubters wrong. Since then, EnergyX opened its new Austin, Texas headquarters, nearly quadrupled its acreage footprint in the lithium-heavy Smackover Formation in East Texas and southwestern Arkansas, completed its Texas and Chile demo projects, and received a $225 million influx from Italian energy giant Eni. Most importantly, in October, major energy trading house Trafigura signed a $2 billion, 10-year contract with EnergyX for 100,000 metric tons of lithium from its Black Giant and Project Lonestar enterprises. “To have that type of customer is not only really encouraging for us, but also really validating to the rest of the market,” Egan said. “This is actually the single-largest DLE offtake in history. That’s a cool little feather in the cap. The major thing that investors or project lenders need to see is that type of contract.” His expectation is that more buyers will quickly follow suit, bringing EnergyX close to commencing construction. The Trafigura deal also boosts EnergyX’s pending $690 million loan with the U.S. Export-Import Bank. While EnergyX’s success is far from assured, Egan has proven his company must be taken seriously. Drilling ahead Egan’s mentor and idol is his father, Michael Egan, who became the majority owner of Alamo Rent a Car, grew the company nationally, and sold it in 1996, continuing to chair the business until 2003. Now retired, Michael Egan sits on the EnergyX board. “I’m a serial entrepreneur. My dad was a serial entrepreneur. I learned from him,” Teague Egan said. “I don’t have an engineering or a chemistry degree. I’m an entrepreneur. I’m a problem solver. I feel like I have a Ph. D. in engineering from working at EnergyX for eight years.” After growing up near Fort Lauderdale, Florida, Egan moved to Los Angeles to attend the University of Southern California. While a college student, he started a record label and sport agency. He quickly found success in music after signing the Boston rapper Sammy Adams, who hit No. 1 on the iTunes hip-hop chart in 2010. Egan said his biggest regret might be declining to sign a deal with his label and Interscope Records because Egan didn’t find much continued success in music. Then again, if he had, EnergyX probably wouldn’t exist, he said. His music profits though led him to invest many of his gains. He was an early investor in Tesla in 2013 when the company still had a market cap of less than $10 billion. Today, Tesla sits above $1.5 trillion. Egan said he used some of those proceeds to help start EnergyX. Ever since, Egan has become an admitted follower of all things Elon Musk and his approach to business. And they’re both Austin, Texas-based now. “He’s transformed into arguably the greatest entrepreneur and innovator in the history of humanity,” Egan said. “People can say what they want about his political views and stuff but, in terms of his contributions to humanity, he’s like unmatched. He’s essentially my idol other than my father. He has that same sense of curiosity and problem solving.” EnergyX Leaning into lithium Driven by EVs and now also by battery energy storage, global lithium demand has jumped more than 400% this decade, to over 1.5 million metric tons per year. By 2035, that demand could approach 4 million tons. With the lithium business focused on traditional hard-rock mining or evaporation ponds, Egan sought another way. Evaporation ponds can take two years to extract the lithium, literally waiting for the sun to evaporate the water and help filter out the lithium. Egan isn’t that patient. He jumped into direct lithium extraction technology. He didn’t invent it, but he wants to perfect and commercialize it. Using advanced filtration technology, DLE operates much like oil and gas by drilling wells, pumping out the brine water, processing and refining the lithium, and returning more than 90% of the brine underground. DLE can take two days instead of two years, although the upfront costs are extensive. But the legacy lithium industry wasn’t ready to embrace DLE, and especially not the required financial investments. “Our original business model was just to license our technology to the existing pond producers. We said, ‘Hey, we have a better mousetrap. This will be much better for you,’” Egan said. “They strung us along and, finally, we realized that, and we said we’re going to have to go acquire our own resources and vertically integrate to prove this and scale it and realize the technology.” That’s when EnergyX began acquiring its own acreage in Chile and the Smackover. Chile and Argentina count among the top lithium producers globally—with Australia and China—but the U.S. only accounts a little more than 1% of global lithium supplies. Those U.S. projects are concentrated in Nevada, including Lithium Americas’ Thacker Pass project currently under construction. events.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
events.summary: Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can W hen you walk up from Haydons Road railway station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium. AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter – but that makes running a loss‑making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board, which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.” Kitcher was speaking before kick‑off in Saturday’s League One game at home against a Blackpool side dealing with a suspected norovirus outbreak in their squad. A superb arrowed strike from Alistair Smith and some vital late saves from Nathan Bishop ended Wimbledon’s winless run of 10 matches in all competitions. The 1-0 victory moved Johnnie Jackson’s side four points clear of the relegation zone and put a positive spin on a week that started with the fallout from the withdrawal of £87m of proposed investment, leaving the club’s finances even tighter. Wimbledon made a £2.6m loss in the 2024-25 season – a figure expected to increase by £500,000 when they publish their accounts next month – which, as Kitcher pointed out, is not as loss-making as a number of other clubs in League One. Those clubs voted in the summer to reduce spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, but now many want to go further to curb the spiralling losses at this level. “It’s an ugly way of running a sport,” said Terry Hunt, a supporter who has been attending matches with his son Billy since AFC Wimbledon were founded in 2002 after the move to Milton Keynes. Wimbledon returned home to Plough Lane in 2020, but had to create a bond to complete the move and the club still owe £7.5m in debts. In November 2025, the DTB warned that competing in the EFL at their new stadium was “not currently sustainable” under their structure at the time. The makeup of the club has since changed. Supporters voted last April in favour of reducing their voting rights from 75% to 50.01% – the same 50+1 model that gives fans the final say on decisions at German clubs – and Wimbledon sought a cash injection. An £87m investment proposal from Sloane Street Capital, a venture including the sole funder, Omar Mir, and the former Chelsea and England defender Ryan Bertrand, was already being voted on by fans when Mir suddenly walked away last Sunday, citing a change in his investment priorities. Mir passed Wimbledon’s due diligence tests, but the tech businessman was not a unifying figure. A Josimar report has detailed his “various connections to some of the most influential and controversial figures in football, technology and global security”. The 44-year-old did not attend either of the information evenings at Plough Lane after the proposal was first made in October, instead sending a two-minute video message, which meant fans could not directly ask him about his intention to purchase 90% of the economic rights of a fan‑owned football club. “We really wanted to have some kind of knight in shining armour,” said Niall Couper, a former member of the DTB and author of three books on Wimbledon. “In this case, I personally wasn’t sure how shiny that armour was.” Couper, who raised questions about Mir’s background before his withdrawal, chose not to attend the Blackpool game owing to anger from some supporters at the deal collapsing. Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football But the SSC deal is not completely dead. Bertrand and his remaining SSC partners Stuart Fiertz, Oliver Ward and Hugh Rosen – who would have owned 1.25% each of Wimbledon’s economic rights in the original proposal – have renamed themselves Sloane Street Football and are talking to other potential investors. In the meantime, the board will seek approval from fans about taking out a loan of up to £3m to “manage the club’s cash position”, but they believe they are able to manage it through to the end of this season and into the next. Which division Wimbledon end up in next season remains to be seen – Jackson’s side survived relegation by four points last April and the manager will probably have his hands tied in January. “I think we’ll probably go down, but bouncing between League Two and League One is absolutely fine by me,” Billy Hunt said.

events.title: ‘I’m scared about my future’: young people on the stress and desperation of jobseeking
events.summary: In the second in our series, four young Britons reveal how the search has taken a toll on their mental and physical health ‘The social contract is broken’: young people on feeling shut out of careers Guardian to follow lives of eight young people in their search for jobs ‘There must be something I could do’ – Celeste, 24 “I had to quit and move back in with my parents because I had developed ME/chronic fatigue syndrome. I am now housebound and cannot look after myself. Although I cannot prove it, I strongly believe that prolonged period of high stress played a big part in the decline of my health.” When Celeste, 24, graduated from the University of Edinburgh last year she spent two months applying for more than 100 jobs in the Scottish capital “just getting rejected or not hearing back at all from applications, 90% of which were waitressing positions”. “It was a really desperate time,” she says. “I was paying rent all of that time, and it was one of the most stressful times of my life.” Celeste had been doing part-time work in cafes since the age of 14 and eventually got full-time work in one, which she described as “very high pressure with terrible hours”. She was feeling unwell before taking on the role, and became increasingly sick until she left to move back in with her parents in Dorset. She had a health assessment for ME/CFS in August this year, but says it could be three to six months before she receives a formal diagnosis. Once she has that, she can start to get more support, including being put on a course to “teach me how to manage my energy” and put in touch with employers “who understand ME and already employ people like me”. She says the wait for a diagnosis is “frustrating”. Meanwhile, her application for a personal independence payment (Pip) has been rejected. She has appealed, but a decision on that could take up to a year and a half, she says, adding that she is relying on her parents to support her. Describing a typical day, she says: “I don’t really go out very much. My mum sometimes takes me to a forest nearby. She pushes me around in a wheelchair, and I can draw for about 20 minutes, and then get too tired and have to stop. It’s mainly just resting.” She hopes once she receives the formal diagnosis she can get on a path to finding employment, but until then, she is trying to think of ways she can work, given her condition. “I’m still trying to figure out how,” she says. “There must be something I could do.” ‘The job market is a lottery’ – Lenny, 26 “I feel like I’m a Neet, but the difference is I’m a Neet who has experienced work. There are different levels to it. You can have Neets who have worked before, but aren’t working now. Neets who haven’t worked at all, or Neets who have gone to school or gone to university but just haven’t found a job since they’ve left.” Lenny, 26, is describing his experience of being Neet – not in education, employment or training. While Alan Milburn’s youth joblessness review is focused on Neets aged 16-24, other economic bodies such as the OECD apply it up to age 29 . He has been unemployed for the past three years, but before then he had worked for two years as a customer assistant at a DIY store, before leaving to take a break for mental health reasons. “I’ve experienced work, I’ve experienced being on the payroll and clocking in, so for me, going into work wouldn’t be unfamiliar.” “Years ago, you could go into a shop and hand in your CV,” says Lenny, who lives with his parents and siblings in Birmingham. “Not that they would necessarily give you a job, but still it was a bit more personal. Now everything’s online and you end up waiting for them to get back digitally.” Lenny, who describes himself as Black British Caribbean, decided against further education after finishing college in 2019, where he gained BTec level 2 in business studies and in music. He did not pass English or Maths GCSE. “I did retake them twice, but I think after the second time, I just wanted to go into employment.” From 2023 to 2025, he was on universal credit. After that, he started doing the odd gardening jobs while receiving some financial support from family. Over the past three years, he has applied for “maybe 30 or 40 jobs” in different fields, including warehouse work, delivery driving and retail. Ideally he would like a manual job or work based outside. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He is also looking at agencies, but says there are drawbacks to this. “I find sometimes you apply to them and then they’ll send you on an induction,” he says. “Then you get to the induction and there’s no work available, and it’s like: ‘We’ll call you if there’s work. So sometimes it can be hit or miss.” He adds: “The job market is a lottery. How many jobs can you apply for without feeling miserable about your prospects? Maybe the lucky number is 100, 200, or 300?

events.title: ‘Prove you are not a robot’: how the Captcha scam captures your computer
events.summary: Unlike familiar Captcha tests, this con asks you to press a series of keys. And that’s a way in for fraudsters to install malicious software Y ou are looking for some gifts for Christmas and want to support small businesses when you shop. When you visit the site of one you’ve heard good things about you are asked to verify that you are human. Instead of clicking on a series of images, or typing letters that appear, just as you have seen before, you are asked to press a series of keys and then press enter. This is a tactic known as the “ClickFix” scam one of the most popular used by criminals to trick people into infecting their own computer with malicious software, according to Chris Fistonich, a researcher with cybersecurity company Malwarebytes. “ClickFix is really one of the most sophisticated malware campaigns there is,” he says. “People are not prepared for this. They are used to solving Captchas every day. They’re used to being able to trust their security software. So it really has opened a new security loophole that’s being exploited extensively.” He adds: “This is the most popular way to get malware on to your computer. Certainly not the only way, but today it is definitely the most popular.” Captcha tests are familiar to many people as ways for a website to distinguish real from automated users. They often involve being shown a photograph and asked to do simple tasks, such as clicking on bikes or trains, or typing out grainy numbers. The ClickFix fraud looks similar. The message may say “Verify you are human by completing the action below” and request you tick a box. By checking the box, you have given the system permission to copy some malicious code to the clipboard on your computer. It will then ask you to carry out a task: “To better prove you are not a robot, please: Press & hold the Windows Key + R. In the verification windows, press Ctrl + V. Press Enter on your keyboard to finish.” This combination of actions pastes the text into your system and means your computer will be infected. In other versions of the same scam, you might be told that “something went wrong when displaying this webpage” with similar instructions to fix the issue. Like many scams, the ClickFix fraud relies on people acting quickly and without thinking through their actions properly, so pause and consider what you are doing whenever you are online. Some security software systems can block malicious websites with malware traps on them, so check what you have in place. If you have been compromised, contact your bank immediately. Then change your passwords, with the most important first.

events.title: Could Budapest be the next digital nomad hotspot?
events.summary: Hungary ranked fifth for digital nomads, behind Spain, the United Arab Emirates, Montenegro and the Bahamas, on a 2025 index compiled by VisaGuide. The country's White Card scheme provides one- or two-year residency permits for digital nomads from outside the EU. AI will further enable the digital nomad trend, according to one workspace operator, because people can create services or businesses without the resources of a large organization. When mechanical engineering graduate and entrepreneur Lexi Vindisch wanted to run her business from a remote location, she didn't pick a town in North America where she lived. Instead, Budapest was top of her list. With its mix of grand sights, cafés, cultural events and inexpensive public transportation, the Hungarian capital has become a popular place for digital nomads — people embracing the "work from anywhere" trend that took off during the Covid-19 pandemic. Based at co-working space Create26 in Budapest, Vindisch runs a domestic cleaning company based in Victoria, Canada, as well as overseeing Lead Machine, a marketing software firm for home service businesses. Why Hungary is a digital nomad hotspot Hungary ranked fifth for digital nomads on a 2025 list of countries, behind Spain, the United Arab Emirates, Montenegro and the Bahamas. The index, compiled by visa information website VisaGuide, considered factors such as taxes, income and cost of living. Vindisch, who has worked in many European and North American cities, but has Hungarian roots, said Budapest feels different. "I've been in locales that are super beautiful, well organized, great facilities, but they lacked a personality ... I've never been able to replicate the feeling that Budapest holds anywhere else," she said. EU citizens can work remotely from Hungary long-term if they meet certain requirements, while Hungary's White Card scheme, which provides one- or two-year residency permits for digital nomads from outside the EU, requires a net monthly income of at least 3,000 euros ($3,370). There are around 35 co-working spots in central Budapest, according to the Coworking Hungary Association, several of which are in the bustling District VI, near the fashionable bars and restaurants of the Jewish Quarter. Alongside these hubs, the city offers around 35 serviced offices, including locations from larger providers such as Regus and DBH Flex. "Budapest has its own vibe," said Áron Levendel, a founder of co-working space Kaptar, which is within view of the city's striking St Stephen's Basilica. "Whoever wants to connect, make friends or meet people, has an easy job. Whoever wants to have fun, learn or get experiences in English, will have the challenge of choosing from hundreds of options every evening," he said. Levendel and his co-founders are organizational developers who wanted a workplace that was both sociable and professional. In 2010, they came up with the idea for Kaptar (the word means "hive" in Hungarian). "Gmail was already there, but most of the work was not in the cloud or online yet; people had folders and papers. Digital nomads were not a thing," Levendel told CNBC by email. "Co-working" also wasn't a term in common use at the time, so he called the space a "közösségi iroda," or community office. Since the Covid-19 pandemic, Kaptar has grown more than 30% every year, according to Levendel, including a "wave" of digital nomads who joined after the pandemic, often arriving initially for a month but staying for up to a year. Overseas members either keep an existing job and work remotely, or they are freelancers who can travel, Levendel said. Mónika Gyurity opened co-working space Liftoff in 2019. After a career as a television executive, she wanted to expand her digital skills and bring different generations together to learn from each other. Located in a former elevator factory close to Budapest's central Nyugati station, Liftoff attracts a mix of professionals — including short-term visitors in need of a workspace, as well as remote employees working for international companies. One of Liftoff's team members is also a remote worker who regularly participates in Nomad Cruise voyages, or "workation" trips that combine a conference program with land excursions. Gyurity expects the digital nomad trend to continue, noting that AI now allows individuals to create and launch services or businesses without the resources of a large organization. "More people will be able to imagine their knowledge, skills and opportunities outside the traditional corporate world," she said. At the same time, she recommends that those in the corporate world spend time in a co-working environment. "Most people are there because they are trying to solve something," she said. "Every day I meet younger people who are at a very different stage of their lives and careers, use different tools, and approach problems differently. We can learn from each other.

events.title: Protesters drive home message to data centre company
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rally organiser Magdalene Lippett says the community does not want to see just a "pause" to the Tungkillo data centre plan. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) More than 250 people rallied at SA Parliament on Sunday, calling for plans for a data centre in the Adelaide Hills to be scrapped. Quantum DC announced earlier this week it would pause its plans to build a data centre at Tungkillo, following a strong community backlash. The SA government says it is working on developing legislation that will "comprehensively deal with the rollout of data centres". Hundreds of protesters have doubled down on their message to data centre company Quantum DC that its plans for a 1,200-megawatt AI data centre are not welcome in the Adelaide Hills. It comes after the company announced it would pause its plans for the development at Tungkillo earlier this week, after deep frustration, anger and protests from the surrounding community. At least 250 people rallied on the South Australian steps of parliament on Sunday, with various political parties including the SA Liberals, Greens, One Nation and independent federal MP Rebekha Sharkie in support of the protest group. Campaign organiser Magdalene Lippett said the community was hopeful it had won the fight against the development. Local farmer Kym Gladigau said the proposed area was prime land for food production. "The Adelaide Hills is a food production area, that's what it's all about," Mr Gladigau said. Kym Gladigau says there is limited prime agricultural land and the area should not be put at risk of bushfires. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) "We're losing farmland at Mt Barker, we've lost it at Virginia. "The risk with this data centre, is that we lose that. "If this thing goes wrong … we cannot afford another big bushfire in the Adelaide Hills, and who is going to tackle it?" Liberal leader Ashton Hurn, who spoke at the rally, agreed the proposed area should be reserved for farming. Ashton Hurn says Tunkillo is prime agricultural land that should be protected. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) "We keep hearing that data centres are a part of our future, there are of course economic opportunities, but we also need to make sure the community is brought along for the ride as well." Greens leader Robert Simms said he wanted to see the Tungkillo plans rejected if they reached the government. "That's why Greens are moving a motion calling on the government to reject this proposal," he said. "We're also calling for a statewide moratorium on data centres. We don't want to see South Australia become the test dummy for the nation." An estimated 250 people were at the rally. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis said he was "very disappointed" with the Tungkillo developers, referencing the company's poor method of community engagement. "I mean, they have behaved in a way that has really lit this fire," he said. Mr Koutsantonis said the developers had not approached government at all about the plans. "I'm the energy minister and the treasurer. They've never spoken to me, and you would've thought the first door you'd knock on is the government's," he said. "Data centres are an essential part of our future. There's no world where Australia cannot have data centres. "If we don't have our own data centres, we'll be price takers rather than price setters." Mr Koutsantonis said the government was working on developing legislation that would "comprehensively deal with the roll-out of data centres". "Data centres have got to have almost no impact on the grid for them to operate in South Australia, and until that time is achieved, we won't license them." In response to Sunday's protest, Quantum DC CEO Alby Tomassi said the company respected the right of community members to express their views. "We want people to know we have heard their concerns," Mr Tomassi said. "That is why we have put our development application on hold and will now prepare a longer-term and more comprehensive engagement program to work through their concerns in a meaningful way.

events.title: No, thank you: Shukran hack a reminder financial details not essential for fraud
events.summary: The perpetrators of this week's data breach of Landmark Group's loyalty programme Shukran may have gained only basic user information, but that could be enough to commit more damaging fraudulent activity. On Wednesday, the Dubai-based conglomerate said it was investigating a cyber incident involving “unauthorised access” to Shukran, involving customer names, contact details and dates of birth. Shukran's initial assessment on its website remained unchanged on Saturday. Analysts caution that this type of data could be used to create convincing impersonation scams, phishing messages and other forms of social engineering in which a victim is coerced to reveal sensitive information. “The key concern is that a data breach does not need to involve financial information to create opportunities for financial fraud,” Mohamed Emam, a security researcher at Singapore-based cybersecurity firm Group-IB, told The National . “Even when financial information is not compromised, exposed customer names and phone numbers can still be valuable to cybercriminals.” How fast can stolen data be shared? After information has been extracted from a compromised system, it has the potential to travel very quickly through the dark web – in mere minutes with some reports even claiming instantly – including in cybercrime forums, illicit marketplaces and private messaging channels. “Stolen information can circulate rapidly within cybercriminal communities. Depending on the nature of the breach and the attacker's intentions, compromised data may be offered for sale or shared on underground forums within hours of being obtained,” Mr Emam said. “However, not every breach results in immediate publication or sale. In some cases, attackers may retain the information for their own operations or distribute it privately.” Stolen data “can also be combined with information obtained from previous breaches to build more detailed profiles of individuals”, Maher Yamout, a lead security researcher at Kaspersky, told The National . That point is related to what US data privacy firm Cloaked calls the archive and enrichment phase, which typically happens two years after the data was stolen. It is a part of a broader journey for stolen data, according to the New York-based company. The first three phases are the triage window, the first 24 to 72 hours in which data is sorted and tested before hitting a marketplace; the general sale from weeks two through eight, where data is made available for bulk buys; and commodity pricing from the third to the 12th month, where a collection of data pulled from multiple breaches is sold at lower rates. A domino effect is also on the table, because threat actors can weaponise the stolen data on a broader scale, particularly involving the other accounts of victims. An example is a scammer calling and coercing you to reset your bank app password. “In the Shukran incident … [the stolen data] may not sound as serious as passwords or payment card details, but this information is typically sold to other criminal organisations on the dark web for use in future attacks on consumers,” Danny Jenkins, chief executive and co-founder of US cybersecurity company ThreatLocker, told The National . “Containing a breach is essential, but it does not mean the risk to affected customers has gone away. Even if the most sensitive data has been protected, any personal identifiable information can be of value to criminals.” Worst-case scenario That's part of more severe outcomes. Mr Yamout said the worst-case scenario is that seemingly basic personal information becomes the starting point for targeted attacks, with names, phone numbers and dates of birth giving criminals the tools to establish credibility and tailor their approach to individual victims. “This could lead to phishing attacks, identity fraud, account takeover attempts or financial scams if the method of the attack is convincing enough to trick victims into disclosing additional information or security credentials,” he said. If scammers successfully obtain login credentials, verification codes or other authentication information, the consequences could extend to account takeover, unauthorised transactions or identity-related fraud, Mr Emam cautioned. “The severity of the risk depends on what information was actually exposed and whether attackers can combine it with data obtained from other sources,” he said. “The immediate concern is not necessarily what criminals can do with a phone number alone, but what they may convince someone to reveal by using that information to gain their trust.”

events.title: Jensen Huang’s ousting sends tech stocks tumbling; Singtel CEO sells shares: Markets this week
events.summary: In this column, ST’s business correspondents unpack the latest developments in Singapore and global markets during the week – and explain what they mean for investors. Jensen Huang’s departure added to the volatility in tech stocks following the US midterm elections. SINGAPORE - Nvidia lost about US$700 billion (S$902 billion) in market value over the past week as its chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned on Nov 12. It was also revealed that he allegedly had a third extramarital affair involving a company executive. The chipmaker’s share price fell by more than 12% through the week, its sixth straight weekly drop and the longest losing streak since 2012. Once the world’s most valuable company, Nvidia has since October lost about US$1.8 trillion in market value. Nvidia announced its chief financial officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO while it commences its search for a new leader. Its board was reported by the media to have approached British chip designer Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor, even as prediction market traders speculated that Huang could make a comeback. Many in the industry, from Nvidia employees to Elon Musk, have voiced support for Huang, who has run Nvidia for the past 30 years and become one of the most influential executives leading the AI boom. Huang’s departure added to the volatility in tech stocks following the US midterm elections. But tech stocks fell again when markets opened the following day, with chipmakers and major cloud providers among the decliners. AMD fell more than 8%, while Broadcom dropped more than 4%. Microsoft’s shares recovered marginally after falling through the week, but still closed 0.3% lower than a week ago as it grappled with a worldwide outage of its Outlook and Teams services on Nov 13 that lasted for more than 24 hours. The Nasdaq closed 0.9% lower, while the S&P 500 also fell 0.4%. Singapore tech stocks closed the week higher, rebounding after the previous week’s rout following the US midterm elections. Semiconductor equipment maker AEM Holdings rose by 14.5% through the week to close at $7.10, while UMS Integration was up 8.9% at $1.84. Frencken Group, another SGX-listed company on the global semiconductor supply chain dealing in high-precision component manufacturing, also closed the week 6.4% higher at $1.84. Singtel CEO sells 2m shares after telco raises guidance Singtel Group CEO Yuen Kuan Moon on Nov 13 sold two million shares in the company at $4.07 per share, or $8.14 million in total. The transaction came hours after Singtel raised its forecast for operating profit growth at the businesses it runs directly. It now expects mid- to high-single-digit growth for the 2027 financial year, up from the low- to mid-single-digit growth it forecast in May. The revision came on the back of an 8.7% rise in first-half earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) for its operating companies to $902 million, led by strong performance by Australian subsidiary Optus, tech service provider NCS and its digital infrastructure arm Digital InfraCo. The group’s operating revenue also rose 5.5% to $7.3 billion, up from $6.9 billion in the year-ago period. But the telco still reported a 54.7% drop in net profit to $1.5 billion for the first half ended Sept 30, in the absence of one-off gains seen in the year-ago period totalling $2.2 billion from the partial stake sale in Indian telco Airtel and Thailand’s Intouch-Gulf Energy merger. Its Singapore business also saw EBIT drop 4.5% as a result of the absence of one-off income in the previous year, though mobile service revenue grew 3.8% in the second quarter compared with the first quarter – its second consecutive quarter of sequential growth. Still, group chief financial officer Arthur Lang said at the media briefing for the telco’s first-half results that the company was entering the second half of the year “with a renewed confidence versus six months ago”. He noted that Singtel had previously set a lower guidance due to the growing level of uncertainty, as the Strait of Hormuz crisis had just broken out and rising inflation was a concern. CEO Yuen added that the Nvidia leadership crisis would likely not have an impact on deliveries of chips for its sovereign artificial intelligence cloud arm RE:AI, under Digital InfraCo. The company provides local infrastructure for enterprises and government agencies to train and deploy AI models while keeping their data within Singapore, and is currently the only Singtel business that purchases chips directly from Nvidia. Around 2 MW of chips is due to be deployed from the fourth quarter of FY2027, and the shipment is expected to arrive on schedule. Singtel shares fell by 3.6% when the market opened on Nov 13, before paring losses to close the week half a per cent higher at $4.11.

events.title: Bitcoin tumbles to three-month low as liquidations accelerate
events.summary: Bitcoin slumped to a four-month low of US$62,112 (S$80,000) over the weekend. Bitcoin fell to a three-month low of just above US$63,000 after leveraged long positions were liquidated, while Ether also dropped sharply. Traders blamed higher rate hopes, US spot Bitcoin ETF outflows, a risk-off mood, and fallout from the US$6 billion Binance hack. Coinglass data showed about US$1.9 billion in crypto liquidations in 24 hours, and GSR’s Rich Rosenblum said Bitcoin may be near a technical floor. WELLINGTON – Cryptocurrencies tumbled over the weekend, with Bitcoin slumping to a four-month low as leveraged long positions were liquidated. The largest digital asset sank 5.7% in the US on Nov 14 and continued to drop in Asia on Nov 15 to as low as US$62,112 (S$80,000), down a further 3.6% and its weakest since July 14. Second-biggest token Ether, which slumped 8% in the US session, fell another 3.4% on Nov 15 to US$1,711, its lowest since July 8. “I think this is a technical move, as Bitcoin broke down through its 200-day moving average of about US$73,000, which has caused a slew of liquidations and new shorts to develop,” said Rich Rosenblum, co-founder of crypto market maker GSR. Crypto has been pummelled in recent weeks by a confluence of factors including the expectation of higher interest rates, large outflows from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, an AI-fuelled risk-off mood and continued fallout from the recent US$6 billion Binance hack. Bitcoin has slumped about 25% since Oct 21. Its low for 2026 is US$57,742, reached on July 1. Large liquidation events – in which more than US$500 million worth of Bitcoin positions are wiped over 24 hours – are becoming a recurring feature in the market, as sharp swings repeatedly flush leveraged traders out of their bets. On Nov 13 , Bitcoin’s slide triggered the liquidation of roughly US$1.3 billion in long crypto bets over 24 hours, with Bitcoin positions accounting for the majority of that sum, according to Coinglass data. In the 24 hours through 7am on Nov 15 in Singapore, exchanges tracked by Coinglass recorded about US$2 billion of crypto liquidations, including US$774 million in Bitcoin and US$488 million in Ether. Long positions accounted for the vast majority of the liquidations. From Oct 30 through Nov 13, US-listed spot Bitcoin ETFs saw almost US$3 billion in net outflows. Richard Galvin, executive chairman at crypto investment firm DACM, said the impending initial public offering of artificial intelligence company Anthropic PBC may be drawing capital away from crypto. “Price performance looks very similar to what happened through the SpaceX IPO pricing period earlier this year,” Galvin said. “It appears crypto remains a short-term funding source, particularly for retail investors. This is in addition to all the other macro headwinds.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: AI retreat fuels India stock comeback in great rotation trade
events.summary: Global funds are turning more positive on India’s US$5.4 trillion equity market as oil prices retreat and earnings growth accelerates. India stocks have rebounded as money moves out of crowded AI trades. The MSCI India gauge is up 11% from an October low and has gained over US$400 billion in value. Foreign investors are buying back into India as earnings improve and oil prices fall. November saw net inflows of US$8.5 billion, the biggest monthly inflow in six years. Many funds still hold India underweight, so more gains may follow. India trades at about 20 times forward earnings, below its five-year average, but 2026 performance still lags the wider region. Indian stocks suffered bruising losses in the first nine months of 2026 as the artificial intelligence trade hoovered up global investor capital . The unwinding of that strategy has turned the Asian nation’s equities into world beaters. The MSCI India gauge has rebounded 11% from a six-month low set in October, adding more than US$400 billion (S$515 billion) in value and almost erasing 2026’s losses, as the country’s relative lack of AI exposure has become a prime advantage. Global funds are also turning more positive on India’s US$5.4 trillion equity market as oil prices retreat and earnings growth accelerates. “We’ve become more positive on India and have added back to our exposure in recent weeks,” said Tan Altundag, an investment manager for emerging equities at Pictet Asset Management in Hong Kong. “We see an improving balance between macro headwinds, portfolio flows and valuations,” while “diversification away from the increasingly volatile AI trade also appears likely to benefit India,” he said. The bounceback in Indian shares over November illustrates a broader rotation by global funds away from crowded tech bets toward markets backed by strong earnings. The shift signals a potential turning point for emerging markets as a whole, testing whether the world’s fastest-growing major economy can reclaim its status as a premier alternative to US tech giants after months of trailing its global peers. A return of overseas investors has underpinned the rebound in Indian stocks, and the process may still have room to run as global funds remain largely underweight. Overseas buyers have snapped up a net US$8.5 billion of Indian shares in November, heading for the biggest monthly inflow in six years, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That has reduced the total 2026 outflow to about US$22 billion. Active long-only funds globally remain US$74 billion underweight on Indian shares relative to the benchmark, Bank of America data show, close to their lightest positioning since the bank began compiling the figures in 2015. Earnings for Nifty 50 Index companies may rise around 18% year-on-year in the September quarter, accelerating from 13% growth in the prior three months since August, Bank of America data also show. US-based Calamos Investments is among those boosting its holdings. The money manager’s emerging-market strategy has lifted its India allocation to more than 10% over the past three to four months from as little as 1% to 2% in 2025 , co-chief investment officer Nick Niziolek said. “We’re adding to India because we’re seeing an inflection in earnings,” he said. “We’re seeing an improvement in fundamentals, and we see really attractive valuations.” Kabouter Management is another overseas investor that is growing more positive. “As long-term investors, we remain constructive on the outlook for India,” said Nikhil Rastogi, portfolio manager at the Chicago-based money manager. Indian shares have faced many challenges since 2024 , “but these headwinds don’t change the long-term picture, and some of the global shifts behind them are working in India’s favour,” he said. “Valuations that looked stretched two years ago have become more attractive, particularly in pockets of the market.” The MSCI India gauge trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of about 20 times one-year-ahead profits, a discount to its five-year average, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The recent decline in oil prices is also helping shares in India, which imports nearly 90% of its energy needs. Global benchmark Brent crude has dropped over 18% from a high set on Oct 30 as investors wager that the Democratic Party’s sweep of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has increased the likelihood of an end to the Middle East conflict. “I’m comfortable on India while Brent sits around US$100 a barrel or below,” said Lauren Hyslop, an investment manager at UK-based Mattioli Woods. Despite the recent rally in Indian stocks, the market remains a relative laggard for 2026. MSCI’s India gauge has still dropped 2.2% in 2026 , whereas the index provider’s regional benchmark has jumped about 12%. The Indian measure is on track for back-to-back years of underperformance against its regional peer for the first time since 2020, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

events.title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
events.summary: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew. Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions. Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals. Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week . (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct . The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him; Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security. Even if it had, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, told TechCrunch that a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said. Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill , Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.” It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible. In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone. What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.” The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed.
