events.title: AI's four colliding crises
events.summary: AI's titans were handed an extraordinary mandate: Police yourselves. But the industry faces a four-pronged crisis of trust as Democrats surge to power and many Americans rebel over AI and data centers. Guardrails for the industry will be a priority for the new Congress, with some populist Republicans eager to pile on. Why it matters: The collision of safety scares, political blows, financial turmoil and leadership scandals threatens to derail AI's once seemingly unstoppable ascent. The big picture: Just six weeks ago, President Trump announced that top AI CEOs had agreed to a voluntary safety accord . But cracks were already showing and, since then, four crises have converged. 🏛️ 1. The political crisis: AI was on the ballot for the first time during the midterm elections through a series of data center measures across America. People voted against data centers in 40 out of 41 cases, and swing-state incumbents linked to the facilities, including Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), were voted out. Now Democrats are planning a flood of AI bills once they take control of Congress in January, Reuters reports . They'll also bring some of the most powerful AI executives to D.C. to testify. 🦺 2. The safety crisis: OpenAI's Hugging Face breach , revealed in July , was a terrifying look at what could happen if machines operate beyond humans' control — and it was the first in a wave of revelations through the summer and fall. AI CEOs and engineers came forward with stark warnings about the dangers of the tech they've been building, including its potential to destroy humanity. Axios' Madison Mills reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of security incidents and that unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts. 💰 3. The financial crisis: The AI trade is looking more vulnerable as investors question when or whether the industry's sky-high spending will deliver sky-high returns. Tech stocks tumbled , with Nvidia falling 13% this week amid the ouster of founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The stock has lost nearly 25% of its value since the first New York Times report in late October about Huang's links to a suspected Chinese spy. Anthropic's IPO may not be what some hoped, with its projected valuation coming in roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago. 🧐 4. The leadership crisis: Huang's stunning resignation, following revelations about affairs, is raising new questions about the vulnerability of the people running America's most powerful companies. Nvidia's stock slide exemplifies the risk of putting so much power in the hands of so few AI executives. Pop culture has turned on the AI titans , with three year-end films — " The Social Reckoning " and " Musk ," out last month, and " Artificial ," opening Christmas Day — savaging Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Reality check: The AI industry's hurdles are partly growing pains — investors start demanding returns, lawmakers seek accountability, the public grows skeptical. The trust collapse echoes the moment social media companies went from Silicon Valley darlings to public enemies. But AI's reckoning — just like its rise — has come much faster.

events.title: MAGA turns on Lutnick amid China spy scandal
events.summary: Commerce Secretary Lutnick has become the face of the Trump administration's troubled response to Chinese espionage and potential national security threats. The most intense scrutiny is coming from Republicans on the Hill, fellow Cabinet members and the MAGA base. Why it matters: Regulators and policymakers on both sides of the aisle want someone's head for an affair that may have exposed sensitive technology to the nation's top foreign adversary. Two names are currently at the top of that list: former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — and now Lutnick. The big picture: Over the past year, Lutnick slow-walked broader administration efforts to address suspicions that Singapore-based company Megaspeed was illegally diverting chips to China, Axios first reported . Administration officials had pushed to place Megaspeed on the Commerce Department's Entity List, which would have restricted exports of U.S. tech to the company. Driving the news: On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed as much. "Treasury, War, USTR, and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC . Trump himself supported taking action on three occasions, but those efforts were delayed by Lutnick, Axios reported . There's a widespread belief in Trump's broad circle of advisers that the Nvidia scandal might be too much for Lutnick to survive — but Trump is standing beside him for now. Behind the scenes, the White House has not expressed concern regarding efforts to have Lutnick testify before Congress. MAGA commentators are also tearing Lutnick apart on shows like "War Room with Steve Bannon," while Republican senators openly take him to task. For the record: " Secretary Lutnick plays a fundamental role in advising the President across many different industries. The reports you have issued are inaccurate and false and literally misstate the topic, creating a false impression," the Commerce Department said in response to Axios' inquiries. Friction point: The brewing scandal hangs in part on a CIA warning that Jensen Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang, who ran Megaspeed and was also alleged to be a Chinese spy. That warning appears to have been ignored by Commerce Department officials, sources told Axios. Context: Last fall, CIA intelligence indicated Huang was the target of the espionage, which was reported in a "book" assembled by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence for a small circle of administration officials with top secret clearance, according to sources familiar with the matter. In March, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who's also White House national security adviser, compiled a memo about the issue to ensure that Cabinet officials with "equities" in Nvidia and AI were informed, one of those sources said. "The memo was made so that Lutnick and Bessent and others knew what was up," said one source. "Howard was given the memo. He ignored the memo," a second source said. In May, as Trump traveled to China aboard Air Force One, Rubio verbally briefed the president as a "reminder," one of the sources said. Reality check: Through it all, Trump has repeatedly been in Lutnick's corner. The president has defended Lutnick time and again, whether over tariffs, immigration or the latest China tussle. There are no indications Trump has changed his stance since publicly defending Lutnick on Thursday. The bottom line: While Trump continues to defend Lutnick, administration officials and congressional Republicans have clearly picked a target.

events.title: Wholesale food prices are on the rise
events.summary: Food prices are rising sharply even before they reach supermarket shelves. Why it matters: Americans are already paying more for groceries. New inflation data this week suggests that the pressure is not letting up. Wholesale fresh and dry vegetable prices surged 27% last month, adding to a 31% price jump the previous month. These are the prices paid by food distributors, grocery chains and other businesses to farmers and other producers for eventual sale to consumers. Wholesale food prices overall are up 1.7% from a year earlier, ending a three-month streak of annual price declines. Zoom in: Unusually warm weather, crop disease and insect infestations have reduced lettuce and other leafy green harvests in California. The Iran war, meanwhile, has driven up the cost of fertilizer and fuel, making it more expensive to grow and transport food. A regional grocery chain recently told Federal Reserve officials that it now costs more to transport a head of lettuce from California than to buy the lettuce itself, citing high diesel fuel prices. Truck freight costs are up almost 25% over the past year, the largest annual increase since 2022 and on par with the surge seen during the pandemic-era inflation shock. The big picture: It's unclear how much of the surge in producer prices will be passed along to consumers. But steeper price increases were already showing up at supermarket checkout counters last month. Grocery prices rose 0.4%, the biggest monthly increase in 6 months, driven by higher prices for meat, dairy products and snack foods. Fresh vegetable prices climbed 2%, including a nearly 8% jump in lettuce prices.

events.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status
events.summary: An international health organization has determined that the United States has lost its measles elimination status, according to multiple news reports. Why it matters: It's an official recognition of how much the country's public health has deteriorated due to a rolling series of outbreaks since early last year. Increased public skepticism about the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, a barrage of distrust from federal officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and funding cuts for response efforts have all factored in the surge of cases, according to public health experts. The big picture: The Pan American Health Organization concluded there has been sustained transmission of the highly contagious virus for longer than 12 months, bringing the U.S. case count to its highest level in 35 years. The measles elimination status hinges on whether the same strain of measles stays in circulation for 12 months or longer without a break. The overwhelming majority of cases are in unvaccinated people. While overall measles vaccination rates remain relatively high, public health officials say they have to remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity. Driving the news: An expert panel convened by the Pan American Health Organization made the widely expected decision following a three-day meeting in Washington, D.C. What they're saying: "It is no surprise that the resurgence of measles has coincided with an administration that has inflicted significant damage to our health care system while spreading false claims about vaccines," said Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and a former acting director of the Centers for Disease Control. "It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026," the Infectious Diseases Society said in comments prior to the decision. The group cited the potential long-term toll on infants infected this year, some of whom could develop serious neurologic disease years after the initial infection. By the numbers: There have been 5,412 confirmed cases so far this year, compared to 2,289 for all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's latest tally. The last time measles cases were higher was in 1991, when the U.S. had 9,643 cases. Pennsylvania is in the grip of an outbreak that has accounted for more than 1,500 cases so far and six measles-associated deaths. Those reports are widely considered to be an undercount, due to the lack of widespread testing and unreported instances of mild illness. While most measles cases aren't severe, they can have long-lasting effects because of the way the virus can suppress the body's immune responses, leaving people more susceptible to other infections. About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles is hospitalized, per the CDC. How it works: Experts rely on disease tracking by local health departments and genetic sequencing, and can also factor vaccination rates and surveillance efforts. Canada and the United Kingdom have both lost their measles elimination status over the past year. The determinations are largely symbolic, but mean the virus has become endemic and is spreading freely in pockets of unvaccinated people, according to Yale epidemiologist Katelyn Jetelina. Since early 2025, there have been large-scale outbreaks in West Texas, along the Utah-Arizona border and in South Carolina.

events.title: No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?
events.summary: On September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the new air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration quickly announced that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.” New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms. None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls. According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe? Depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this new technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” says a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.” Aviation’s embrace of AI traces back to the early 2000s, when advances in batteries and microelectronics suddenly made drones much more capable and inexpensive. The surge convinced officials that robots and humans would eventually need to share the airways, and that new infrastructure would be necessary to allow that. At the time, virtually all aircraft were human-piloted, and there was no way for drones to avoid human-flown planes or each other. In 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed. Joby’s aircraft flying past Lower Manhattan, New York, in April. With a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, big players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious plans for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia . The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia . Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come. Around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the company unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year. For more than a decade, various eVTOL builders have been promising that production models were just around the corner .

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Collabora and Nextcloud pitch alternatives as education customers weigh the cost of losing free services Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China 1 hour ago LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in 16 hours ago Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum 1 day ago FAA blames ground stop on faulty copper wiring 2 days ago Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 2 days ago The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure. "Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy." Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service.

events.title: I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account.
events.summary: ProPublica reporter Jake Pearson tests DraftKings’ guardrails at a Manhattan bar this spring. After a ProPublica investigation published this fall, the company closed Pearson’s account. Gerardo del Valle/ProPublica Late last month, I was getting dinner on the table when an email hit my inbox with some bad news. “Upon review your account has been closed at DraftKings’ discretion,” the message read. “We understand that this is not the decision that you were hoping for but this decision is final.”  I hadn’t bet on sports in months and had withdrawn all but a few cents of my balance. Why, I wondered, would my account even be under review? Was it something I’d said? In September, I’d published an investigation into how online sports betting companies like DraftKings court customers — and whether the internal guardrails they’ve put in place to stop their users from spiraling out of control are firm enough. For that piece, I’d intentionally bet like a problem gambler , recklessly escalating my betting behavior over 10 weeks. My wagering had been informed by a panel of professional sports bettors, recovering addicts and addiction specialists. As I flagrantly waved the red flags, DraftKings made me a VIP and assigned me my very own personal host. My recklessness was being rewarded. It just took three weeks and about $6,000 of losses. What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out. If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files. Share Your Experience The company, like the rest of the industry, says it doesn’t want to profit off of addiction, and has invested heavily in a system of tools and in-app prompts designed to help bettors put conditions on their gambling and slow them down. But my experiment raised serious questions about the effectiveness of this system, what’s known as “responsible gaming.”   So on one hand, I could understand how a story like mine, which scrutinized a core business function, might rankle company executives. But on the other hand, DraftKings had been downplaying the significance of my story for weeks.  In an interview for the piece, the company’s chief responsible gaming officer, Lori Kalani, had told me that the system “worked the way it was supposed to” in my case by feeding me some 30 responsible gaming messages over the course of my 10-week betting spree. And on Oct. 22, about a month after publication, DraftKings CEO Jason Robins doubled down, telling a CNBC journalist that he had “personally looked” at my entire betting history and was “pretty proud of how we handled it.” (He also made false claims about my reporting, but I’ve already addressed that on X .) So as I read the notice of my account closure, I wondered: What changed, exactly? DraftKings didn’t respond when I asked. All I got was a check in the mail for 94 cents, the remainder of my balance. But what was clear was that my investigation was reaching more and more people — including state regulators and federal lawmakers. Since publication, it had gone viral. A 27-minute, behind-the-scenes documentary of our work that we posted on YouTube on Oct. 10 had been viewed more than 6 million times in just three weeks. Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting Experiment Lisa Seville and Nadia Sussman/ProPublica The video offered viewers who may not be familiar with ProPublica (or perhaps not inclined to read 4,000-word stories) a way to learn about the reporting in the venue where so much sports betting content lives. Most of our viewers were young men — the prime sports betting demographic. And boy did they engage, leaving 3,500 comments on YouTube and flooding my inbox with messages about the same features and VIP perks detailed in my story. Regulators from across the country were citing my investigation when announcing that they were going to take a look for themselves at how DraftKings and its ilk incentivize users to keep betting. Federal and state officials were also demanding answers about how the company lures in its customers and keeps them in the action . In Ohio, regulators were even proposing a rule to restrict the apps’ marketing practices that spoke directly to one of the findings in my piece.   On the morning of Oct. 27, I sent DraftKings a series of questions for a story about that impact .  That evening is when the unsigned notice from DraftKings Support about my account closure appeared in my inbox. Two hours later, the company sent me a formal response to my questions, writing, in part, that “regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business” and denying that the company improperly targets losing gamblers. I may no longer be able to access my account, but I’m still reporting on DraftKings and the online gambling industry. In fact, right now, we’re collecting wagering data from bettors to better understand how the major operators handle problem gambling. You can help by submitting your data here . If you’ve got a tip, you can also reach me directly at 917-512-0276 and jake.pearson@propublica.org . The post I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account. appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Tesla invites select customers to order their own driverless Cybercab
events.summary: Elon Musk's Tesla Motors is inviting select customers in the US to order its fully autonomous Cybercab, the company's new focus after scrapping the Cybertruck earlier this month . The Cybercab, also dubbed the Robotaxi , is being sold for personal use for $29,990 before taxes and is expected to be delivered in December, the Texas-based company said in a post on X. That makes it Tesla's cheapest vehicle, $7,000 lower than the entry-level variant of the Model 3. Select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use pic.twitter.com/LDIkKuseAZ — Robotaxi (@robotaxi) November 13, 2026 However, the Cybercab requires a $3,600 annual autonomy subscription, which is the fee to use its driverless capabilities – a non-optional feature as the vehicle does not have a steering wheel or pedals. Maintenance and insurance costs are excluded from Tesla's pricing. Also, Cybercab deliveries are limited to Texas, one of only two states – the other being Florida – where Tesla's Robotaxi services are authorised to operate in a handful of cities. The driverless cab will be arriving in Arizona and Nevada soon, according to the company's website. Tesla described the launch as “early access” and “limited release”. It is unclear how many customers have been invited, whether the period will be extended and whether deliveries will be made available in Florida. “Select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use,” Tesla said. The Cybercab was released to much hype in October 2024, nearly a decade after Mr Musk first told Tesla shareholders that the company's cars would achieve full autonomy within three years. In 2016, he said that by the end of 2017, a Tesla car would be able to drive across the US without human intervention. In 2019, he said Tesla would have one million robotaxis on roads in 2020. None of those came to fruition. There were several reasons for the delay and failed promises, most notably the challenge of developing the technology, as well as regulatory scrutiny – especially after accidents involving driverless cars, and what has been perceived as grandiose ambitions in such a short period. The company, however, was able to stick to its roll-out plan for the Cybercab after its pledge in 2024. The Cybercab is also one of Tesla's focal points moving forward after it announced on November 6 that it would cease production of the polarising Cybertruck pickup. Mr Musk defended the Cybertruck this week, saying that its order rate “far exceeds” the production rate and that “the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production”. Tesla also unveiled its next-generation Roadster in another hyped launch last month, with its top-end Rocket variant model having the ability to “fly” using thrusters made by Mr Musk's other venture, SpaceX.

events.title: ‘It’s like the wild west’: how AI has rocked the literary world
events.summary: With authors losing lucrative deals and writers removed from prize shortlists, accusations of AI use are sending shock waves through the publishing industry. Is it too late to turn the tide on machine writing? T he romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time. Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself “high six figures”. Continue reading...

events.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
events.summary: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories. With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process. Success of user reports trails away As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially. Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent. Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures. The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly. Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limbo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests. Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report , it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny. Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment. The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference " to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves. Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms. She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.' "In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered. "So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

events.title: Football kit giveaway aims to boost participation
events.summary: Millie Bright said she wanted girls to feel "comfortable and confident" in their kit Former England captain Millie Bright has helped hand out new kit to grassroots football teams in Leeds as part of an initiative aimed at keeping girls in sport for longer. Thirty teams based in communities facing social or economic challenges were chosen by anti-discrimination charity Kick it Out for the donation. Bright, who began her career at Doncaster Belles, said it was "vital" to keep girls playing sport. "Every young girl deserves a kit, no matter what level they play at, and, whilst the top of the game is doing really well, real life still exists. People can't afford to give their children kits, but that doesn't mean they should go without." Craig Gilmore set up Champions CIC, in Beeston, six years ago, to provide free Saturday morning training for children in the local area, as well as breakfast and lunch. "With the cost of living, football's expensive [and] bills come first," he said. "We work with a lot of families that can't afford the direct debits and the ongoing costs of grassroots sport nowadays. "The new kit is amazing. It gives them that sense of belonging, that team pride, it's a massive boost for them." Bright spoke with young footballers during the event in Leeds The new kit was provided by Kick it Out, in partnership with the Morrisons Foundation. They hope it will inspire these girls to continue sport as young women and adults. "Girls' participation struggles with drop-out rates," said Gemma Clark, from Kick it Out. "One of the barriers is kit. We want to remove that barrier so that more local girls can keep playing." Bright told the BBC she was fully behind the campaign. "As a girl or a woman, it's about feeling wanted and equal," she said. "We deserve to have kits. I don't want to see any girl dropping out of the game because they don't feel valued or comfortable. "These are the days that really make a difference. Hopefully this shows the girls that the people at the top care. The power of having a kit is a small gesture, but has a massive impact." events.title: What do Christmas market traders say about rising prices?
events.summary: Nils Borstel said his business was making less money despite more than doubling the price of a sausage Mention Christmas markets these days and the conversation often turns to rising prices – from £8 bratwursts, £11 Yorkshire pudding wraps and even £5 for a few marshmallow sticks. But what do the people behind the stalls think? Are they benefiting from the hikes or are their own profits being squeezed? Traders at Manchester's Christmas markets told the BBC they were feeling the pressure of increasing bills for staff, ingredients and energy, with some saying they were making less money despite charging more. One trader said it costs at least £4,000 a day to run each her four stalls, while another has cut prices to keep customers coming back. Nils Borstel, 25, helps run Bratwurst King, a family business which has operated at the markets since 1999. He said a sausage that previously cost £3.50 now sold for £8, with much of the increase taking place over the past five or six years. "But we don't earn more money," he said. Manchester Christmas market traders explain prices Borstel, whose family operates four stalls across the city centre, said rising costs for meat, electricity, staffing and accommodation had forced the business to increase prices. About 15 workers travel from Germany to help run the stalls, alongside staff recruited in the UK. He said that despite busy crowds and dry weather during the opening weekend, people appeared more cautious about spending than in previous years. For example, some customers were now buying one portion of food to share, rather than purchasing one each, he said. Borstel said he had seen a change in spending habits since 2019, when customers were more willing to buy food and drinks without worrying about the cost. He acknowledged that prices were high and did not want to increase them, but said the they were necessary to cover expenses. Poppy (left) and Neve questioned whether the portions they bought justified the prices Among those questioning the costs were Neve and Poppy, both 18. Neve, a student, said she had spent about £15 on one dish, while Poppy, who is taking a gap year, paid £11 for a Yorkshire pudding wrap. "I think it was pricey for what it was," Neve said. Poppy also felt she had not received much food for the money, although said it was tasty. Both said they enjoyed going into the city and looking around the markets, while Neve sympathised with traders, saying she thought the cost of renting space could force businesses to raise prices. Charlotte Whittle, director of CT Catering, has been trading at the markets for 10 years and now operates four stalls. She said each stall cost at least £1,000 a day to run, bringing her total daily operating costs to at least £4,000. Whittle, who employs a range of staff, said customers often underestimated the work and expense involved. Before the markets opened, her business spent two weeks preparing its stalls, with another two weeks needed to dismantle them after Christmas. CT Catering director Charlotte Whittle says her business employs 57 people across four Manchester market sites She said the costs included staff wages, accommodation, deliveries, storage, packaging and card payment fees. Parking three vans in Manchester city centre could cost £100 a day alone, she said, with the vehicles needed to replenish stock throughout busy trading periods. "They think that you're just selling cookies," she said. Whittle, who began her business selling homemade cakes at street food markets, said the cost of stock and packaging had increased significantly over the years. Although she had increased some prices, she said she had chosen to absorb part of those costs rather than risk putting customers off. "We've had to take a massive cut on profits," she said. She also argued that the standard of street food had improved and customers were receiving food comparable in quality to that served in restaurants. But not every trader has responded to rising costs by putting up prices. Clark Murphy, whose family has traded at the markets for 22 years, runs Mr Crimble Crumble, which sells fruit crumbles from two stalls. He said the business had kept most prices unchanged for three years and had reduced the cost of its largest portion by £2. Clark Murphy (left), pictured with his nephew Davis, said his business had reduced the price of its largest crumble Murphy said cooking oil and biodegradable packaging had become more expensive, but the business wanted to retain customers who returned each Christmas. "We haven't increased our prices for three years now," he said. A notice at one food stall offered customers £1 off each drink or dish if they paid in cash He said the business remained profitable, although margins were under pressure and card payments added to operating costs. At another food stall, a notice offered customers £1 off each drink or dish when paying cash. "Card fees are crazy – help us keep it simple," it said.

events.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
events.summary: Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption. The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected. The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide. Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent. Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers. Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday. By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America. Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge. Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost? Published 2 days ago Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world Published 2 days ago In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected , as were some schools and police forces. UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network. In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails. In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook. Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday. In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook. The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals. Pete says his business has been brought to a standstill Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill". His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations". Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that. "The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she said. "We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible." Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally. It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world. By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region. Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously." A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review. Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services. "The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure. Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

events.title: Food bank sees donations drop by 10% each year
events.summary: The year ending in 2024 saw a 9% drop, then another 13% in 2025, and finally a 6% drop in 2026 A food bank that has seen a drop in donations of about 10% each year since 2023 is hoping government stockpiling advice will not affect the public's generosity. Someone eats a meal provided by Cambridge City Foodbank "every two minutes" and it claims to have provided more than 260,000 in the past year. In October, the government launched its "Be Ready" campaign and encouraged households to stock up with enough non-perishable food and water to survive for three days in case of an emergency. Chief executive Steve Clay says he does not know if this will affect the Christmas appeal - their busiest period - but confesses: "It is a concern." A government spokesperson said it had "no serious evidence of stockpiling or indeed a supply shortage" with the campaign and it had worked with voluntary organisations and charities to address any concerns. Steve Clay, chief executive of Cambridge City Foodbank, said they had discussed the possibility that stockpiling would affect donations The food bank team estimates it will provide more than 45,000 meals to people in the city between 13 November and 15 January. Clay says that with cold weather and pressure on spending, Christmas is "more difficult" than the rest of the year. "Budgets are tighter, more has to be spent on fuel and energy," he said. "So people are contacting us all the time for emergency support and we need to make sure that the support is always there and is continuing to be there." Donations are used to purchase emergency hampers, treats or provide advice and assistance. While the food bank's doors close on Christmas Day, meals they have provided mean more people can enjoy the festivities. Every pound donated, up to the first £15,000, would be doubled as part of a match-funding commitment. Dr Liam Loftus, development director of the food bank, said: "As we head into winter and the cold draws in, thousands of individuals and families will be forced to make the heart-breaking choice between heating or eating. "This winter, can you take two minutes of your time to support our Winter Appeal? "You'll be helping restore hope and dignity to people facing hardship and providing one of your neighbours with their next meal at what should be one of the happiest times of year." The government spokesperson said of the Be Ready campaign: "We've worked hand-in-hand with voluntary organisations and charities, including food banks, to address any concerns and ensure the guidance is as accessible as possible. Unilever had spotted in the 1960s that farming salmon, which until then was caught wild and remained a relative luxury, would create a mass market, lower costs and provide steady profits. events.title: UAE Property: 'Should I waive the penalty if my tenant can no longer afford the rent?'
events.summary: Question: I own a one-bedroom apartment that I rent out. My tenant renewed only three months ago but has now lost his job and says he needs to leave the UAE . The tenancy contract says early termination requires two months' rent as a penalty. He has asked me to waive it because he has a family and says he genuinely cannot afford it. I'm sympathetic, but I'm also paying a mortgage and I'm worried the apartment could sit empty while I find another tenant. What would you do? Am I being foolish if I let him leave without enforcing the penalty? DH, Dubai Answer: There's the legal answer and then there's the answer I would give you after many years of dealing with landlords and tenants, and they aren't always exactly the same. Let's start with the contract. If you have an agreed early termination clause requiring two months' rent, that is the basis from which the two of you negotiate. A tenant losing their job doesn't automatically erase their contractual obligations. But of course, I wouldn't immediately turn this into a dispute . Ask the tenant when they realistically need to leave and whether they'll co-operate with viewings (presumably you will want to find an immediate replacement). Then, speak to a good local brokerage firm to establish how quickly the apartment could be re-let and at what level of rent. Suppose your existing tenant helps you secure a replacement who moves in immediately after he leaves. If you suffer little or no financial loss, insisting on the full two-month penalty may achieve very little other than making an already difficult situation for him worse. On the other hand, if the property is likely to sit vacant for six weeks and you'll incur cleaning, maintenance/preparation costs, or perhaps agency fees, it's therefore perfectly reasonable to negotiate compensation. If I had to be practical and you pressed me for my view, I would release him early provided he allows viewings , returns the apartment properly, settles utilities and rent up to the agreed handover date and perhaps pays a reduced termination amount if there's a genuine vacancy period. One piece of advice though: whatever you both decide ensure you put everything in writing. I've always believed the best landlord-and-tenant outcomes aren't necessarily the ones where somebody squeezes every last dirham out of the contract. They're the ones where both sides walk away feeling the agreement was fair. You have a mortgage to pay, so this isn't charity. But if you can replace the tenant quickly and help somebody through a genuinely difficult period without leaving yourself out of pocket, I'd call that sensible property management rather than weakness. Q: I own an apartment in Dubai that I bought as a long-term investment. My service charges have increased over the years, but the condition of the building seems to be going in the opposite direction. The gym has had broken equipment for months, there are regular problems with the lifts, the swimming pool has been closed several times and the common areas look tired. I don't mind paying reasonable service charges if the money is being spent properly, but as an individual owner I feel I have absolutely no influence. Can I refuse to pay until these issues are fixed, and how can I actually find out what I'm paying for? LM, Dubai A: Straight off the bat, I wouldn't refuse to pay. This puts you in a weak position and ultimately you will be falling foul of the law. Service charges in Dubai's jointly owned properties are regulated and the budgets are subject to Rera's approval. The charges can include security, cleaning, maintenance, utilities for common areas, insurance, management costs, master-community charges and contributions to any reserve funds. Your first step should therefore be to establish what the approved charge actually is. You can check this through the DLD Service Charge Index, Mollak or Dubai REST. DLD specifically states that management entities should not demand service charges before they have been approved by Rera. After you have thoroughly checked this out you can go ahead and separate the two issues of how much you're being charged and what standard of service you're receiving. A high service charge isn't automatically unreasonable if you're in a building with extensive facilities, cooling of common areas, several lifts, pools, landscaping and 24-hour security. But owners are entitled to question why facilities they are funding are not being fully maintained. Document the problems. Dates, photographs, emails and previous complaints are far more useful than simply saying the building is badly managed. Raise them formally with the management company first. If the standard of common-area maintenance remains unacceptable, DLD says owners can submit a complaint through Dubai REST using the Real Estate Violations System. From an investment perspective, I'd take this seriously. Poor building management doesn't just irritate residents, over time it can affect rents, tenant retention and of course resale values. Two identical apartments in neighbouring buildings can perform very differently simply because one building is well run and the other isn't. The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. Please send any questions to mario@evadxb.com

events.title: 'The line-up is huge': Australians caught up in US flight chaos
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australians stranded as US flight chaos grounds thousands of planes Adelaide woman Trish Crabb is stranded at JFK Airport in New York after thousands of flights were cancelled and delayed. ( Supplied: Trish Crabb ) A major air traffic control outage in the US has disrupted thousands of flights, leaving Australians stranded and warnings about global flow-on impacts, including international delays. Airlines are working to clear the backlog as US authorities investigate what caused the outage. Australians have been caught up in widespread flight disruptions across the United States after a communications outage forced aviation authorities to ground flights nationwide. More than 11,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, with passengers left stranded at airports across the country after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an unprecedented ground stop. The grounding has since been lifted, but airlines are warning it could take time to clear the backlog, with disruptions also affecting flights departing Australia for the US. Look back on our live blog for the latest on the issues affecting flights in the US and Australia. Sydney Airport said flights to the US would now resume from Mascot after being temporarily grounded on Saturday morning, and urged passengers to contact their airlines. The disruption has affected travellers at major airports including New York's JFK, Los Angeles International Airport and San Diego. Adelaide traveller Trish Crabb snapped this photograph while in line at JFK airport in New York. She was among thousands of travellers caught up in US flight cancellations. ( Supplied: Trish Crabb ) Trish Crabb, from Adelaide, was among those caught up in the chaos after her flight from New York to Miami was grounded. She and her husband were due to fly out of JFK Airport when they discovered their Delta flight had been cancelled. The couple are holidaying in the US and had planned to drive from Miami to Fort Lauderdale to board a cruise. "My husband is going to try and find us a hotel room somewhere close by, and hopefully we will be able to get a flight out at some stage," she said. Despite the disruption, Ms Crabb said passengers appeared to be keeping their composure. "Everyone was very calm," she said, adding most people were taking the situation in their stride. Rivkah Brown, from Myrtleford in Victoria, was stranded at San Diego Airport after her Delta flight was cancelled. Rivkah Brown from Victoria was stranded at San Diego Airport following a cruise in the US. She's now boarding a bus to get to Las Vegas. ( Supplied: Rivkah Brown ) Ms Brown had just disembarked from a cruise and was stopping over in San Diego before travelling to Las Vegas, where she was due to meet her fiancé. She said she would now take a bus to Las Vegas instead, a journey of almost 10 hours. "It's disappointing but it is what it is," Ms Brown said. The FAA ordered the nationwide ground stop on Friday, local time, after communications problems affecting air traffic control centres across the United States. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the issue was affected all Air Route Traffic Control Centres, with technicians investigating the cause. What we know about the US flight groundstop Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage. The FAA said the decision was made because of "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety". US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said preliminary investigations pointed to a telecommunications outage, with no immediate indication of a deliberate attack. "There's no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It's just a telecommunications outage as of right now," he said. The outage affected the 22 regional air traffic control centres responsible for directing aircraft between airports across the country. At least 600 flights had been diverted, including aircraft sent back to their departure airports or redirected elsewhere. The order to ground all departing US flights was finally lifted after more than five hours. ( AP Photo: Tony Gutierrez ) About 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to depart US airports after 4pm Eastern time on Friday. Planes already in the air were able to continue to their destinations, with authorities prioritising their safe landing. The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a computer system failure at the FAA caused thousands of delays.

events.title: 'Plastic farmers' in Indonesia unaware of the dangers of burning waste
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Researchers investigate health impact of burning plastic waste in Indonesia Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Plastic waste was regularly burned in limestone kilns in Sumberejo, a village in East Java. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Ahmad Yani spent hours each day sifting through piles of rubbish, searching for recyclable materials to sell to help make ends meet. For decades, his family and other people in his village in East Java, in Indonesia, would buy truckloads of waste residue from factories recycling imported paper and cardboard. They would spread the waste on the ground, and separate plastics from paper and cardboard. The paper would be sold back to the recycling factories and most of the plastics to industries that needed fuel for furnaces. "It had become a source of livelihood for many low-income residents," Mr Yani said, adding he would make about 300,000 rupiah ($24) a month. Any plastics still left over would be used in his village to fire limestone kilns, to produce building materials to sell or use. Ahmad Yani says plastic waste from overseas has been coming to his village for decades. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Mr Yani said among the rubbish he noticed food sachets and cat and dog food packaging with Australian labels, as well as labels of countries in Europe. While burning plastic has helped support the family's livelihood, the smoke from their home and neighbouring households may be having a devastating impact on health. Mr Yani said some people he knew who had operated the limestone kilns had died from respiratory diseases and causes were never determined. He said the burning of plastics in his village was no longer happening. It stopped about a year ago. Several local media reported companies had stopped distributing waste to his community to sort, which had sparked anger among locals who lost their source of income. The ABC couldn't independently verify the reasons for the change. But health concerns for people who have been exposed to air pollution from burning plastics remain. Women sort through waste in East Java. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Researchers from the Climate and Health Centre at Brawijaya University were investigating the health effects of air pollution in East Java when they found locals were burning plastic waste. One of the researchers, Sekar Aqila Salsabilla, said pre-screening tests earlier this year on those in their study produced some worrying findings. She said at least 20 per cent of the more than 4,000 participants across six East Java villages were at high risk of cardiovascular disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Sekar Aqila Salsabilla has been researching the health effects of air pollution in villages in East Java. ( Supplied: Sekar Aqila Salsabilla ) "When we first entered these communities, one of the most distressing findings was that many people were unaware of the dangers associated with burning plastic waste," said Ms Salsabilla, who, as part of a broader study, worked with more than 30 researchers, the majority of whom had medical backgrounds. People earning money from sorting waste, known as "plastic farmers", knew their health was "slowly declining" but did not understand the source of the problems, she said. "Despite the income they generate, many do not realise that the long-term health burden they may face is likely to be far greater than the money they earn from handling and burning this waste," Ms Salsabilla said. Environmental activists say Australian plastic waste was in this rubbish heap in East Java, Indonesia, in 2024. ( Supplied: Ecoton ) Most plastic waste was no longer burned in people's homes but rather converted into refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and burned in a designated facility, she said. "But I think this only relocates the problem rather than actually solving it," Ms Salsabilla said, adding the facility still required humans to sort the waste. Emissions from open waste burning, such as burning plastics, include a variety of air pollutants, some of which have particularly harmful effects on both the climate and health, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). "Exposure to these pollutants, whether short or long-term, can lead to adverse health effects such as coughing, skin irritation, respiratory diseases, and other negative outcomes," the WHO says on its website. Environmentalists say plastic waste from Australia is often found in East Java. ( Supplied: Ecoton ) Ms Salsabilla said the waste imported to East Java was coming from places including Australia, the US and Europe.

events.title: India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain
events.summary: India has set an ambitious goal to install enough clean energy to power over 1 billion homes by 2035 BENGALURU, India -- With the United Nations climate talks underway, India has set an ambitious goal of installing enough clean power to supply more than 1 billion homes by 2035, and has approved nearly $20 billion in power grid upgrades to ease bottlenecks that prevent some solar and wind energy from reaching consumers. The world's most populous country and one of the biggest carbon polluters is also among the fastest to expand clean power. Accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels is a key goal of this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, in Turkey. India announced the 900-gigawatt goal in late September. It covers nonfossil power sources, including solar, wind, hydropower and nuclear energy. It is nearly twice India’s existing target of 500 gigawatts of clean power by 2030. India's current clean power capacity of just over 300 gigawatts ranks it third behind China and the United States. Experts say meeting the target could lower electricity costs, curb coal construction and accelerate the transition to clean energy. The push comes as India struggles to use all the renewable electricity it can generate because of inadequate transmission infrastructure . The new goal refers to installed generating capacity, rather than the amount of electricity actually produced. “If the grid doesn’t catch up, then there is no way India can meet this target,” Nikit Abhyankar from the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley, said. “A robust and innovative transmission grid is an absolute must.” The government also approved nearly $20 billion in funding for transmission infrastructure and battery storage under its Green Energy Corridor plan. Economist Ajay Shah of the Mumbai-based XKDR Forum described the transition as the emergence of an Indian “electrostate,” in which electricity increasingly replaces coal and petroleum products. “So now in India you have two assets — not only do you have cheap labor, you also have cheap energy,” Shah said. The shift mirrors a global trend toward cleaner power, even as fossil fuel energy remains a key energy source amid rising electricity demand. Brazil, which ranks close behind India in clean energy capacity, projects renewables will supply nearly 90% of its electricity in the next decade, even as it expands oil and gas production. In the United States, where President Donald Trump supports fossil fuels, electricity demand is expected to grow by 40%, with natural gas remaining a major source. India’s clean energy expansion could help industries replace costly imported fossil fuels with domestically produced electricity. Abhyankar said solar and wind power, even when combined with battery storage, are increasingly cost-competitive with power from coal, oil and natural gas. Lower generation costs could eventually translate into cheaper electricity for households, though utilities also factor in transmission costs and other expenses. However, India’s continued dependence on coal presents a major challenge to its clean energy transition. Coal generated about 71% of the country’s electricity in 2025, according to energy think tank Ember. India’s power planners remain concerned about meeting growing demand and maintaining reliable electricity when solar and wind output fluctuates. Ghanshyam Prasad, chair of the Central Electricity Authority, said earlier this month that India could need as much as 150 gigawatts of additional coal-fired generating capacity by 2035. Ember energy analyst Neshwin Rodrigues said coal will remain important for years, particularly until large-scale batteries can store solar energy to reliably meet demand when the sun isn't shining. Existing coal plants also pose operational challenges. Many cannot quickly reduce output when renewable electricity becomes available, making it difficult for the grid to accommodate growing solar and wind power. Glenn Gawdin scores his first 2 NHL goals in the Rangers' 5-1 victory over the Canucks China and ASEAN make progress on South China Sea pact but can't finish talks this year Trump administration cancels mandatory pay hike for Head Start teachers Researchers at Berkeley estimate that beyond approximately 35 gigawatts of coal capacity already under construction, additional coal plants would not be economically necessary under the country's new clean energy goals. Berkeley's Abhyankar warned that newly built coal plants could become stranded assets if the government meets its renewable energy targets. Meeting the 2035 target requires more than building more renewable power plants. Their electricity must be able to reach consumers. India’s rapid clean energy expansion is already testing the grid's limits. Although clean power accounted for 55% of installed power capacity by September, it generated about a third of the country’s electricity in the preceding three months, according to government data.

events.title: FAA ends hours-long nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday night after hours of chaos and thousands of delays and cancellations. Why it matters: The effects of the rare and extreme move will likely ripple through the weekend, with travelers stranded and airlines' planes and crews out of position. Driving the news: In a Friday evening press conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was issued after outdated air traffic control communications equipment suffered from "overloaded data, and they went down." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin added that officials are looking into incompatibilities between that older equipment and newer technology currently being installed. Mullin added that there's no evidence that the problems were tied to a cyberattack. Yes, but: Duffy and Mullin didn't specify the exact initial cause of the problems. "We're still working on the details of what went wrong today," Duffy said. Duffy spent much of the press conference pushing Congress for more funding for air traffic control upgrades. "I can't build things if I don't have money," he told reporters at the White House briefing room. He later added that similar problems could occur again without more funding. Catch up quick: The FAA initially issued the stop due to "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety." "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the agency said in an earlier statement after the ground stop was issued. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates." Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often simply called "centers," mostly handle high-altitude en route airspace between airports. Between the lines: The FAA has been rolling out a new AI tool designed to help manage airspace congestion, but it's unclear if that system has any connection to Friday's communication issues. The developer of that tool denied any connection. By the numbers: As of 9 p.m. ET, FlightAware reported more than 6,000 cancellations over the course of the day Friday. Many travelers are stuck at the airport or on their planes on the tarmac Friday evening. Editor's note: This story has been updated with details from a press briefing.

events.title: PearlBone gets FDA clearance for world's largest orthopaedic market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts PearlBone from WA wins FDA approval for US orthopaedic market The PearlBone FDA approval follows years of testing, evaluation and development. ( Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls ) A bone graft substitute made from Kimberley pearl shells has received clearance from the US Food and Drug Adminstration (FDA). The product is the first of its kind to repair bone fractures using nacre, commonly known as mother-of-pearl. Marine Biomedical says there is more to be done before the product can treat patients, but regulatory approval is an important first step. Mother-of-pearl harvested in Western Australia's north could soon be used to fill bone fractures for patients in the United States. WA biotech company Marine Biomedical has received clearance from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its bone graft substitute, PearlBone. A manufacturing facility for PearlBone was built in Broome in 2022. ( Supplied: Rolee Kumar ) The product is the first of its kind to be developed from nacre, commonly known as mother-of-pearl. The iridescent material has been used for ornamental items, jewellery and even buttons. But Marine Biomedical chief executive Rolee Kumar said it was also effective for bone repair and regeneration. PearlBone will be used to repair bone fractures for patients in the United States. ( Supplied: Rolee Kumar ) "The material of what the mother-of-pearl is made out of, all of these are actually building blocks of our bone too," she said. "So in a way, it's not surprising when we do these studies we see PearlBone facilitates bone healing." The United States is the world's largest orthopaedics market, with the bone grafts and substitutes sector valued at $US1.1 billion ($1.5 billion). Ms Kumar said FDA clearance was an important first step in entering the US market, but there were more hurdles to be overcome before it could be sold. Rolee Kumar says PearlBone is as safe and effective as existing bone repair materials. ( Supplied: Rolee Kumar ) "We've gone through a process where PearlBone was compared against another existing bone graft that's established itself in the market," she said. "We've been able to demonstrate PearlBone is as safe and efficacious as the predicate device ." She said the company also hoped to bring the product to Australian customers in future and expand into other treatments like dental work. 'Exciting' opportunity for pearl industry Marine Biomedical was established in 2021 through a partnership with local Broome pearling business Willie Creek Pearls and research expertise from the University of Western Australia (UWA). Paul Birch says shells are prepped at the farm before being transported to the manufacturing facility in Broome. "And with more research, there might be other parts of the oyster that can be used for other biomedical technologies." The shells farmed by Willie Creek for pearl production undergo cleaning and preparations before being transported to the Marine Biomedical manufacturing facility in Broome. Mr Birch said there was an abundance of pearl shell available at the farm to meet current requirements, but this could change as the product demand increased. "So hopefully at one point in time, it might be something the entire industry is able to be involved in and supply to Marine Biomedical," he said.
