The professor said it was common for products to gain approval in the United States market before returning to Australia. "One of the big reasons is because even though we're a very large country geographically, we've got a relatively small population," Professor Pfleger said. "So if we get approval in the US first, it means it's much more economically viable for us to then come back and market in Australia." Willie Creek Pearls, based on the outskirts of Broome in WA's north, will provide the product for PearlBone. events.title: FAA lifts rare nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The FAA on Friday lifted a rare nationwide ground stop that impacted more than 14,500 flights after a major outage affecting the US’ air communications system. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed “an incredibly old air traffic control system,” and said the government didn’t suspect any nefarious causes, such as a terrorist or cyber attack. He said the issues were connected to old equipment that was overloaded, and that flights should start taking off again over the next day. “Hopefully tomorrow, we are going to start to see far better movement,” he said, while trying to reassure travelers that the US remains “the safest system in the world.” The stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, caused widespread disruption and prompted shares in airlines to drop. American Airlines shares dropped more than 2% in after-hours trading, while United shares fell 1.6%. Those airlines are now navigating thousands of rebookings and frustrated passengers. This is only the third time the agency has ever issued such an order. The most recent was in January 2023; before that, air traffic was halted nationwide on Sept. 11, 2001. Duffy used a large portion of a press conference on Friday evening to blame the Republican-controlled Congress for withholding funds for air-traffic control repairs. He urged lawmakers to approve $50 billion to upgrade infrastructure through an emergency funding bill. “I’ve asked, the president’s asked for $30 billion. I want $50 billion,” Duffy said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Albanese, Bowen caught talking phones and 'dicks' in hot-mic gaffe
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts PM Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen caught on hot mic at COP31 climate summit A private exchange between Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen was inadvertently recorded at the COP31 summit in Türkiye. The prime minister's office said the pair were joking between meetings, but the Coalition has criticised the hot mic moment as "weird and gross". Mr Albanese has travelled to the Philippines for the ASEAN summit, while Mr Bowen remains in Türkiye. A conversation between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen about phone radiation and "dicks" has been caught on camera on the sidelines of a UN conference. The Coalition has criticised the hot mic moment as "weird and gross", accusing the pair of behaving like "14-year-old schoolboys". Mr Albanese's office said the pair was sharing a "joke" between meetings when the exchange was recorded by Australian media at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye. The comments were captured shortly before a business roundtable spruiking renewable energy transition investment opportunities in Australia began overnight on Friday. Anthony Albanese left Türkiye shortly after a business roundtable. ( AAP ) Cameras were rolling ahead of the event, during which time Mr Albanese and Mr Bowen were privately chatting to each other. Mr Albanese put his phone in his jacket pocket and — as he did so — told Mr Bowen he had heard it was better to store the device away from the heart because "it can interfere with your rhythm". Mr Bowen responded in a joking tone, asking if it was because the phone was "a little bit radioactive". The prime minister laughed, saying the idea "makes absolute sense". Mr Bowen then responded he was more conscious about putting his phone in his pants pocket. Mr Albanese asked, "Because of your dick?" The pair laughed and Mr Bowen agreed, adding it was "arguably more important than the heart". On Sunday, Liberal deputy leader Jane Hume said the gaffe undermined Labor's message about pitching Australia to the world on climate. "It's bad enough that these guys sent almost 200 bureaucrats to Türkiye at a cost of more than $2 million and spent $36,000 [sic] of your taxpayer money on a coffee cart so that Greta Thunberg could have a free latte, but they justified it on the basis they were 'selling Australia to the world', 'attracting investment from overseas'," she said. "Well, great salesmen you clowns are. "The only thing you've attracted to Australia is ridicule on the world stage." Hot-mic gaffe came ahead of roundtable The exchange, which did not appear to be overheard by anyone in the room but was captured by a news camera microphone preparing to record the opening remarks at the event, was later broadcast by Channel 7 after it was noticed in production. A spokesperson for Mr Albanese's office said, "They were having a joke in between meetings." Labor frontbencher Murray Watt agreed that the comments were made in jest. "This is really just about people having a joke," he said. Mr Watt laughed off a question about where he kept his own phone, and defended Australia's presence and performance at COP31. "I know there's been a lot of criticism from some quarters about every aspect of this COP, but the reality is participating in and in fact leading the discussions at COP is in Australia's national interest," he said. During the official proceedings of the business roundtable, the prime minister made a pitch to international investors to back Australia's clean energy transition. "If you're an investor, there's nowhere you'd rather be than Australia," he said. Mr Albanese said having abundant renewable resources, critical minerals and a stable investment environment meant Australia was well placed to capitalise on the multi-trillion-dollar industry. The prime minister left Türkiye shortly after the roundtable to travel to the Philippines for the ASEAN summit in Manila. Mr Bowen has remained in Antalya, where he is playing a critical role as the co-president of negotiations for COP31.

events.title: Mississippi River cruise crash has no fatalities, critical injuries
events.summary: Thirty-two people are in local hospitals and all passengers and crew are accounted for after a tanker collided with a Mississippi River cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans , officials said Friday. The big picture: With approximately 180 people on the ship, the rescue of all aboard is "truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a press conference. What they're saying: While the investigation remains ongoing, officials said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker appeared to have lost control, causing it to collide with the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking after the collision, the cruise ship began to sink and eventually toppled over and flipped — leaving people in the cold water. Video from the scene shows passengers, in life preservers, swimming in the river toward safety. The first 87 passengers got off while the ship was still afloat, Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. She added it "was normal conditions" on the river and that there wasn't a high current, despite how notoriously challenging that stretch of the Mississippi River usually is. "The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said. He added, "I've never been prouder of a group of people than those people that came off of that boat." Catch up quick: The American Heritage, a vessel operated by American Cruise Lines, had docked for passengers to disembark at the port Friday afternoon about two hours before it was hit, according to a press release from the Port of New Orleans. A city spokesman confirmed to Axios that the riverboat had rolled onto its side in the water, which social media videos appear to corroborate. Zoom out: The Atlantic Asphalt tanker is registered in the Marshall Islands, and had arrived at the Port of New Orleans on Nov. 11. Per data from myshiptracking.com, the tanker began its current journey in Paulsboro, New Jersey, in late October. Zoom in: The tanker was immobilized on the river Friday at about 2pm CT, with two tugs positioned on either side. Another dozen vessels were in the water nearby as a helicopter roamed overhead and sirens rang out over the water. Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

events.title: Questions remain after Nvidia CEO's departure
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Despite Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, questions remain over the whole affair Jensen Huang was one of the world's most influential figures in the tech and AI industry. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) Mounting speculation over an espionage plot against Jensen Huang and his multiple alleged affairs reached a tipping point on Friday, when the tech billionaire quit as Nvidia's CEO. The controversy centred around his relationship with Alice Huang, who US intelligence reportedly suspects to be a Chinese spy, before claims emerged he had another two extra-marital affairs. While Mr Huang's resignation puts an end to his long reign over Nvidia, questions about America's national security and the US president's knowledge of the whole saga remain. China's foreign ministry said allegations of spying in relation to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang (no relation) were "unsubstantiated" and "smears against China". ( Reuters: CTI ) When reports of an espionage plot against Mr Huang first emerged almost a week ago, top Republicans called on the tech executive to front Congress later this month. Senator Tim Scott reiterated those demands after Mr Huang's resignation, saying there were "serious concerns" to address. Separately the chairs of three House committees — the foreign affairs panel, the China select committee and the intelligence committee — wrote to Mr Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter requiring them to appear for closed-door transcribed interviews on December 1 and 2. After news broke of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset Nvidia's value plummeted. Why? Mr Huang and Mr Teter have not publicly commented on the requests, but they could face subpoenas to compel their appearances. "There are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three committee chairs wrote in the letter. Mr Huang is also yet to comment publicly after reports emerged he allegedly had another two extra-marital affairs — both with Nvidia employees. His last statement was on Sunday, local time, when he admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife of over 40 years but did not name who he had been intimate with. In that statement, he said he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security". Meanwhile, Nvidia and Mr Huang are facing a ‌proposed class action accusing them ‌of ⁠defrauding ‌shareholders . Questions for the US administration Next to Mr Huang, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been called on to testify in front of Congress on concerns he did not do enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China. In December 2025 Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to China in exchange for a cut of the sales, after Mr Huang argued that restrictions only accelerated Beijing's own AI development. That was despite concerns from both sides of Congress about China's access to the technology. Howard Lutnick is facing pressure over whether the US government was properly overseeing Nvidia's exports to China. ( Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz ) Mr Lutnick has also been criticised for the administration's refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a trade blacklist. In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration had held ⁠off adding more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the list. The US ⁠has not added to the list since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in more than a decade. Previous reports said that Mr Lutnick's US Commerce Department had not blacklisted new Chinese companies for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China. Under-Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler has been called on to testify at a December 3 hearing as well. The Commerce Department did not respond to Reuters' request for comment. In America's pursuit to lead the AI race, Mr Huang had become a close ally of Mr Trump and was one of the few people known to have a direct line to him. He has visited the White House at least five times during Mr Trump's second term, is part of a council advising the president on science and technology, and accompanied Mr Trump on a trip to Beijing in May. The Washington Post reported in mid-October that Nvidia committed $US25 million ($36.7 million) for Mr Trump's contentious White House ballroom project, while the president disclosed buying and selling Nvidia stock earlier this year. The New York Times reported Mr Trump was briefed on intelligence findings about a suspected espionage effort against Mr Huang about a year ago, and took no action.

With the cost of regional airfares soaring, musicians and band managers say touring has become untenable for both famous bands and emerging artists from regional Australia. An interim Productivity Commission report released this week revealed a significant price gap between regional and metropolitan flight routes. It found long regional and remote flights cost 67 per cent more on average than major city routes, while short regional flights cost 173 per cent more per kilometre. Alan James says high airfares are pricing Yothu Yindi "out of the market" for live music. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Yothu Yindi manager Alan James said the cost of travel had forced the internationally-renowned band from Arnhem Land to turn down shows within Australia. "It's $5,200 return from Gove to Brisbane, it would be cheaper for us to go do a concert in London than it would be to do a concert in a capital city of Australia," he said. Yothu Yindi bassist Stuart Kellaway — who now manages fellow Arnhem Land rock band King Stingray — said the next generation band's recent flights to shows in the United States cost less than domestic flights. Yothu Yindi played the 2025 Garma Festival but had to turn down shows interstate. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) "We've had to turn down three or four shows in the past month or so because it just wasn't going to work financially with the airfare components," he said. Mr Kellaway the sky-high airfares were affecting the ability even of artists in the prime of their careers to make a living. "With streaming and everything else, gigs are one of the last, decent income streams for bands," he said. Limited options limiting opportunities Mr James said while all bands were impacted by the exorbitant airfares, for new artists in particular, the costs could make sustainable careers in the music industry impossible. "If you're an emerging group, you've got no shot, you're out of the business," he said. "It really means for musicians, if you're not based in a capital city, then you're not in the market anymore." King Stingray manager Stuart Kellaway (third from left) says bands based outside capital cities are "not in the market anymore". ( ABC / Matt Garrick ) Both Mr James and Mr Kellaway said they had noticed a decline in the number of airlines servicing Arnhem Land throughout the course of Yothu Yindi's career. Their observations align with the findings of the Productivity Commission's report, which noted competition in regional aviation was severely limited. Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients Fears FIFO specialists will soon need to pass rising flight costs onto vulnerable country patients. Several airlines have reduced NT services recently, leaving flights between Darwin and capitals such as Sydney, Adelaide and Canberra serviced only by Qantas and its subsidiary Jetstar. In a statement, a Qantas spokesperson said rising costs had dramatically influenced the price of tickets in and out of the NT. "Aviation costs, including labour, airport charges and government air traffic control fees, are rising faster than the rate of inflation, while fuel costs also remain significantly higher," they said. "Great value fares can still be found on flights to and from the Northern Territory and we encourage customers to book ahead whenever possible to secure the best fare.

events.title: How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
events.summary: A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade. On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips. For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets. With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years. Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns. But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere. Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips. It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. The city-state has had some success in policing this. It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places. They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties. In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore. The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere. Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed. But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department. Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud. In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months. Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case. Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing. In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times. Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses. Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity. On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". China has also long rebuffed accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips. Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meeting How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness. In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.

events.title: Amazon’s new Kindle Colorsoft is a premium e-reader with a premium price
events.summary: Amazon recently unveiled its refreshed Kindle lineup , introducing a new basic Kindle , Paperwhite, and Colorsoft. The new Kindle Colorsoft starts at $290, while the Signature Edition, which I’ve spent the past few weeks testing, costs $320. The base model comes with 16GB of storage, while the Signature Edition doubles that to 32GB and is available in graphite or a maroon-like Fig finish with an aluminum back. Amazon first brought color to its Kindle lineup in 2024 with the launch of the original Colorsoft. The latest model is lighter and thinner than its predecessor and features an edge-to-edge display. If you already own the first-generation Colorsoft, there’s little reason to upgrade. The core reading experience remains largely the same. Both models have a 7-inch color E-Ink display, 300ppi resolution for black-and-white content and 150ppi for color. However, if you’ve been eyeing a color e-reader, the new Colorsoft is worth considering if you can get past the hefty price tag. Unlike standard Kindles, which display everything in black and white, the Colorsoft brings your digital bookshelf to life with their original colors. This makes it a particularly appealing option for readers who enjoy comics, graphic novels, or cookbooks, where color makes a big difference. It’s also great for readers who like highlighting passages in different colors. It’s worth noting that colors on the Colorsoft are still relatively muted and not as vibrant as what you’d see on an iPad. Still, they add a welcome splash of color and make a noticeable difference compared to the black-and-white displays of standard Kindles. The Colorsoft lets you adjust the screen’s color temperature, so you can switch to a warmer, more yellow-toned display that’s easier on the eyes when reading at night. There’s also an auto-adjusting brightness option that comes in handy. When it comes to battery life, Amazon says that the Colorsoft can last up to eight weeks on a single charge, compared to up to 12 weeks for the Paperwhite. During my testing, I didn’t have to stress about charging the Colorsoft because like other Kindles, its battery lasts a relatively long time compared to other everyday electronics. One small but welcome improvement on the new Colorsoft is the repositioned power button. On the previous generation, it was on the bottom of the device next to the charging port, making it easy to accidentally press it when handling the Kindle. On the new model, Amazon has moved it to the top-right edge, where it’s less likely to get in the way. I quite like this change, and found the new location more intuitive when powering the device on and off. I enjoyed the premium feel of the aluminum back on the Signature Edition. Although Amazon provided a case with my review unit, I rarely used it, and the finish held up well. While the slimmer design isn’t a major change, I found the new Colorsoft quite comfortable to hold compared to older Kindle devices. For those who enjoy reading in the bath or by the pool, the Colorsoft is waterproof, so you don’t have to worry about accidental splashes or spills damaging the e-reader. One thing I appreciated about the Colorsoft was how infrequently the screen needed to refresh, which was something I noticed more often with the larger Kindle Scribe Colorsoft . I also didn’t experience any noticeable ghosting, where text from previous pages lingers on the screen, which is common on some e-readers. The Signature Edition supports a magnetic cover with built-in page-turn buttons that connects to the pogo pins on the back of the device, but I can’t speak to this experience because I didn’t have access to the case. The biggest drawback of the Colorsoft is its price. It’s a steep investment for a device that’s just used for reading. That said, if you really want a color display, the Colorsoft is definitely worth considering. For everyone else, it’s a nice upgrade, but far from a must-have. Many readers would be better off with the basic Kindle or Paperwhite, which start at $169.99 and $199.99, respectively. events.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
events.summary: The Trump administration announced a six-month delay Friday in enforcing the Medicaid work requirements that were scheduled to take effect in January. Why it matters: The announcement pauses a set of rules that officials in many states warned they're not ready to handle — and that could cause millions of people to lose their health coverage. A federal court last month struck down a portion of the rules that required chronically ill Medicaid recipients to prove their condition significantly impairs the ability to work in order to qualify for an exemption. Driving the news: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said Friday there will be an "optional hold harmless period" through June 30 that will give states "a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes, and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience." Hospitals have been so worried about the impact of the work requirements that they've created their own outreach campaign to prepare people on Medicaid, per the New York Times . The concern is not that people will be kicked out of the program for not working, but that a chaotic rollout of the requirements will disenroll more people because they don't understand the reporting rules and won't be able to prove they've met the requirements. What they're saying: "States have made real progress, and they've been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries — at scale and for the long term," said Deputy Administrator and Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Dan Brillman. How it works: The first-ever work rules mean Medicaid enrollees must report at least 80 hours a month of work, school or volunteering or get an exemption. States were facing tight timetables for setting up systems to notify millions of recipients about the requirements — and to track whether they're complying. Nebraska's early rollout of the work requirements in May led to confusion and coverage denials due to unsubmitted paperwork, per KFF Health News . What we're watching: Democrats who will control Congress next year intend to push for more delays, or to scrap the work requirements altogether. events.title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
events.summary: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.” Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . “Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.” It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said.

events.title: FAA blames ground stop on faulty copper wiring
events.summary: The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevented the takeoff of flights in US airspace for around five hours, creating chaos for travelers and airports. The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded. In a press conference Saturday, Transportation Secretary Duffy attributed the FAA ground stop to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade. Duffy said it has yet to be determined whether the issue was incompetence or a faulty router. In a statement provided to The Register on Saturday, a spokesperson for L3Harris said, “L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” The stop was issued on Friday around the middle of the day ET. "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement on Friday. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone at the time said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement. The FAA ATCSCC advisory halted departing flights and said international flights would be dealt with individually. The notice said, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis." Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now." An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage." The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. ® Updated at 0039 UTC Sunday UTC with the administration's explanation for the stop. Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop. Updated to add at 2353 UTC CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.” Updated to add at 2340 UTC Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

events.title: Airlines scramble to get flights in air after planes grounded across US — as it happened
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts US officials lift order grounding flights after thousands of travellers affected — as it happened Here is a summary of the day's key events: US officials have lifted a national ground stop order for all departing flights hours after thousands of travellers, including Australians, were impacted. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has blamed an "old air traffic control system" for an outage that led to the ground stop. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says there is not yet any evidence suggesting a cyber attack was the cause. More than 7,000 flights were cancelled during the order. The halt is just the second ground stop issued by regulators since the September 11 terror attacks in 2001. Choose what information you see below by using filters Thank you for sticking with us throughout our coverage of today's US air traffic control centre outage . We're ending our live updates here but, as always, you can keep up to date with the latest information on this story and other news via the ABC News website and mobile app . Until next time, have a fantastic afternoon! How Australians were caught in the mayhem of a nationwide US flights ground stop As we've been reporting to you throughout the day, Australians have found themselves among the thousands of people whose travels have been halted due to the US ground stop order. My ABC News colleague Kristy Sexton-McGrath has collated some of their stories in the link below. 'The line-up is huge': Australians caught up in US flight chaos 📷: US airspace, flights and airports come to a standstill Everything you need to know about the US air traffic ground stop In the hours after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued an immediate pause of departing flights across the country due to "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety" , air traffic ground to a halt. If you're looking to catch up on everything that happened following that order and the impact it had on national and international air traffic, my colleague Audrey Courty has covered it all in the link below: What we know about the US air traffic communications outage Safety investigators heading to earlier ship crash affected by air traffic outage In other news from the US today, more than 100 people were rescued after a tanker collided with a river cruise boat near the port of New Orleans . In the aftermath of that accident, the US's National Transport Safety Bureau (NTSB) announced it was launching an investigation and sending a team to Louisiana . While initially unrelated to today's nationwide halt on flights, both news stories have since merged. The NTSB has released a statement in the past 20 minutes saying the ground stop order has impacted its earlier plans. "Due to the residual delays from the nationwide ground stop, the NTSB will no longer send a board member and will instead send a team of investigators by ground to the scene of the vessel collision in New Orleans," it said in a statement on X. Passengers stuck on tarmac for more than 5 hours after cross-country flight Frustration is continuing to grow for travellers who are still impacted by the fallout of today's ground stop order. Among them is Ruth Coles , who jumped on an Alaska Airlines plane from Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey and flew five hours across the country to Los Angeles . But, after her plane landed on the tarmac at Los Angeles International Airport , that is where she currently remains. She has told The Associated Press she was flying to visit her sister and attend a festival when she learnt about the ground stop order mid-flight. Passengers on her plane have been told they are waiting for a gate to open up, she said. "The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line," Coles said, but that was more than five hours ago . Coles said they have been given soft drinks and cookies and been allowed to use the restroom. Frustrated, she posted on X multiple times asking the airport for help and messaged Alaska Airlines support. The airline told her they were trying to park the flight in a remote area and provide bus transportation back to the terminal. FAA systems 'reliable' after earlier disruptions With flight services resuming across the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has released its own message to assure travellers the country is safe for air travel. It's worth pointing out that while thousands of planes were grounded and many more pulled out of the skies over the US, Donald Trump was mostly silent.

events.title: ‘The machine doesn’t stop’: Abu Dhabi’s wartime plan for keeping its cultural ambition alive
events.summary: The Signal Interview “We have plan A’s all the way to plan Z’s, from our best-case scenarios to our worst-case scenarios,” Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak says, when asked how the culture, tourism, and property groups he leads are preparing for what might happen next in the conflict that has shaken the Middle East. Many of those plans are contingent on the US-Israeli conflict with Iran ending, but “if this conflict gets worse, we also have a very clear route,” says the chairman of the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi. The manga-loving 44-year-old member of Abu Dhabi’s Executive Council, whose other interests include sneakers, rap music, and basketball, has spent more than a decade at the heart of the city’s strategy to diversify its economy using museums, UFC fights, and theme parks. Last year alone, the city opened five museums and welcomed a record 26.6 million visitors. Culture and tourism are “the building blocks of our future,” he says. But the conflict has forced him to craft a response that combines a strategic pivot, reassurance to local staff and foreign partners, and continued commitment to his city’s long-term aims. When the Iran war started in February, flights and events were canceled and the number of Western tourists to the Gulf plunged, emptying local hotels. “We had to basically rethink how we’re…promoting ourselves,” Al Mubarak says. But, he adds, “We always understood that, no matter what happens… the machine doesn’t stop.” A pivot to new growth markets Before the conflict, Abu Dhabi was working toward a goal of attracting 39.3 million visitors a year by 2030, up from 24 million in 2023. It projected that those tourists would contribute AED 90 billion a year to the city’s economy. Al Mubarak is still sticking to his 2030 goals, but he says the assumptions underlying them have changed. He now expects a 10-15% drop in visitors from the US and Europe compared to its original estimates, for example, with growth from other parts of the globe making up the difference. So he has changed the focus of Abu Dhabi’s marketing, looking to pull in far more visitors from its own region, and from Eastern Europe, India and the rest of Southeast Asia, and Africa. The city is already seeing 5-8% growth in visitors from “some of our Eastern geographies,” he says, and much larger numbers from around the Gulf. On Yas Island this summer, he says, “Some days I felt I was in Saudi, some days I felt I was in Qatar, some days I felt I was in Moscow.” He recalls talking to two tourists as they watched the smoke from a drone attack on a French navy base in the first week of the conflict: when he asked if they were alright, they replied: “We’re Russians, so this is nothing.” Abu Dhabi has been a magnet for wealthy Westerners, with its Formula 1 track and outpost of the Louvre. But Al Mubarak wants to use the current crisis to broaden its appeal to other parts of the world whose populations’ economic power is growing. Under his worst-case scenarios for the war’s outcome, his plans would focus Abu Dhabi’s culture and tourism strategy much more on its immediate region and the Global South. That grouping of poorer countries comprises more than 70% of the world’s population, he notes, and its people want “to experience a lot more than they have.” Westerners have been more put off by news coverage that he says exaggerates the security threat, but he has not stopped marketing to them, too. “We haven’t stopped acknowledging that they are a traveler and they are a future potential traveler,” he says. “We’ve kept [at the] front of their mind that the UAE is here and Abu Dhabi is here, and it’s going to continue to develop, it’s going to continue to grow. So when the time is right for you as a traveler, our doors are wide open.” Three-quarters of Abu Dhabi’s hotel rooms were full again by August, Al Mubarak notes. At Aldar Properties, the commercial real estate developer he also chairs, new sales dropped 34% in the first nine months of this year, but at AED 18.9 billion were still higher than for the same period in 2024. Overseas buyers — from China, the UK, Russia, and elsewhere — made up 28% of the total. After the first day of Iranian attacks, he maintains, “business has really been as usual.” Projecting normality, and an alluring vision Informed by its experience during the pandemic, Abu Dhabi kept cultural institutions open throughout the conflict to give residents places to connect and “a sense of comfort,” Al Mubarak says. To reassure his own teams, he set up daily management group meetings, and a stream of video conferences, emails, and helplines for employees. What mattered most was to show that leaders were listening rather than just talking, he says. “Small things like that make a difference,” he notes, adding that his strategy starts with Abu Dhabi’s own residents. The city wants to be a “home away from home” for the world’s culture-lovers, he says, but “we did not develop our cultural strategy and our cultural infrastructure for people to come [to Abu Dhabi]. We developed it for people that are here.” But Al Mubarak is equally keen to project a sense of normality for potential visitors who are contemplating Abu Dhabi from afar. “Imagine yourself in Abu Dhabi today,” he says. The weather’s good this time of year, so “you’d wake up in the morning and you’d sink your feet in beautiful white sand,” then maybe go for a swim, he suggests. Then a tourist could go for an AI-personalized museum tour, a round of golf, some shopping, a concert at the Sphere (a $1.7 billion entertainment venue opening in 2029), or a comedy show. It’s “an imaginary story,” he says, but one “that could be a reality” for a visitor. The next step in realizing that vision will come on Dec. 11, when a branch of New York’s Guggenheim Museum opens on Saadiyat Island. Some of Abu Dhabi’s partners have expressed fears about the region’s suitability as a home for their artwork in a period of conflict — “our French partners raised concerns on some of the loans that they’ve had at the Louvre,” Al Mubarak acknowledges — but he was able to reassure them that its buildings are “built to withstand things of this sort of nature.” The opening of the Frank Gehry-designed Guggenheim will be a symbolic and emotional moment for Abu Dhabi, he says, but also one that “highlights our aspirations.” The case for not outgrowing your imagination What outsiders looking at Abu Dhabi’s transformation often miss is what has powered its economic growth, Al Mubarak says. “What they don’t see is that just three generations ago — my grandfather and my great-grandfather — they lived a very, very difficult life. They went days where they couldn’t find food.” The city’s ambition “comes from hunger and it comes from struggle,” he says. Even as it builds ever more glittering projects, he adds, “That struggle I’m talking about, we feel it. That taste is still in our mouth.” Abu Dhabi is still “the new kid on the block,” he says — an underdog

events.title: Shifting HBM4 Controller Functions Closer To Memory (UC Riverside)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Tharunya Yogananda and Wantong Li of the University of California, Riverside published a technical paper titled “Beyond Host-Side Control: HBM Controller Partitioning Across Host and HBM Base Dies.” “Recent generations of high bandwidth memory (HBM), such as HBM4, allow the base die of the memory stack to be manufactured using a logic process that can accommodate more complex controller functions next to the DRAM. We present the first systematic quantitative study of function-level controller placement between the host and the HBM4 base die on a silicon interposer. We divide the controller into its main functions and evaluate four placements, from a complete host controller to a complete base die controller, with intermediate placements that move maintenance or scheduling to the base die. “ Find the technical paper here . events.title: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy
events.summary: The Campaign Legal Center is calling for an investigation into whether Alicia Jackson, director of the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, violated ethics laws. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics laws after a recent ProPublica investigation revealed actions experts called “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest.”  Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.  In a letter to the department’s inspector general , the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm. The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.  Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though health officials have not publicly explained why. In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center cited the ProPublica investigation that found Jackson spoke at an HHS press conference last November and was quoted in a department news release announcing the decision to remove “black box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.  At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone replacement treatments, according to her financial disclosures . Read More Top U.S. Health Official Backed a Medication Policy Shift That Benefited a Company She Has Stock In It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson became her agency’s director in October 2025. Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press conference or in a news release.   The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest waiver before participating in the policy announcement.  “Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote. The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in private investment funds. ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by her husband, Alex Jacobson . The company invests in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical device companies. Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency.  137 Ventures founders Alex Jacobson, left, and Justin Fishner-Wolfson Kimberly White/Getty Images for 137 Ventures The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms. Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black box warning announcement, the center said. Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago — remain uncertified.  HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly 100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 party-line vote . President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the president’s second term. ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137 Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”  Jackson was appointed by Trump as her agency’s second director and sworn in on Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-related illnesses. Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to ProPublica’s Trump Team Financials database , a searchable tool launched in March. The records detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased. Read More Explore Financial Disclosures From President Trump and 2,300 of His Appointees The post Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: US government grounds all flights across the United States ‘due to extraordinary circumstances’
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday afternoon that it has grounded all flights across the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances” and issues related to safety. The FAA’s website said the cause is an “equipment outage.” The site itself was down for a brief period at the time of publication, with a note that the website was “experiencing technical difficulties.” Per an alert sent by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center , or ATCSCC, the FAA said the ground stop means that aircraft cannot take off from departure gates. The message said that the disruption was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” but did not specify further. The alert was not visible on the ATCSCC website at press time. The alert stated that all departing flights must remain on the ground “until further notice.” Inbound international flights will be “managed on a case-by-case basis,” it said. A spokesperson for the FAA told TechCrunch that it issued the ground stop “following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” which manage the airspace across the United States. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a post on X : “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.” It’s not clear what caused the ongoing FAA equipment outage. The outage comes in the same week that the administration rolled out an AI-powered tool for air traffic controllers to save aircraft flight time and fuel costs — though it’s unclear if the ongoing outage is related. Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that there is “no indication yet that this was a nefarious act,” but warned that the recovery “is going to take some time.” Updated with comment from the FAA, and remarks from Homeland Security. events.title: The Big Fly Swat unleashed after bar flies' inspired idea
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tiny outback town builds world's biggest fly swat It's hoped The Big Fly Swat will encourage "big thing" tourism and give others a reason to detour off the highway and visit Kingoonya. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) A seven to eight hour drive into the outback north-west of Adelaide brings you to a micro town so small it's almost a ghost town. Kingoonya, with its population of roughly 13, offers an authentic slice of Australian country life rarely glimpsed by outsiders. That is, until now. It's hoped that the installation of Australia's latest "big thing" will draw more people to venture off the highway, visit the local pub or cafe and take a selfie to say they have seen the world's biggest fly swat. The official opening of The Big Fly Swat took place this week at Kingoonya. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) Once a railway maintenance town for the tracks that criss-cross Australia from Sydney to Perth and Adelaide to Darwin, Kingoonya once had a population of over 100. The trains still come — as many as 70 a week pass through — but few stop. While the railway workers and their families are long gone. Up until the 1980s Kingoonya was still a busy petrol stop on the main road that travels up the middle of the country from Adelaide to Darwin. But then the highways department decided to shift it 40 kilometres to the east, to Glendambo. Kingoonya was a busy petrol stop on the highway between Adelaide and Alice Springs before the road was shifted 40km to the east in the 1980s. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) Overnight, the town nearly disappeared, with even the pub closing for a time. "The population went down to one for a while," said Leesa Carty from the Kingoonya and Area Progress Association. These days, visitors come in the form of four-wheel-drive adventurers and those en route to local stations. It has brought revenue for the pub, cafe and caravan park. And also more carrots and apples for the retired horses who freely roam the dusty streets, mooching treats and seeking out shady spots. The idea for the swat was thought up on the verandah of the Kingoonya Bush Hotel, where fly swats are always on hand for the customers. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) Throughout all the ups and downs for Kingoonya over the many years, there has always been one constant: the flies. Ms Carty was sitting on the front porch of the Kingoonya Bush Hotel one night with former publican Johnny Brett when the idea for the swat was born. The tables were scattered, as they always are, with beers, ashtrays and fly swats. Leesa Carty runs the caravan park and cafe in Kingoonya and is also a member of the Kingoonya and Area Progress Association. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) The question was how to best spend a $30,000 grant from the Outback Communities Authority to bring people to town. "I think I just went 'flies' and he went 'fly swat' and we just went, 'Yes!" she recalled. "That's the one. We could do a big fly swat." Many months later, the Big Fly Swat, with its accompanying fly (the eyes made from red kitchen strainers), is complete. The fly on the fly swat now looks back over the town. ( Supplied: Grayson Cooke ) Painted blue, the metal swat was 8 metres long (or in South Australian parlance, about one Stobie pole high). With its location decided on, it was cemented in place between the main street and the railway track. At the official opening this week, Ms Carty, holding one of the pub's plastic swats, was invited by Marg Howard of the outback authority to "bash the crap" out of the ceremonial red bow placed on the big swat for the occasion. Leesa Carty was invited to "bash the crap" out of the ribbon on the big swat at the opening ceremony. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) A cheer went up from the gathered crowd of Kingoonya and surrounding residents as The Big Fly Swat was declared open. Ms Howard was enthusiastic about the project and the town, which is one of the many little populations the authority oversees. "I think some people will come to see it because it's a Big Thing and big things are big things in Australia." Paul Willis watches over the resident three free-roaming horses which amble through town and wait under the shade in the heat of the day. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) The new owner of the 89-year-old Kingoonya Bush Hotel, Jeff Verning, was among those in the crowd at the swat opening. A frequent visitor to the region for many years, he and wife Catherine took over the pub this year. After the celebrations died down, they joined their customers on the verandah for a drink and a smoke as they did most nights, watching the sun go down and the trains pass by.

Flipboard Reddit Whatsapp Whatsapp Email The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports on Friday afternoon, citing “extraordinary circumstances” for safety. According to Sean Duffy, U.S. Secretary of Transportation, the issue stems from communication issue impacting “all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” nationwide. “The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” Duffy posted to X Friday afternoon. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.” Was the FAA hit by a cyberattack? The cause of the air traffic control communications disruption remains unclear. Federal officials have yet to publicly identify what triggered the problem, and it is unclear if the incident is linked to a cyberattack. The FAA directed departing flights to remain on the ground until further notice and said it would handle inbound international flights case by case. The agency had already halted traffic in Chicago over air traffic control communications problems before issuing the nationwide order. UPDATE : US officials found no evidence of hacking in the FAA outage that halted flights nationwide, as the FBI reportedly probes an update. events.title: US aviation administration resumes flights after grounding
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts US Federal Aviation Administration says flights can resume after national ground stop It is only the second time flights have been grounded in the US since the September 11, 2001, terror attacks. ( Reuters: Joshua Lott ) Flights in the United States have resumed after the US Federal Aviation Administration earlier issued a national ground stop due to safety. It was only the second time flights have been grounded in the US since the September 11 terror attacks in 2001. The grounding had been called due to a communication issue affecting 22 regional air traffic control centres. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says flights can now resume, after it earlier issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstance and reasons for safety". US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the ground stop was due to a communication issue affecting all air route traffic control centres. Look back on our live blog for the latest on the issues affecting flights in the US and Australia. Mr Duffy said there was a communications issue affecting 22 regional air traffic control centres that direct planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians were investigating the cause of the issue. US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet of a nefarious act behind the communication issue. "It's just a telecommunications outage … everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying." Mr Mullin said investigators would look at whether there was any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But the system operates out of one location near Washington DC, and only sends recommendations to the air traffic control centres. What we know so far about why US flights were grounded Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage. Shortly before the announcement, the FAA halted traffic in Chicago due to air traffic control issues. The agency said: "All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice." The FAA said international flights would be managed on a case-by-case basis. According to the Eurocontrol website, all US-bound traffic from its member states were suspended at the FAA's request because of technical issues. There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including Israel. FlightAware, an online aircraft-tracking website, is reporting that about 10,500 flights in and out of the US have already been delayed today. The website also said more than 1,800 flight services had been cancelled. Traveller Jeff Dubner was still waiting to disembark from his plane an hour and a half after leaving the gate at Los Angeles International Airport. "It's frustrating. This certainly sounds like it's going to be more than the usual run-of-the-mill delay. I look forward to finding out why," he said. This is only the second nationwide ground stop in the US since the September 11 terror attacks in 2001. The last one was in January 2023, when domestic departures were paused for less than two hours.

events.title: Trump’s AI task force discusses cyber risks
events.summary: The White House’s AI task force convened Thursday to discuss the “evolving cyber threat environment” and strengthening critical infrastructure against potential attacks, an administration official told Semafor. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who leads the task force, informed the members about the work that tech CEOs who signed the White House AI accord are doing to prepare “a common set of industry standards,” the administration official said. Clayton also alluded to adding more firms to the accord. Officials including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross also gave an update on the pre-release testing of AI models being conducted at the National Institute of Standards & Technology’s AI unit. The task force wants Congress to reauthorize cyber and information-sharing related bills and is still assessing whether it wants to recommend the passage of new bills. Notably, the ongoing Nvidia scandal was not discussed during the meeting, the official said.

events.title: Activists call for Pressley to launch House speaker bid against Jeffries
events.summary: House Democrats are all but certain to elect House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries as their speaker designate next week. There could still be some turbulence, though , with progressive activists calling for Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., to launch a bid against Jeffries. Ricardo Sanchez, a Pressley spokesperson, said she was in “active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people. She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership.” Most Democrats don’t believe Pressley will actually launch a bid ahead of next week’s leadership elections. She’s privately denied interest in running to other lawmakers, according to people familiar with her comments, and she hasn’t laid the groundwork for a bid by sounding out support from other lawmakers. House Democrats are staring down brewing fights as younger lawmakers jostle for power and influence ahead of the party assuming its largest majority in decades. Once their leadership slate is set, the caucus will weigh major changes like implementing term limits, shaking up panel leaders, and standing up select committees on controversial policy issues. “We can have the fight about how many terms should be the limit, but I think the time is right — with all these new members coming into the caucus — to set some limits,” said Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt. At the “What’s Next” conference on Friday, Jeffries said discussion about term limits was the “right conversation to have.” And Rep. Janelle Bynum, D-Ore., launched an effort this morning to change the seniority system for subcommittee leadership positions. Jeffries and Democratic leaders could face an influx of new members who aren’t as beholden to caucus traditions when it comes to picking leaders based on seniority. “I think it’s going to be important for the Democratic Caucus to make sure that the voices of this large, energetic, new class of members are included at the table, and in general, I think we, as a party and as a Congress, are healthier when we allow for new perspectives and more renewal,” said Rep.-elect Luke Bronin, who’s coming to office after unseating a longtime Democratic incumbent. Democrats are also weighing the future of the select panel on China and whether to stand up a select committee on AI. Some Democrats have argued for changing the China committee, keeping it as is , or sunsetting it altogether. Top House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., who is close to Jeffries, has advocated for folding the China committee into his panel, and for standing up a separate Foreign Affairs subpanel on AI and chips. Doing so could set off a turf war with other powerful committee leaders.

events.title: Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer
events.summary: US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer. Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models." "This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," said DePue in a social media post . "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model." It doesn't sound that insane. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed from revelations that he had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who, in 2023, founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International. That company is reportedly under investigation by US authorities for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China. Huang's departure coincides with a renewed push to tighten US chip export controls. House Speaker Mike Johnson supports the idea . And there are at least four bills awaiting consideration that aim to limit China's access to leading edge AI tech: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, Match Act, and the Cloud Security Act. On Monday, US Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) cited Jensen Huang's "relationship with a suspected Chinese spy" as a justification for passing the AI Overwatch Act, which would codify the Trump administration's existing chip export controls. The Trump administration on Thursday said it's not sure whether Alice Huang was a spy, an allegation denied by Beijing and currently under investigation by the FBI. Whatever the case, the current rules clearly are not working. Only a few weeks ago, Lava, an Israel-based security company, said it had found "32 Nvidia B300 GPUs, part of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra generation, through publicly exposed monitoring endpoints with IP addresses geolocated to China." These GPUs, Lava noted, are subject to US export controls [PDF]. The security biz said its findings followed from the exposure of monitoring systems intended for internal infrastructure management that were publicly exposed. How DePue reached his conclusion The analysis published through DePue's consultancy, "Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs," takes a different approach: analyzing the published weights of various models from Chinese AI labs. As described in the report, model weights – the parameters that change in relation to training data – must be initialized with some value. One method for doing so involves a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox. The algorithm starts with a seed value that produces the same set of initial values whenever it's run. Using PyTorch, initialization can be done by creating multiple GPU threads that work in parallel, with the help of Nvidia's cuRAND library. And because this process is not truly random, it's possible to select a chip and a seed value, generate the initial weights for that hardware and compare that pattern to a model's published weights. "I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models," said DePue. "In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models – including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3 – were initialized on Nvidia Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in Nvidia's flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems." Noting that this is the first time MiniMax and Ant Group have been publicly linked to usage of Nvidia's Blackwell, he also cited several limitations to his approach. One is that usage of Blackwell GPUs doesn't prove where the GPUs were located, so it's possible some of these Chinese labs used this hardware through US providers – a loophole the Cloud Security Act aims to close. DePue's report includes initial seed values that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Nvidia's Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, for those who wish to attempt to reproduce the results. DuPue claims that multiple senior researchers, both independent and inside frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, have confirmed the result. Coincidentally, OpenAI and Anthropic have each complained about Chinese labs copying their models through distillation, a pastime also noted by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. ®
